title: מבנה הסוגיות – Niddah
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).
note_de: KI-erzeugte Einteilung in Sugjot und Argumentationsschritte von talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum); englisch, hebräisch wo dort vorhanden.
note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Three opinions on retroactive impurity
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Three opinions on retroactive impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Shammai's view that a woman is impure only from the moment she sees blood (דייה שעתה), Hillel's view that impurity extends back to the last examination (מפקידה לפקידה), and the Sages' compromise combining both timeframes.

sub.desc_en: Shammai rules that a woman's impurity begins only from the moment she sees blood (דייה שעתה).
Hillel rules that impurity extends retroactively to the last examination (מפקידה לפקידה), even if many days have passed.
The Sages compromise: a twenty-four-hour period reduces the time from examination to examination, and vice versa.
A woman with a fixed cycle (וסת) has her time sufficient; one who uses examination cloths (עדים) is like having an examination.

items.text: Mishnah: Practical application of דייה שעתה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Practical application of דייה שעתה
items.desc_en: The Mishnah clarifies the case of a woman who was engaged with pure items and then saw blood: she is impure but the items remain pure, and she only counts impurity from the moment of seeing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the practical case: a woman sitting with pure items who then sees blood — she is impure but the items remain pure.
The Mishnah adds that even though the Rabbis said she transmits impurity retroactively for a twenty-four-hour period, she only counts her days from the moment she saw blood.

items.text: Gemara: Shammai's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara: Shammai's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Shammai's rationale, explaining that he applies the principle of חזקה (presumption) that a woman is presumed pure until proven otherwise. It then begins to question Hillel's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Shammai's rationale, introducing the principle of חזקה (presumption) that a woman is presumed pure.
Shammai applies the principle of חזקה (presumption) that a woman stands in a state of purity until proven otherwise.
The Gemara begins to question Hillel's position, noting that Hillel also applies the principle of חזקה (presumption) but with a limitation.
Hillel limits the application of חזקה (presumption) to cases where there is no inherent flaw, but a woman has a potential flaw, so the presumption does not apply.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge from the mikveh
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge from the mikveh
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Shammai's ruling differs from the case of a mikveh that was found deficient, where all purifications performed retroactively are deemed impure. This suggests that retroactive impurity should apply here as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by challenging Shammai's ruling: since the blood is visible from the source itself, we do not apply the principle of establishing the woman on her presumptive status of purity.

items.text: Citation of the mikveh mishnah
items.text_en: Citation of the mikveh mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about a mikveh found deficient, which states that all purifications performed retroactively are impure, whether in public or private domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of a woman differs from the Mishnah's rule of a mikveh found deficient, where all prior purifications are retroactively impure.

items.text: Difficulty for Shammai and Hillel
items.text_en: Difficulty for Shammai and Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this mikveh case is difficult for Shammai because it imposes retroactive impurity, and even more difficult for Hillel because the mikveh case declares impurity definitively, whereas Hillel's ruling for a niddah is only a stringency (suspension) for the period from time to time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mikveh case is difficult for Shammai because it imposes retroactive impurity.

The Gemara notes that the mikveh case is even more difficult for Hillel because it declares impurity definitively, whereas Hillel's ruling for a niddah is only a stringency (suspension) for the period from time to time.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the mikveh challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the mikveh challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes the mikveh case: there, one can argue that the person was impure (standing on his presumptive impurity) and never immersed, whereas here the woman was pure. The mikveh's deficiency is present before us, but the blood is only seen now. The Gemara further notes that in the mikveh case there are two factors for stringency (deficiency and the person's impurity), while here there is only one (the blood).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers the mikveh challenge by arguing that there one can place the person on his presumptive impurity (חזקה) and say he never immersed.
The Gemara objects: one could equally place the mikveh on its presumptive status and say it was not deficient.
The Gemara rejects the objection: the mikveh's deficiency is present before us, overriding its presumptive status.
The Gemara objects: here too the blood is present before us, and the mikveh's deficiency is only now discovered, just as the blood is only now seen.
The Gemara rejects the objection: in the mikveh case one can say the deficiency came gradually, but here one cannot say the blood came gradually; the objection is dismissed.
The Gemara briefly suggests that perhaps she saw a large clot, but this is not pursued.
The Gemara resolves: in the mikveh case there are two factors for stringency (deficiency and the person's impurity), while here there is only one (the blood), so the cases are not analogous.

items.text: Challenge from the wine cask
items.text_en: Challenge from the wine cask
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new challenge from the case of a wine cask that was found to be vinegar: within the first three days, the separation is definitely valid, but afterward it is uncertain. This is difficult for Shammai, who would presumably rule leniently here as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shammai by comparing the case of a woman who saw blood to a wine cask that turned to vinegar, where within three days the separation is certain but afterward uncertain, posing a difficulty for Shammai's lenient position.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the wine cask challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the wine cask challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara similarly distinguishes the wine cask case: one can argue that the produce was untithed (standing on its presumptive status), and the wine's change is only now apparent. Again, there are two factors for stringency (the produce's untithed status and the change), whereas here there is only one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that in the wine cask case, one can place the untithed produce on its presumptive status and say it was not yet fixed.
The Gemara objects that one could equally place the wine on its presumptive status and say it did not turn to vinegar.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the wine is now vinegar before you, and similarly the blood is now seen, so the change is only now apparent.
The Gemara objects that in the wine case one could say the vinegar came gradually, but here the blood could not have appeared gradually, though it might have been seen in a clump.
The Gemara resolves that in the wine case there are two factors for stringency (untithed produce and the change), whereas here there is only one (the blood), so the cases are not comparable.

items.text: Contradiction between mikveh and wine cask resolved by Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Contradiction between mikveh and wine cask resolved by Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the mikveh case rules definitively impure, while the wine cask case rules only uncertain. Rabbi Chanina from Sura resolves this by attributing the wine cask ruling to Rabbi Shimon, who also rules leniently regarding the mikveh in public domain (suspension rather than definite impurity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the wine cask case (which rules uncertain after three days) and the mikveh case (which rules definitively impure), asking why the rulings differ.
Rabbi Chanina from Sura resolves the contradiction by attributing the wine cask ruling to Rabbi Shimon, who also treats the mikveh case as uncertain (suspension) rather than definite impurity.

The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon rules that in the mikveh case, items in the public domain are pure and in the private domain are suspended (uncertain), confirming his lenient approach.

items.text: The Rabbis' derivation from Sotah and the objection of public domain
items.text_en: The Rabbis' derivation from Sotah and the objection of public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that both Shammai and Hillel derived their positions from the Sotah. The Rabbis (Sages) argue that just as the Sotah, who is a case of uncertainty, is treated as certain in the private domain, so too here uncertainty is treated as certain. An objection is raised: from Sotah we might also learn that in the public domain she is pure. The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the Sotah's purity in the public domain is due to the absence of 'סתירה' (seclusion), whereas here the issue is 'חסר' (lack of blood), which applies equally in both domains. Furthermore, since there are two factors for leniency, it is considered like certain impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that both Shammai and Hillel derived their positions from the Sotah.
The Rabbis argue that just as the Sotah, a case of uncertainty, is treated as certain, so too here uncertainty is treated as certain.
An objection is raised: from Sotah we might also learn that in the public domain she is pure.

The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the Sotah's purity in the public domain is due to the absence of 'סתירה' (seclusion), whereas here the issue is 'חסר' (lack of blood), which applies equally in both domains.
The Gemara resolves that since there are two factors for leniency, it is considered like certain impurity.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's derivation from Sotah and the objection of certain impurity
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's derivation from Sotah and the objection of certain impurity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon also derives from Sotah, but argues that just as the Sotah in the public domain is pure, so too here. An objection is raised: from Sotah we might also learn that in the private domain she is definitely impure. The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the Sotah has 'רגלים לדבר' (grounds for suspicion) because her husband warned her and she secluded herself, whereas here there are no such grounds.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives from Sotah that in the public domain the woman is pure.
An objection is raised: from Sotah one might also learn that in the private domain she is definitely impure.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that Sotah has 'רגלים לדבר' (grounds for suspicion) due to warning and seclusion, whereas here there are no such grounds.

items.text: Alternative explanation for Rabbi Shimon: analogy from beginning of impurity
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for Rabbi Shimon: analogy from beginning of impurity
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: Rabbi Shimon derives from the beginning of impurity (ספק נגע ספק לא נגע) where in the public domain it is pure, so too at the end of impurity (ספק טבל ספק לא טבל) it is pure. The Rabbis reject this, arguing that in the beginning the person is presumed pure, so we do not remove him from his presumption, whereas here the person is presumed impure, so we do not remove him from his impurity.

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation is introduced: Rabbi Shimon derives his ruling from an analogy between the beginning of impurity (תחילת טומאה) and the end of impurity (סוף טומאה).

The analogy is spelled out: just as at the beginning of impurity a doubt about contact in the public domain is pure, so too at the end of impurity a doubt about immersion in the public domain is pure.

The Rabbis object: in the beginning of impurity the person stands in a presumption of purity (חזקת טהרה), so we do not remove him from that presumption, whereas here the person stands in a presumption of impurity (חזקת טומאה), so the analogy fails.
The Rabbis conclude: since here the person is presumed impure, we do not remove him from his impurity on the basis of a doubt.

items.text: Objection from the alleyway (Mavoi) and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the alleyway (Mavoi) and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the Mishnah about a dead creeping animal found in an alleyway, which retroactively imparts impurity. The Gemara answers that there too, since there are both its own creeping animals and those from outside, it is considered like two factors for leniency.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from the Mishnah about a dead creeping animal found in an alleyway, which retroactively imparts impurity, seemingly contradicting the principle of two factors for leniency.
The Gemara answers that in the alleyway too, since there are both its own creeping animals and those from outside, it is considered like two factors for leniency, resolving the objection.

items.text: Shammai's reasoning: woman feels herself, and Hillel's response
items.text_en: Shammai's reasoning: woman feels herself, and Hillel's response
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is given for Shammai's position: because a woman feels herself (when she discharges), and Hillel says she might think it is urine. The Gemara asks about a sleeping woman, and answers that even she wakes up due to pain, thinking it is urine. The Gemara then asks about a mentally incompetent woman (שוטה), and answers that Shammai admits in that case, and the Mishnah's phrase 'כל הנשים' refers only to competent women.

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation is given for Shammai's position: because a woman feels herself (when she discharges), and Hillel says she might think it is urine.
The Gemara objects: what about a sleeping woman, who does not feel herself?
The Gemara answers: even a sleeping woman wakes up due to pain, thinking it is urine.
The Gemara objects: what about a mentally incompetent woman (שוטה), who cannot feel or reason?
The Gemara answers: Shammai admits in the case of a mentally incompetent woman, and the Mishnah's phrase 'כל הנשים' refers only to competent women.

items.text: Why the Mishnah says 'all women' and not just 'women'
items.text_en: Why the Mishnah says 'all women' and not just 'women'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah could have simply said 'women', but it says 'all women' to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, who said only four women, teaching that all women are included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'all women' (כל הנשים) instead of simply 'women' (נשים).
The Gemara answers that the word 'all' excludes the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, who said only four women, teaching that all women are included.

items.text: Shammai's position on stains (ketamim) and the case of a woman using a cloth
items.text_en: Shammai's position on stains (ketamim) and the case of a woman using a cloth
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about stains (כתמים), suggesting that the Mishnah's ruling is not in accordance with Shammai. Abaye answers that Shammai admits regarding stains, because there is no source for the blood. An alternative explanation is given: Shammai says that if there was blood originally it would have come, while Hillel says the walls of the uterus held it. The Gemara then asks about a woman using a cloth (מוך), and Abaye says Shammai admits there. Rava says that even the cloth might shrink due to sweat, but Rava admits in the case of a tightly packed cloth. The Gemara concludes by asking what difference there is between these versions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about stains (כתמים), suggesting that the Mishnah's ruling is not in accordance with Shammai.
Abaye answers that Shammai admits regarding stains, because there is no source for the blood.
An alternative explanation is given: Shammai says that if there was blood originally it would have come, while Hillel says the walls of the uterus held it.
The Gemara asks about a woman using a cloth (מוך).
Abaye says Shammai admits in the case of a woman using a cloth.
Rava objects that even the cloth might shrink due to sweat.
Rava admits in the case of a tightly packed cloth.
The Gemara asks what difference there is between these versions.

items.text: Distinction between the two versions of the dispute
items.text_en: Distinction between the two versions of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a practical difference between two versions of the dispute: one version allows raising objections from cases of a barrel, a mikveh, and a mavoy, while the other does not. Abaye and Rava further differ regarding the status of a 'moch' (absorbent cloth) and a 'moch dachuk' (tightly packed cloth).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a practical difference between two versions of the dispute: one allows raising objections from cases of a barrel, a mikveh, and a mavoy, while the other does not.

items.text: Hillel's analogy to a basket with a found rodent
items.text_en: Hillel's analogy to a basket with a found rodent
items.desc_en: A beraita supports one version of the dispute, where Hillel argues that if blood were present from the beginning it would have come out, analogous to a basket used for pure items in one corner where a rodent is later found in another corner—the first items are impure. Shammai responds by distinguishing between a basket with a bottom (shulayim) and one without.

sub.desc_en: A beraita is cited that supports the first version of the dispute, stating that if blood had been present from the beginning it would have come out.
Hillel asks Shammai whether he agrees that in a basket used for pure items in one corner where a rodent is later found in another corner, the first items are impure.
Shammai agrees but distinguishes between a basket with a bottom (שוליים) and one without.

items.text: Rava's explanation: Shammai's concern for nullification of procreation
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: Shammai's concern for nullification of procreation
items.desc_en: Rava states that Shammai's reasoning is based on the concern that declaring the woman pure would lead to nullification of procreation (bitul priya u'reviya). A beraita confirms this, where Shammai tells Hillel that his ruling would cause Jewish daughters to cease from procreation.

sub.desc_en: Rava states: Shammai's reasoning is due to nullification of procreation.
A baraita supports: Shammai said to Hillel: If so, you have nullified the daughters of Israel from procreation.

items.text: Reconciling the two versions: Hillel's misunderstanding
items.text_en: Reconciling the two versions: Hillel's misunderstanding
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the second version, Hillel mistakenly thought Shammai's reasoning was that blood would have come from the beginning, so he challenged him with the basket analogy. Shammai then clarified that his actual reasoning was nullification of procreation, and regarding the basket analogy, he distinguished between a basket with a bottom and one without.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the second version, noting that it is supported by the baraita that assumes blood would have come from the beginning.
The Gemara explains that Hillel misunderstood Shammai's reasoning, thinking it was about blood coming from the beginning, so he challenged him with the basket analogy.
Shammai clarifies that his actual reasoning is nullification of procreation, and regarding the basket analogy, he distinguishes between a basket with a bottom and one without.

items.text: Alternative reconciliation: Hillel's suggestion of a safeguard
items.text_en: Alternative reconciliation: Hillel's suggestion of a safeguard
items.desc_en: According to another version, Hillel acknowledged Shammai's reasoning but suggested making a safeguard (seyag) for his words, similar to other Torah laws. Shammai responded that this would nullify procreation, and Hillel clarified he only meant for purity matters. Shammai countered that even for purity, the woman's heart would pound and she would separate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the dispute, where Hillel acknowledges Shammai's reasoning but proposes a safeguard.
Hillel suggests that Shammai make a safeguard (סְיָיג) for his words, similar to other Torah laws.
Shammai objects that a safeguard would nullify procreation (בִּטּוּל פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה).
Hillel clarifies that he only meant the safeguard for matters of purity (טְהָרוֹת), not for marital relations.
Shammai rejects even the purity safeguard, arguing that the woman's heart would pound (לִבּוֹ נוֹקְפוֹ) and she would separate from her husband.

items.text: Dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan on the basket case
items.text_en: Dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan on the basket case
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Chizkiya says the first pure items are pure, while Rabbi Yochanan says they are impure. The Gemara questions this, noting that Beit Shammai and Hillel agreed that the first items are impure. It resolves that they agreed only regarding a basket with a bottom, while Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan dispute a basket without a bottom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Chizkiya says the first pure items are pure, and Rabbi Yochanan says they are impure.
The Gemara objects: Beit Shammai and Hillel both agreed that the first pure items are impure, so how can Chizkiya disagree?
The Gemara resolves: Beit Shammai and Hillel agreed only regarding a basket with a bottom, while Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan dispute a basket without a bottom.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning and the support from Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning and the support from Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning is that even without a bottom, the basket has 'oganim' (rims) that can transfer impurity. This is supported by a beraita about drawing water with buckets, where Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai says that if the buckets have rims, all are impure. The Gemara questions whether Chizkiya rejects Rabbi Yannai's principle, and answers that water flows (sharki) but fruits do not, or that one is not particular about water but is particular about fruits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning for ruling that the first pure items are impure even in a basket without a bottom?
The Gemara answers: Even without a bottom, the basket has rims (אוגנים) that can transfer impurity from the dead creeping animal to the pure items.
A baraita is cited: One who draws ten buckets of water one after another, and a dead creeping animal is found in one of them — that bucket is impure, but all the others are pure.
Reish Lakish says in the name of Rabbi Yannai: The baraita's leniency applies only when the buckets have no rims, but if they have rims, all are impure — supporting Rabbi Yochanan's principle.
The Gemara questions: Does Chizkiya reject Rabbi Yannai's principle, since he rules that the first pure items are pure even in a basket without a bottom?
The Gemara answers: Water flows (שרקי) through the rims and connects the buckets, but fruits do not flow, so Chizkiya's case with fruits is different.
Alternatively, the Gemara answers: One is not particular about water (so it is considered connected), but one is particular about fruits (so they are considered separate).

items.text: Alternative resolution: Dispute about an unchecked basket
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: Dispute about an unchecked basket
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: Beit Shammai and Hillel agreed only regarding a basket that was not checked (bduka) for a rodent, implying that Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute may be about a different scenario.

sub.desc_en: And if you wish, say: Since Shammai and Hillel agree regarding a box that is not checked.

items.text: First resolution: dispute about a checked basket
items.text_en: First resolution: dispute about a checked basket
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about a checked basket, where one assumes the item fell when the hand was removed and the other does not. The Gemara objects that the analogy to a woman is problematic because a woman is checked, but answers that since blood is common, she is considered unchecked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about a checked basket (קופה בדוקה), where one assumes the item fell when the hand was removed and the other does not.
The Gemara objects that the analogy to a woman is problematic because a woman is checked (בדוקה).
The Gemara answers that since blood is common in a woman, she is considered unchecked (כשאינה בדוקה דמיא).

items.text: Second resolution: dispute about a covered basket
items.text_en: Second resolution: dispute about a covered basket
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Shammai and Hillel agree about an uncovered basket, and Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about a covered basket accessed through its cover. The objection that a woman is covered is answered by noting that since blood is common, she is considered uncovered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative resolution: Shammai and Hillel agree about an uncovered basket, while Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about a covered basket accessed through its cover.
The Gemara objects that the analogy to a woman is problematic because a woman is covered (like a covered basket), yet the mishnah compares her to an uncovered basket.
The Gemara answers that since blood is common in a woman, she is considered like an uncovered basket despite being physically covered.

items.text: Third resolution: dispute about a corner of a house
items.text_en: Third resolution: dispute about a corner of a house
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Shammai and Hillel agree about the corner of a basket, while Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about the corner of a house. The Gemara clarifies that the basket was moved from one corner to another, and the dispute is whether we assume impurity moved from place to place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a third resolution: Shammai and Hillel agree about the corner of a basket, while Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about the corner of a house.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'basket' (קופה), not 'house'.
The Gemara clarifies that the basket was moved from one corner of a house to another, and the dispute is whether we assume impurity moved from place to place.

items.text: Challenge from a mishnah: touching at night
items.text_en: Challenge from a mishnah: touching at night
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle of assuming impurity from place to place with a mishnah where one touched a person at night and found him dead in the morning. Rabbi Meir declares pure, and the Sages declare impure based on the rule that all impurities are judged at the time of finding, and a baraita adds 'and at the place of finding.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle of assuming impurity from place to place by citing a mishnah where one touched a person at night and found him dead in the morning, and Rabbi Meir declares pure.
The Sages declare impure based on the rule that all impurities are judged at the time of finding.
A baraita adds that the rule applies both at the time of finding and at the place of finding.

items.text: Attempt to distinguish: lenient suspension vs. burning
items.text_en: Attempt to distinguish: lenient suspension vs. burning
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the rule applies only for burning, but for suspension we might assume impurity. This is refuted by a mishnah about a rusty needle and a burnt carcass on olives, which are declared pure based on the rule of 'at the time of finding,' implying no suspension.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the rule of 'at the time of finding' applies only for burning, but for suspension we might assume impurity, and then immediately questions whether we actually suspend.
The Gemara cites a mishnah about a rusty or broken needle found on teruma being pure, arguing that if suspension were allowed, we would suspect the needle was originally impure.
The Gemara cites another mishnah about a burnt carcass or tattered rag on olives being pure, reinforcing that no suspension is made based on the rule of 'at the time of finding.'

items.text: Further challenge: not in the place of finding
items.text_en: Further challenge: not in the place of finding
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the rule applies leniently and stringently at the place of finding, but not in the place of finding we might suspend. This is challenged by a mishnah about a loaf on a shelf above a contaminated press, which is declared pure even though contact is possible, because we assume a pure person moved it. Rabbi Elazar adds that this applies even in a drainage area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the principle of 'as at the time of finding' applies both leniently and stringently at the place of finding, but not in the place of finding we might suspend the status.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita about a loaf on a shelf above a contaminated press, which is declared pure even though contact was possible, and Rabbi Elazar adds that this applies even in a drainage area, showing that we do not suspend even when movement is involved.

items.text: Conclusion: reason stated in the mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion: reason stated in the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the case of the loaf is different because the mishnah itself gives the reason: we assume a pure person entered and took it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the case of the loaf is different because the mishnah itself gives the reason: we assume a pure person entered and took it.

items.text: Rejecting the raven analogy
items.text_en: Rejecting the raven analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that a raven could have moved the loaf, because a raven acts unintentionally, while the case involves a person who acted intentionally. The distinction is that we do not attribute unintentional actions to a raven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the raven analogy by distinguishing between intentional human action and unintentional raven action, concluding that we do not attribute unintentional acts to a raven.

items.text: Two alternative explanations for the Mishnah's leniency
items.text_en: Two alternative explanations for the Mishnah's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two explanations for why the loaf is considered pure. First, since it is a case of uncertain impurity in a private domain, but the loaf has no consciousness to be asked, its status is pure even in a private domain. Alternatively, the impurity discussed is rabbinic, as indicated by the term 'madef' (a light impurity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the loaf is pure, given that uncertain impurity in a private domain is normally impure, but resolves that since the loaf has no consciousness to be asked, its status is pure even in a private domain.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the impurity here is rabbinic, as indicated by the term 'madef' (a light impurity), which is derived from the verse 'עלה נדף' (a driven leaf).

items.text: Baraita on the Sages' ruling
items.text_en: Baraita on the Sages' ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited explaining the Sages' statement that they follow neither Shammai nor Hillel: Shammai did not make a fence for his words, and Hillel was excessive in his measures.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited explaining the Sages' ruling that they follow neither Shammai nor Hillel: Shammai did not make a fence for his words, and Hillel was excessive in his measures.

items.text: The Sages' compromise: from time to time and from examination to examination
items.text_en: The Sages' compromise: from time to time and from examination to examination
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Sages' compromise: the period from time to time (24 hours) reduces the period from examination to examination, and vice versa. Examples are given for each case. The Gemara then notes that the second case is obvious, but it was taught for symmetry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the Sages' compromise: the period from time to time (24 hours) reduces the period from examination to examination, and vice versa.

The Gemara gives an example: a woman examined on Sunday and found clean, did not examine Monday or Tuesday, and found blood on Wednesday — she is retroactively impure only from time to time (24 hours), not from the last examination.

The Gemara gives the reverse example: a woman examined at the first hour and found clean, did not examine for the next two hours, and found blood at the fourth hour — she is retroactively impure only from the last examination, not from time to time.
The Gemara notes that the second example is obvious, but it was taught for symmetry with the first example.

items.text: Reason for the Sages' ruling and the dispute with Abaye
items.text_en: Reason for the Sages' ruling and the dispute with Abaye
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the Sages' reasoning is that a woman feels herself (when she becomes impure). Abaye objects that if so, she should be deemed pure only from the moment of discovery. Rabbah admits he was testing Abaye. The true reason is given by Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel: the Sages instituted that women examine themselves morning and evening to permit pure items; if she did not examine, she loses an extra period. Rav Papa asks about cases where three periods occur within 24 hours, and the Gemara answers that the Sages equalized their measures so that the law would not vary. An alternative reason is given: so that the sinner should not profit. The difference between these reasons is a case where she was ill and did not examine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks what the Sages' reasoning is for their ruling, and proposes that a woman feels herself when she becomes impure.
Abaye objects that if the woman feels herself, she should be deemed pure only from the moment of discovery, not retroactively.
The Gemara explains that Rabbah was only testing Abaye's sharpness, not giving the true reason.
The Gemara asks again for the true reason of the Sages, and introduces the answer from Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel.
Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel explains that the Sages instituted that women examine themselves morning and evening to permit pure items; if she did not examine, she loses an extra period.
Rav Papa asks Rava about cases where three periods occur within 24 hours, challenging the consistency of the measure.
Rava answers that the Sages equalized their measures so that the law would not vary between cases.
The Gemara offers an alternative reason: so that the sinner should not profit from her negligence.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two reasons, and answers that it is a case where she was ill and did not examine.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a woman with a fixed cycle
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a woman with a fixed cycle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that a woman with a fixed cycle is deemed pure only at her expected time follows Rabbi Dosa or the Sages. It concludes that it can be reconciled with either: if it follows the Sages, they agree with Rabbi Dosa during her expected time; if it follows Rabbi Dosa, he agrees with the Sages outside her expected time. The Mishnah deals with the expected time, so it is the view of all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that a woman with a fixed cycle is deemed pure only at her expected time follows Rabbi Dosa and not the Sages.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer lists four women whose status is determined only from the moment of discovery, and Rabbi Dosa extends this to any woman with a fixed cycle.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah can even follow the Sages, because they only dispute Rabbi Dosa outside the expected time but agree with him during the expected time, so the Mishnah, which deals with the expected time, represents the view of all.

The Gemara infers that Rabbi Dosa must hold his view even outside the expected time, citing a baraita that a woman with a fixed cycle whose bloodstain is found outside her expected time is retroactively impure from the last examination.
The Gemara now asks whether the baraita about retroactive impurity follows the Sages and not Rabbi Dosa.

The Gemara answers that the baraita can even follow Rabbi Dosa, because he only disputes the Sages during the expected time but agrees with them outside it, and the baraita deals with outside the expected time, so it is the view of all.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who sees a blood stain outside her expected menstrual period is impure from that time forward, but the Sages argue she is only impure from the time of discovery. Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus holds that women who are deemed 'sufficient for their time' have no retroactive impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the baraita's ruling about retroactive impurity for blood not at the fixed time is agreed upon by all.
The Gemara questions why the mishna was not interpreted in the opposite manner to give precedence to the mishna.
The Gemara answers that since the interpretation can lead to either leniency or stringency, the stringent interpretation is adopted.
The Gemara cites the baraita's ruling that a woman with a fixed cycle has retroactive impurity for stains, implying that other women have stains treated like their sightings.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel quoting Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel quoting Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus
sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the baraita as following Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, who rules that women with sufficient time have stains like sightings, except for a minor girl.

items.text: Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Does Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus hold that stains are never retroactively impure? It cites a baraita where he says women who are 'sufficient for their time' have no stain at all, implying no retroactive impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus holds that stains cause impurity at all, citing a baraita where he says women who are 'sufficient for their time' have no stain, implying no retroactive impurity.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus means they have no retroactive stain impurity, but they do have impurity from the time of discovery onward.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the first Tanna (Rabbi Meir) holds stains are retroactively impure, while Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus holds they are only impure from the time of discovery. The baraita's statement 'no stain at all' means no retroactive stain, but there is a stain from now onward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the first Tanna holds that stains are retroactively impure.
The Gemara answers that the first Tanna is Rabbi Meir, who is stringent regarding stains, as cited in a baraita.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's full position
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's full position
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus explicitly states: Women deemed 'sufficient for their time' have stains like their sightings (only from discovery), and a girl who has not reached maturity has no stain at all. Maturity is defined as reaching the days of youth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus states his full position: women deemed 'sufficient for their time' have stains like their sightings, a girl who has reached maturity has a stain, and one who has not reached maturity has no stain, defining maturity as reaching the days of youth.

items.text: Witnesses for marital relations
items.text_en: Witnesses for marital relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the requirement of witnesses before and after marital relations. Rabbi Yehuda quoting Shmuel says a witness before intercourse does not reduce the need for a post-intercourse witness. The reason is that the woman may be distracted and fail to check properly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda quoting Shmuel states that a witness before intercourse does not reduce the need for a post-intercourse examination.
Rabbi Katina explains the reason: because the woman is distracted by her household concerns, she does not insert the cloth into crevices and cracks properly.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of witnesses
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers an alternative: perhaps the Mishnah means one witness before and one after, but the text says 'one for him and one for her' — both after intercourse. The Gemara rejects this, noting the explicit phrase 'the one who serves' implies a pre-service witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's two witnesses are one before intercourse and one after, based on the phrase 'one for him and one for her'.
The Gemara rejects the question, explaining that both witnesses are after intercourse, one for him and one for her, as taught in a baraita.
The Gemara objects that if both witnesses are after intercourse, the Mishnah's statement is obvious and unnecessary, whereas the alternative interpretation would have justified the teaching.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah teaches that even if a tiny drop of blood might be concealed by semen, the witness still counts as a valid check.

items.text: Gemara's concern about blood drops
items.text_en: Gemara's concern about blood drops
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: perhaps the woman might see a tiny drop of blood like a mustard seed and cover it with semen, misleading the examiner. This is why the Mishnah requires a post-intercourse check.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that a woman might see a tiny drop of blood like a mustard seed and cover it with semen, misleading the examiner, and the Mishnah teaches that the post-intercourse check is necessary.

items.text: Two required checks
items.text_en: Two required checks
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Rabbis require two checks: one before intercourse and one after. The Mishnah's phrase 'like a deposit' refers to the post-intercourse check, while 'the one who serves' refers to the pre-intercourse check.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the Rabbis required two checks (one before and one after intercourse), and the Mishnah's phrase 'like a deposit' refers to the post-intercourse check, while the text should be emended to read 'וּמְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת' (and she who serves) to include the pre-intercourse check.

The Gemara notes that the check reduces the retroactive impurity from מעת לעת (a full day) to the time of the check only, implying that without the check the impurity would extend retroactively for a full day.

items.text: Question about the scope of retroactive impurity
items.text_en: Question about the scope of retroactive impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that a woman is impure only from the last examination (מפקידה לפקידה) is necessary, or if one might think she is impure for the full 24 hours (מעת לעת). The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that even from examination to examination, the Sages were concerned about loss of pure items, but not for the full 24-hour period.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling of impurity from examination to examination (מפקידה לפקידה) is even necessary to state.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that the Sages were concerned about loss of pure items only from examination to examination, not for the full 24-hour period (מעת לעת).

items.text: The Mishnah's example of the bed and support for Ze'iri
items.text_en: The Mishnah's example of the bed and support for Ze'iri
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that the woman was sitting on a bed engaged with pure items, rather than simply saying she was engaged with pure items and then withdrew. It answers that this teaches that only because of the principle of דייה שעתה (she is deemed impure only from the time of finding) is the bed pure; otherwise, if she were impure for the full 24 hours, the bed would also be impure. This supports Ze'iri's statement that a woman in her 24-hour period renders her bed and seat a source of impurity that can transmit impurity to a person and their garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that the woman was sitting on a bed engaged with pure items, rather than simply stating she was engaged with pure items and then withdrew and saw blood.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that only because of the principle of דייה שעתה (she is deemed impure only from the time of finding) is the bed pure; otherwise, if she were impure for the full 24 hours, the bed would also be impure.
The Gemara notes that this supports Ze'iri's statement that a woman in her 24-hour period renders her bed and seat a source of impurity that can transmit impurity to a person and their garments.

items.text: The problem of the bed as an object without intent and Ze'iri's resolution
items.text_en: The problem of the bed as an object without intent and Ze'iri's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the bed is an object without intent (דבר שאין בו דעת לישאל), and such an object's doubtful impurity is pure. Ze'iri resolves this by explaining that the case is where her friends are carrying her on the bed, giving it a 'hand' of friends (יד חברותיה). The Gemara then notes that according to Rabbi Yochanan's principle that doubtful impurity coming through human agency is treated as if the object has intent, even without friends carrying it, the bed would be impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the bed is an object without intent (דבר שאין בו דעת לישאל), so its doubtful impurity should be pure.
Ze'iri resolves the objection by explaining that the case is where her friends are carrying her on the bed, giving it a 'hand' of friends (יד חברותיה).

The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yochanan's principle that doubtful impurity coming through human agency is treated as if the object has intent, even without friends carrying it, the bed would be impure.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and an objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and an objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's principle that doubtful impurity coming through human agency is treated as if the object has intent, even for a vessel placed on the ground. An objection is raised from a baraita about a person wrapped in a garment with pure and impure items nearby, where doubt is resolved as pure. The Gemara explains that the baraita deals with a different case, as taught by Rav Hoshaya: in a private domain the doubt is impure, in a public domain it is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's principle that doubtful impurity coming through human agency is treated as if the object has intent, even for a vessel placed on the ground.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a person wrapped in a garment with pure and impure items nearby, where doubt is resolved as pure, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's principle.
The Gemara questions why the baraita rules pure, since it involves doubtful impurity coming through human agency.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rav Hoshaya's teaching that the baraita deals with a public domain, where doubt is pure, unlike Rabbi Yochanan's case in a private domain.

items.text: Ze'iri's statement challenged by Avimi's tradition and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Ze'iri's statement challenged by Avimi's tradition and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines Ze'iri's statement that a woman's bed and seat in her 24-hour period transmit impurity to a person and garments. Avimi brought a tradition that her bed and seat are like her touch, implying they do not transmit impurity to a person. Rava argues by a kal vachomer that they must transmit impurity, but the Gemara objects that Avimi's tradition is authoritative. The Gemara resolves that the tradition means her bed and seat are like her touch in that they do not require a vessel for impurity, but they do transmit impurity to a person.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri states that the retroactive twenty-four-hour period of a menstruating woman renders her bed and seat impure to the extent that they transmit impurity to a person and his garments.
The Gemara objects by citing Avimi's tradition that her bed and seat are like her touch, implying they do not transmit impurity to a person.
Rava argues by a kal vachomer that her bed and seat must transmit impurity to a person, as they are not spared from impurity even where earthenware vessels are spared.
The Gemara resolves that Avimi's tradition means her bed and seat are like her touch in that they do not require a vessel for impurity, but they do transmit impurity to a person.

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer for bed and seat
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer for bed and seat
items.desc_en: Rava argues that just as a niddah's touch (מגע עצמה) defiles a person to defile garments, so too her bed and seat (משכבה ומושבה) defile a person to defile garments, using a kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that just as a niddah's own touch defiles a person to defile garments, so too her bed and seat defile a person to defile garments.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava and distinction between blood and stain
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava and distinction between blood and stain
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's view, detailing the laws of a woman who sees blood (מטמאה מעת לעת) and one who sees a stain (מטמאה למפרע). Rabbi Akiva adds that the blood-seer defiles her husband, but she counts only from the time she saw. Both cases are treated as suspended (תולין), not eaten or burned.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the law of a woman who sees blood (מטמאה מעת לעת) and lists what she defiles, adding that she is not retroactively disqualified from her count and does not defile her husband retroactively.
Rabbi Akiva adds that the blood-seer does defile her husband, but she counts only from the time she saw.

The baraita states the law of a woman who sees a stain (מטמאה למפרע), listing what she defiles and that she is retroactively disqualified from her count and defiles her husband, but counts only from the time she saw.
The baraita concludes that both cases are treated as suspended (תולין), not eaten or burned.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rava's source and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rava's source and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava: if he knew the baraita, why not cite it; if not, how did he derive the kal vachomer? It answers that he knew the baraita, but the baraita might imply only one of the two (person or garments), so the kal vachomer was needed to teach both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava: if he knew the baraita, why not cite it; if not, how did he derive the kal vachomer?
The Gemara answers that Rava knew the baraita, but the baraita might imply only one of the two (person or garments), so the kal vachomer was needed to teach both.

items.text: Rav Huna's limitation of 'me'et le'et' to kodashim
items.text_en: Rav Huna's limitation of 'me'et le'et' to kodashim
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the 'me'et le'et' rule in niddah applies only to kodashim, not to terumah. The Gemara objects that if so, it should have been taught in the context of מעלות (degrees of sanctity). It answers that the Mishnah only teaches where there is a real impurity (דררא דטומאה), not where there is none.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the 'me'et le'et' rule in niddah applies only to kodashim, not to terumah.
The Gemara objects that if Rav Huna is correct, the Mishnah should have taught this rule in the context of מעלות (degrees of sanctity).
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only teaches where there is a real impurity (דררא דטומאה), not where there is none.

items.text: Attempted refutations and resolution regarding terumah
items.text_en: Attempted refutations and resolution regarding terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to refute Rav Huna from the baraita listing what she defiles, asking if it includes both kodashim and terumah. It answers only kodashim. Another attempt from Rabbi Yehuda's statement about terumah is dismissed as referring to a past situation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Huna's ruling by citing the baraita that lists what a woman with a stain defiles, and asks whether this includes both kodashim and terumah.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers only to kodashim, not terumah.
The Gemara attempts another refutation from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that a woman with a stain is prohibited from eating terumah even during the time of transition.
The Gemara dismisses this objection, explaining that Rabbi Yehuda's statement refers to a past situation (what was, was) and does not apply to the current case.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rav Huna on the practical application
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Huna on the practical application
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the ruling is needed only to prepare the remnants (שיריים) in her presence. Rav Huna teaches that she must burn the remnants in her hands if she examined herself at the time of her fixed period.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the ruling of the baraita is needed only to prepare the remnants (שיריים) in her presence, not to burn them.
Rav Huna teaches that she must burn the remnants in her hands if she examined herself at the time of her fixed period (וסת).

items.text: Rabbi's practice following Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rabbi's practice following Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: A story is brought that Rabbi acted in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer. After recalling this, he said that Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story that Rabbi acted in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer's position.
After recalling the story, Rabbi declared that Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon for halachic practice.

items.text: Clarifying the meaning of 'after he remembered'
items.text_en: Clarifying the meaning of 'after he remembered'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what 'after he remembered' means in the context of a ruling by Rabbi Eliezer. It concludes that it refers to a case where no halakhic ruling was issued, and since many disagree with Rabbi Eliezer, one may rely on him only in a pressing situation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'after he remembered' means, rejecting the possibility that it refers to a case where the halakha was already decided against Rabbi Eliezer, because then one could not rely on him even in a pressing situation.
The Gemara answers that 'after he remembered' refers to a case where no halakhic ruling was issued, and since many disagree with Rabbi Eliezer, one may rely on him only in a pressing situation.

items.text: Question about terumah and kodash in Rabbi's time
items.text_en: Question about terumah and kodash in Rabbi's time
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the case involves terumah or kodash, noting that terumah existed in Rabbi's time but kodash did not. It resolves by citing Ulla that colleagues would purify in the Galilee, implying kodash was relevant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the case involves תרומה (priestly portion) or קודש (sacred food), noting that קודש did not exist in Rabbi's time.
The Gemara resolves by citing Ulla that colleagues would purify in the Galilee, implying קודש was relevant in Rabbi's time.

items.text: Story of Rabban Gamliel's maidservant with terumah loaves
items.text_en: Story of Rabban Gamliel's maidservant with terumah loaves
items.desc_en: A maidservant of Rabban Gamliel was baking terumah loaves, checking her hands between each. After the last loaf, she found herself impure. Rabban Gamliel ruled all loaves impure, but when she mentioned her checks, he said only she is impure and the loaves are pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story about Rabban Gamliel's maidservant who baked terumah loaves, checked her hands between each, and after the last found herself impure; Rabban Gamliel initially ruled all loaves impure, but upon hearing of her checks, ruled only she is impure and the loaves are pure.

items.text: Clarifying the type of terumah loaves
items.text_en: Clarifying the type of terumah loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what terumah is involved, suggesting it is terumah of loaves of thanksgiving. It explains that the separation was done at the kneading stage, citing Rav Tovi bar Rav Katina that baking four loaves fulfills the mitzvah, and that one must separate a whole loaf, not a piece.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of תרומה (priestly portion) is involved, suggesting it is the תרומה of the loaves of the thanksgiving offering.
The Gemara objects that the תרומה of thanksgiving loaves is separated at the baking stage, not at the kneading stage mentioned in the story.

The Gemara answers that the separation was done at the kneading stage, citing Rav Tovi bar Rav Katina that baking four loaves fulfills the mitzvah, and that one must separate a whole loaf, not a piece.

sub.text: Rav Tovi bar Rav Katina's statement
sub.text_en: Rav Tovi bar Rav Katina's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Rav Katina states that if one baked the thanksgiving loaves as four loaves, he has fulfilled the mitzvah, and the Gemara clarifies that the requirement of forty loaves is only for the ideal standard (למצוה).

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the separation of תרומה was done at the kneading stage, as the Torah requires a whole loaf, not a piece, and the loaves were separated before baking.

items.text: Second story with wine barrels and distinction between terumah and kodash
items.text_en: Second story with wine barrels and distinction between terumah and kodash
items.desc_en: Another story is brought about the same maidservant sealing wine barrels. The Gemara argues that if both stories involved kodash, she wouldn't need to ask again; therefore, one story is about kodash and the other about terumah, or they involved two different maidservants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a second story about the maidservant of Rabban Gamliel sealing wine barrels, with the same pattern of checking and ruling.
The Gemara argues that if both stories involved קודש (sacred food), the maidservant would not need to ask again, so one must be about תרומה (priestly portion) and the other about קודש.
The Gemara resolves that the two stories involved two different maidservants, not the same one.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling and its limitation to kodash
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling and its limitation to kodash
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the entire day of a niddah's impurity applies to both kodash and terumah, based on its absence from the list of stringencies. Rav Nachman objects that a baraita explicitly says it applies only to kodash. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak accepts this, explaining it refers to hullin prepared with kodash purity, not terumah purity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the entire day of a niddah's impurity applies both to kodash and terumah, inferred from its absence from the list of stringencies.
Rav Nachman objects that a baraita explicitly states the rule applies only to kodash, not to terumah.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's acceptance and explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's acceptance and explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak accepts Rav Nachman's objection and explains that the baraita refers to hullin prepared with kodash purity, not terumah purity.

items.text: Mishnah about doubt of impurity before and after kneading
items.text_en: Mishnah about doubt of impurity before and after kneading
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about a doubt of impurity arising before or after kneading dough. Before kneading, it is treated as impure because hullin may be made impure in Israel; after kneading, it must be pure because the dough is designated for challah, and causing impurity to challah is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about a doubt of impurity arising before or after kneading dough: before kneading it is treated as impure, after kneading it must be pure.

The Gemara explains the mishnah: before kneading, the dough is ordinary hullin (חוּלִּין) and it is permitted to cause impurity to hullin in the Land of Israel; after kneading, the dough is designated for challah (חַלָּה) and causing impurity to challah is forbidden.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when challah is in a suspended state, it is neither eaten nor burned. The Gemara asks: what kind of doubt is this referring to? It specifies: the doubt of challah. The Gemara then asks: what is the doubt of challah?

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when challah is in a suspended state, it is neither eaten nor burned.
The Gemara asks what kind of doubt this refers to, and answers: the doubt of challah.
The Gemara further asks: what is the doubt of challah?

items.text: Abaye and Rava's explanation of the doubt
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's explanation of the doubt
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava explain that the doubt is not like the case of two paths (שני שבילין), where even ordinary unconsecrated food becomes impure. Rather, it is like the case of leaning (נשען), as taught in a mishnah about a zav and a pure person loading a donkey, where the status depends on the weight of the load.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava explain that the doubt is not like the case of two paths (שני שבילין), where even ordinary unconsecrated food becomes impure, but rather like the case of leaning (נשען), as taught in a mishnah about a zav and a pure person loading a donkey, where the status depends on the weight of the load.

items.text: Question: Are חולין הטבולין לחלה like challah?
items.text_en: Question: Are חולין הטבולין לחלה like challah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether ordinary food that is designated for challah (חולין הטבולין לחלה) is considered like challah itself. It cites a baraita where a woman who is a tevul yom separates challah from dough and sets it aside, because a tevul yom is only a third-degree impurity and is pure regarding ordinary food. If חולין הטבולין לחלה were like challah, then the tevul yom would render the dough impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether חולין הטבולין לחלה (ordinary food designated for challah) is considered like challah itself, and begins citing a baraita about a tevul yom woman who separates challah from dough.

The baraita explains that a tevul yom is a third-degree impurity and pure for ordinary food, and the Gemara argues that if חולין הטבולין לחלה were like challah, the tevul yom would render the dough impure.

items.text: Abaye's answer: Distinction between certain and uncertain impurity
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: Distinction between certain and uncertain impurity
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the Sages decreed uncertainty about a source that certainly imparts impurity to ordinary food, due to the concern for חולין הטבולין לחלה. However, a tevul yom does not certainly impart impurity to ordinary food, so no such decree was made regarding it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the Sages decreed uncertainty about a source that certainly imparts impurity to ordinary food (חולין), due to the concern for חולין הטבולין לחלה (ordinary food designated for challah), but a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) does not certainly impart impurity to ordinary food, so no such decree was made regarding it.

items.text: Objection from the case of מעת לעת in niddah
items.text_en: Objection from the case of מעת לעת in niddah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the case of מעת לעת in niddah certainly imparts impurity to ordinary food, yet the Sages did not decree regarding its uncertainty because of חולין הטבולין לחלה. The Gemara answers that the case of מעת לעת was discussed in the context of חולין שנעשו על טהרת קודש, not חולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה. Here, with challah, terumah is mixed in, unlike there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the case of מעת לעת (within the previous 24 hours) in niddah certainly imparts impurity to ordinary food, yet the Sages did not decree regarding its uncertainty because of חולין הטבולין לחלה (ordinary food designated for challah).

sub.text: Mar's statement via Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Mar's statement via Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: Mar said that Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak accepted from him that the case of מעת לעת was discussed in the context of חולין שנעשו על טהרת קודש (ordinary food prepared in purity of sacrificial food), not חולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה (ordinary food prepared in purity of terumah).
The Gemara resolves: there (in the case of מעת לעת) terumah is not mixed in, but here (with challah) terumah is mixed in, so the decree applies.

items.text: Alternative answer: מעת לעת is rabbinic
items.text_en: Alternative answer: מעת לעת is rabbinic
items.desc_en: Alternatively, the Gemara says: set aside the case of מעת לעת, as it is a rabbinic decree, not a Torah law, so the comparison does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: set aside the case of מעת לעת (the twenty-four-hour period) because it is a rabbinic decree (דְּרַבָּנַן), not a Torah law, so the comparison with חולין הטבולין לחלה (ordinary food designated for challah) does not apply.

items.text: Beginning of the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Beginning of the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: Rabbi Eliezer says: Four women are sufficient with their time (i.e., they only need to consider the time of their current experience, not retroactively): a virgin, a pregnant woman, a nursing woman, and an elderly woman. Rabbi Yehoshua says: I only heard (this leniency) regarding a virgin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that four women are sufficient with their time, and Rabbi Yehoshua's qualification that he only heard this leniency regarding a virgin.

items.text: Mishnah: Definitions of virgin, pregnant, nursing, and elderly women regarding impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definitions of virgin, pregnant, nursing, and elderly women regarding impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines which women are considered 'virgin', 'pregnant', 'nursing', and 'elderly' for the purposes of impurity. It records disputes between Rabbi Meir and the Sages, and between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei, regarding the duration of impurity for these women.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Eliezer, then defines a virgin as any woman who has never seen blood, even if married.

The Mishnah defines a pregnant woman as one from the time her pregnancy is known, and a nursing woman until she weans her child, with a dispute between Rabbi Meir (who says she is טמאה (impure) for a full day) and the Sages (who say she is only טמאה for the moment).

The Mishnah defines an elderly woman as one for whom three periods have passed near her old age, and records the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer (who says any woman with three missed periods is only טמאה for the moment) and Rabbi Yosei (who limits this rule to pregnant and nursing women).

The Mishnah clarifies that the leniency of 'דייה שעתה' (she is only טמאה for the moment) applies only to the first sighting, but for a second sighting she is טמאה for a full day, unless the first was due to אונס (an external cause), in which case even the second sighting is lenient.

items.text: Gemara: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua and its aftermath
items.text_en: Gemara: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua and its aftermath
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer tells Rabbi Yehoshua that he heard many traditions while Rabbi Yehoshua heard only one. It explains that during Rabbi Eliezer's lifetime, the Sages did not follow his rulings out of concern for his excommunication, but after his death, Rabbi Yehoshua restored the practice to its original state.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer tells Rabbi Yehoshua that he heard many traditions while Rabbi Yehoshua heard only one.

The baraita continues with a principle about testimony and reports that during Rabbi Eliezer's lifetime the Sages followed Rabbi Yehoshua, but after Rabbi Eliezer's death Rabbi Yehoshua restored the practice to its original state.

The Gemara asks why the Sages did not follow Rabbi Eliezer during his lifetime, and answers that it was because Rabbi Eliezer was excommunicated and they feared that following him in one matter would lead to following him in others.
The Gemara explains that out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer they could not protest, but after his death they could, so Rabbi Yehoshua restored the practice.

items.text: Introduction: Shmuel's statement that halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four cases
items.text_en: Introduction: Shmuel's statement that halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four cases
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four specific cases. The first case is the one already mentioned in the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four cases, the first being the one already mentioned in the Mishnah.

items.text: Second case: The woman in difficult labor
items.text_en: Second case: The woman in difficult labor
items.desc_en: The second case is about a woman in difficult labor and how long she can have a discharge and still be considered a zavah. Rabbi Eliezer says it is from time to time (24 hours), and the halakha follows his view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the second case: a woman in difficult labor, asking how long she can discharge and still be considered a זבה (zavah).
Rabbi Eliezer rules that the period is מעת לעת (from time to time, 24 hours), and the Gemara states that the הלכה (binding law) follows his view.

items.text: Third case: Zav and zavah who examined themselves only on first and seventh days
items.text_en: Third case: Zav and zavah who examined themselves only on first and seventh days
items.desc_en: The third case involves a zav or zavah who examined themselves on the first and seventh days and found themselves pure, but did not check on the other days. Rabbi Eliezer considers them pure, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva disagree. A baraita states that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the third case: a zav or zavah who examined themselves on the first and seventh days and found themselves pure, but did not check on the other days.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that they are presumed pure for the entire period.
Rabbi Yehoshua rules that only the first and seventh days are considered pure.
Rabbi Akiva rules that only the seventh day is considered pure.
A baraita reports that Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei deem Rabbi Eliezer's view more convincing than Rabbi Yehoshua's, and Rabbi Akiva's more convincing than all, but the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Fourth case: The backs of vessels that became impure through liquids
items.text_en: Fourth case: The backs of vessels that became impure through liquids
items.desc_en: The fourth case concerns the backs of vessels that became impure through liquids. Rabbi Eliezer rules that they render liquids impure but do not disqualify foods, while Rabbi Yehoshua argues they also disqualify foods. The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning based on rabbinic decrees and the distinction between liquids and foods.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the fourth case: Rabbi Eliezer rules that the backs of vessels that became impure through liquids render liquids impure but do not disqualify foods, while Rabbi Yehoshua argues they also disqualify foods.

Rabbi Yehoshua argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori reasoning): if a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) who does not render חולין (non-sacred) liquids impure nevertheless disqualifies תרומה (priestly portion) foods, then the backs of vessels that do render חולין liquids impure should certainly disqualify תרומה foods.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's position: the impurity of the backs of vessels is a rabbinic decree (דרבנן), while the impurity of a טבול יום is Torah law (דאורייתא), and one cannot derive a rabbinic law from a Torah law via קל וחומר; the rabbis decreed impurity for liquids because they are prone to become impure, but not for foods.

sub.text: Gemara's question and answer about the choice of case
sub.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the choice of case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifically mentions the backs of vessels, and answers: because they are קילי (lenient), as a vessel that becomes impure on its back has its inside, rim, and handles remain pure, but if the inside becomes impure, the entire vessel is impure.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer: What does Shmuel teach us?
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer: What does Shmuel teach us?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Shmuel's statement adds, since the halakha in these cases is already stated in the Mishnah. It answers that Shmuel teaches that one does not derive halakha from a student's teaching (i.e., from a Mishnah that is not authoritative).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Shmuel's statement teaches, since the halakha in all these cases is already stated in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel teaches that one does not derive halakha from a student's teaching (i.e., from a Mishnah that is not authoritative).

items.text: Transition: Are there more cases?
items.text_en: Transition: Are there more cases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if there are no more cases where the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, and begins to cite another case from a Mishnah about Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks if there are no more cases where the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, and begins to cite another case from a Mishnah about Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling and its proof
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and its proof
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in the case of teaching a minor to refuse. The Gemara notes that Shmuel only said this for four cases in Seder Taharot, but not for other orders. It then brings a proof from a similar ruling about the basket joining dough for challah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one teaches a minor girl to perform refusal (מיאון) against her husband.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Eliezer in this case.
The Gemara notes that Shmuel only applied this rule to four cases in Seder Taharot, but not to other orders where there are many.
The Gemara brings a supporting baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a basket joins dough for חלה (challah), and Shmuel similarly rules the הלכה follows Rabbi Eliezer there, proving the pattern.

items.text: Questioning the proof and offering a better support
items.text_en: Questioning the proof and offering a better support
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the proof from the challah case is strong, and suggests it is because Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Eliezer. However, it then notes that Rabbi Elazar's statement is not identical to the mishnah, so it instead supports the ruling from Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the proof from the challah case is stronger than the direct mishnah, and suggests it is because Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar explicitly rules that one teaches a minor girl to refuse her husband.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar's statement is not identical to the mishnah, so it instead supports the ruling from Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's testimony.

items.text: Analyzing Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's testimony
items.text_en: Analyzing Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the five things Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava testified about, including that minors may be made to refuse. It then questions whether 'minor girls' refers to the cases of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Eliezer, but concludes it means minor girls in general. A further objection is raised and resolved.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's five testimonies, beginning with the rule that minor girls may be made to refuse.
The baraita continues listing the remaining four testimonies: marrying a woman on one witness, stoning a rooster, libated wine, and the morning tamid offering.
The Gemara asks whether 'minor girls' in the baraita refers specifically to the cases of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara rejects that interpretation and explains that 'minor girls' means minor girls in general, not limited to those specific cases.
The Gemara objects: if so, regarding the case of 'woman' in the baraita, why not teach 'women' and say it means women in general?
The Gemara resolves: since the baraita uses 'woman' in the singular and 'minor girls' in the plural, the distinction is deliberate, proving the point.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's similar ruling and a challenge from Shevi'it
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's similar ruling and a challenge from Shevi'it
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar also said the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four cases. The Gemara challenges this by citing a mishnah in Shevi'it where Rabbi Eliezer's view is followed, and Rabbi Zeira points out the inconsistency with his father's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing Rabbi Elazar's statement that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four cases, then questions whether there are no more cases, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Elazar himself ruled like Rabbi Eliezer regarding a minor's refusal.
The Gemara cites a mishnah in Shevi'it where Rabbi Eliezer's view is followed regarding balsam, and Rabbi Pedat identifies Rabbi Eliezer as the tanna who considers balsam a fruit.
