Rabbi Zeira objects to Rabbi Pedat, pointing out the inconsistency: Rabbi Pedat says Rabbi Eliezer is the tanna, but Rabbi Pedat's father (Rabbi Elazar) said the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer only in four cases.

The Gemara resolves that if Rabbi Elazar's statement were limited to Seder Teharot, Rabbi Pedat could have replied that his father meant only four cases in Seder Teharot, but there are other cases in other orders.

items.text: Resolving the challenge with the same support
items.text_en: Resolving the challenge with the same support
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by again invoking Rabbi Elazar's and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's support for the ruling about teaching a minor to refuse, showing that the Shevi'it case is not a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by noting that the case of Shevi'it is not a contradiction because Rabbi Elazar holds in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion about teaching a minor to refuse.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar's opinion is not identical to Rabbi Eliezer's, as both are necessary for different cases.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer because Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava supports his opinion.

items.text: Another case and its attribution
items.text_en: Another case and its attribution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another case where Rabbi Elazar ruled like Rabbi Eliezer, regarding the fourth blessing of the bride. Rabbi Abba attributes this ruling to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, whose statement is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there are no more cases, and cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer dispute the fourth blessing of the bride, with Rabbi Elazar ruling like Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Abba explains that Rabbi Elazar's ruling was actually said in the name of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, citing the baraita where Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel holds the same position as Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position seems inconsistent with a baraita about Yom Kippur prayers. It resolves that he follows his own tradition, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that he cites his ancestors' view but does not necessarily hold it himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position seems very old and inconsistent, and suggests he follows his own tradition.
The Gemara objects further, citing a baraita about Yom Kippur prayers that seems to contradict Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel cites his ancestors' view but does not necessarily hold it himself.

items.text: Discussion on the identity of the Tanna who holds that קְטָף is a fruit
items.text_en: Discussion on the identity of the Tanna who holds that קְטָף is a fruit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira if the Tanna who considers קְטָף a fruit is Rabbi Eliezer. The Gemara suggests that even the Rabbis might agree in certain cases, citing a Mishnah about the sap of orlah and a baraita about Sabbatical year.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the Tanna who taught that קְטָפָא (a fruit bud) is considered a fruit is Rabbi Eliezer, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer forbids curdling milk with the sap of orlah fruit.
Rabbi Zeira answers that even if the Tanna is the Rabbis, they only dispute Rabbi Eliezer regarding a branch bud, but agree regarding a fruit bud, citing Rabbi Yehoshua's tradition.

An alternative answer is offered: the Rabbis only dispute Rabbi Eliezer regarding a fruit-bearing tree, but agree regarding a non-fruit-bearing tree, citing Rabbi Shimon's statement about the Sabbatical year.

items.text: Clarification of the identity of the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer's response
items.text_en: Clarification of the identity of the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the Sages are in the baraita, and an elder cites Rabbi Yochanan that they are actually Rabbi Eliezer. The Gemara then explains that Rabbi Eliezer's statement was made in response to the Rabbis, conceding only in the case of a non-fruit tree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the 'Sages' are in the baraita, and an elder cites Rabbi Yochanan that they are actually Rabbi Eliezer himself.

The Gemara objects that if it is Rabbi Eliezer, why mention a non-fruit-bearing tree? The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer is speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning, but they reject his argument.
The Gemara objects: if the Sages are Rabbi Eliezer, why does the baraita specify a non-fruit tree? Rabbi Eliezer would say the same even for a fruit tree.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer was speaking to the Rabbis according to their own logic: he concedes only for a non-fruit tree, but the Rabbis reject even that.

items.text: Baraita defining a virgin and the three types of virginity
items.text_en: Baraita defining a virgin and the three types of virginity
items.desc_en: A baraita defines a virgin as one who has not seen blood due to marriage or childbirth, emphasizing 'virginity of blood' not 'virginity of hymen'. Rav Kahana's baraita lists three types of virginity: human, land, and fig tree, each with practical halachic implications. The Gemara questions why the baraita does not include the case of a woman who saw blood due to marriage.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines a 'virgin' for halachic purposes as one who has not seen blood from marriage or childbirth, i.e., a 'virgin of blood' not of hymen.

Rav Kahana objects by citing a baraita listing three types of 'virginity' (human, land, and fig tree), and argues that if the Mishnah's definition were correct, it should have been included in that list.

items.text: Amoraic explanations for why the baraita omitted the case of a woman who saw blood due to marriage
items.text_en: Amoraic explanations for why the baraita omitted the case of a woman who saw blood due to marriage
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, Rav Sheishet, Rabbi Chanina, and Ravina offer different criteria for why the baraita only lists cases where the item loses its original name or status. The Gemara objects that blood is actually beneficial for a woman, citing Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Meir, and resolves that the baraita lists only items that are eagerly sought by buyers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the baraita only lists items that have lost their original name (שֵׁם לְוַוי), not those that retain it, so blood from marriage is excluded because it still has a secondary name.

Rav Sheishet explains that the baraita only lists items dependent on an action (תְּלֵי בְּמַעֲשֶׂה), not those independent of action, so blood from marriage is excluded because it is not action-dependent.

Rabbi Chanina explains that the baraita only lists items that do not return to their original state (לָא הָדַר לִבְרִיָּיתוֹ), not those that do, so blood from marriage is excluded because it can return.

Ravina explains that the baraita only lists items that buyers are particular about (קָפֵיד עֲלֵיהּ זָבוֹנָא), not those they are not particular about, so blood from marriage is excluded because buyers are not particular about it.

The Gemara objects that buyers are indeed particular about blood, citing Rabbi Chiya that blood is beneficial for a woman like leaven for dough, and Rabbi Meir that abundant blood leads to many children.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita lists only items that buyers eagerly seek (קָפֵיץ עֲלֵיהּ זָבוֹנָא), not those they are merely particular about, so blood from marriage is excluded because it is not eagerly sought.

items.text: Baraita defining 'virgin land'
items.text_en: Baraita defining 'virgin land'
items.desc_en: A baraita defines virgin land as that which produces clods and whose soil is not loose. Finding a potsherd indicates it was worked, while finding צוּנְמָא indicates it is virgin.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines 'virgin land' as land that produces clods and whose soil is not loose, and notes that finding a potsherd indicates it was worked.

items.text: Discussion on the recognition of pregnancy
items.text_en: Discussion on the recognition of pregnancy
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a pregnant woman's status changes once her pregnancy is recognizable. Sumchos cites Rabbi Meir that this is after three months, with a biblical allusion. The Gemara questions why it is only a 'remembrance' and not a proof, explaining that some women give birth at nine months and others at seven.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a pregnant woman's status begins when her pregnancy is recognizable, and Sumchos cites a verse as a memory aid for three months.
The Gemara objects that the verse is a strong proof, not just a memory aid, and explains that it is only a memory aid because some women give birth at nine months and others at seven.
The Gemara answers that the verse is only a remembrance because some women give birth at nine months and others at seven, so the three-month marker is not universally conclusive.

items.text: Baraita on a woman presumed pregnant who miscarries a non-viable fetus
items.text_en: Baraita on a woman presumed pregnant who miscarries a non-viable fetus
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that a woman presumed pregnant who sees blood and then miscarries a non-viable substance remains in her presumption, and her blood is considered only for that moment. The Gemara questions the prooftext and then raises a contradiction with another baraita that considers such a case as a full birth for the laws of זוֹב.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a woman presumed pregnant who sees blood and then miscarries a non-viable substance remains in her presumption and her blood is considered only for that moment.
The Gemara questions why the baraita calls the verse a mere 'reminder' when it seems to be a clear proof.
The Gemara answers that the verse refers to males, not women, so it is only a reminder, not a direct proof.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that considers such a case as a full birth for the laws of זוֹב (abnormal discharge).

items.text: Gemara's question and answers on the leniency for a pregnant woman
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answers on the leniency for a pregnant woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a pregnant woman who experiences a discharge close to birth is deemed pure, given that the Torah declared her pure. Rav Pappi and Rava offer explanations: Rav Pappi says to set aside the rabbinic rule of 'from time to time', and Rava says the reason is that her head and limbs are heavy, which applies here as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a pregnant woman who experiences a discharge close to birth is deemed pure, given that the Torah declared her pure.
Rav Pappi answers that the leniency is because the rabbinic rule of 'from time to time' is set aside.
Rava explains that the reason is that her head and limbs are heavy, and this applies here as well.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry about a woman who saw blood and then her pregnancy was recognized
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry about a woman who saw blood and then her pregnancy was recognized
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether a woman who saw blood and later her pregnancy was recognized is impure, since at the time of seeing the pregnancy was not recognized, or perhaps she is pure because the seeing was close to the recognition. Rabbi Zeira responds that the reason is that her head and limbs are heavy, but at the time she saw, her head and limbs were not heavy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether a woman who saw blood and later her pregnancy was recognized is impure or pure.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the reason for purity is heavy limbs, but at the time she saw, her limbs were not heavy, so she is impure.

items.text: Inquiry about a pregnant woman who reached her fixed period and did not examine
items.text_en: Inquiry about a pregnant woman who reached her fixed period and did not examine
items.desc_en: A certain elder asks Rabbi Yochanan about a pregnant woman whose fixed period arrived and she did not examine herself, according to the opinion that fixed periods are Torah law. Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir says that if a woman was in hiding and her fixed period arrived and she did not examine, she is pure because fear suspends the blood. The Gemara concludes that here too her blood is suspended and she does not require examination.

sub.desc_en: An elder asks Rabbi Yochanan about a pregnant woman whose fixed period arrived and she did not examine herself, questioning whether she requires examination according to the view that fixed periods are Torah law.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers by citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that a woman in hiding whose fixed period arrived and she did not examine is pure because fear suspends the blood, implying that without fear she would be impure.
The Gemara concludes that fixed periods are Torah law, and since the pregnant woman's blood is suspended due to her condition, she does not require examination.

items.text: Baraita on a nursing woman whose child died within 24 months
items.text_en: Baraita on a nursing woman whose child died within 24 months
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a nursing woman is considered like all women until she weans. A baraita elaborates: if her child died within 24 months, she is like all women and is impure from time to time and from examination to examination. Rabbi Meir says that if she nursed for four or five years, she only counts her hour. Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon say she counts her hour only during the 24 months, but after that she is impure from time to time. The Gemara explains the rationale: according to Rabbi Meir, blood is transformed into milk; according to the other rabbis, her limbs are disintegrating and her soul does not return until 24 months.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the Tanna Kamma's ruling: a nursing woman whose child died within 24 months is like all women, impure from time to time and from examination to examination; Rabbi Meir adds that if she nursed for four or five years, she only counts her hour.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon state that she counts her hour only during the 24 months; after that, she is impure from time to time and from examination to examination.

The Gemara explains the rationale: according to Rabbi Meir, blood is transformed into milk; according to Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon, her limbs are disintegrating and her soul does not return until 24 months.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the term 'therefore' in the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the term 'therefore' in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Meir needs the term 'therefore' and why Rabbi Yosei needs it. It explains that Rabbi Yosei's 'therefore' teaches that he holds two leniencies, and the term is used to prevent a misunderstanding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir needs the term 'לְפִיכָךְ' (therefore) in the baraita, and answers that it is needed because of Rabbi Yosei's use of the same term.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei's 'לְפִיכָךְ' (therefore) teaches that he holds two leniencies, and the term is used to prevent a misunderstanding that he holds only one.

items.text: Tosefta and discussion on the source for Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.text_en: Tosefta and discussion on the source for Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.desc_en: A Tosefta states that Rabbi Meir says blood is transformed into milk, citing the verse 'Who can bring a pure thing from an impure?' The Gemara discusses the interpretation of this verse: Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to semen, Rabbi Elazar says it refers to the water of purification, leading to a discussion about the carrier of the water and the required measure for sprinkling. The Gemara concludes with a verse from Solomon.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited that supports Rabbi Meir's view that blood turns into milk, citing the verse 'Who can bring a pure thing from an impure?'
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse as referring to semen, which is impure but produces a pure person.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse as referring to the water of purification, where the sprinkler is pure but the one who touches is impure.
The Gemara objects that the verse says 'the sprinkler' requires laundering, implying impurity, so it cannot mean the sprinkler is pure; rather it means 'the carrier'.

The Gemara explains that the verse uses 'sprinkler' to teach that the carrier must carry a measure fit for sprinkling, and then questions this for those who hold sprinkling does not require a measure.
The Gemara resolves that even for those who say sprinkling does not require a measure, that applies to the person, but the vessel requires a measure, as taught in a Mishnah.
The Gemara concludes with Solomon's verse 'I said I would be wise, but it is far from me' as a reflection on the difficulty of the discussion.

items.text: Definition of an old woman
items.text_en: Definition of an old woman
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines an old woman as one for whom three periods have passed close to her old age. The Gemara asks what 'close to her old age' means, and Rav Yehuda answers that it is when her friends say she is old. Rabbi Shimon offers a different definition, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines an old woman as one for whom three periods have passed close to her old age.
The Gemara asks what 'close to her old age' means.
Rav Yehuda answers that it is when her friends say she is old.
Rabbi Shimon offers a different definition, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Definition of a zekenah
items.text_en: Definition of a zekenah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's description of a zekenah as one who is called 'mother' without embarrassment. Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak dispute whether the key criterion is that she is not particular about being called old or that she is not embarrassed by it. The difference between them is a case where she is embarrassed but not particular.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's definition of a zekenah as one who is called 'mother' without embarrassment.
The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak over whether the criterion is not being particular or not being embarrassed.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions.
The Gemara answers that the difference is a case where she is embarrassed but not particular.

items.text: Length of an onah
items.text_en: Length of an onah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how long an onah is. Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah says an average onah is thirty days, while Rava in the name of Rav Chisda says twenty days. The Gemara resolves that they do not disagree: one counts days of impurity and purity, the other counts only days of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how long an onah is.

sub.text: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish citing Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah says an average onah is thirty days.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rava citing Rav Chisda says an average onah is twenty days.
The Gemara resolves that they do not disagree: one counts days of impurity and purity, the other counts only days of impurity.

items.text: Baraita on the zekenah's status
items.text_en: Baraita on the zekenah's status
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a zekenah has three onot pass without seeing blood, and then she sees, she only counts from that moment. If another three onot pass and she sees again, she still only counts from that moment. But if a third set of three onot passes and she sees, she is like all other women and must count retroactively from the last examination.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the rule for a zekenah (elderly woman) who experiences three sets of three onot (periods) without seeing blood, establishing that after the third set she is treated like all other women and must count retroactively.

items.text: Analysis of the baraita's wording
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's statement that it is not necessary that she had a fixed pattern, but even if she shortened or lengthened the interval. It raises a difficulty: if she had a fixed pattern, she would have established a vest, and then she would only count from the moment of sighting. The Gemara suggests that the baraita might follow the Sages who disagree with Rabbi Dosa, but then the wording should be reversed. It resolves by offering two versions: one that the text should read 'not that she shortened or lengthened, but even if she had a fixed pattern,' and another that the original text is correct and refers to Rabbi Dosa's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that it is not necessary that she had a fixed pattern, but even if she shortened or lengthened the interval.

The Gemara questions the baraita's wording: if she had a fixed pattern, she would have established a vest, and then she would only count from the moment of sighting, so the baraita should have prioritized the fixed pattern case.

The Gemara suggests that the baraita might follow the Sages who disagree with Rabbi Dosa, but then the wording should be reversed to say 'not that she shortened or lengthened, but even if she had a fixed pattern.'

The Gemara resolves by offering two versions: one that the text should read 'not that she shortened or lengthened, but even if she had a fixed pattern,' and another that the original text is correct and refers to Rabbi Dosa's opinion.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and the Sages' response
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and the Sages' response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that any woman who has three onot pass without seeing blood is considered a zekenah. He brings a precedent of an old woman in Haitalu who stopped for three onot, and the Sages ruled that she only counts from the moment of sighting. The Sages respond that a time of pressing need is not proof. Two explanations are given for 'time of pressing need': either it was a time of scarcity, or there were many pure items at stake and the Sages were concerned for the loss of pure items.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that any woman who has three onot pass without seeing blood is considered a zekenah, and brings a precedent of an old woman in Haitalu who stopped for three onot and the Sages ruled that she only counts from the moment of sighting.

The Sages respond that a time of pressing need is not proof, and two explanations are given for 'time of pressing need': either it was a time of scarcity, or there were many pure items at stake and the Sages were concerned for the loss of pure items.

items.text: Rabbi's ruling in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rabbi's ruling in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: A baraita relates that Rabbi acted in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer. After he remembered, he said that Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in a time of pressing need. The Gemara questions what 'after he remembered' means: if he remembered that the halakhah is not like Rabbi Eliezer but like the Sages, how could he have acted like him in a time of pressing need? Rather, it means that no halakhah had been stated either way, and 'after he remembered' means he remembered that not just an individual but many disagreed with him, so he said Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in a time of pressing need.

sub.desc_en: A baraita relates that Rabbi acted in accordance with רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer), and after remembering, said that רבי אליעזר is worthy to rely upon in a time of pressing need.
The Gemara questions what 'after he remembered' means: if he remembered that the halakhah is not like רבי אליעזר but like the Sages, how could he have acted like him in a time of pressing need?

The Gemara answers that no halakhah had been stated either way, and 'after he remembered' means he remembered that not just an individual but many disagreed with him, so he said רבי אליעזר is worthy to rely upon in a time of pressing need.

items.text: Laws of a minor girl who sees blood
items.text_en: Laws of a minor girl who sees blood
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches the laws of a minor girl who has not yet reached the age of seeing blood. If she sees blood, the first three times she only counts from the moment of sighting. If three onot pass and she sees, she only counts from that moment, and this pattern repeats for three cycles. Once she reaches the age of seeing blood, the first time she sees she only counts from the moment, but the second time she must count retroactively. However, if three onot pass and she sees, she again only counts from the moment. The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly states that after three onot pass, she only counts from the moment.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the law of a minor girl who has not yet reached the age of seeing blood: the first three sightings only count from the moment of sighting.
The baraita continues: if three onot pass and she sees, she only counts from that moment, and this pattern repeats for three cycles.

The baraita concludes: once she reaches the age of seeing blood, the first time she sees she only counts from the moment, but the second time she must count retroactively; however, if three onot pass and she sees, she again only counts from the moment.
The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly states that after three onot pass, she only counts from the moment.

items.text: Rav Giddel's first ruling on sightings in intervals
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's first ruling on sightings in intervals
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel, citing Rav, rules that if a woman sees blood on the first and second intervals (onot), she is only impure from the time of sighting; on the third interval, she is impure retroactively from the previous examination and from the previous interval.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if she then sees blood again at intervals (עונות), what is the law?

Rav Giddel in the name of Rav rules: first and second sightings — she is only impure from the time of sighting (דייה שעתה); third sighting — she is impure retroactively from the previous examination and from the previous interval (מטמאה מעת לעת ומפקידה לפקידה).

items.text: Second question: after three intervals
items.text_en: Second question: after three intervals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if after three intervals have passed she sees blood, what is the ruling? The answer is that she is only impure from the time of sighting. Then the Gemara repeats the initial question about sightings in intervals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if after three intervals have passed she sees blood, what is the ruling? The answer is that she is only impure from the time of sighting.
The Gemara then repeats the initial question about sightings in intervals: what is the ruling if she sees again during intervals?

items.text: Rav Kahana's version of Rav Giddel's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's version of Rav Giddel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana, citing Rav Giddel citing Rav, gives a different version: on the first interval she is only impure from the time of sighting; on the second interval she is impure retroactively from the previous examination and from the previous interval.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Rav Giddel citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Rav Giddel citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana transmits Rav Giddel's version of Rav's ruling: on the first interval she is only impure from the time of sighting; on the second interval she is impure retroactively from the previous examination and from the previous interval.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that this ruling follows Rabbi, who holds that a presumption (chazakah) is established after two occurrences.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the preceding ruling follows Rabbi (רבי), who holds that a presumption (חזקה) is established after two occurrences.

items.text: Contradiction from the later clause and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from the later clause and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the later clause (about three intervals) follows Rabbi Eliezer, not Rabbi. It then resolves that the entire ruling is Rabbi Eliezer's, but he agrees with Rabbi regarding the establishment of a veset (fixed cycle).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the later clause (three intervals) follows Rabbi Eliezer, not Rabbi.
The Gemara resolves that the entire ruling is Rabbi Eliezer's, but he agrees with Rabbi regarding the establishment of a veset (fixed cycle).

items.text: Dispute about a stain between sightings
items.text_en: Dispute about a stain between sightings
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan argue about the status of a blood stain found between the first and second sightings (pure) and between the second and third (Chizkiyah says impure, Rabbi Yochanan says pure). Their reasoning is given.

sub.desc_en: The Stam introduces the dispute: a stain found between the first and second sightings is pure, but between the second and third, Chizkiyah says it is impure.
Chizkiyah rules the stain impure, reasoning that since if she had actually seen blood at that point she would be impure, the stain (כתם) likewise renders her impure.
Rabbi Yochanan rules the stain pure, reasoning that since she has not yet established a fixed pattern (חזקה) of seeing blood, we do not render her impure via the stain.

items.text: Rabbi Il'ai's challenge and Rabbi Zeira's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Il'ai's challenge and Rabbi Zeira's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Il'ai challenges the earlier ruling by comparing the minor girl to a virgin whose blood is pure. Rabbi Zeira responds that the difference is that the minor's 'burning' (sirpah) is common, while the virgin's is not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Il'ai challenges the earlier ruling by asking what distinguishes the minor girl from a virgin whose blood is pure.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the minor's 'burning' (sirpah) is common, while the virgin's is not.

items.text: Ulla's report in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
items.text_en: Ulla's report in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
items.desc_en: Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak that a minor girl who has not reached the age of seeing blood and sees a first and second time — her saliva and her midras are pure in the market, and even her bloodstain is pure. The Gemara questions whether this ruling is from Rabbi Shimon or from his teacher, and notes the practical difference for the status of a single opinion against two.

sub.text: Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak that a minor girl who has not reached the age of seeing blood and sees a first and second time — her saliva and midras are pure in the market, and even her bloodstain is pure; Ulla adds uncertainty whether the stain ruling is from Rabbi Yochanan or his teacher.
The Gemara asks what practical difference the uncertainty makes, and answers that it affects whether the ruling is considered the statement of one Sage against two.
When Ravin and all the seafarers came, they stated the ruling as that of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, resolving that Rabbi Yochanan was transmitting his teacher's opinion.

items.text: Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi's ruling and the clarification of 'shofa'at'
items.text_en: Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi's ruling and the clarification of 'shofa'at'
items.desc_en: Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi states that a minor girl who has not reached the age of seeing blood, even if she flows (shofa'at) for all seven days, is considered only one sighting. The Gemara initially questions whether this applies even to a continuous flow versus a stopping flow, then corrects the formulation, and finally Rav Shimi bar Chiyya clarifies that a dripping (madlefet) is not like seeing, but like a continuous flow (shofa'at).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi rules that a minor girl who has not reached the age of seeing blood, even if she flows for all seven days, is considered only one sighting.
The Gemara questions whether the ruling applies even to a continuous flow, arguing that a stopping flow should be considered two sightings.
The Gemara corrects the formulation: the ruling applies specifically to a continuous flow for all seven days, which is considered only one sighting.

Rav Shimi bar Chiyya initially states that a dripping woman is not like a full sighting, but the Gemara objects that she did see blood, so he rephrases: she is like a stopping flow, not a continuous one.
The Gemara rejects the comparison to a river and concludes that a dripping woman is like a continuous flow, both considered one sighting.

items.text: The baraita on the presumption of daughters of Israel before and after reaching puberty
items.text_en: The baraita on the presumption of daughters of Israel before and after reaching puberty
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that daughters of Israel who have not reached puberty are presumed pure and women do not examine them. Once they reach puberty, they are presumed impure and women examine them. Rabbi Yehuda adds that they should not be examined by hand, but anointed with oil inside and wiped outside, so they are examined naturally.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the presumption that daughters of Israel before puberty are presumed pure and not examined, while after puberty they are presumed impure and examined.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that they should not be examined by hand, but anointed with oil inside and wiped outside, so they are examined naturally.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's ruling on a pregnant or nursing woman and the clarification of the baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's ruling on a pregnant or nursing woman and the clarification of the baraita
items.desc_en: A tanna recites before Rabbi Elazar that Rabbi Yose says a pregnant or nursing woman who has passed three seasons is presumed pure (dayah sha'atah). Rabbi Elazar objects that the tanna began with two categories (pregnant and nursing) and ended with one. The Gemara explains that the tanna meant a woman who is both pregnant and nursing, and teaches that days of pregnancy count toward nursing and vice versa. The Gemara then discusses how this is possible, offering three answers: a dry birth, separate blood of niddah and birth, or teaching one case.

sub.desc_en: A tanna recites before Rabbi Elazar that Rabbi Yose rules a pregnant or nursing woman who has passed three seasons is presumed pure (דייה שעתה).
Rabbi Elazar objects that the tanna began with two categories (pregnant and nursing) but ended with one (דייה שעתה).
The Gemara explains that the tanna meant a woman who is both pregnant and nursing, and the baraita incidentally teaches that days of pregnancy count toward nursing and vice versa.
The Gemara cites a baraita that explicitly states days of pregnancy count toward nursing and nursing days count toward pregnancy.
The Gemara questions how nursing days can count toward pregnancy, since a nursing woman who becomes pregnant is already in both states.
The Gemara offers the first answer: the case involves a dry birth (לידה יבשתא), where the woman did not nurse but the pregnancy period counts as nursing.
The Gemara offers the second answer: the blood of niddah (דם נדה) and the blood of birth (דם לידה) are separate, so the woman can be in niddah status while nursing.
The Gemara offers the third answer: simply teach one case (תני חדא) — the baraita refers only to a woman who is both pregnant and nursing.

items.text: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel (and Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan) regarding the scope of 'dayah sha'atah'
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel (and Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan) regarding the scope of 'dayah sha'atah'
items.desc_en: Rav says the ruling of 'dayah sha'atah' applies to all women (virgin, elderly, pregnant, nursing). Shmuel says it was only taught for a virgin and an elderly woman, but a pregnant or nursing woman is presumed pure for all her days of pregnancy or nursing. Reish Lakish agrees with Rav, and Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Shmuel. The Gemara notes this is like a dispute among tannaim.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the ruling of 'דייה שעתה' (she suffices with her time) applies to all women listed in the Mishnah.
Shmuel limits the ruling to a virgin and an elderly woman, while a pregnant or nursing woman is presumed pure for all her days of pregnancy or nursing.

sub.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish agrees with Rav, and Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Shmuel, showing the dispute is parallel among later Amoraim.

sub.text: Gemara's note of a tannaitic dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's note of a tannaitic dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this Amoraic dispute mirrors a tannaitic dispute, introducing the baraita about a pregnant and nursing woman.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: R. Meir holds that a woman who sees blood throughout pregnancy and nursing is deemed pure (her status is determined by the first sighting). R. Yose, R. Yehuda, and R. Shimon argue that this leniency applies only to the first sighting; subsequent sightings render her impure retroactively.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that a woman who sees blood throughout pregnancy and nursing is deemed pure (her status is determined by the first sighting), while Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon argue that this leniency applies only to the first sighting; subsequent sightings render her impure retroactively.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rav Huna's statement on jumping and veset
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rav Huna's statement on jumping and veset
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if a woman jumped and saw blood three times, she establishes a veset. The Gemara questions whether this applies to days or to jumps, citing a baraita that an onset (ones) does not establish a veset. Rav Ashi explains that the case is where she jumped on the same day of the week each time, but once jumped without seeing, and later saw without jumping—the Gemara concludes that the jump is still a factor, not just the day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if a woman jumped and saw blood three times, she establishes a וסת (fixed menstrual pattern).
The Gemara asks: does Rav Huna mean the pattern is fixed for days or for jumps? It rejects the possibility of days, since she did not see blood on days she did not jump.
The Gemara objects: if it is for jumps, a baraita teaches that anything established due to an אונס (uncontrollable onset) does not establish a pattern at all.
The Gemara answers: the baraita means she does not establish a pattern for days alone or jumps alone, but she does establish a pattern for days and jumps combined.
The Gemara questions: that she does not establish a pattern for days alone is obvious, so why mention it?

Rav Ashi explains the case: she jumped on a certain day of the week and saw blood three times, but once jumped without seeing, and later saw without jumping; the Gemara concludes that the jump is still a factor, not just the day.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Huna said the woman establishes a veset for days but not for jumps. Rav Ashi explains the case: she jumped on the same day of the week and saw, but once jumped without seeing, and later saw without jumping—this reveals that the day is the cause, not the jump.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version of Rav Huna's statement is presented: the woman establishes a veset for days but not for jumps, and Rav Ashi explains the case where the day is revealed as the cause.

items.text: Mishnah on bedikah requirements
items.text_en: Mishnah on bedikah requirements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that although a woman is deemed pure by her current status, she must still perform internal examinations (bedikah), except for a niddah and a woman sitting on pure blood (yoshevet al dam tohar). It lists times when examination is required: morning, twilight, and when serving her household. Kohanot have additional requirements when eating terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that despite the principle of דייה שעתה (her current status suffices), a woman must perform internal examinations (בדיקה), except for a niddah and a woman sitting on pure blood (יושבת על דם טוהר).
The Mishnah adds that a woman uses examination cloths (עדים), except for a woman sitting on pure blood and a virgin whose blood is pure.

The Mishnah lists times when examination is required: morning, twilight, when serving her household; additional times for priestesses when eating תרומה (priestly portion), and Rabbi Yehuda adds also when they pass from eating terumah.

items.text: Gemara on the niddah exemption from bedikah
items.text_en: Gemara on the niddah exemption from bedikah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a niddah does not require bedikah during her menstrual days. This works well for R. Shimon ben Lakish, who holds that a woman cannot establish a veset during niddah days, but R. Yochanan, who holds she can, would require bedikah. R. Yochanan responds that his ruling applies only when she sees from a closed source (ma'ayan satum), not an open one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's exemption from bedikah applies to a niddah during her menstrual days.

The Gemara questions that this exemption works well for Reish Lakish, who holds a woman cannot establish a veset during niddah days, but for Rabbi Yochanan, who holds she can, she would need to perform bedikah.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that his ruling applies only when she sees from a closed source (מעיין סתום), not from an open one (מעיין פתוח).

items.text: Gemara on the yoshevet al dam tohar exemption
items.text_en: Gemara on the yoshevet al dam tohar exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the case of a woman sitting on pure blood (yoshevet al dam tohar). This works well for Rav, who holds there is one source that the Torah alternately renders impure and pure, but for Levi, who holds there are two sources, she would need to check lest the impure source has not ceased. Levi responds by questioning the authorship of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the case of a woman sitting on pure blood (יושבת על דם טוהר) and initially assumes she is seeking to sit on pure blood.
The Gemara notes that this works well for Rav, who holds there is one source (מעין אחד) that the Torah alternately renders impure and pure.
The Gemara objects that for Levi, who holds there are two sources (שני מעיינות), she would need to check lest the impure source has not ceased.
Levi responds by questioning the authorship of the Mishnah, implying it follows a different opinion.

items.text: Identifying the anonymous Mishnah as Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Identifying the anonymous Mishnah as Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Beit Shammai, who hold that there is only one source (the uterus) for both menstrual and virgin blood. It questions whether the Tanna can state an anonymous Mishnah like Beit Shammai, and explains that this is a case of an anonymous ruling followed by a dispute, where the halakha does not follow the anonymous ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous Mishnah as Beit Shammai, who hold that there is only one source (the uterus) for both menstrual and virgin blood.
The Gemara questions how the Tanna can state an anonymous Mishnah like Beit Shammai, since the halakha usually follows Beit Hillel.
The Gemara answers that this is a case of an anonymous ruling followed by a dispute, where the halakha does not follow the anonymous ruling.

items.text: Alternative explanation: the Mishnah says 'yoshevet' not 'mevakeshet'
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: the Mishnah says 'yoshevet' not 'mevakeshet'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the Mishnah says 'yoshevet' (sitting) not 'mevakeshet' (seeking to sit), implying she is already sitting. The concern that she might establish a fixed cycle is dismissed because a pure source does not establish a cycle for an impure source. This works for Levi who holds there are two sources, but for Rav who holds one source, the Gemara explains that pure days do not establish a cycle for impure days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah says 'יוֹשֶׁבֶת' (sitting) not 'מְבַקֶּשֶׁת לֵישֵׁב' (seeking to sit), implying she is already sitting. The concern that she might establish a fixed cycle is dismissed because a pure source does not establish a cycle for an impure source.

The Gemara notes that this answer works for לוי (Levi) who holds there are two sources, but for רב (Rav) who holds one source, she should be required to examine herself. The Gemara resolves that even according to Rav, pure days do not establish a cycle for impure days.

items.text: The Mishnah's ruling on a young bride and Rav Giddel's qualification
items.text_en: The Mishnah's ruling on a young bride and Rav Giddel's qualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a minor who married before reaching puberty: Beit Shammai give her four nights, Beit Hillel say until the wound heals. Rav Giddel in the name of Shmuel qualifies: this applies only if she did not stop bleeding due to intercourse and then saw blood not due to intercourse; but if she stopped due to intercourse and then saw blood, she is impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a minor who married before reaching puberty: Beit Shammai give her four nights, Beit Hillel say until the wound heals.

Rav Giddel in the name of Shmuel qualifies the Mishnah: it applies only if she did not stop bleeding due to intercourse and then saw blood not due to intercourse; but if she stopped due to intercourse and then saw blood, she is impure.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yona and resolution by Rava
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yona and resolution by Rava
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona objects: if a virgin's blood is pure, why does she need bedikot? Perhaps her blood color changed. Rava resolves by distinguishing: one case is where she engaged in intercourse (the act may have discolored the blood), the other where she did not. The Mishnah's statement that a virgin's blood is pure applies only when she did not engage in intercourse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona objects: if a virgin's blood is pure, why does she not need bedikot (examinations)? Perhaps her blood color changed, rendering her impure.

Rava initially answers by reinterpreting the Mishnah: the statement that a virgin's blood is pure applies only to the case of a woman sitting on pure blood, not to all virgins, but then notes the contradiction between the two parts of the Mishnah.

Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: one case is where she engaged in intercourse (the act may have discolored the blood), the other where she did not; the Mishnah's statement that a virgin's blood is pure applies only when she did not engage in intercourse.

items.text: Supporting baraita for the distinction
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for the distinction
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the distinction: the ruling that a virgin's blood is pure applies only when she did not stop bleeding due to intercourse and saw blood not due to intercourse. But if she stopped due to intercourse and saw blood, or passed a night without intercourse and saw blood, or her blood color changed, she is impure.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the supporting evidence, stating that the lenient ruling applies only when she did not stop bleeding due to intercourse and saw blood not due to intercourse.

The baraita lists the three cases where the blood is impure: if she stopped bleeding due to intercourse and then saw blood, if she passed a night without intercourse and saw blood, or if her blood color changed.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on bedikot for the husband vs. terumah
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on bedikot for the husband vs. terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says the Mishnah's requirement of two bedikot applies only for terumah, but for her husband she is permitted without bedikah. The Gemara questions this, noting the Mishnah explicitly says 'shacharit' (morning). It then reinterprets: Shmuel's statement was about the case where she is engaged in handling terumot, so she must check for terumah and consequently for her husband too. The Gemara discusses whether this is novel, given the principle that all women are presumed pure for their husbands, and notes that Shmuel had already said a woman without a fixed cycle must check, but that was qualified to one engaged in terumot.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling that the Mishnah's requirement of two bedikot applies only for terumah, but for her husband she is permitted without bedikah.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'shacharit' (morning), implying the requirement is for her husband as well, so Shmuel's ruling seems obvious and contradictory.

The Gemara reinterprets: Shmuel's statement was actually said about the end of the Mishnah, referring to a woman engaged in handling terumot, so she must check for terumah and consequently for her husband too.
The Gemara questions what novelty Shmuel teaches, given the principle that all women are presumed pure for their husbands.
The Gemara answers that without Shmuel, one might have thought the presumption applies only to a woman with a fixed cycle, but a woman without a fixed cycle requires a bedikah.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah deals with a woman who has a fixed cycle, so Shmuel's novelty is that even such a woman, because she must check for terumah, also checks for her husband.

The Gemara objects that Shmuel already said this once before, citing Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeya's report that Shmuel ruled a woman without a fixed cycle is forbidden until she checks, and that was qualified to one engaged in terumot; the Gemara resolves that one statement was said as part of the other.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Shmuel's distinction
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Shmuel's distinction
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel: the requirement of bedikah applies only for terumot, but for her husband she is permitted. It adds that if she was left in a state of purity, she remains pure; but if left in a state of impurity, she remains impure until she says 'I am pure'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's distinction: the requirement of bedikah applies only for terumot, but for her husband she is permitted; if left in a state of purity she remains pure, but if left in impurity she remains impure until she says 'I am pure'.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Yehuda about self-examination for her husband
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Yehuda about self-examination for her husband
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Yehuda whether a woman may examine herself for her husband's sake before intercourse. Rav Yehuda responds that she should not, because if she does, her husband's heart will strike him and he will separate.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Yehuda whether a woman may examine herself for her husband's sake before intercourse.
Rav Yehuda responds that she should not examine herself, because if she does, her husband's heart will strike him and he will separate.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna about examination for veset shiur
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna about examination for veset shiur
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether a woman may examine herself at the time of her veset shiur to obligate her husband in a chatat offering. Rav Huna responds that such a bedikah is impossible because the veset shiur is defined as the moment the sun sets and the moon rises, which is instantaneous. The Gemara concludes that veset refers to wiping (kinuach), not examination (bedikah), and then asks whether she may wipe.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether a woman may examine herself at the time of her veset shiur (fixed cycle interval) in order to obligate her husband to bring a chatat (sin-offering).
Rav Huna responds that such a bedikah (examination) is impossible because the veset shiur is defined as an instantaneous moment, like the sun setting and the moon rising simultaneously.
The Gemara concludes that the term veset (fixed cycle) in this context refers to kinuach (wiping), not bedikah (examination).
The Gemara then asks whether a woman may wipe herself at that moment.

items.text: Alternative version: examination to obligate an asham taluy
items.text_en: Alternative version: examination to obligate an asham taluy
items.desc_en: Some say the inquiry was about examination to obligate her husband in an asham taluy. The answer is the same: she should not examine, because it would cause him to separate.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Abba's question
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Abba's question
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rabbi Abba asked whether a woman may examine herself to obligate her husband to bring a conditional guilt-offering (אשם תלוי).
Rav Huna responds that she should not examine herself, because her husband's heart will strike him and he will separate.

items.text: The time of passing and the dispute about 'tzenuot'
items.text_en: The time of passing and the dispute about 'tzenuot'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions the time when she passes. Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Yannai says this is the time of modest women (tzenuot). Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects that the Tanna teaches 'tzerichot' (needy ones), not 'tzenuot'. Rabbi Ami explains that anyone who fulfills the words of the Sages is called modest. Rava then clarifies that one who does not fulfill them is not called wicked, and reinterprets: modest women examine themselves before this intercourse but not before another, while immodest women examine without concern.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase about the time when she passes.
Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yannai identifies this time as the period of modest women (צנועות).
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects that the Tanna teaches 'צריכות' (needy ones), not 'צנועות' (modest ones).
Rabbi Ami explains that anyone who fulfills the words of the Sages is called modest (צנוע).
Rava objects that one who does not fulfill the Sages' words is not called wicked (רשע), only not called modest.
Rava reinterprets: modest women examine themselves before this intercourse but not before another, while immodest women examine without concern.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on women without a veset and the distinction between awake and asleep
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on women without a veset and the distinction between awake and asleep
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Shmuel that a woman without a veset is forbidden to have intercourse until she examines herself. Rabbi Zeira asks whether a woman with a veset does not need examination. Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeyah answers that a woman with a veset who is awake needs examination, but if asleep does not; one without a veset always needs examination. Rava notes that Shmuel could have distinguished between taharot and ba'al, implying Shmuel holds that for ba'al no examination is needed at all.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites Shmuel's ruling that a woman without a veset (fixed menstrual cycle) is forbidden to have intercourse until she examines herself.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeyah: if a woman without a veset requires examination, does a woman with a veset not require examination?
Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeyah answers that a woman with a veset who is awake needs examination, but if asleep does not; one without a veset always needs examination.
Rava objects that Shmuel could have distinguished between taharot (ritually pure foods) and ba'al (intercourse), implying that for ba'al no examination is needed at all.
The Gemara infers from Shmuel's failure to make that distinction that Shmuel holds that for ba'al (intercourse) no examination is needed at all.

items.text: The baraita about donkey drivers and workers, and its reconciliation with Shmuel
items.text_en: The baraita about donkey drivers and workers, and its reconciliation with Shmuel
items.desc_en: A baraita states that donkey drivers and workers, and those returning from mourning or feasting, may assume their wives are pure, whether asleep or awake. The Gemara asks how Shmuel reconciles this: if she has a veset, the case of an awake woman is difficult; if she has no veset, both cases are difficult. The answer is that she has a veset, and since he requested her, there is no greater examination than this. Rav Pappa then asks Rava whether one may act according to this baraita.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that donkey drivers, workers, and those returning from mourning or feasting may assume their wives are pure, whether asleep or awake, unless they left them in a state of impurity.
The Gemara asks how Shmuel reconciles this baraita with his ruling: if she has a veset, the case of an awake woman is difficult; if she has no veset, both cases are difficult.
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a woman who has a veset, and since the husband requested her, there is no greater examination than this.
Rav Pappa asks Rava whether one may act according to this baraita.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry about bedikah practice
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry about bedikah practice
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks the household members of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna whether the rabbis from the house of Rav required bedikah, and they answer no. The Gemara questions why not ask them directly, suggesting they may be stringent on themselves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks the household members of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna whether the rabbis from the house of Rav required bedikah, and they answer no.
The Gemara objects that Rav Kahana should have asked the rabbis directly, and suggests that the household members may have been stringent on themselves.

items.text: Baraita: Three opinions on a woman without a fixed cycle
items.text_en: Baraita: Three opinions on a woman without a fixed cycle
items.desc_en: The baraita presents three views: Rabbi Meir says she is forbidden to have intercourse and loses all ketubah rights; Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus says she may use two cloths to check; and Abba Chanan says woe to her husband.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the first opinion: Rabbi Meir rules that a woman without a fixed cycle is forbidden to have intercourse and loses all ketubah rights.
Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus presents the second opinion: she may use two cloths to check, which either expose her or correct her.
Abba Chanan adds a third opinion: woe to her husband, implying the situation is dire.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Meir's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Meir's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: she is forbidden lest she cause a stain; she has no ketubah because she is unfit for intercourse; other ketubah conditions are like the ketubah itself; and the divorce is permanent even if she later becomes fixed, to prevent retroactive nullification and mamzerim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's first two rulings: she is forbidden to have intercourse lest she cause a stain, and she has no ketubah because she is unfit for intercourse.
The Gemara explains that the additional conditions of the ketubah (fruit, sustenance, worn garments) are treated like the ketubah itself, so she also loses them.
The Gemara asks why it is obvious that he must divorce her permanently, and answers that the ruling is needed even if she later becomes fixed.
The Gemara explains that the permanent divorce prevents a scenario where she remarries, becomes fixed, and then retroactively nullifies the get, producing mamzerim.

items.text: Two interpretations of Abba Chanan's statement
items.text_en: Two interpretations of Abba Chanan's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two possibilities for Abba Chanan's 'woe to her husband': either he said it to Rabbi Meir, who wants to collect her ketubah, or to Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, because she might cause a stain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the statement of Abba Chanan: 'Woe to her husband.'
One interpretation suggests that Abba Chanan said 'woe to her husband' to Rabbi Meir, who seeks to collect her ketubah.
Another interpretation suggests that Abba Chanan said it to Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, because she might cause a stain.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: halakhah like Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, and a contradiction resolved
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: halakhah like Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, and a contradiction resolved
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says Shmuel rules like Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus. The Gemara questions this: if she is engaged in taharot, Shmuel already said she needs bedikah; if not, Shmuel said she does not need bedikah. The Gemara resolves that the two statements refer to different cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel rules the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus.
The Gemara asks: in which case does Shmuel's ruling apply? If she is engaged in טהרות (ritually pure foods), Shmuel already stated the law once.
If she is not engaged in טהרות, Shmuel already said she does not need בדיקה (examination) for her husband.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeya citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeya citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a tradition that Shmuel ruled a woman without a fixed cycle is forbidden to have relations until she performs a בדיקה (examination).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the two statements of Shmuel are transmitted by different tradents — one who teaches this ruling does not teach that one.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any hand that frequently checks women is praiseworthy, but for men, it should be cut off.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the distinction between men and women, explaining that women are not prone to arousal from touch, while men are. It clarifies that the Mishnah's emphasis on 'frequent' applies only to men, and a baraita adds that this applies only to checking for semen, but for זוב, it is praiseworthy for men as well.

items.text: Exception for checking with a shard or cloth
items.text_en: Exception for checking with a shard or cloth
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even for semen, one may check with a shard or potsherd, and questions whether a cloth is permitted. It cites a baraita allowing any material, and Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a thick cloth (permitted) and a thin one (prohibited).

items.text: Debate on holding the penis while urinating
items.text_en: Debate on holding the penis while urinating
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one feels arousal while eating terumah and must hold his penis to avoid emission. It cites Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that holding the penis is like bringing a flood, but Abaye permits it with a thick cloth. Rava argues that even a thin cloth is permitted once arousal has passed, and defends against an objection about repeated stimulation.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's debate with the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's debate with the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that holding the penis while urinating is like bringing a flood. The Sages object that not holding it causes splashing and slander about his children being mamzerim. Rabbi Eliezer responds that it is better to suffer slander than to sin. The Gemara clarifies the order of his statements: he first offered a solution (high place or soft earth), and only when that was unavailable did he say to suffer slander.

items.text: Severity of wasting seed
items.text_en: Severity of wasting seed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason for the strictness: wasting seed is a grave sin. Rabbi Yochanan says it is punishable by death, Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Ami compare it to bloodshed, and Rav Asi compares it to idolatry, each citing verses.

items.text: Samuel's ruling and its justification
items.text_en: Samuel's ruling and its justification
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Yehuda and Samuel were on a roof, and Samuel told Rav Yehuda to hold his penis and urinate outside. The Gemara questions this against Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and offers multiple answers: Abaye says Samuel treated it as a pressing need (like a bolshet), and various explanations are given for the fear that prevented arousal (night, roof, teacher, Shechinah, Samuel's awe, being married, or supporting the testicles from below).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that touching from the crown (corona) and above is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that touching from the corona and above is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara on the severity of masturbation and sinful thoughts
items.text_en: Gemara on the severity of masturbation and sinful thoughts
items.desc_en: Rav says one who intentionally causes an erection should be excommunicated; Rabbi Ami calls such a person a transgressor. Rabbi Ami also says one who brings himself to sinful thoughts is not admitted into God's presence. Rabbi Elazar and the school of Rabbi Yishmael interpret verses to include manual and foot adultery.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that one who intentionally causes an erection should be excommunicated, and the Gemara explains why he did not simply say 'forbidden' — because it provokes the evil inclination.
Rabbi Ami says such a person is called a 'transgressor' because the evil inclination's pattern leads from minor sins to idolatry.
Rabbi Ami says one who brings himself to sinful thoughts is not admitted into God's presence, citing verses about evil not dwelling with God.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse 'your hands are full of blood' as referring to those who commit adultery with the hand.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets the commandment 'do not commit adultery' to include adultery by hand or by foot.

items.text: Converts and those who play with children delay the Messiah
items.text_en: Converts and those who play with children delay the Messiah
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that converts and those who play with children delay the Messiah. The Gemara explains that converts are difficult like a scab, and 'playing with children' refers to marrying young girls who cannot bear children, as Rabbi Yose says the son of David will not come until all souls in the body are exhausted.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that converts and those who play with children delay the coming of the Messiah.
The Gemara asks: Converts are understandable per Rabbi Helbo's teaching, but what does 'playing with children' mean?
Rabbi Helbo said that converts are as difficult for Israel as a scab (a skin affliction).
The Gemara objects: If 'playing with children' means homosexual intercourse, they are liable for stoning; if it means masturbation, they are liable for the flood generation's punishment.
Rather, it refers to those who marry young girls who cannot bear children, as Rabbi Yose said the son of David will not come until all souls in the body are exhausted.

Rabbi Yose said that the Messiah will not come until all the souls in the body (the treasury of souls) are exhausted, as the verse says 'For the spirit from before Me will be exhausted, and souls I have made.'

items.text: The debate on whether 'let the hand be cut off' is a law or a curse
items.text_en: The debate on whether 'let the hand be cut off' is a law or a curse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the statement 'let the hand be cut off' is a halakhic ruling or a curse. It brings a baraita where Rabbi Tarfon says one who puts his hand below his navel should have it cut off, and the Sages object. The Gemara concludes it is a law, not a curse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does the mishna's statement 'let the hand be cut off' teach a practical halakha or a mere curse?
The Gemara elaborates on the two possibilities: either it is a practical halakha like Rav Huna who actually cut off a hand, or it is a curse.
The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Tarfon says that if one's hand goes to his penis, it should be severed upon his navel, and he defends this ruling against the Sages' objection.

The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if it is a practical halakha, the Sages' objection about the belly splitting makes sense; if it is a curse, the objection is meaningless. It then questions why the hand must be cut off specifically upon the navel.

The Gemara reinterprets Rabbi Tarfon's statement: anyone who inserts his hand below his navel should have it cut off, and the Sages' objection about a thorn is answered with the principle that it is better to suffer physical harm than to descend to the pit of destruction.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on deaf, insane, and blind women regarding terumah
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on deaf, insane, and blind women regarding terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a deaf, insane, or blind woman, or one whose mind is disturbed, if they have sane women, they prepare them and they eat terumah. The Gemara questions why a deaf woman cannot check herself, and distinguishes between one who cannot speak and one who cannot hear. For a blind woman, Rabbi Yose bar Chanina says she is not a Mishnah (i.e., she cannot check). The Gemara clarifies that 'one whose mind is disturbed' is due to illness, not insanity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a deaf, insane, or blind woman, or one whose mind is disturbed, if they have sane women, they prepare them and they eat terumah.
The Gemara questions why a deaf woman cannot check herself, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said a deaf woman in his neighborhood was so proficient she even helped her friends.
The Gemara distinguishes: there the deaf woman could speak but not hear, while here the mishna refers to a deaf-mute who can neither speak nor hear.
The Gemara asks why a blind woman cannot check herself and show the cloth to her friend.
Rabbi Yose bar Chanina says that the correct version of the mishna does not mention a blind woman.
The Gemara asks why the mishna separately mentions a woman whose mind is disturbed, as that seems to be the same as an imbecile.
The Gemara clarifies that this refers to a woman who went insane due to illness, which is a different category from an imbecile.

items.text: The case of a mad priest and the protective covering
items.text_en: The case of a mad priest and the protective covering
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that a mad priest is immersed and fed terumah in the evening, and guarded from sleeping. Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok says to make a leather pouch for him, but the Sages object that it might cause heat. Another version says to make a metal pouch, and Abaye specifies copper, citing Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that a mad priest is immersed, fed terumah in the evening, and guarded from sleeping, with the consequence that if he slept he is impure, if not he is pure.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok proposes making a leather pouch for the mad priest, but the Sages object that it might cause heat, and he retorts that according to them a mad person has no remedy.
The Sages counter that according to their view the status is clear, but according to his view a tiny drop might be seen and then absorbed in the pouch, causing uncertainty.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught in the name of Rabbi Elazar that they make a metal pouch instead of leather.
Abaye specifies that the pouch should be of copper, citing Rabbi Yehuda who compares the hyssop stalks to copper.

items.text: Discussion on trousers and the priestly undergarments
items.text_en: Discussion on trousers and the priestly undergarments
items.desc_en: Rav Papa infers that trousers are forbidden, but the Gemara objects with the verse about priestly breeches. It explains that the priestly breeches were like horse riders' trousers, with openings but no place for the genitals. Abaye adds a final comment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa infers that trousers are forbidden, citing the verse about priestly breeches.
The Gemara explains that priestly breeches were like horse riders' trousers, with openings but no place for the genitals.
Abaye begins a final comment, but the text cuts off at the section boundary.

items.text: Camel riders and terumah
items.text_en: Camel riders and terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that camel riders are all wicked, sailors are all righteous, and donkey drivers are mixed. Two explanations are given for the distinction among donkey drivers: one based on whether they use a saddle, and another based on whether they jostle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita classifying camel riders as all wicked, sailors as all righteous, and donkey drivers as mixed.
One explanation distinguishes donkey drivers based on whether they use a saddle (מכף) or not.
Another explanation distinguishes donkey drivers based on whether they jostle (מטרטין) or not.

items.text: Sleeping on one's stomach
items.text_en: Sleeping on one's stomach
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi curses one who sleeps on his stomach. The Gemara questions this based on Rav Yosef's statement that a prone person should not recite Shema, implying sleeping is fine. It resolves that for sleeping it is permitted, but for Shema it is prohibited, and Rabbi Yochanan is an exception because he was fleshy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi curses one who sleeps on his stomach.
The Gemara questions the curse, citing Rav Yosef's statement that a prone person should not recite Shema, implying sleeping in that position is fine.
The Gemara resolves that sleeping on one's stomach is permitted, but reciting Shema in that position is prohibited, and Rabbi Yochanan is an exception because he was fleshy.

items.text: Mishnah: Examination cloths
items.text_en: Mishnah: Examination cloths
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the practice of using two cloths for examination, one for the husband and one for the wife, with modest women adding a third. It details the rules of impurity and sacrifice when blood is found on each cloth, and defines 'after a time' as the interval to wash her face. Rabbi Akiva adds that she also renders her husband impure, and the Sages agree regarding a stain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the standard practice of using two examination cloths, one for the husband and one for the wife, with modest women adding a third to prepare the home.

The Mishnah states the impurity and sacrifice rules: if blood is found on the husband's cloth or on the wife's cloth immediately, both are impure and liable for a sacrifice; if found on her cloth after a time, they are impure due to doubt but exempt from sacrifice.
The Mishnah defines 'after a time' as the interval to wash her face, and adds that she then renders things impure retroactively for a day but does not render her husband impure.
Rabbi Akiva adds that she also renders her husband impure.
The Sages agree with Rabbi Akiva regarding a stain (כתם) that she renders her husband impure.

items.text: Gemara: Concern for blood from a wound
items.text_en: Gemara: Concern for blood from a wound
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the blood might be from a wound. Rabbi Zeira answers that the place is checked regarding wounds, or alternatively that it is pressed against wounds. The difference between these versions is if a wound is found adjacent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the blood found might be from a wound (מאכלת) rather than menstrual blood.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the place (the vagina) is checked regarding wounds, meaning it is known to be free of wounds.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Zeira's answer
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Zeira's answer
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that the place is pressed against wounds, meaning the vaginal walls are tight and would not allow a wound to bleed freely.

items.text: Blood on a checked cloth
items.text_en: Blood on a checked cloth
items.desc_en: A case is presented where a woman checked with a cloth that was checked for her, placed it on her thigh, and found blood the next day. Rav rules she is a niddah, and Rav Shimi bar Chiyya questions this because Rav had previously said she is 'suspected'. Shmuel and the study hall also rule she is a niddah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a woman checked with a cloth that was checked for her, placed it on her thigh, and found blood the next day.
Rav rules that the woman is a niddah (ritually impure).
Rav Shimi bar Chiyya objects that Rav had previously taught them the woman is only 'suspected' (חוֹשֶׁשֶׁת), not definitively impure.

sub.text: Supporting statement from Shmuel and the study hall
sub.text_en: Supporting statement from Shmuel and the study hall
sub.desc_en: Shmuel and the study hall also rule that the woman is a niddah, supporting Rav's position.

items.text: Blood on an unchecked cloth
items.text_en: Blood on an unchecked cloth
items.desc_en: A case is presented where a woman checked with an unchecked cloth and placed it in a box, finding blood the next day. Rav Yosef reports that Rabbi Chiyya initially ruled impure and later pure. A dilemma arises about whether he changed from niddah to ketem or from ketem to nothing. A baraita resolves it: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says impure as niddah, Rabbi Chiyya says impure as ketem.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a woman checked with an unchecked cloth and placed it in a box, finding blood the next day.
Rav Yosef reports that Rabbi Chiyya initially ruled impure and later ruled pure.
