The gemara raises a dilemma about the meaning of Rabbi Chiyya's change: whether he initially ruled impure as a niddah and later ruled pure as a niddah but impure as a ketem.
The gemara presents the alternative possibility: that Rabbi Chiyya initially ruled impure as a ketem and later ruled pure entirely.
A baraita is cited to resolve the dilemma: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules impure as a niddah, while Rabbi Chiyya rules impure as a ketem.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's challenge and Rabbi's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's challenge and Rabbi's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya challenges Rabbi's position by noting that if a stain requires a k'gris v'od (a bean-sized amount plus a bit), then Rabbi himself treats it as a כתם. The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds that the requirement of k'gris v'od excludes blood from meat, and since it is not from meat, it must come from her body, making her a Niddah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya challenges Rabbi: if a stain requires a k'gris v'od (a bean-sized amount plus a bit), then Rabbi himself treats it as a כתם (stain).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds the requirement of k'gris v'od excludes blood from meat, so since it is not from meat, it must come from her body, making her a Niddah.

items.text: Inference about Rabbi's youth vs. old age
items.text_en: Inference about Rabbi's youth vs. old age
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the previous statement refers to Rabbi in his old age, implying that in his youth he ruled that the stain renders her a Niddah. The Gemara concludes that this is conclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the previous statement refers to Rabbi in his old age, implying that in his youth he ruled that the stain renders her a Niddah.
The Gemara concludes that this inference is conclusive.

items.text: Story of Rabbi, Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabbi Chama bar Bisa
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi, Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabbi Chama bar Bisa
items.desc_en: Rabbi praises Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei as a great man. When he arrives, Rabbi Yishmael asks him a halakhic question about a woman who examined with an unchecked cloth and later found blood. Rabbi Yishmael offers to answer either like his father or like Rabbi. Rabbi chooses Rabbi's view, but Rabbi Yishmael criticizes him for abandoning the teacher's view for the student's. The Gemara explains Rabbi Chama bar Bisa's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi praises Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei as a great man and asks to bring Rabbi Chama bar Bisa to him.
Rabbi Chama bar Bisa asks Rabbi Yishmael about a woman who examined with an unchecked cloth and later found blood.
Rabbi Yishmael offers to answer either like his father Rabbi Yosei or like Rabbi, and Rabbi Chama chooses Rabbi's view.
Rabbi Yishmael criticizes Rabbi Chama for abandoning the teacher's (Rabbi Yosei's) view for the student's (Rabbi's).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chama bar Bisa reasoned that Rabbi, as head of the academy, had sharper halachic reasoning due to frequent engagement with the sages.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei explained via Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei explained via Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the positions of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei regarding blood found after urination. Rabbi Zeira explains that when Rabbi ruled impure, he followed Rabbi Meir, and when Rabbi Yosei ruled pure, he ruled for himself. A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir distinguishes between standing (impure) and sitting (pure), while Rabbi Yosei rules pure in both cases. Rav Acha bar Rava challenges that Rabbi Meir's impurity was due to a כתם, not Niddah, but Rav Ashi resolves that the statement was made regarding Niddah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei regarding blood found after urination?
Rav Adda bar Masna cites a baraita: Rabbi declares impure, Rabbi Yosei declares pure.
Rabbi Zeira explains: When Rabbi ruled impure, he followed Rabbi Meir; when Rabbi Yosei ruled pure, he ruled for himself.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir distinguishes between standing (impure) and sitting (pure), while Rabbi Yosei rules pure in both cases.
Rav Acha bar Rava objects: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said Rabbi Meir's impurity was due to a כתם (stain), not Niddah, but Rabbi's ruling was about Niddah.
Rav Ashi resolves: The statement about Rabbi Meir's impurity was made regarding Niddah, not a stain.

items.text: Definition of a fixed period (וסת) for wiping
items.text_en: Definition of a fixed period (וסת) for wiping
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita defining the measure of a וסת: like a servant and a witness standing at the threshold, when the sun sets the witness enters. This applies to wiping (קינוח), not to examination (בדיקה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that defines the measure of a fixed period (וסת) through a parable of a servant and a witness at the threshold.
The Gemara clarifies that this fixed period (וסת) applies to wiping (קינוח), not to examination (בדיקה).

items.text: Liability for a provisional guilt-offering and the need for two pieces
items.text_en: Liability for a provisional guilt-offering and the need for two pieces
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for finding blood 'after a time', one is liable for a provisional guilt-offering (אשם תלוי). It questions why our Tanna does not mention this, and answers that we require a piece from two pieces (i.e., a definite doubt).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for finding blood 'after a time', one is liable for a provisional guilt-offering (אשם תלוי).
The Gemara asks why our Tanna (in the Mishnah) does not mention this liability.
The Gemara answers that a provisional guilt-offering requires a definite doubt (a piece from two pieces), which is not the case here.

items.text: Defining 'after a time' – dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the Mishnah
items.text_en: Defining 'after a time' – dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines 'after a time' as enough time to lower herself from the bed and wash her face. A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok defining it as enough time to reach under the pillow, take a cloth, and examine. Rav Chisda explains 'after' means 'after after'. The Gemara reconciles: the baraita refers to a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages. Rav Ashi says both measures are the same: if the cloth is in hand, it's the time to get down and wash; if not, it's the time to reach and take it. A challenge is raised from a question Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok asked the Sages in Usha.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines 'after a time' as enough time to get down from the bed and wash her face; a baraita cites Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok defining it as enough time to reach under the pillow, take a cloth, and examine.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's definition and Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's definition.
Rav Chisda explains that 'after' in the baraita means 'after after' (a later time), resolving the contradiction by distinguishing the two measures.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly states 'after a time' with the same wording as the baraita, undermining Rav Chisda's distinction.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita actually refers to a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages, not a separate definition.
The Gemara objects that the baraita uses the term 'after that' (אחר כך), not 'after a time' (אחר זמן), challenging the resolution.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita means 'this is the 'after that' about which Rabbi Akiva and the Sages disputed.'
Rav Ashi says both measures are the same: if the cloth is in hand, it's the time to get down and wash; if not, it's the time to reach and take it.
A challenge is raised from a question Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok asked the Sages in Usha, which seems to contradict Rav Ashi's reconciliation.

items.text: The ruling of the Sages in Yavneh regarding a woman who did not wait
items.text_en: The ruling of the Sages in Yavneh regarding a woman who did not wait
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that the Sages in Yavneh ruled that if a woman did not wait long enough to wash her face after intercourse, the couple is impure with uncertainty, exempt from a fixed sin-offering but liable for a suspensive guilt-offering. If she waited that long, it is considered after the fact. The same applies when she waited from one time to the next or from one examination to the next, with Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda offering differing opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the Sages whether they follow Rabbi Akiva's view that a woman who did not wait renders her husband impure.
The Sages in Yavneh rule that if a woman did not wait long enough to wash her face, the couple is impure with uncertainty, exempt from a fixed sin-offering but liable for a suspensive guilt-offering.
The Sages add that if she waited that long, it is considered after the fact.

The Sages generalize the ruling to cases of waiting from one time to the next, with Rabbi Akiva adding impurity as a בעל (husband) and Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai stating the husband may enter the Temple and burn incense.

items.text: Question on Rav Ashi's position
items.text_en: Question on Rav Ashi's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rav Chisda, it is understandable why the Rabbis declare the woman pure, but according to Rav Ashi, why do they declare her pure? If one suggests it is because she has no witness in her hand, the Gemara objects that the distinction between having a witness and not having one is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that according to Rav Chisda, the Rabbis' ruling of purity is understandable.
The Gemara questions why the Rabbis declare the woman pure according to Rav Ashi's position.
The Gemara objects that the suggested distinction between having a witness and not having one is already needed elsewhere, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Defense of Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Defense of Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's statement that the husband may enter the Temple and offer incense, asking why he is not considered impure as one who touched a woman who had a discharge from one time to the next. The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda follows Shammai, who says all women suffice with their time. Another question arises that he might be a ba'al keri, and the Gemara answers that he did not complete his intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda's husband is not considered impure as one who touched a woman who had a discharge from one time to the next.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda follows Shammai, who says all women suffice with their time, so the husband is not retroactively impure.
The Gemara raises another objection: the husband might be a ba'al keri (one who emitted semen) and thus impure.
The Gemara answers that the case is where he did not complete his intercourse, so he is not a ba'al keri.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a stain
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a stain
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Sages agree with Rabbi Akiva regarding a woman who sees a stain. Rav says this applies retroactively, and it is the opinion of Rabbi Meir. Shmuel says it applies from now onward, and it is the opinion of the Rabbis. The Gemara questions why Shmuel's statement is not obvious, and explains that one might have thought that since both the law of 'from one time to the next' and stains are rabbinic, the stain should not render her husband impure retroactively, but the Gemara teaches that it does, because there is a 'slaughtered ox before you' (a clear sign of impurity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Sages agree with Rabbi Akiva regarding a woman who sees a stain.
Rav says the stain renders her husband impure retroactively, and this is the opinion of Rabbi Meir.
Shmuel says the stain renders her husband impure from now onward, and this is the opinion of the Rabbis.
The Gemara questions why Shmuel's statement is not obvious.

The Gemara explains that one might have thought that since both the law of 'from one time to the next' and stains are rabbinic, the stain should not render her husband impure retroactively, but the Gemara teaches that it does.
The Gemara objects: why not say that the stain should indeed not render her husband impure retroactively?
The Gemara resolves that in the case of 'from one time to the next' there is no clear sign of impurity, but here there is a 'slaughtered ox before you' (a clear sign of impurity).

items.text: Reiteration of the dispute by Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Reiteration of the dispute by Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says the ruling applies retroactively, following Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yochanan says it applies from now onward, following the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the ruling applies retroactively (למפרע), aligning with Rabbi Meir's position.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the ruling applies from now onward (מכאן ולהבא), aligning with the Rabbis' position.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the presumption of purity for wives of travelers
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the presumption of purity for wives of travelers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all women are presumed pure for their husbands, and those coming from a journey find their wives presumed pure. The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'those coming from a journey', and explains that one might have thought the presumption applies only when the husband is in town, as the wife is concerned and checks herself, but when he is away she is not concerned, so the Mishnah teaches that she is still presumed pure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all women are presumed pure for their husbands, and those coming from a journey find their wives presumed pure.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'those coming from a journey'.

The Gemara explains that one might have thought the presumption applies only when the husband is in town, as the wife is concerned and checks herself, but when he is away she is not concerned, so the Mishnah teaches that she is still presumed pure.

items.text: Dispute about the presumption when the husband finds her within her expected period
items.text_en: Dispute about the presumption when the husband finds her within her expected period
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a says the presumption applies only if he finds her within her expected period. Rav Huna initially says it applies only if she has no fixed cycle, but the Gemara objects and corrects him to say it applies only if her expected time has not arrived, as he holds that fixed cycles are biblical. Rabba bar bar Chana permits even if her time has arrived, as he holds fixed cycles are rabbinic. Rav Ashi teaches this version.

sub.text: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a states that the presumption of purity for a husband returning from a journey applies only if he finds his wife within her expected period.
Rav Huna initially says the mishna's presumption applies only to a woman without a fixed cycle, but one with a fixed cycle is forbidden to her husband.
The Gemara objects that the opposite seems more logical: a woman without a fixed cycle is suspect, while one with a fixed cycle is presumed pure.

sub.text: Corrected version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.text_en: Corrected version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara corrects Rav Huna's statement: the presumption applies only if her expected time has not arrived; if it has arrived she is forbidden, because Rav Huna holds that fixed cycles are biblical.
Rabba bar bar Chana says even if her expected time has arrived she is permitted, because he holds that fixed cycles are rabbinic.
Rav Ashi teaches the corrected version of Rav Huna's statement, introducing the dispute as transmitted.

items.text: First opinion: woman with a fixed cycle is forbidden
items.text_en: First opinion: woman with a fixed cycle is forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when she has no fixed cycle for days; if she has a fixed cycle for days, she is forbidden to have intercourse, because the presumption of a fixed cycle is biblical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when a woman has no fixed cycle for days; if she has a fixed cycle for days, she is forbidden to have intercourse.
The Gemara explains that this opinion holds that the presumption of a fixed cycle (וסתות) is biblical in origin.

items.text: Second opinion: woman with a fixed cycle is permitted
items.text_en: Second opinion: woman with a fixed cycle is permitted
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah argues that even if she has a fixed cycle for days, she is permitted, because the presumption of a fixed cycle is rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah argues that even a woman with a fixed cycle for days is permitted, because the presumption of a fixed cycle (וסתות) is rabbinic (דרבנן).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: husband calculates her cycle
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: husband calculates her cycle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a woman with a fixed cycle is permitted; her husband calculates her expected cycle days and may have intercourse on them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a woman with a fixed cycle is permitted; her husband calculates her expected cycle days and may have intercourse on them.

items.text: Question about a young girl and the certainty-uncertainty principle
items.text_en: Question about a young girl and the certainty-uncertainty principle
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yeiva asks Rabbi Abba whether Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies even to a young girl who is hesitant to immerse. Rabbi Abba clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan only spoke of a case of uncertainty, not when she definitely saw blood, because uncertainty cannot override certainty.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yeiva's question to Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yeiva's question to Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yeiva asks Rabbi Abba whether Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies even to a young girl who is hesitant to immerse.
Rabbi Abba clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan only spoke of a case of uncertainty, not when she definitely saw blood, because uncertainty cannot override certainty.

items.text: First challenge: case of a colleague's produce
items.text_en: First challenge: case of a colleague's produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty with a baraita about a colleague who died leaving a storehouse of produce, which is presumed tithed even though it was certainly untithed. The Gemara answers that this is a case of certainty versus certainty, based on the presumption that a colleague does not release untithed produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty by citing a baraita about a colleague who died leaving a storehouse of produce, which is presumed tithed even though it was certainly untithed.
The Gemara answers that this is a case of certainty versus certainty, based on the presumption (חזקה) that a colleague does not release untithed produce from his hand.

items.text: Alternative answer: case of uncertainty versus uncertainty
items.text_en: Alternative answer: case of uncertainty versus uncertainty
items.desc_en: Alternatively, the Gemara answers that the case of the colleague's produce is actually uncertainty versus uncertainty, based on Rabbi Oshaya's ruling that one can circumvent tithing by feeding produce to his animal while it is still in the chaff.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the case of the colleague's produce is actually a case of uncertainty versus uncertainty, citing Rabbi Oshaya's ruling that one can circumvent tithing by feeding produce to his animal while it is still in the chaff.

items.text: Second challenge: case of the maidservant's miscarriage
items.text_en: Second challenge: case of the maidservant's miscarriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle again with a story of a maidservant who miscarried into a pit, and the Sages ruled the fetus pure because a weasel or lizard might have dragged it away. Here, certainty (the miscarriage) is overridden by uncertainty (whether it was dragged).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty by citing a baraita about a maidservant who miscarried into a pit.
The baraita reports that the Sages ruled the fetus pure because a weasel or lizard might have dragged it away.
The Gemara objects that here certainty (the miscarriage) is overridden by uncertainty (whether it was dragged), contradicting the principle.

items.text: Resolution: reinterpretation of the case
items.text_en: Resolution: reinterpretation of the case
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by reinterpreting the story: the maidservant did not definitely miscarry into the pit; rather, she was suspected of having miscarried, so it is a case of uncertainty versus uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by reinterpreting the story: the maidservant did not definitely miscarry into the pit; rather, she was suspected of having miscarried, so it is a case of uncertainty versus uncertainty.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'to know if it is a male or female', given the context of a miscarried fetus. It reinterprets the Mishnah: the priest first examines to determine if it is a miscarriage or a wind, and if it is a miscarriage, then to know the gender. Alternatively, since weasels and martens are common there, they surely dragged it away.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: a woman miscarried something like a fetus (נפל).
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'to know if it is a male or female' when the context is a miscarried fetus that may not be identifiable.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: the priest first examines to determine if it is a miscarriage or a wind, and if it is a miscarriage, then to know the gender.
An alternative answer: since weasels and martens are common there, they surely dragged the miscarried fetus away, so the Mishnah's phrase is irrelevant.

items.text: Are vesatot biblical or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Are vesatot biblical or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: The students asked Rav Nachman whether the laws of fixed cycles (vesatot) are biblical or rabbinic. He replied with a proof from Rav Huna's statement that a woman who has a fixed cycle and did not check at its time but later saw blood is concerned for both her cycle and her sight, implying vesatot are biblical. Another version says he argued the opposite: since she is only concerned if she actually saw blood, vesatot are rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rav Nachman whether the laws of fixed cycles (vesatot) are biblical (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא) or rabbinic (דְרַבָּנַן).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's first answer (citing Rav Huna)
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's first answer (citing Rav Huna)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Rav Huna's statement that a woman with a fixed cycle who did not check at its time but later saw blood is concerned for both her cycle and her sight, proving that vesatot are biblical.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's answer
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's answer
sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Rav Nachman argued the opposite: since she is only concerned if she actually saw blood, vesatot are rabbinic.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute on vesatot
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute on vesatot
items.desc_en: It was stated: A woman with a fixed cycle who did not check at its time but later checked. Rav says: if she checked and found herself impure, she is impure; if pure, she is pure. Shmuel says: even if she checked and found herself pure, she is impure, because the time itself brings the discharge. The Gemara suggests they dispute whether vesatot are biblical or rabbinic. Rabbi Zeira resolves: everyone agrees vesatot are biblical; the dispute is whether she checked within the time of the cycle or not.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states: A woman with a fixed cycle who did not check at its time but later checked.
Rav rules: if she checked and found herself impure, she is impure; if pure, she is pure.
Shmuel rules: even if she checked and found herself pure, she is impure, because the time itself brings the discharge.
The gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel dispute whether vesatot (fixed cycles) are biblical or rabbinic.
Rabbi Zeira resolves: everyone agrees vesatot are biblical; the dispute is whether she checked within the time of the cycle or not.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's view
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's view
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says that Rav and Shmuel actually dispute the very status of vesatot: one holds they are biblical, the other rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that Rav and Shmuel actually dispute the status of וסתות (menstrual cycles): one holds they are biblical, the other rabbinic.

items.text: Support from Tannaitic disputes
items.text_en: Support from Tannaitic disputes
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet connects the dispute to Tannaim: Rabbi Eliezer says she is impure as a niddah, Rabbi Yehoshua says she must be examined. Similarly, Rabbi Meir says impure, and the Sages say she must be examined. Abaye adds support from a Mishnah: if she was in hiding and her cycle time came without checking, she is pure because fear suppresses blood; implying that without fear she would be impure, showing vesatot are biblical.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet opens by linking the dispute about vesatot to a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer declares her impure as a niddah.
Rav Sheshet cites Rabbi Yehoshua's position that she must be examined, and parallels it with a baraita where Rabbi Meir says impure and the Sages say she must be examined.

Abaye adds support from a Mishnah: if she was in hiding and her cycle time came without checking, she is pure because fear suppresses blood; implying that without fear she would be impure, showing vesatot are biblical.

items.text: Dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the Tannaim in a baraita also dispute about vesatot. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a woman who sees blood due to a wound is pure even within her niddah days; Rabbi says if she has a fixed cycle, she is concerned for her cycle. Ravina explains: all agree vesatot are rabbinic; they dispute whether the source (makor) is impure in its place. Rabban Shimon holds the woman is pure but the blood is impure; Rabbi argues that if you are concerned for the cycle, the woman is also impure, otherwise the source is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Tannaim in the baraita about a woman seeing blood due to a wound also dispute about the nature of vesatot (fixed cycles).
Rabbi states that if a woman has a fixed cycle, she is concerned for her cycle even if the blood came from a wound.
The Gemara infers that the dispute is about whether vesatot are de-oraita (Torah law) or de-rabbanan (rabbinic).
Ravina rejects the inference, explaining that all agree vesatot are rabbinic, and the dispute is about whether the source (מקור) is impure in its place.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the woman is pure but the blood is impure because it comes through the source (מקור).
Rabbi argues that if one is concerned for the cycle, the woman is also impure; otherwise, the source (מקור) is pure in its place.

items.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on witnesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: Beit Shammai say a woman needs two witnesses for each act of intercourse, or she may use a lamp. Beit Hillel say it is sufficient to have two witnesses for the entire night.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Beit Shammai require two witnesses for each act of intercourse or use of a lamp, while Beit Hillel suffice with two witnesses for the entire night.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about witnesses for each act of intercourse
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about witnesses for each act of intercourse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Shammai requires two witnesses for each act of intercourse, while Beit Hillel says two witnesses suffice for the entire night. Beit Shammai objects that a drop of blood might be covered by semen in a second act, and Beit Hillel responds with a counter-argument about saliva. Beit Shammai then distinguishes between one-time and two-time dissolution.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the dispute: Beit Shammai requires two witnesses for each act of intercourse, while Beit Hillel says two witnesses suffice for the entire night.
Beit Shammai objects to Beit Hillel's leniency: a drop of blood from the first act might be covered by semen in the second act, so witnesses for the whole night are insufficient.
Beit Hillel counters with a parallel: according to Beit Shammai's logic, one should also worry that saliva in the mouth might dissolve and be lost, which is absurd.
Beit Shammai rejects the analogy: dissolving once (saliva) is not comparable to dissolving twice (blood covered by semen), so their objection stands.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling and Rabbi Zeira's conclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling and Rabbi Zeira's conclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua sides with Beit Shammai, and his students complain about his lengthy discourse. Rabbi Zeira concludes from all opinions that a scrupulous person should not engage in intercourse twice in one night.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that Rabbi Yehoshua sides with Beit Shammai's position.

sub.text: Students' complaint and Rabbi Yehoshua's response
sub.text_en: Students' complaint and Rabbi Yehoshua's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's students complain about his lengthy discourse, and he replies that it is better to lengthen in this world so their days are extended in the World to Come.
Rabbi Zeira concludes from all the opinions that a scrupulous person (בעל נפש) should not engage in intercourse twice in one night.

items.text: Rava's distinction: the baraita applies only to purity
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: the baraita applies only to purity
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the baraita about not repeating intercourse applies only to matters of purity (terumah), but for the husband himself it is permitted. A supporting baraita clarifies that the restriction applies only when she was left in a state of purity, but if left in a state of impurity she remains in that state until she declares herself pure.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a man may repeat intercourse, and the baraita's restriction applies only to matters of purity (טהרות).
A supporting baraita confirms Rava's distinction: the restriction applies only to purity matters, and if she was left in a state of impurity she remains in that state until she declares herself pure.

items.text: Dispute about checking with a lost cloth
items.text_en: Dispute about checking with a lost cloth
items.desc_en: Rav rules that if a woman checked with a cloth and it was lost, she is forbidden to have intercourse until she checks again. Rabbi Ila objects that if the cloth were present she would not know its status, so she should be permitted. Rava distinguishes between a cloth that is present (which can be examined) and one that is lost.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that if a woman checked with a cloth and it was lost, she is forbidden to have intercourse until she checks again.
Rabbi Ila objects that if the cloth were present she would not know its status and would still be permitted, so she should be permitted now as well.
Rava distinguishes between a cloth that is present (which can be examined) and one that is lost (which cannot), resolving the objection.

items.text: Prohibition of daytime intercourse and the angel of conception
items.text_en: Prohibition of daytime intercourse and the angel of conception
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan prohibits daytime intercourse, citing a verse. Rav Hamnuna and Reish Lakish offer different prooftexts. The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish uses the verse for a different teaching about the angel named 'Layla' who brings the drop before God, and Rabbi Yochanan's verse teaches that night is for conception, not day.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) prohibits daytime intercourse, and the Gemara cites Rav Hamnuna and Reish Lakish offering different prooftexts from verses.
The Gemara asks how Reish Lakish interprets the verse cited by Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara answers that Reish Lakish uses the verse for the teaching of רבי חנינא בר פפא (Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) about the angel named 'לילה' (Night) who brings the drop before God.
The Gemara notes that the angel does not ask about righteousness, consistent with רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) that everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse's unusual wording that night is given for conception, not day.

items.text: Things God hates: entering suddenly and other behaviors
items.text_en: Things God hates: entering suddenly and other behaviors
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a verse from Ben Sira about four things God hates, including entering a friend's house suddenly. Rabbi Yochanan adds that this applies even to one's own house. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai lists four things God hates, including entering suddenly and holding the penis while urinating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse that Reish Lakish used.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan uses the verse to support a teaching from the book of Ben Sira about four things God hates.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the prohibition of entering suddenly applies even to one's own house.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai lists four things God hates, including entering suddenly and holding the penis while urinating.

items.text: Opening discussion on marital relations in front of others
items.text_en: Opening discussion on marital relations in front of others
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asks Shmuel whether the prohibition of marital relations in front of all living beings applies even in front of mice. Shmuel clarifies that it refers to specific households that engage in relations in front of their servants, who are considered like donkeys.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions including urinating naked before one's bed and having marital relations in front of any living being.
Rav Yehuda asks Shmuel whether the prohibition of marital relations in front of all living beings applies even in front of mice.
Shmuel clarifies that the prohibition refers to specific households that engage in relations in front of their servants, who are considered like donkeys.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the scriptural basis
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the scriptural basis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that these households derive from the verse 'Sit here with the donkey' — a people comparable to a donkey.

items.text: Examples of modest behavior by Amoraim
items.text_en: Examples of modest behavior by Amoraim
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples of how Rabbah bar Rav Huna, Abaye, and Rava would engage in marital relations discreetly, using various methods to avoid being seen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides three examples of Amoraim who engaged in marital relations discreetly: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rattled the bells of a basket, Abaye used door bolts, and Rava used flying bolts.

items.text: Five dangerous actions according to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.text_en: Five dangerous actions according to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai lists five actions that endanger one's life, including eating peeled garlic or onion, drinking liquids left overnight, sleeping in a cemetery, cutting nails and throwing them in public, and bloodletting followed by marital relations. The Gemara elaborates on the danger of peeled items even if sealed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai lists five actions that endanger one's life, including eating peeled garlic, onion, or egg, drinking liquids left overnight, sleeping in a cemetery, cutting nails and throwing them in public, and bloodletting followed by marital relations.
The Gemara elaborates that even if peeled items are sealed in flour and wrapped, a harmful spirit rests upon them, unless some root or peel remains.

items.text: Details on drinking liquids left overnight
items.text_en: Details on drinking liquids left overnight
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan specify that the danger applies only when the liquids were left in metal vessels, and Rav Pappa adds that earthenware vessels are similar.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel limits the danger of drinking mixed liquids left overnight to those left in metal vessels.
Rav Pappa adds that earthenware vessels (כלי נתר) are similar to metal vessels in this regard.
Rabbi Yochanan independently states the same limitation to metal vessels and agrees that earthenware vessels are similar.

items.text: Sleeping in a cemetery and cutting nails
items.text_en: Sleeping in a cemetery and cutting nails
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that sleeping in a cemetery invites a spirit of impurity, and cutting nails and throwing them in public can cause a pregnant woman to miscarry. Exceptions are made for certain methods of cutting and disposal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that sleeping in a cemetery invites a spirit of impurity (רוח טומאה) which can sometimes endanger the person.

The Gemara explains that cutting nails and throwing them in public can cause a pregnant woman to miscarry, with exceptions for certain methods of cutting and disposal, but ultimately concludes that concern applies to all cases.

items.text: Three categories for nail disposal
items.text_en: Three categories for nail disposal
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that burning nails is pious, burying them is righteous, and throwing them away is wicked.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach a baraita listing three categories for nail disposal: burning (pious), burying (righteous), and throwing away (wicked).

items.text: Bloodletting and marital relations
items.text_en: Bloodletting and marital relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the consequences of bloodletting followed by marital relations, stating that it leads to weak children. Rav adds that this applies only if one has not eaten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that bloodletting followed by marital relations produces weak children.
The Gemara adds that if both partners bled and then had relations, the children will be leprous.
Rav qualifies that this applies only if one has not eaten, but if he has eaten, there is no concern.

items.text: Prohibition of marital relations during the day
items.text_en: Prohibition of marital relations during the day
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda prohibits marital relations during the day due to the verse 'Love your neighbor as yourself', lest one see something unseemly. Rav Huna states that Jews are holy and do not engage in relations during the day. Rava allows it in a dark house or if one creates darkness with a garment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda prohibits marital relations during the day, citing the verse 'Love your neighbor as yourself', and Abaye explains the reason: lest one see something unseemly in his wife and she becomes repulsive to him.
Rav Huna adds that Jews are holy and do not engage in relations during the day, reinforcing the prohibition.
Rava permits relations during the day in a dark house, and a Torah scholar may create darkness with his garment and then engage.

items.text: Reinterpretation of mishnaic sources about bed-checking
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of mishnaic sources about bed-checking
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets sources that seem to permit marital relations by candlelight or during the day, explaining that they actually refer to bed-checking. The case of the house of Monbaz is discussed, where they would check beds during the day, not engage in relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna that seems to permit marital relations by candlelight, posing a contradiction to the earlier ruling that relations by candlelight are forbidden.
The Gemara reinterprets the mishna as referring to bed-checking by candlelight, not marital relations.
The Gemara brings a baraita that explicitly states that one who engages in relations by candlelight is contemptible, supporting the reinterpretation.
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as referring to bed-checking by candlelight, which is also contemptible.
The Gemara brings a baraita about the house of Monbaz that seems to praise daytime marital relations, challenging the reinterpretation.
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as referring to daytime bed-checking, and explains that even if it meant relations, the praise is due to the constraint of sleep, not the act itself.

items.text: Materials for bed-checking
items.text_en: Materials for bed-checking
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Shmuel's statement that bed-checking is done only with flax or clean soft wool. Rava suggests using worn linen garments, but a baraita from the school of Menashe prohibits linen. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between linen and linen garments, or new vs. worn garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita about the house of Monbaz checking beds with flax (מֵילָא פַּרְהֲבָא) as support for Shmuel's ruling that bed-checking is done only with flax or clean soft wool, and adds Rav's anecdote about not understanding the term.
Rava proposes that worn linen garments (שַׁחֲקֵי דְּכִיתָּנָא) are suitable for bed-checking.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from baraita of the school of Menashe
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from baraita of the school of Menashe
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing the baraita of the school of Menashe, which explicitly prohibits checking with linen (פִּשְׁתָּן), contradicting Rava's suggestion.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between raw flax (כִּיתָּנָא) which is prohibited, and linen garments (מָאנֵי דְּכִיתָּנָא) which are permitted, or alternatively between new garments (חַדְתֵי) which are prohibited and worn garments (שַׁחֲקֵי) which are permitted.

items.text: Discussion on snow and impurity
items.text_en: Discussion on snow and impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the laws of snow regarding impurity: snow is neither food nor drink, but if designated for food it does not convey food impurity, and for drink it conveys drink impurity. A contradiction is raised about partial impurity and purification, and Abaye resolves it with the case of passing snow over the airspace of an oven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah from elsewhere (מסכת מכשירין) that snow is neither food nor drink, but if designated for food it does not convey food impurity, and if designated for drink it conveys drink impurity.
The Mishnah adds a rule about partial impurity and purification of snow: if part becomes impure, the whole is not impure; if part becomes pure, the whole becomes pure.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says partial impurity does not affect the whole, but then says partial purification purifies the whole, implying that the whole was impure.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining the case as snow passed over the airspace of an oven, where the Torah testified that an earthenware vessel's airspace conveys impurity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a metaphor: the chamber (inner), hallway (middle), and attic (outer). Blood from the chamber is impure, from the attic pure, and from the hallway is a safek (doubtful) because its presumption is from the source.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's initial teaching
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's initial teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna finds Rami bar Shmuel and Rav Yitzchak studying the Mishnah's layout. He reports that his father taught: blood found from the skylight inward is a safek tamei, from the skylight outward is a safek tahor.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's correction
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's correction
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna reports his father's teaching to Rav Huna, who corrects him: from the skylight inward is definitely impure, from the skylight outward is a safek tamei.

items.text: Abaye's two frameworks
items.text_en: Abaye's two frameworks
items.desc_en: Abaye questions the distinction: why is outward a safek? Perhaps it came from the chamber. Inward could also be from the attic. He then offers two approaches: if we follow concern (חֲשָׁשָׁא), both are safek; if we follow presumption (חֲזָקָה), inward is definitely impure and outward is definitely pure.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute and alignment with Abaye's frameworks
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute and alignment with Abaye's frameworks
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya and Rav Katina dispute the halachic consequences of blood found in the hallway: Rabbi Chiya says it obligates sacrifice and burning terumah, Rav Katina says not. The Gemara notes that Abaye's first framework (following concern) supports Rav Katina and disputes Rabbi Chiya, while his second framework (following presumption) supports Rabbi Chiya.

items.text: Resolving the dispute about blood found in the courtyard
items.text_en: Resolving the dispute about blood found in the courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the contradiction between Rav Katina and Rav Huna by distinguishing between blood found inside the courtyard and outside. It then resolves the difficulty for Rami bar Shmuel and Rav Yitzchak by attributing their ruling to the case of blood found inside, and rejects the suggestion that it contradicts Rabbi Chiya by distinguishing between blood found on the floor of the corridor and on its roof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rav Katina and Rav Huna, and resolves it by distinguishing between blood found inside the courtyard (מן הלול ולפנים) and outside (מן הלול ולחוץ).

sub.text: Gemara's answer for Rami bar Shmuel and Rav Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for Rami bar Shmuel and Rav Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rami bar Shmuel and Rav Yitzchak's ruling applies specifically to blood found inside the courtyard (מן הלול ולפנים), resolving the difficulty.
The Gemara objects that the ruling might contradict Rabbi Chiya's position.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between blood found on the floor of the corridor (קרקע פרוזדור) and on its roof (גג פרוזדור).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's three places where majority is treated as certain
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's three places where majority is treated as certain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that in three places the Sages followed the majority and treated the doubt as certain: the source (מקור), the placenta (שליא), and a cut limb (חתיכה). The Gemara briefly explains each: the source as previously discussed, the placenta because it never occurs without a child (despite Rabbi Shimon's opinion), and a cut hand or foot because we do not suspect it came from a sealed body part.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that in three places the Sages followed the majority and treated the doubt as certain: the source (מקור), the placenta (שליא), and a cut limb (חתיכה).
The Gemara briefly explains the first case: the source (מקור) is as previously discussed.

The Gemara cites a baraita about the placenta (שליא) in a house: the house is impure because a placenta never occurs without a child, despite Rabbi Shimon's opinion that the child may have dissolved before emerging.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a cut limb (חתיכה): a woman who miscarries a cut hand or foot is impure from childbirth, and we do not suspect it came from a sealed body part (גוף אטום).

items.text: Question from the case of nine stores
items.text_en: Question from the case of nine stores
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of nine stores selling kosher meat and one selling non-kosher is not included, citing a baraita where the doubt is forbidden but when found one follows the majority. The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan was discussing ritual impurity (טומאה), not prohibition (איסור).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of nine stores (תשע חנויות) is not included in Rabbi Yochanan's list, citing a baraita where the doubt is forbidden but when found one follows the majority.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan was discussing ritual impurity (טומאה), not prohibition (איסור).

items.text: Question from the case of nine frogs and one reptile
items.text_en: Question from the case of nine frogs and one reptile
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of nine frogs and one reptile, where touching one in a private domain is doubtful and in a public domain is pure, but when found one follows the majority, is not included. The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking specifically about a woman's impurity (טומאה דאישה), not general impurity (טומאה בעלמא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of nine frogs and one reptile, where touching one in a private domain is doubtful and in a public domain is pure, but when found one follows the majority, is not included in Rabbi Yochanan's list.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking specifically about a woman's impurity (טומאה דאישה), not general impurity (טומאה בעלמא).

items.text: Beginning of another question from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Beginning of another question from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to raise another case from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about a woman who crossed a river, but the segment is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another case from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about a woman who crossed a river, challenging the previous limitation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and principle of majority
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and principle of majority
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who miscarries brings a sacrifice and it is eaten, following the majority of women who give birth to viable offspring. This establishes the principle of relying on רוב.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who miscarries brings a sacrifice which is eaten, relying on the majority of women who give birth to viable offspring.

items.text: Gemara's question about the scope of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the scope of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling applies only to the Mishnah itself or also to other traditions (שמעתתא). It cites a report from Ravin that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina raised a difficulty, but the Gemara is unsure whether it is a refutation or support, concluding it might be neither.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling applies only to the Mishnah itself or also to other traditions (שמעתתא).
The Gemara cites a report from Ravin that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina raised a difficulty, but the Gemara does not know what the refutation is.
The Gemara asks whether the report is not a refutation but rather support for the Mishnah's ruling.
The Gemara concludes that the report might be neither a refutation nor support.

items.text: Discussion of majority versus presumption (חזקה)
items.text_en: Discussion of majority versus presumption (חזקה)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's principle excludes, considering a case where a majority is opposed by a חזקה. It cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about a child near dough, and a debate between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan about whether such a חזקה allows burning terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's principle of following the majority excludes.
The Gemara objects that if the exclusion is a majority opposed by a חזקה (presumption), Rabbi Yochanan already addressed this.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a child found near dough, where Rabbi Meir declares it pure and the Sages declare it impure.
Rabbi Meir holds that the majority of children handle dough, but the minority does not, and the dough's presumption of purity combines with the minority to weaken the majority.
The Sages consider the minority as non-existent, and when a majority opposes a חזקה (presumption), the majority prevails.

sub.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Oshaya says this is a חזקה (presumption) upon which one may burn terumah, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is not.

items.text: Alternative exclusion: majority of Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Alternative exclusion: majority of Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's principle excludes the majority of Rabbi Yehuda, who rules that a woman who miscarries a piece of flesh is always impure. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan clarify the dispute, limiting it to cases of four types of blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's principle excludes the majority view of Rabbi Yehuda, who rules that a woman who miscarries a piece of flesh is always impure, citing the Mishnah's dispute.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel clarifies that Rabbi Yehuda only deemed impure a piece of flesh from four types of blood, but other types are pure.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that for four types of blood all agree she is impure, for other blood all agree she is pure, and the dispute is only when she miscarried.

items.text: Opening dispute on רוב חתיכות
items.text_en: Opening dispute on רוב חתיכות
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis regarding a woman who miscarried without knowing what she expelled. Rabbi Yehuda holds we follow the majority of pieces (רוב חתיכות), which are typically from four types of blood, while the Rabbis reject this principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis regarding a woman who miscarried without knowing what she expelled: Rabbi Yehuda follows the majority of pieces (רוב חתיכות), which are typically from four types of blood, while the Rabbis reject this principle.

items.text: Mishnah: Five types of impure blood
items.text_en: Mishnah: Five types of impure blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five types of blood that render a woman impure: red, black, like saffron, like earth-water, and like diluted wine. Beit Shammai adds two more, Beit Hillel declares them pure. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei debate the status of green blood. The Mishnah then defines the shades of each color.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing five types of impure blood and records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding two additional shades.
The Mishnah records the dispute about green blood: Akavya ben Mahalalel declares it impure, the Sages pure, Rabbi Meir says it at least renders liquids impure, and Rabbi Yosei rejects both positions.

The Mishnah defines the precise shades for each of the five impure blood types: red like wound blood, black like ink, saffron-like, earth-water from Beit Kerem valley, and diluted wine in a two-to-one ratio.

items.text: Gemara's question: Source for pure blood
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Source for pure blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How do we know there is pure blood in a woman? Perhaps all blood from her is impure. Rabbi Chama bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Oshaya answers with a verse: 'between blood and blood' implies a distinction between pure and impure blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How do we know there is pure blood in a woman? Perhaps all blood from her is impure.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Oshaya answers with a verse: 'between blood and blood' implies a distinction between pure and impure blood.

items.text: Objection and resolution: Alternative interpretations of the verse
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Alternative interpretations of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: The same verse could apply to negaim, but there is no pure negaim. It then suggests the verse refers to different types of negaim (human, houses, garments), all impure. Similarly, it could refer to menstrual blood and zivah blood, all impure. The Gemara rejects this: in negaim there are disputes (e.g., Rabbi Yehoshua vs. Sages, Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon vs. Sages, Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtulmos vs. Sages), but here if there is no pure blood, what dispute exists in the Mishnah?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'between blood and blood' could equally apply to negaim, but there is no pure negaim, as the only candidate (all-white skin) is called bohak, not a negah.
The Gemara suggests that the verse refers to different types of negaim (human, houses, garments), all of which are impure, and similarly to menstrual blood and zivah blood, all impure.

The Gemara objects that in negaim there are disputes (e.g., Rabbi Yehoshua vs. Sages, Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon vs. Sages, Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtulmos vs. Sages), but here if there is no pure blood, what dispute exists in the Mishnah?

sub.text: Supporting baraita for dispute in human negaim
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for dispute in human negaim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita showing a dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and the Sages regarding the order of a bright spot and white hair in negaim.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for dispute in house negaim
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for dispute in house negaim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita showing a dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon and the Sages regarding the minimum size of a house negah.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's reasoning from the verses 'קיר' and 'קירות' to require a corner.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for dispute in garment negaim
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for dispute in garment negaim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita showing a dispute between Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtulmos and the Sages regarding the purity of a garment that has completely spread with a negah.

items.text: Source for the five bloods: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Source for the five bloods: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu derives from the verse 'the waters were red as blood' that blood is red, but this only gives one. He then cites the repeated word 'דָּמֶיהָ' to yield four, and Rabbi Chanina explains that black is a form of red that has deteriorated, making five. A baraisa supports this with a simile of wound blood that turns black.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know which bloods are pure and which are impure.
Rabbi Avahu derives from the verse 'וַיִּרְאוּ מוֹאָב אֶת הַמַּיִם אֲדוּמִּים כַּדָּם' that blood is red, but this only yields one color.
Rabbi Avahu cites the repeated word 'דָּמֶיהָ' to derive four bloods.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah lists five bloods, not four.
Rabbi Chanina explains that black is a form of red that has deteriorated, making five bloods.
A baraita supports this with a simile of wound blood that turns black only after being detached.

items.text: Beit Shammai's additional bloods and the dispute with Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's additional bloods and the dispute with Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Beit Shammai can add two more bloods if the verse only implies four. Two answers are given: either they do not accept the derivation, or they do and consider the additional colors as deteriorated forms. The Gemara then notes that Beit Hillel's ruling seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, and identifies a practical difference between them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Beit Shammai can add two more bloods if the verse only implies four.
The Gemara offers the first answer: Beit Shammai does not accept the derivation of four bloods from the verse.

The Gemara offers the second answer: Beit Shammai does accept the derivation, but considers the additional colors as deteriorated forms of the four, similar to Rabbi Chanina's explanation of black being a deteriorated red.
The Gemara notes that Beit Hillel's ruling seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, and questions the difference between them.
The Gemara identifies a practical difference between Beit Hillel and the Tanna Kamma.

items.text: Opening statement on green blood
items.text_en: Opening statement on green blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by noting that green blood is a matter of dispute, with Akavya ben Mahalalel declaring it impure. The text then questions whether Akavya's position contradicts the principle that only red blood is considered menstrual blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the word 'לתלות' (to suspend), introducing the topic of green blood.
The Gemara notes that Akavya ben Mahalalel declares green blood impure, and questions whether this contradicts the principle that only red blood is considered menstrual blood.

The Gemara offers two resolutions: either Akavya rejects the principle, or he accepts it, citing Rabbi Chanina's principle that black blood is actually red blood that has become discolored, and green blood is similarly a discolored form of red.

The Gemara notes that the Sages declare green blood pure, and questions whether this is identical to the first Tanna, concluding that the difference between them is the matter of 'לתלות' (suspending judgment).
Rabbi Meir states that if green blood does not impart impurity as a כתם (stain), it still imparts impurity as a liquid.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Meir adopted Akavya's position and argued to the Sages that even if they do not declare a green stain impure, they should declare green blood seen from her body impure.

The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Meir's argument is as stated, the phrase 'if it does not impart impurity as a stain, it imparts impurity as a liquid' is problematic, because the proper term should be 'because she sees' rather than 'as a liquid'.

The Gemara revises Rabbi Meir's argument: even if they do not declare green blood impure when seen initially, they should declare it impure when seen after red blood, because it then has the status of a liquid of a זב (male with discharge) or זבה (female with discharge).

The Sages respond by analogy to saliva: just as saliva is round and comes out, so only that which is round and comes out is considered a liquid of a זב, excluding green blood which does not come out round.

The Gemara offers another version: Rabbi Meir argued that green blood should be like a liquid to enable seeds to become susceptible to impurity, but the Sages require 'דם חללים' (blood of a corpse) for that, which is absent.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir derived the impurity of green blood through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the verse 'שלחיך פרדס רמונים' and the verse 'ושולח מים על פני חוצות'.
The Sages respond that while one may derive a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) independently, one may not derive a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) independently.

The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yosei's statement is identical to the first Tanna, and explains that the purpose is to identify the first Tanna as Rabbi Yosei and to teach that one who says something in the name of its speaker brings redemption to the world.
The Mishnah states that red blood is like the blood of a wound, and the Gemara asks what this means.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that it is like the blood of a slaughtered ox, and the Gemara clarifies that the phrase 'blood of a wound' teaches that it is like the initial strike of a knife, not the entire slaughter.
Ulla says it is like the blood of a live bird, and the Gemara raises a doubt whether 'live' excludes a slaughtered bird or a weak bird, concluding with תיקו (let it stand unresolved).

sub.text: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina says it is like the blood of the head's knife, and the Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a woman who killed with a knife, resolving that it refers to the head of the knife.

sub.text: Ammi Vardina'a in the name of Rabbi Abahu
sub.text_en: Ammi Vardina'a in the name of Rabbi Abahu
sub.desc_en: Ammi Vardina'a in the name of Rabbi Abahu says it is like the blood of the small finger of the hand that was struck, healed, and struck again, specifically of a young man who has not married, up to age twenty.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that a woman may attribute blood to her son or her husband, questioning how she can attribute it to her husband.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that it refers to a case where she entered the wedding canopy but was not yet intimate with her husband.
Rav Nachman says it is like the blood of bloodletting, and the Gemara raises an objection from a story where Rabbi Meir attributed blood to bloodletting.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction for Akavya
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction for Akavya
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two answers: either Akavya does not hold the principle of 'dameha dameha' (her blood is her blood), or he does, but considers green blood as a form of red blood that has become discolored, similar to Rabbi Chanina's explanation of black blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Akavya can hold that green blood is impure, given that he does not accept the principle of 'דָּמֶיהָ דָּמֶיהָ' (her blood is her blood) which would limit the colors.
The Gemara offers the first answer: Akavya does not hold the principle of 'דָּמֶיהָ דָּמֶיהָ' at all.

The Gemara offers the second answer: Akavya does hold the principle, but considers green blood as red blood that has become discolored, analogous to Rabbi Chanina's explanation that black blood is red blood that has been afflicted.

items.text: Difference between Tanna Kamma and Sages
items.text_en: Difference between Tanna Kamma and Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Sages also declare green blood pure, which seems identical to the Tanna Kamma. It clarifies that the difference between them is the issue of 'litlot' (suspending impurity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The Sages also declare green blood pure — this is identical to the Tanna Kamma's ruling, so what is the difference between them?
The Gemara answers: The difference between them is the issue of 'litlot' (suspending impurity) — whether one may suspend impurity in a case of doubt regarding green blood.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's position and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's position and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that if green blood is not impure as a stain, it is impure as a liquid. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Meir follows Akavya's view, arguing that while a green stain on a garment is not impure, green blood from the body should be. The Gemara refines this: Rabbi Meir's argument is about a woman who first sees red blood and then green blood, making it like the fluids of a zav or zava.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir's statement that if green blood is not impure as a stain (כתם), it is impure as a liquid (משקה).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Meir adopted Akavya's view, arguing that while a green stain on a garment is not impure, green blood from the body should be impure.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Meir's argument is about blood from the body, he should have said it is impure as 'blood of a woman who sees a discharge' (רואה), not as 'liquid' (משקה).

The Gemara refines Rabbi Meir's argument: it applies specifically to a woman who first saw red blood and then green blood, making the green blood like the fluids of a זב (zav) or זבה (zava), which are impure as liquids.

items.text: Sages' responses and alternative interpretations
items.text_en: Sages' responses and alternative interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents three possible responses of the Sages to Rabbi Meir: first, that green blood does not resemble saliva (rok) which is round; second, that it cannot make seeds susceptible to impurity; third, a gezeirah shava (verbal analogy) from 'shlachayich' to 'sholeach'. The Gemara then notes that one cannot derive a gezeirah shava on one's own.

sub.desc_en: The Sages respond to Rabbi Meir that green blood does not resemble saliva (rok) which is round, so it is excluded from the category of fluids that convey impurity.
The Gemara notes that this first response would be a valid refutation of Rabbi Meir's position.
The Sages alternatively argue that green blood cannot make seeds susceptible to impurity (הכשר), since only blood of a slaughtered animal (דם חללים) qualifies.
The Gemara again notes that this second response would also be a valid refutation.
The Sages propose a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'שלחיך' to 'שולח' to include green blood as a fluid that conveys impurity.
The Gemara rejects this third response, noting that one cannot derive a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on one's own authority, unlike a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument).

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's statement and its implication
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's statement and its implication
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says something similar to the Tanna Kamma. The Gemara explains that this teaches us that the Tanna Kamma is actually Rabbi Yosei, and that one who says something in the name of its original speaker brings redemption to the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: 'Rabbi Yosei says: Not so etc.'

items.text: Defining the color red for blood
items.text_en: Defining the color red for blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that red is like the blood of a wound. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines it as the blood of a slaughtered ox. Ulla says it is like the blood of a live bird. Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina says it is like the blood of the head's knife. Rabbi Avahu says it is like the blood of a small finger that was struck and healed repeatedly, specifically of a bachelor under twenty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the color red for blood as like the blood of a wound.

The Gemara asks what 'like the blood of a wound' means, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers it is like the blood of a slaughtered ox, specifying it means the initial cut of the knife, not the entire slaughter.
Ulla says the red is like the blood of a live bird, and the Gemara leaves unresolved whether 'live' excludes a slaughtered bird or a weak one.

sub.text: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina says it is like the blood of a head knife, and the Gemara clarifies from a baraita that it refers to the head part of the knife, not the whole body.
Rabbi Avahu defines the red as the blood of a small finger repeatedly struck and healed, specifically of a bachelor under twenty.

items.text: Discussion on hanging impurity on a husband
items.text_en: Discussion on hanging impurity on a husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a woman can attribute blood to her husband, given that he is not usually present. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it refers to a case where she entered the wedding canopy but was not yet intimate. Rav Nachman then defines red as the blood of bloodletting, and cites a story where Rabbi Meir used this as a basis for leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a woman can attribute blood to her husband, given that he is not usually present.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the case is where she entered the wedding canopy but was not yet intimate.
Rav Nachman defines red as the blood of bloodletting (הקזה).
A supporting baraita is cited, recounting a story where Rabbi Meir used this definition as a basis for leniency.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'red' comparison
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'red' comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's comparison of red blood to the 'kilor' (a red dye) and Rabbi's comparison to burnt sycamore wood refer to the color red itself. It answers that these comparisons are for other red-colored bloods, not for the primary red blood.

items.text: Practical test for red blood by Amemar and Mar Zutra
items.text_en: Practical test for red blood by Amemar and Mar Zutra
items.desc_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi sit before a craftsman who shows them a red horn. Amemar identifies it as the 'red' of the Mishnah. When shown another horn, he says it changed color. Rav Ashi concludes that one who cannot distinguish between these shades should not examine blood.

items.text: Definition of 'black' as ink and its shade
items.text_en: Definition of 'black' as ink and its shade
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says black blood is like 'cheres' (ink). Rabbah bar Rav Huna specifies that the ink is dry ink. A baraisa supports this. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah uses 'cheres' rather than 'dyo' to indicate the shade of ink, not its liquid form. A question arises whether the ink is moist or dry, and Rabbi Ammi's practice of scraping dry ink and testing with it shows it is dry.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar on shades of red and black
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar on shades of red and black
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel states that blood as dark as a wall, ink, or a grape is impure, corresponding to the Mishnah's 'deeper than this – impure'. Rabbi Elazar states that blood as light as olive oil, pitch, or a raven is pure, corresponding to 'lighter than this – pure'.

items.text: Ulla's definition of black as a black garment
items.text_en: Ulla's definition of black as a black garment
items.desc_en: Ulla says black is like a black garment. He once saw an Arab wearing a black garment and declared it the 'black' of the Mishnah. They plucked threads from it, which were sold for 400 zuz.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's definition and resolution of a contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's definition and resolution of a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says black is like 'olya'irin' garments from overseas. The Gemara questions whether these are black, citing Rabbi Yannai's instruction to his sons not to bury him in black or white garments, but in 'olya'irin' garments. The Gemara resolves that the garments in Rabbi Yochanan's statement are black cloaks, while those in Rabbi Yannai's are white linen garments.

items.text: Dispute about testing blood on a white cloth
items.text_en: Dispute about testing blood on a white cloth
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel says all bloods are tested only on a white cloth. Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi adds that black blood is tested on a red cloth. Rav Yirmiya from Difti says they do not disagree: one refers to black blood, the other to other bloods. Rav Ashi objects, arguing that if so, Shmuel should have said 'except for black'. Rav Ashi concludes they actually disagree about black blood itself.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on black blood and its rationale
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on black blood and its rationale
items.desc_en: Ulla rules that for all bloods, deeper than the specified shade is impure, lighter is pure, except for black blood. The Gemara explains that one might have thought black blood is impure even when lighter, because Rabbi Chanina said black is merely red that has spoiled. Therefore, the Mishnah teaches that black blood is pure when lighter.

items.text: Rabbi Ammi bar Abba and Rami bar Abba's opposing rulings
items.text_en: Rabbi Ammi bar Abba and Rami bar Abba's opposing rulings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi bar Abba says all bloods are impure when deeper or lighter, except black blood, which is pure when lighter. The Rabbis' measurement (the shade of black) excludes a lighter shade of black. An alternative version: Rami bar Abba says all bloods are pure when deeper or lighter, except black blood, and the measurement serves to include black blood as impure when it is exactly that shade.

items.text: Bar Kappara's ruling on all bloods and wine sediment
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's ruling on all bloods and wine sediment
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara rules that all bloods are impure when deeper, pure when lighter, except for wine sediment (mezeg), which is pure both when deeper and lighter. The Gemara notes that Bar Kappara's rulings are consistent: when they deepened the color, it was pure; when they lightened it, it was pure. Rabbi Chanina remarks how great is a person whose rulings align with his teachings.

items.text: Discussion of the saffron-colored stain and contradictory baraisos
items.text_en: Discussion of the saffron-colored stain and contradictory baraisos
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions a stain like saffron. A baraisa specifies it is moist, not dry. Four baraisos contradict each other regarding whether the stain is like the lower (darker) or upper (lighter) part of the saffron. Abaye resolves that there are three layers and three leaves of saffron; one should take the middle layer and the middle leaf. When people came before Rabbi Avahu, he said they taught the baraisos according to their own interpretations.

items.text: Discussion of earth-colored water and its testing procedure
items.text_en: Discussion of earth-colored water and its testing procedure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions water resembling earth. A baraisa details the procedure: bring rich soil from the Valley of Beit Kerem (or other places per different Tannaim), pour water over it. Another baraisa adds that the water should be like garlic peel, with no fixed measure for water or earth, and it must be tested when cloudy, not clear. A question arises whether the prohibition against stirring with the hand means one cannot stir at all, or just that one should use a vessel. The Gemara cites a baraisa that testing is done with a cup, but the stirring method remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Final ruling on earth-colored water and a curse
items.text_en: Final ruling on earth-colored water and a curse
items.desc_en: When people came before Rabbah bar Avuh, he said they taught the baraisa according to its location (i.e., the Valley of Beit Kerem). Rabbi Chanina would scrape a piece of gurgishta (a type of earth) and test with it. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei cursed him with askara (diphtheria) for this practice.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's unique wisdom
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's unique wisdom
