items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chanina was uniquely wise, implying others are not as knowledgeable.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Zeira on seeing blood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Zeira on seeing blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan attributes his inability to see blood to Rabbi Chanina's wisdom, Rabbi Elazar attributes his ability to see blood to Rabbi Chanina's humility, and Rabbi Zeira blames his Babylonian nature for not seeing blood.

items.text: Challenge and Ulla's story
items.text_en: Challenge and Ulla's story
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the matter depends on nature, citing Rabbah who knew nature but not blood. Ulla, when visiting Pumbedita, could not see blood, comparing himself to Rabbi Elazar who also failed in Rabbi Yehuda's place.

items.text: Why Rabbi Elazar was called 'Master of the Land of Israel'
items.text_en: Why Rabbi Elazar was called 'Master of the Land of Israel'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar was called 'Master of the Land of Israel' because he correctly identified a woman's blood as 'blood of desire' (dam chimud), and Rabbi Ami later confirmed her story.

items.text: Ifra Hormiz and Rava's test
items.text_en: Ifra Hormiz and Rava's test
items.desc_en: Ifra Hormiz, mother of King Shapur, sent blood to Rava. Rava identified it as 'blood of desire'. She later sent sixty types of blood, all identified except for louse blood, but Rava sent a louse-killer, showing his wisdom.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's change in practice
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's change in practice
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says he used to see blood, but after his mother told him not to bring the first drop to the Sages because it is dangerous, he no longer sees it. He only sees blood when it is clearly between impure and pure.

items.text: Yalta's blood and the principle of overturning a ruling
items.text_en: Yalta's blood and the principle of overturning a ruling
items.desc_en: Yalta brought blood to Rabbah bar bar Chanah who declared it impure, then to Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda who declared it pure. The Gemara questions this, citing a baraita that a sage cannot overturn another's ruling. The answer is that she told him the first sage only ruled due to an eye ailment, and a woman is believed to say 'I saw such and lost it'.

items.text: Inquiry about believing a woman's claim 'a sage declared this pure'
items.text_en: Inquiry about believing a woman's claim 'a sage declared this pure'
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a woman is believed to say 'a sage declared this pure'. It attempts to prove from Yalta's case that she is believed, concluding that Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda relied on her statement.

items.text: Rabbi's changing ruling on blood
items.text_en: Rabbi's changing ruling on blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi saw blood at night and declared it impure, then in the morning declared it pure, but later changed again and declared it impure. The Gemara explains that he initially thought it was pure but the night view was unclear, then realized it was actually impure and changing color.

items.text: Methods of examining blood and the Mishnah's teaching
items.text_en: Methods of examining blood and the Mishnah's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses proper methods for examining blood: Rabbi examined by candlelight, Rabbi Yishmael on a cloudy day between pillars, and others specify between sun and shade. The Mishnah's teaching about 'two parts mixed' is cited.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Ruling on a miscarried piece
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Ruling on a miscarried piece
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman miscarries a piece and there is blood with it, she is impure; otherwise she is pure. Rabbi Yehuda says she is impure in either case.

items.text: Mishnah: Other forms of miscarriage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Other forms of miscarriage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues with cases of miscarrying a form like a husk, hair, dirt, or red gnats; if they dissolve in water she is impure. Also cases of fish, locusts, etc., and animals; if there is blood she is impure. For an animal, she observes the days for a male or female. If unknown, Rabbi Meir says she observes for both, but the Sages say that without human form it is not a fetus.

items.text: Gemara: Samuel and Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Samuel and Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Samuel that Rabbi Yehuda only ruled impure for a piece of the four types of blood, but for other bloods she is pure. Rabbi Yochanan says that for the four types all agree she is impure, and for other bloods all agree she is pure; the dispute is only when she miscarried and does not know what she miscarried, with Rabbi Yehuda following the majority of pieces being from the four types, while the Rabbis do not.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that lists a red, black, green, and white piece, with Rabbi Yehuda disputing in all cases. This challenges Samuel (who limits Rabbi Yehuda to four types) and Rabbi Yochanan (who says the Rabbis agree on the four types). After analyzing the difficulties, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the dispute is about the possibility of opening the womb without blood, and cites a related Tannaitic dispute.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who miscarries a piece of tissue, uncertain whether it is a birth or a zivah, brings a sacrifice that is not eaten. Rabbi Yehoshua argues it is eaten, because it is impossible for the womb to open without blood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of a woman who miscarries a piece of tissue, uncertain whether it is a birth or a zivah, and rules that she brings a sacrifice that is not eaten.
Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the sacrifice is eaten, because it is impossible for the womb to open without blood.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on colored pieces
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on colored pieces
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a version where Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel limits Rabbi Yehuda's impurity to a piece of four types of blood. A baraita is brought listing colored pieces (red, black, green, white) where Rabbi Yehuda declares impurity even without blood, contradicting the limitation. The Gemara analyzes the baraita, concluding that Rabbi Yehuda disputes all colors.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel limited Rabbi Yehuda's impurity ruling to a piece of four types of blood, but other types are pure.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita brought by Rav Hoshaya that lists colored pieces (red, black, green, white) where Rabbi Yehuda declares impurity even without blood, contradicting the limitation.
The Gemara notes that the baraita lists all four colors and Rabbi Yehuda disputes all of them, not just red and black.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rabbi Yehuda only disputes red and black, asking who then teaches the green and white cases.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must be attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, who disputes all colors, thus contradicting the limitation.

items.text: Resolution: dispute over 'impossible without blood'
items.text_en: Resolution: dispute over 'impossible without blood'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the dispute is about the principle of 'impossible for the womb to open without blood', citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehoshua holds that view, while the first Tanna disagrees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda resolves that the dispute is about the principle of 'impossible for the womb to open without blood'.
The gemara cites a baraita where the first Tanna holds the woman brings a sacrifice that is not eaten, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds it is eaten because the womb cannot open without blood.

items.text: Tannaitic opinions on tearing the piece
items.text_en: Tannaitic opinions on tearing the piece
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings several baraitot: Sumchos (in the name of Rabbi Meir) and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya say to tear the piece; if blood is inside, she is impure. Rabbi Acha says if the inside reddens, she is impure. Rabbi Binyamin says if there is a bone, she is impure for childbirth. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says if there is congealed blood, she is impure. These opinions are compared to the earlier ones.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the case of a woman who miscarries a piece, and Sumchos in the name of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rule to tear it; if blood is inside, she is impure.
The Gemara explains that Sumchos agrees with the Rabbis that bleeding can occur without a birth, but is more stringent by requiring tearing even when blood is inside the piece.
A second baraita cites Rabbi Acha who says to tear the piece; if the inside reddens, she is impure.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Acha's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Acha's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Acha's position is like Sumchos but more stringent, requiring reddening rather than just blood inside.
A third baraita cites Rabbi Binyamin who says to tear the piece; if there is a bone inside, the mother is impure for childbirth, and Rav Chisda specifies this applies to a white piece.
Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says to tear the piece; if there is congealed blood inside, she is impure, and this is the most lenient of all the opinions.

items.text: Question about blood in a tube (שפופרת)
items.text_en: Question about blood in a tube (שפופרת)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether a woman who sees blood in a tube is impure. Rabbi Zeira answers that the verse says 'in her flesh' (בבשרה), not in a tube, and the word 'בבשרה' teaches both that impurity is from inside like outside and excludes a tube. The Gemara objects with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about blood in a piece, but distinguishes because women typically see blood in a piece, not in a tube.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether a woman who sees blood in a tube (שפופרת) is impure, presenting two possible interpretations of the verse 'בבשרה' (in her flesh).

Rabbi Zeira answers that the verse 'בבשרה' excludes a tube, and that the word 'בבשרה' (in her flesh) rather than 'בבשר' (in flesh) teaches both that impurity is from inside like outside and that a tube is excluded.

The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai that a woman who miscarries a piece (חתיכה) must tear it, and if it contains congealed blood she is impure, implying that blood inside a container can convey impurity.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing that women typically see blood in a piece (חתיכה), but not in a tube (שפופרת), so the tube is excluded.

items.text: Analysis: Is the tube case a Tannaitic dispute?
items.text_en: Analysis: Is the tube case a Tannaitic dispute?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the tube case might be a dispute between Tannaim, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says 'in her flesh' excludes a sac (שפיר) and a piece, while the first Tanna agrees but distinguishes between intact and torn pieces. The Rabbis hold that even torn, it is not menstrual blood. Abaye concludes that regarding a tube, all agree she is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the tube case might be a dispute between Tannaim.
A baraita is cited: the first Tanna rules that a woman who miscarries a piece is pure unless accompanied by blood, while Rabbi Eliezer says 'in her flesh' excludes a sac and a piece.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's position seems identical to the first Tanna, and clarifies that the baraita should read 'that Rabbi Eliezer says...' as a separate statement.

The Gemara explains that the Rabbis say this is not menstrual blood but blood of the piece, and the difference between the first Tanna and the Rabbis is whether a torn piece is considered 'in her flesh'.

The Gemara resolves: the first Tanna holds that 'in her flesh' excludes a sac and piece, but a torn piece is considered 'in her flesh' and impure; the Rabbis hold that even a torn piece is not menstrual blood, but actual menstrual blood is impure even in a tube.
Abaye concludes that regarding a tube, all agree she is pure.

items.text: Dispute about blood on a piece of flesh
items.text_en: Dispute about blood on a piece of flesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two interpretations of a prior dispute. Rava explains that all agree a woman does not typically see blood on a piece of flesh; the dispute is about a pure woman and whether the source is impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about whether a woman typically sees blood on a piece of flesh, presenting two opposing views.
Rava asserts that all agree a woman does not typically see blood on a piece of flesh.
Rava resolves that the dispute is about a pure woman and whether the source (מקור) is impure, with Rabbi Eliezer holding the blood is impure and the Rabbis holding the source is pure.

items.text: Question about semen emitted via a splinter
items.text_en: Question about semen emitted via a splinter
items.desc_en: Rabba asks Rav Huna whether one who sees a seminal emission via a splinter is impure. Rav Huna answers that the person himself is not impure except when the emission is at the opening of the membrum.

sub.desc_en: Rabba asks Rav Huna whether a man who sees a seminal emission via a splinter (קיסם) becomes impure, questioning whether the Torah's 'from him' (ממנו) requires direct bodily emission or includes any exit, even via an object.

Rav Huna answers that the person himself is not impure except when the emission is at the opening of the membrum (בחתימת פי האמה), implying that emission via a splinter does not convey impurity to the person.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding zavah and semen
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding zavah and semen
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the person is not impure, then semen should not interrupt the zavah count. Rav Huna explains that it does interrupt because it is impossible without some discharge of zivah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the person is only a touch-contactor (נוגע), then semen should not interrupt the zavah count.
The Gemara cites a baraita that equates semen to zivah in interrupting the count, based on the verse 'זאת תורת הזב'.
Rav Huna answers that semen interrupts because it is impossible without some discharge of zivah (צחצוחי זיבה).

items.text: Question about whether semen interrupts all seven days
items.text_en: Question about whether semen interrupts all seven days
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if semen should interrupt all seven days like zivah. It answers that a verse limits it to one day, and Rav Huna explains that pure zivah interrupts seven days, but zivah mixed with semen interrupts only one day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if semen interrupts the counting of zivah, why should it not interrupt all seven days like pure zivah? It cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'זאת תורת הזב' that semen also interrupts.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'לטהרה בה' limits the interruption to one day only, not seven.
Rav Huna explains that pure zivah (זיבה גמורה) interrupts seven days, but zivah mixed with semen (צחצוחי זיבה) interrupts only one day, as a decree of the verse.

items.text: Question about dry menstrual blood
items.text_en: Question about dry menstrual blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina asks Rabbi Elazar whether dry menstrual blood is impure. Rabbi Elazar cites a mishnah that menstrual blood is impure wet or dry. Rabbi Yosei clarifies he meant initially dry, and Rabbi Elazar cites another mishnah about a woman who miscarries various forms that must be placed in water.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina asks Rabbi Elazar whether dry menstrual blood is impure, posing two possible interpretations of the verse.
Rabbi Elazar answers by citing a mishnah that menstrual blood is impure both wet and dry.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's clarification
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's clarification
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei clarifies that his question was about blood that was initially dry, not blood that became dry after being wet.
Rabbi Elazar answers by citing another mishnah about a woman who miscarries various forms that must be placed in water, implying that initially dry forms are also impure.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's condition
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies that if the miscarried matter dissolves in water it is impure, arguing that even if it does not dissolve it should be impure. Rabba answers that when it does not dissolve, it is considered a separate entity (בריה בפני עצמה) and thus not impure.

items.text: Supporting baraitot from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if such a case exists, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok recounts two incidents brought by his father Abba from Tivon to Yavne: one of a woman miscarrying red peels and another of red hairs, both tested by dissolving in water. In both cases, the doctors said the source was an internal wound or mole, and the test determines impurity.

items.text: Resh Lakish's ruling on lukewarm water and the dispute with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's ruling on lukewarm water and the dispute with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the test must be done with lukewarm water (פושרין), and a baraita supports this. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one can crush it with saliva on the fingernail. Ravina explains the difference between them is whether the substance is crushed by pressure (מעוך על ידי הדחק).

items.text: Question about the duration of soaking
items.text_en: Question about the duration of soaking
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the soaking in lukewarm water must be for a full day (מעת לעת), as in the case of a creeping thing or carcass, or not, since blood is soft. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.text_en: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute in the case of fish-shaped miscarriages. Resh Lakish says the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, while Rabbi Yochanan says even Rabbi Yehuda would agree, as he only disputes regarding a piece (where blood congeals) but not a creature. A second version of the dispute is presented where both agree the Mishnah follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's reason for animal-shaped miscarriages
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's reason for animal-shaped miscarriages
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explaining Rabbi Meir's reasoning: because the term 'יצירה' (formation) is used for animals as for humans, as in Genesis 2:19.

items.text: Hermeneutical debate on גזירה שוה between 'יצירה' and 'בריאה'
items.text_en: Hermeneutical debate on גזירה שוה between 'יצירה' and 'בריאה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the criterion is 'יצירה', then a woman miscarrying a tannin (sea monster) should also be impure, since 'בריאה' is used for it. The Gemara engages in a detailed discussion of the principles of גזירה שוה, distinguishing between 'יצירה' and 'בריאה', and between a גזירה שוה that is מופנה (free) from one side or two sides, citing Rabbi Yishmael's rule. The discussion concludes with the distinction between מופנה מצד אחד and מופנה משני צדדין.

items.text: Introduction of the principle of מופנה משני צדדין and its application
items.text_en: Introduction of the principle of מופנה משני צדדין and its application
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah made the word "בהמה" free (מופנה) from both sides to prevent deriving a leniency from a one-sided מופנה. Rav Acha bar Rava cites Rabbi Elazar's distinction between types of גזירה שווה: non-מופנה, מופנה מצד אחד, and מופנה משני צדדין, and the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis regarding מופנה מצד אחד. The Gemara then asks what practical difference exists for the Rabbis between מופנה מצד אחד and non-מופנה, and answers that when both are available without refutations, we prefer the מופנה מצד אחד.

items.text: Objection to the derivation from אדם
items.text_en: Objection to the derivation from אדם
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a refutation against the גזירה שוה: one can argue that the comparison to אדם is flawed because אדם is unique in being impure while alive.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's first explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's first explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Meir's reason is that the word "יצירה" is used for both animals and humans, implying a comparison.

items.text: Objections to Rabbi Yochanan's explanation and resolution
items.text_en: Objections to Rabbi Yochanan's explanation and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami challenges: if the word "יצירה" is the criterion, then a woman who miscarries a mountain-like form should be impure, since the verse says "יוצר הרים". Rabbi Yochanan responds that a mountain is not miscarried; it is a clod. Rabbi Ami further challenges with a wind-like form, citing "ובורא רוח". Rabbi Yochanan responds that we do not derive laws from the Torah using verses from the Prophets (דברי קבלה).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's second explanation: eyes like a human
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's second explanation: eyes like a human
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Meir's reason is that animals' eyes resemble human eyes. The Gemara objects: if so, a snake with a round eye should also be considered a viable fetus. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah in Masechet Nega'im distinguishes between a black eye (אוכמא) and a white eye (ציריא), implying that only a black eye is considered human-like.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's explanation and the dispute about birds
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's explanation and the dispute about birds
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai says Rabbi Meir's reason is that animals' eyes face forward like humans. The Gemara objects: birds' eyes do not face forward, yet Rabbi Meir considers some birds impure. Abaye answers that this applies only to קרייא and קיפופא (types of birds with forward-facing eyes). A baraita from Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus is cited, and the Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Meir agrees with the Rabbis regarding other birds.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the distinction for birds
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the distinction for birds
items.desc_en: A baraita states: for Rabbi Meir, a miscarriage of an animal is a viable fetus; for the Rabbis, it is not. For birds, it is uncertain (תיבדק). The Gemara clarifies that this uncertainty is for the Rabbis, who consider קרייא and קיפופא as viable because they have eyelids like humans.

items.text: Question about betrothal and the viability of the animal fetus
items.text_en: Question about betrothal and the viability of the animal fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: according to Rabbi Meir, if a woman miscarries an animal, is it considered a viable offspring such that if her father accepted betrothal for her, she is forbidden to her sister? The Gemara notes that Rav Yehuda said Rabbi Meir only said this because the species survives, not that the individual lives. Rav Acha bar Yaakov comments that Rabbi Yirmeya almost made Rabbi Zeira laugh, but he did not.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Fetal forms and their halachic status
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Fetal forms and their halachic status
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various fetal forms (like a sandal, afterbirth, or shaped fetus) and rules that a subsequent birth is the firstborn for inheritance but not for priestly gifts, unless the first was a non-viable sandal or afterbirth. It also debates whether a fetus resembling an animal is a valid offspring.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Is a human fetus in an animal womb viable?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Is a human fetus in an animal womb viable?
items.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava asks Abaye: according to Rabbi Meir who says an animal fetus in a woman's womb is viable, what about a human fetus in an animal womb? The practical issue is whether it can be eaten. Abaye attempts to resolve from Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about a dove found in a slaughtered animal.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution: Comparing dove and human fetus cases
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution: Comparing dove and human fetus cases
items.desc_en: Abaye notes the dove case lacks hooves, while the human fetus in an animal womb has hooves, so the analogy fails. He then cites a Mishnah where Sages require a human face for viability, implying a human fetus in an animal womb is not viable.

items.text: Dispute over required facial features for viability
items.text_en: Dispute over required facial features for viability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Jeremiah bar Abba reports Rav's ruling that all agree a goat-faced human body is invalid, but dispute arises over a human face with one animal-like eye: Rabbi Meir requires full human form, Sages accept any human face. The Gemara notes a Tannaitic dispute mirroring this.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: 'All form' vs 'From form' in Tannaitic sources
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: 'All form' vs 'From form' in Tannaitic sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one Tanna says 'all form of a face' (כֹּל צוּרַת) while another says 'from the form' (מִצּוּרַת). Rabbi Jeremiah bar Abba resolves that both are valid, just different phrasing. Abaye then explains the practical difference: 'all form' requires all features, 'from form' suffices with one.

items.text: Rava's rulings on fetal form and purity
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on fetal form and purity
items.desc_en: Rava rules: a fetus created with one eye and one thigh from the side renders the mother impure; in the middle, pure. A perforated womb renders impure; an sealed womb pure. These relate to the Mishnah's discussion of 'atimus' (sealed) vs 'nakuv' (perforated) forms.

items.text: Baraita: Defining 'atimus' (sealed) fetal form
items.text_en: Baraita: Defining 'atimus' (sealed) fetal form
items.desc_en: A Baraita defines 'atimus' as a fetus from which enough flesh must be removed to cause death. Rabbi Zakai specifies the amount: a needle's puncture. This connects to the Mishnah's rule that an 'atimus' fetus does not render the mother impure for childbirth.

items.text: Opening dispute on the definition of a formed fetus
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the definition of a formed fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan (citing Rabbi Yosei ben Yehoshua) argue about the anatomical landmark that determines a viable birth: up to the knees, up to the navel, or up to the anus.

items.text: Gemara clarifies the practical differences between the opinions
items.text_en: Gemara clarifies the practical differences between the opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the halakhic difference between Rabbi Zakkai and Rabbi Yannai (whether a tereifah can live), and between Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan (based on Rabbi Elazar's ruling about a missing thigh and socket).

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Giddel's rulings on miscarriages
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Giddel's rulings on miscarriages
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the dispute applies only when the fetus is expelled feet-first, but head-first even a small amount renders the mother pure. Rav Giddel cites Rabbi Yochanan that a closed skull or a palm-like shape renders the mother pure.

items.text: Dispute about a miscarried fetus with smeared face
items.text_en: Dispute about a miscarried fetus with smeared face
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue whether a fetus with a smeared face renders the mother impure. Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita about a cut hand or foot to challenge Reish Lakish. Rav Pappi clarifies the dispute is about a 'smeared' face, not 'smudged', and the positions are reversed.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's sons and the practical ruling
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's sons and the practical ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya's sons ruled a case of a 'smeared face' as impure, but their father rebuked them, explaining that such a stringency leads to leniency by granting the woman days of purity.

items.text: Dispute about a creature with two backs and two spines
items.text_en: Dispute about a creature with two backs and two spines
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue whether such a creature is a valid birth for a woman (Rav: no, Shmuel: yes) and whether it is forbidden to eat in an animal (Rav: forbidden, Shmuel: permitted). The Gemara explains their dispute is based on the interpretation of the Torah's term 'shasu'ah'.

items.text: Gemara challenges Rav and Shmuel with a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara challenges Rav and Shmuel with a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita lists forbidden animal fetuses and excludes one with two backs and spines. The Gemara questions whether this exclusion means it is permitted in the womb. Rav and Shmuel each resolve the baraita according to their own positions.

items.text: Shmuel's resolution regarding a fetus with two backs and two spines
items.text_en: Shmuel's resolution regarding a fetus with two backs and two spines
items.desc_en: Shmuel resolves his own statement: a fetus born at four months for a small animal or eight months for a large animal is forbidden only if its months were not completed, but if completed it is permitted. However, a fetus with two backs and two spines is forbidden even if its months were completed, but permitted while still in the womb.

items.text: Baraita on a miscarried body with uncut limbs and Rav's addition
items.text_en: Baraita on a miscarried body with uncut limbs and Rav's addition
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav: a woman who miscarries a body that is not cut or a head that is not cut might be impure with childbirth impurity, but the verse teaches that only those fit for circumcision on the eighth day are considered, excluding these. Rav added: and one with two backs and two spines.

items.text: Rav Huna advises against following Shmuel's leniency
items.text_en: Rav Huna advises against following Shmuel's leniency
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba intended to rule leniently like Shmuel, but Rav Huna warned him that this leniency leads to a stringency (requiring days of purity), and advised him to follow Rav, as the halakha follows Rav in prohibitions, whether lenient or stringent.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on whether a large animal can give birth at seven months
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on whether a large animal can give birth at seven months
items.desc_en: Rava raises a question: a woman can give birth at nine or seven months; can a large animal give birth at seven months? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak suggests a proof from Shmuel's statement, but the Gemara clarifies that Shmuel's statement refers to a small animal, not a large one. The Gemara then explains why the statement was necessary even for a small animal.

items.text: Ruling on a miscarriage resembling a Lilith
items.text_en: Ruling on a miscarriage resembling a Lilith
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: a woman who miscarries a creature resembling a Lilith is impure with childbirth impurity; it is a fetus but has wings. A baraita supports this with a story from Simonia.

items.text: Ruling on a miscarriage resembling a snake and the lesson about giving a reason
items.text_en: Ruling on a miscarriage resembling a snake and the lesson about giving a reason
items.desc_en: Chanina ben Rabbi Yehoshua's brother ruled that a woman who miscarries a snake-like creature is impure. Rabbi Yehoshua initially sent for him, but later, after his daughter-in-law questioned him, he remembered that Chanina had ruled based on the round eye. Abaye learns that a scholar should give a reason for his ruling so that when reminded, he will remember.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on a sac filled with liquid or sandal/shi-lya
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on a sac filled with liquid or sandal/shi-lya
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman who miscarries a sac filled with water, blood, or 'geninim' (colored matter) is not concerned for a fetus, but if it was 'merukam' (formed), she must observe impurity for male and female. A sandal or shilya also requires impurity. The Gemara questions why geninim is not suspected to be a dissolved fetus, and Abaye, Rava, and Rav Adda bar Ahava offer explanations.

items.text: Aggadic stories of Abba Shaul and the chain of tall scholars
items.text_en: Aggadic stories of Abba Shaul and the chain of tall scholars
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul recounts his experiences as a grave-digger, describing the effects of wine on bones, and stories of running after a deer through the bone of Og and standing in the eye socket of Absalom. The Gemara then notes that Abba Shaul was not a dwarf, listing a chain of tall scholars.

items.text: Opening analogy
items.text_en: Opening analogy
items.desc_en: A parable about a ferryman standing up to his waist while others stand only to his chest, setting the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a parable: the ferryman of Pumbedita stands up to his waist in water, while everyone else stands only up to his chest.

items.text: Rabbi's ruling on a sac filled with flesh
items.text_en: Rabbi's ruling on a sac filled with flesh
items.desc_en: Rabbi is asked about a woman who miscarries a sac filled with flesh. He says he hasn't heard. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei reports his father's ruling: if filled with blood she is a niddah, if filled with flesh she is impure due to childbirth. Rabbi questions the authority, suspecting it follows Rabbi Yehoshua's view.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Rabbi about the status of a woman who miscarries a sac filled with flesh.
Rabbi responds that he has not heard a ruling on this matter.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's report
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's report
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei reports his father's ruling: a sac filled with blood renders her a niddah, filled with flesh renders her impure due to childbirth.
Rabbi objects that the ruling is not novel and may follow Rabbi Yehoshua's rejected view, so he does not accept it.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about a non-formed sac
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about a non-formed sac
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehoshua says a non-formed sac is a viable birth, while the Sages say it is not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting the dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua considers a non-formed sac a viable birth, while the Sages disagree.

items.text: Amoraic dispute about the scope of the dispute
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute about the scope of the dispute
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi debate whether the dispute applies to a cloudy (akur) or clear (tzalul) sac. A query is raised but remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states in the name of Rabbi Oshaya that the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and the Sages applies only to a cloudy (עכור) sac, but for a clear (צלול) sac, all agree it is not a viable fetus.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees and asserts that the dispute applies specifically to a clear (צלול) sac.

The Gemara raises an unresolved query: does Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi mean that the dispute is only about a clear sac, while all agree a cloudy sac is a fetus, or that the dispute applies to both cases?
The query remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Proof from a verse about skin
items.text_en: Proof from a verse about skin
items.desc_en: A baraita citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya from a verse about God making skin garments for Adam is brought to argue that a sac without skin is not a viable birth. The Gemara deduces that the dispute is specifically about a clear sac.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is brought citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's interpretation of the verse about God making skin garments for Adam, teaching that God only creates skin for a human once the body is formed.
The Gemara deduces from the baraita that the matter depends on the presence of skin, regardless of whether the sac is clear or cloudy.
The Gemara resolves the objection by arguing that the verse is necessary only if the dispute is about a clear sac, proving that the dispute is indeed about a clear sac.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the dispute is only about a cloudy sac, but for a clear sac all agree it is not a viable birth. Rava challenges from a baraita about animal signs, and the Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehoshua's doubt is only rabbinic, leading to stringency in different cases.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the dispute (between Rabbi Yehoshua and the Sages) is only about a cloudy sac (עָכוּר), but for a clear sac (צָלוּל) all agree it is not a viable birth.

Rava challenges Rav Nachman from a baraita that lists signs of birth in animals: if the dispute were only about a cloudy sac, why would a clear sac exempt a woman but not an animal, since the reasoning is the same?

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehoshua's position is only a doubt (סְפֵק), not a certainty, so he rules stringently in each case: for a woman regarding טומאה (ritual impurity), for an animal regarding איסור (prohibition of shearing and working), and for monetary matters (בכור) leniently.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yehoshua's doubt is only rabbinic (מִדְּרַבָּנַן), and the verse cited earlier is merely an אסמכתא (scriptural support), not a biblical source.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's practical ruling
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's practical ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina bar Shelemia asks Rav which opinion he follows. Rav says in either case she need not be concerned. Shmuel says she must be concerned, consistent with his practice of examining a sac with a hair to determine if it is a viable birth.

sub.text: Rav Chanina bar Shelemia's question to Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanina bar Shelemia's question to Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina bar Shelemia asks Rav which opinion he follows among the conflicting Amoraim.
Rav rules that in either case (cloudy or clear sac) the woman need not be concerned about impurity.
Shmuel rules that she must be concerned in either case, consistent with his practice of examining a sac with a hair to determine if it is a viable birth.

items.text: Description of a formed sac
items.text_en: Description of a formed sac
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's phrase 'if it was formed' is explained: Abba Shaul and Rabbi Chiya describe the features of a formed sac, including eyes like fly specks, nostrils, mouth, and body shape, and the verse from Job is cited. The Gemara notes that one does not test it with water because water is harsh.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by defining a formed sac (שפיר מרוקם) and cites Abba Shaul's description: its initial formation begins from the head, with two eyes like fly specks.
Rabbi Chiya adds that the two eyes are distant from each other, and the two nostrils are like two fly specks.
Rabbi Chiya further describes the nostrils as close together, the mouth stretched like a hair, the body like a lentil, and for a female the body is judged like a barley grain lengthwise.
The baraita notes that the formed sac has no cut limbs, and cites the verse from Job (10:10-12) describing embryonic formation.
The Gemara concludes that one does not test the formed sac with water because water is harsh and would dissolve it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Testing with oil
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Testing with oil
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a miscarried fetus is not immediately discarded but is examined with oil in sunlight to determine its sex.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abba Shaul's method
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abba Shaul's method
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to examine the fetus to determine if it is male or female. Abba Shaul bar Nash (or bar Remes) answers: insert a smooth stick and see if it catches; if so, it is male.

items.text: Rav Nachman's limitation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's limitation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha limits the test: it works only when probing from below upward, not from the sides, as the sides might be the walls of the womb.

items.text: Rav Adda's baraita and Rav Nachman's objection
items.text_en: Rav Adda's baraita and Rav Nachman's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah teaches a baraita: if the fetus is female, it is judged like a split barley grain. Rav Nachman objects that it might be the tube of the testes. Abaye retorts that if the testes themselves are unknown, how can the tube be known?

items.text: Rabbi Amram's baraita on limbs
items.text_en: Rabbi Amram's baraita on limbs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Amram teaches a baraita describing the fetus's thighs and arms as like threads of crimson, with specific comparisons to the woof and warp of a garment.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on waiting for hair
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on waiting for hair
items.desc_en: Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda not to rule on a case until the fetus grows hair. The Gemara questions this, citing Shmuel's own statement that one must be concerned for both male and female. Rav Ammi bar Shmuel explains: she is concerned, but we do not give her days of purity until it grows hair. The Gemara then questions whether Shmuel was uncertain, citing a case where he calculated 41 days and declared the child conceived during niddah, but concludes that Shmuel is different because he is a great man.

items.text: Baraita on sandal and halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Baraita on sandal and halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions a sandal (flat fetus). A baraita describes it as resembling a sea fish or a tongue of a large ox. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it requires a face. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that a sandal requires a face, and Rav Adda citing Rav Yosef citing Rabbi Yitzchak adds that even from behind, like a person whose face is turned backward.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: In the days of Rabbi Yannai, they sought to purify a sandal without a face. Rabbi Yannai said: You have purified the offspring! The Gemara objects that a baraita already requires a face. Rav Bibi bar Abaye citing Rabbi Yochanan explains that this mishnah was taught based on the testimony of Rabbi Nechunyah. Rabbi Zeira notes that he and Rav Bibi were present when Rabbi Yochanan said this, and Rav Bibi merited to say it first.

items.text: Why mention sandal if always with a child?
items.text_en: Why mention sandal if always with a child?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions sandal separately, since a sandal always comes with a child. It answers that the case is where a male child is born with it. One might think that since the woman's seed determines a male, the sandal is also male, but the Mishnah teaches that both may have been emitted simultaneously, one male and one female. Alternatively, if the female child is born before sunset and the sandal after, she counts a separate niddah period for each.

items.text: Return to Mishnah text
items.text_en: Return to Mishnah text
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah's phrase 'sandal' as taught.

items.text: Question about the sandal in the context of firstborns
items.text_en: Question about the sandal in the context of firstborns
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Regarding the sandal mentioned in the Mishnah about firstborns, what is the practical halakhic implication?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Regarding the sandal mentioned in the Mishnah about firstborns, what is the practical halakhic implication?

items.text: Answer: Firstborn status for inheritance, not for priest
items.text_en: Answer: Firstborn status for inheritance, not for priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: The sandal's halakhic implication is that if a live birth follows the sandal, the live birth is a firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the sandal's halakhic implication regarding firstborn status is that a live birth following a sandal is a firstborn for inheritance (בְּכוֹר לְנַחֲלָה) but not for the priest (וְאֵין בְּכוֹר לְכֹהֵן).

items.text: Question and answer about the sandal in the context of sin-offerings
items.text_en: Question and answer about the sandal in the context of sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Regarding the sandal mentioned in the Mishnah about sin-offerings, what is the halakhic implication? It answers: If a woman gives birth to a live child through the side of the womb (caesarean) and a sandal through the natural birth canal, she brings a sin-offering for the sandal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Regarding the sandal mentioned in the Mishnah about sin-offerings, what is the halakhic implication?
The Gemara answers: If a woman gives birth to a live child through the side of the womb (caesarean) and a sandal through the natural birth canal, she brings a sin-offering for the sandal.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's objection and Rabbi Yirmeya's alternative answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's objection and Rabbi Yirmeya's alternative answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Shimon, who considers a child born by caesarean a viable birth, the previous answer fails. Rabbi Yirmeya offers an alternative: the sandal's implication is for a case where the woman gives birth to a live child while still a gentile and then a sandal after converting, so she brings a sin-offering for the sandal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Shimon, who considers a child born by caesarean a fully viable birth (ולד מעליא), what can be said to explain the halacha of the sandal in the context of kareitot?

Rabbi Yirmeya answers: the sandal's implication is for a case where the woman gave birth to a live child while still a gentile, and then a sandal after converting, so she brings a sin-offering for the sandal.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Pappa object: Are these distinctions valid? A baraita states that when a sandal and a live child emerge, they are always intertwined. Rav Pappa answers: The live child wraps around the sandal at its side and slides it toward its head. For firstborns, they emerge head-first, so the sandal comes out first. For sin-offerings, they emerge feet-first, so the live child comes out first.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Pappa object: Are these distinctions valid? A baraita states that when a sandal and a live child emerge, they are always intertwined.

Rav Pappa answers: The live child wraps around the sandal at its side and slides it toward its head. For firstborns, they emerge head-first, so the sandal comes out first. For sin-offerings, they emerge feet-first, so the live child comes out first.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Tahlifa's alternative explanation in the name of Rava
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Tahlifa's alternative explanation in the name of Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Tahlifa says in the name of Rava: Even if the fetuses are tightly packed, reverse the rulings. For firstborns, they emerge feet-first; the live child clings and does not emerge, while the sandal slips out. For sin-offerings, they emerge head-first; once the live child's head emerges, it is considered a birth, but the sandal requires most of its body to emerge.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Tahlifa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Tahlifa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Tahlifa presents Rava's alternative explanation: even if fetuses are tightly packed, reverse the rulings — for firstborns, the live child clings and does not emerge while the sandal slips out; for sin-offerings, once the live child's head emerges it is a birth, but the sandal requires most of its body to emerge.

items.text: Mishnah: The placenta and its tumah
items.text_en: Mishnah: The placenta and its tumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If a placenta is found in a house, the house is impure, not because the placenta is a child, but because there is no placenta without a child. Rabbi Shimon says: The child may have dissolved before it emerged.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a placenta found in a house renders the house impure, not because the placenta itself is a child, but because there is no placenta without a child.
Rabbi Shimon dissents, arguing that the child may have dissolved (נִימּוֹק) before it emerged, so the placenta does not necessarily indicate a child.

items.text: Baraita on the appearance and size of the placenta, and other items with a tefach measure
items.text_en: Baraita on the appearance and size of the placenta, and other items with a tefach measure
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the placenta's shape and states it is never less than a tefach. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel compares it to a gizzard. Another baraita lists five items with a minimum size of a tefach: placenta, shofar, spine, sukkah wall, and hyssop. The Gemara explains each: the shofar must be a tefach to be visible, the spine of the lulav must protrude a tefach from the myrtle, the sukkah's third wall can be a tefach, and hyssop for sprinkling must be a tefach.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes the placenta's shape and states it is never less than a tefach.
Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel compares the placenta to a chicken gizzard with small tubes emerging from it.
A baraita lists five items with a minimum size of a tefach: placenta, shofar, spine, sukkah wall, and hyssop.
The Gemara explains that the shofar must be a tefach so that it is visible when held in the hand.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of spine (Rabbi Parnakh citing Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of spine (Rabbi Parnakh citing Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the spine of the lulav must protrude a tefach from the myrtle.
The Gemara explains that the sukkah's third wall can be as small as a tefach.
The Gemara explains that hyssop for sprinkling must be a tefach, citing Rabbi Chiyya.

items.text: Discussion about the number of tefach measures and other cases
items.text_en: Discussion about the number of tefach measures and other cases
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa reports that Sheilah of Kfar Tamarta taught three Mishnayot and two halakhot with a tefach measure. Abaye corrects: say one halakha (Rabbi Chiyya's hyssop). The Gemara asks if there are more, citing a tefach-square that brings tumah and a stone from a furnace that is a tefach. It answers: we are discussing items that are useless if less than a tefach, but those are different (the stone is considered a handle).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa reports that Sheilah of Kfar Tamarta taught three Mishnayot and two halakhot with a tefach measure.
The Gemara objects that Sheilah's list actually contains only one halakha, not two.
Abaye corrects the count: say one halakha, namely Rabbi Chiyya's teaching that hyssop requires a tefach.
The Gemara asks whether there are not more tefach measures, citing the case of a tefach-square that brings tum'ah and interposes against tum'ah.
The Gemara answers that we are discussing items whose measure is a tefach, not a tefach-square.
The Gemara asks further about the stone from a furnace that is a tefach and connects for tum'ah.
The Gemara answers that we are discussing items useless if less than a tefach, but the stone is considered a handle (יד תנור) even when smaller.

items.text: Minimum size of a small oven
items.text_en: Minimum size of a small oven
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the initial and remaining size of an oven, with Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagreeing. Rabbi Yannai explains that 'any amount' for a small oven is a handbreadth, as they make 'תנורי בנות טפח', and this is not part of the dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that an oven's initial and remaining size is four handbreadths, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages distinguish between a large oven (initial size four) and a small oven (initial size any amount, remaining size in its majority).
Rabbi Yannai explains that 'any amount' for a small oven is a handbreadth, because they make 'תנורי בנות טפח' (ovens for girls a handbreadth), and this is not part of the dispute.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute and excluding other cases
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute and excluding other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara realizes that the previous statement is itself a dispute, as the continuation mentions Rabbi Yehuda's opinion. It then addresses potential objections about other items with a handbreadth measure (e.g., מסגרת, כפורת, קורה), explaining that the discussion excludes cases where the measure is written or rabbinic, focusing only on written but unspecified measures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous statement is itself a dispute, as the continuation cites Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
The Gemara raises objections about other items with a handbreadth measure (מסגרת, כפורת, קורה) and answers that the discussion excludes cases where the measure is written or rabbinic.
The Gemara resolves the objection by stating that the discussion focuses only on written but unspecified measures, excluding rabbinic measures.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement about the placenta and Rav's apparent contradiction
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement about the placenta and Rav's apparent contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta reports in the name of Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that for the first three days the placenta is attributed to the fetus, but afterward one suspects another fetus. Rav Kahana objects because Rav said one fetus does not delay another. Rav Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by specifying that Rav's statement applies to a miscarriage followed by a placenta, but if a live birth preceded the placenta, there is no concern even after ten days.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta quoting Rav Yehuda quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta quoting Rav Yehuda quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta, sitting before Rav Kahana, reports in the name of Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that for the first three days the placenta is attributed to the fetus, but afterward one suspects another fetus.
Rav Kahana objects, citing Rav's own statement that one fetus does not delay another, implying the placenta cannot be attributed to a later fetus.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's tentative answer
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's tentative answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak is silent, then suggests tentatively that the contradiction might be resolved by distinguishing between a miscarriage (נפל) and a live birth (בן קיימא).

sub.text: Rav Kahana's definitive resolution quoting Rav explicitly
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's definitive resolution quoting Rav explicitly
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana provides Rav's explicit ruling: if a miscarriage preceded the placenta, the three-day rule applies; but if a live birth preceded the placenta, there is no concern for another fetus even after ten days.

items.text: Shmuel's inquiry about Rav's view on the placenta
items.text_en: Shmuel's inquiry about Rav's view on the placenta
items.desc_en: Shmuel and Rav's students are sitting when Rav Yosef bar Menashya from Devil approaches. Shmuel asks him what Rav said about the placenta. He reports that Rav said the placenta is only attributed to a viable fetus. Shmuel then asks all of Rav's students, who confirm this, and Shmuel later sees Rav Yehuda's embarrassment.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Shmuel, Rav's students, and Rav Yehuda are sitting, and they anticipate the arrival of Rav Yosef bar Menashya from Devil, whom they plan to interrogate.
When Rav Yosef bar Menashya arrives, Shmuel asks him what Rav said about the placenta.
Rav Yosef bar Menashya reports that Rav said the placenta is only attributed to a viable fetus (דבר של קיימא).
Shmuel asks all of Rav's students, and they confirm that this is indeed what Rav said.
Shmuel then sees Rav Yehuda's embarrassment, concluding the episode.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's question about a placenta with a non-human form
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's question about a placenta with a non-human form
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul asks Rabbi whether a placenta from a miscarriage of a raven-like form is attributed to it. Rabbi answers that it is only attributed to a species that normally has a placenta. Rabbi Yosei then asks about a placenta attached to the form, and Rabbi initially says it is not relevant. Rabbi Yosei cites a baraita that if the placenta is attached to a non-human form, there is no concern for another fetus, but if not attached, there is concern, and he challenges Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul asks Rabbi whether a placenta from a miscarriage of a raven-like form is attributed to it.
Rabbi answers that the placenta is only attributed to a species that normally has a placenta.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's follow-up question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's follow-up question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul asks about a placenta attached to the non-human form.
Rabbi initially says the question about an attached placenta is not relevant.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's objection with a baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's objection with a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul cites a baraita that distinguishes between attached and unattached placenta regarding concern for another fetus, challenging Rabbi's dismissal.

items.text: Opening challenge: the stringency of two births
items.text_en: Opening challenge: the stringency of two births
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a contradiction: a previous ruling stated that a placenta indicates a birth, but here it is said that a placenta might be from a dissolved fetus. This is presented as a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a contradiction: a previous ruling that a placenta indicates a birth is challenged by the possibility that the placenta might be from a dissolved fetus, concluding with 'תְּיוּבְתָּא' (a refutation).

items.text: Three traditions on how long a placenta can be attached
items.text_en: Three traditions on how long a placenta can be attached
items.desc_en: Three Amoraim report traditions about how long after a birth a placenta can be attached and still be considered from that birth: Shmuel says up to ten days, Rabbi Yochanan says up to twenty-three (or twenty-four), and Rabbi Yitzchak says up to thirty-three (or thirty-four).

sub.text: Rabbah bar Sheilah citing Rav Mattanah citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Sheilah citing Rav Mattanah citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Shmuel reports a tradition that a placenta was attached to a child for up to ten days, but only when the placenta comes after the child.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports a tradition of attachment up to twenty-three days, and Rav Yosef corrects him to twenty-four days.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Avira citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Avira citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak reports a tradition of a child delayed after its fellow for thirty-three days, and Rav Yosef corrects him to thirty-four days.

items.text: Reconciling the traditions with different views on gestation
items.text_en: Reconciling the traditions with different views on gestation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how these traditions fit with the view that a woman can give birth at nine months in parts. It then suggests reversing the traditions: the longer period refers to the placenta, the shorter to the fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the traditions of delayed births fit with the view that a woman gives birth at nine months in parts, and challenges the view that she does not give birth in parts.
The Gemara answers by reversing the traditions: the longer period (33 days) refers to the placenta, the shorter (23 days) to the fetus.

items.text: A case of a three-month delay and its explanation
items.text_en: A case of a three-month delay and its explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda reports a case where one fetus was delayed three months after another. The Gemara objects that a woman cannot become pregnant again while already pregnant. Abaye explains that it was a single drop that split, with one part forming early and the other late.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rav Menachem
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rav Menachem
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda reports in the name of Rav Menachem a case where one fetus was delayed three months after another, and the children (Yehuda and Chizkiya, sons of Rabbi Chiya) are alive and present in the study hall.
The Gemara objects: the master said that a woman cannot become pregnant while already pregnant, so how could one fetus be delayed three months after another?
Abaye explains that it was a single drop that split into two, with one part forming at the beginning of seven months and the other at the end of nine months.

items.text: Dispute about a placenta found in a house
items.text_en: Dispute about a placenta found in a house
items.desc_en: A Tannaitic dispute: if a placenta is found in a house, Rabbi Meir declares the house impure because a placenta always accompanies a fetus, even if the fetus dissolved. Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon declare it pure. The Sages challenge Rabbi Meir with a case where the placenta was brought in a bowl, and he concedes. They argue that the same logic should apply to a house, but Rabbi Meir distinguishes between one-time dissolution and two-time dissolution.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the ruling: a placenta found in a house renders the house impure, not because the placenta itself is a fetus, but because no placenta exists without a fetus — this is Rabbi Meir's position.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon dispute Rabbi Meir and declare the house pure.
The Sages challenge Rabbi Meir: if the placenta was brought in a bowl to an outer house, he concedes it is pure.
The Sages argue that the same logic should apply to the inner house, since the fetus dissolved there as well.
Rabbi Meir distinguishes between one-time dissolution (in the bowl) and two-time dissolution (in the house), maintaining his position.

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that any impurity mixed with a different type is nullified. Rav Pappa then notes that this is also the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, and he is laughed at for stating the obvious. He defends himself by citing a verse about not speaking before one's teacher.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa, sitting behind Rav Beivai before Rav Hamnuna, explains that Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is that any impurity mixed with a different type is nullified.
Rav Pappa adds that this is also the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, and the others laugh at him for stating the obvious.
Rav Pappa defends himself by citing a verse about not speaking before one's teacher, asserting that even such an obvious point should be said.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Shimon from a baraita about a kav of decay
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Shimon from a baraita about a kav of decay
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that a kav of decay mixed with any amount of earth is pure, consistent with his view. Rabbah explains that the Sages of Rav's school said it is impossible for two particles of earth not to outnumber one particle of decay, but Rabbah argues the opposite: two particles of decay outnumber one of earth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that a kav of decay mixed with any amount of earth is pure, consistent with his general position.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Shimon's ruling.

sub.text: Rabbah's report of the Sages of Rav's school
sub.text_en: Rabbah's report of the Sages of Rav's school
sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports that the Sages of Rav's school argued that two particles of earth inevitably outnumber one particle of decay, making the mixture impure, but Rabbah rejects this reasoning.
Rabbah counters that, on the contrary, two particles of decay outnumber one particle of earth, supporting Rabbi Shimon's ruling of purity.

items.text: Rabbah's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbah's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that Rabbi Shimon's leniency regarding a k'zayis of rot mixed with any amount of dirt is based on the principle 'sofo k'techilaso' — just as at the beginning (the corpse) it becomes a different entity (ganngilon), so too at the end (the rot) it becomes a different entity (ganngilon) when mixed with dirt.

items.text: Definition of a corpse that produces rot
items.text_en: Definition of a corpse that produces rot
items.desc_en: A baraita defines which corpses produce rot (rakav) and which do not: one buried naked in a marble coffin or on a stone floor produces rot, while one buried in a shroud, a wooden coffin, or on a brick floor does not. Rot applies only to a corpse, excluding a slain person.

items.text: The Mishnah and the need for both cases
items.text_en: The Mishnah and the need for both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the core dispute: a k'zayis of rot mixed with any dirt is tamei according to the Rabbis, but Rabbi Shimon declares it tahor. Similarly, if a k'zayis of rot is scattered in a house, the house is tamei according to the Rabbis, but Rabbi Shimon declares it tahor. The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary to avoid assuming the Rabbis would concede in the other case.

items.text: Another baraita: a k'zayis plus more grave dirt
items.text_en: Another baraita: a k'zayis plus more grave dirt
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a k'zayis plus more of grave dirt is tamei, but Rabbi Shimon declares it tahor. The Rabbis' reasoning is that it is impossible for such a measure of grave dirt not to contain a k'zayis of rot.

items.text: Applying Rabbi Shimon's principle to the shilya and chararah
items.text_en: Applying Rabbi Shimon's principle to the shilya and chararah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is based on 'sofo k'techilaso', what is his reasoning regarding a shilya (stillborn sac)? Rabbi Yochanan answers: it is due to 'bittul b'rov' (nullification in the majority). Rabbi Yochanan then links Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that a large animal that discharged a blood clot (chararah) must be buried and is exempt from the firstborn. Rabbi Chiya teaches that this clot does not convey tumah through touch or carrying, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that this is also due to 'bittul b'rov'.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon concedes the mother is tamei leidah
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon concedes the mother is tamei leidah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami quotes Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Shimon agrees that the mother is tamei with the tumah of childbirth. An elder explains to Rabbi Ami that this is derived from the verse 'Isha ki tazria v'yaldah zachar' — even if she gave birth only to something resembling what she conceived, she is tamei leidah.

items.text: Reish Lakish's alternative explanation and Rabbi Yochanan's objection
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's alternative explanation and Rabbi Yochanan's objection
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains that a shilya is like a fetus whose form was disturbed by its waters, making it like a corpse whose form is disturbed (and thus tahor). Rabbi Yochanan challenges this, asking for a source that a corpse whose form is disturbed is tahor, and suggests a possible source from a case of a burned corpse with a preserved spine.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a burned fetus with intact skeleton
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a burned fetus with intact skeleton
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if the skeleton is not intact, the fetus is pure. Ravina and Rav Ashi debate the opposite inference: that if the skeleton is intact, small openings are pure, but if not, even small openings are impure because each could emit a limb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only when the skeleton is intact are small openings pure, implying that without an intact skeleton the fetus is pure.
Ravina and Rav Ashi counter-infer that if the skeleton is intact, small openings are pure, but if not, even small openings are impure because each could emit a limb.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna behind Rabbi Yochanan's view and defining 'skeleton intact'
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna behind Rabbi Yochanan's view and defining 'skeleton intact'
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Eliezer, who measures ash of a burned corpse by a quarter-log. Abaye, Rava, and Ravina then define a case where the skeleton remains intact: burning on a brazier, on coals, or merely charred.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether Rabbi Yochanan's view aligns with Rabbi Eliezer, who measures the ash of a burned corpse by a quarter-log.
The gemara asks for a concrete example of a corpse that was burned yet its skeleton remains intact.
Abaye answers that the case is when the corpse was burned on a brazier, so the skeleton remains intact.
Rava answers that the case is when the corpse was burned on coals, so the skeleton remains intact.
Ravina answers that the case is when the corpse was merely charred, so the skeleton remains intact.

items.text: Mishnah: Miscarriage of a severed limb and Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah: Miscarriage of a severed limb and Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who miscarries a severed hand or foot is impure with childbirth impurity, and we do not suspect it came from an amorphous body. Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna rule that she is not given days of purity, because perhaps her birth was distant.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a woman who miscarries a severed hand or foot is impure with childbirth impurity, and we do not suspect it came from an amorphous body.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna rule that she is not given days of purity, because perhaps her birth was distant.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects from a Mishnah that a woman who miscarries an unknown substance sits for both male and female, implying she does have days of purity. Abaye explains that if the Mishnah had mentioned niddah, one might think her offering is not eaten, so it teaches that it is eaten.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects from a Mishnah that a woman who miscarries an unknown substance sits for both male and female, implying she does have days of purity, and asks why the Mishnah did not also mention niddah.
Abaye explains that if the Mishnah had mentioned niddah, one might think her offering is not eaten, so it teaches that it is eaten.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a fetus that extended its hand and Rav Yehuda's objection
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a fetus that extended its hand and Rav Yehuda's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a fetus extended its hand and retracted it, the mother is impure with childbirth impurity, citing a verse. Rav Yehuda objects from a baraita that she is not concerned at all. Rav Nachman clarifies that Rav Huna meant she is concerned, but we do not give her days of purity until most of the fetus emerges. Abaye explains that the concern is rabbinic, and the verse is merely a support.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a fetus extended its hand and retracted it, the mother is impure with childbirth impurity, citing the verse 'וַיְהִי בְלִדְתָּהּ וַיִּתֶּן יָד' (and it was in her giving birth, and he put out a hand).
Rav Yehuda objects by citing a baraita that states if a fetus extended its hand, the mother is not concerned at all.
Rav Nachman clarifies that Rav Huna meant she is concerned (חוֹשֶׁשֶׁת), but we do not give her days of purity until most of the fetus emerges.
The gemara objects that the baraita explicitly says 'she is not concerned at all', contradicting Rav Nachman's interpretation.
Abaye resolves that she is not concerned at all from the Torah (מִדְּאוֹרָיְיתָא), but she is concerned rabbinically (מִדְּרַבָּנַן), and the verse is merely a support (אַסְמַכְתָּא).

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of tumtum, androgynos, and partial birth
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of tumtum, androgynos, and partial birth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman who miscarries a tumtum or androgynos sits for both male and female. If with a male or female, different rules apply. A fetus that emerges cut or crushed is considered born only after most emerges; if born normally, after most of the head, defined as the forehead.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: a woman who miscarries a tumtum or an androgynos sits the impure periods for both male and female.
The Mishnah continues: if a tumtum or androgynos was with a male, she sits for male and female; with a female, she sits for female only.
The Mishnah concludes: a fetus that emerges cut or crushed is considered born only after most of its body emerges; if born normally, only after most of the head, defined as the forehead.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy and Rabbi Yitzchak's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy and Rabbi Yitzchak's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state the case of tumtum with a male, since it already rules for tumtum alone. It explains that one might think, based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that if the woman emits seed first she bears a male, that the male indicates the tumtum is also male; so the Mishnah teaches that both may have emitted simultaneously, one male and one female.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to separately state the case of a tumtum with a male, since it already rules for a tumtum alone.

The Gemara answers that the extra case is necessary, because one might think based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that the male indicates the tumtum is also male; the Mishnah teaches that both may have emitted simultaneously, one male and one female.

items.text: Rav Nachman citing Rav: Laws of zav for tumtum and androgynos
items.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav: Laws of zav for tumtum and androgynos
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says in the name of Rav that a tumtum or androgynos who sees a discharge of white or red is not liable for entering the Temple, and terumah is not burned for them. If they see both colors together, they are still not liable for entering the Temple, but terumah is burned, based on the verse 'from male to female'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states in the name of Rav that a tumtum or androgynos who sees a white or red discharge is not liable for entering the Temple and terumah is not burned for them.
Rav Nachman adds that if they see both colors together, they are still not liable for entering the Temple, but terumah is burned, based on the verse 'from male to female'.

items.text: Opening citation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening citation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the verse "מִזָּכָר וְעַד נְקֵבָה תְּשַׁלֵּחוּ" excludes tumtum and androgynos, applying only to definite male or female zavim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the verse 'מִזָּכָר וְעַד נְקֵבָה תְּשַׁלֵּחוּ' to exclude tumtum and androgynos from the laws of zav, applying only to definite male or female.

items.text: Gemara's question and Ulla's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Ulla's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about tumtum and androgynos who see discharge, and asks if it supports the Mishnah's derivation. Ulla deflects, attributing the baraita to Rabbi Eliezer, who requires knowledge of the specific source of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a baraita about tumtum and androgynos who see discharge supports the Mishnah's derivation from the verse.
Ulla deflects, attributing the baraita to Rabbi Eliezer, who requires knowledge of the specific source of impurity.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva regarding the requirement to know the specific source of impurity. Rabbi Eliezer requires knowing whether the impurity came from a sheretz or neveilah, and similarly here whether from white or red discharge. Rabbi Akiva only requires awareness of impurity in general.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that one is liable only for forgetting the impurity of a sheretz (creeping creature), not for forgetting the Temple.
Rabbi Akiva rules that one is liable for forgetting the impurity itself, not for forgetting the Temple.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the positions of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva.
Chizkiyah explains that the difference is whether one must know if the impurity came from a sheretz or neveilah (carcass); Rabbi Eliezer requires this knowledge, Rabbi Akiva does not.
The Gemara applies the principle: just as Rabbi Eliezer requires knowing whether the impurity came from a sheretz or neveilah, so too here he requires knowing whether the discharge was white or red.
