For Rabbi Akiva, who holds that liability is based on awareness of impurity in general, here too liability is based on awareness of impurity alone, without specifying the color.

items.text: Rav's challenge and the inconsistency
items.text_en: Rav's challenge and the inconsistency
items.desc_en: Rav questions why the baraita exempts from liability for entering the Temple but burns terumah. If the verse excludes tumtum and androgynos from the laws of zav, then terumah should also not be burned. The Gemara notes a parallel verse that could also exclude them.

sub.desc_en: Rav asks why the baraita exempts a tumtum or hermaphrodite from liability for entering the Temple but burns terumah they touched, given the verse 'מִזָּכָר וְעַד נְקֵבָה תְּשַׁלֵּחוּ' (from male to female you shall send out) excludes them from Temple entry.

Rav objects that if the verse excludes them from Temple entry, then by the same logic the verse 'וְהַזָּב אֶת זוֹבוֹ לַזָּכָר וְלַנְּקֵבָה' (and the zav with his issue, to the male and to the female) should also exclude them from the laws of zav, so terumah should not be burned either.

items.text: First answer: Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation
items.text_en: First answer: Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse "לַזָּכָר וְלַנְּקֵבָה" is needed for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching about including a male or female leper for their spring-like issues. Another answer suggests it excludes clay vessels, per Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse 'לַזָּכָר וְלַנְּקֵבָה' is needed for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching about including a male or female leper for their spring-like issues.
Another answer suggests the verse excludes clay vessels, per Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Refinement of the derivation for Rav
items.text_en: Refinement of the derivation for Rav
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the verse were only for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching, it could have said "אָדָם". The phrase "מִזָּכָר וְעַד נְקֵבָה" teaches that anything that has purification in a mikveh is included, supporting Rav's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the verse 'לַזָּכָר וְלַנְּקֵבָה' is only for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching, then the Torah could have simply written 'אָדָם' (a person) instead.

The Gemara answers: if the Torah wrote 'אָדָם', one might exclude metal vessels, but they are already derived from 'כֹּל טָמֵא לָנָפֶשׁ'; therefore the terms 'זָכָר' and 'נְקֵבָה' are needed for Rav's teaching.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the entire verse is only for Rav's teaching, and the phrase 'מִזָּכָר וְעַד נְקֵבָה' teaches that anything with purification in a mikveh is included.

items.text: Clarification of the exclusion
items.text_en: Clarification of the exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the exclusion applies only to impurity that emanates from a male (zav), not to other impurities. The phrase "מִזָּכָר" limits the exclusion to that specific type of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the exclusion of tumtum and androgynos from being sent outside the camp applies only to impurity emanating from a male (zav), not to other impurities.

items.text: Comparison with valuations and conclusion
items.text_en: Comparison with valuations and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares to the verse about valuations, where "הַזָּכָר" excludes tumtum and androgynos, but only because it says "הַזָּכָר... וְאִם נְקֵבָה". Without that, the simple terms "זָכָר" and "נְקֵבָה" would not exclude them, as they are needed for other teachings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether every instance of 'מִזָּכָר עַד נְקֵבָה' (from male to female) is intended to exclude tumtum and androgynos, citing the case of valuations.
A baraita is cited regarding valuations, where 'הַזָּכָר' (the male) excludes tumtum and androgynos, but only because the verse also says 'וְאִם נְקֵבָה' (and if female).

The Gemara concludes that the exclusion in valuations depends on the specific phrase 'הַזָּכָר... וְאִם נְקֵבָה' (the male... and if female), not on the simple terms 'זָכָר' (male) and 'נְקֵבָה' (female), which are needed for other teachings.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on the head of a malformed fetus
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on the head of a malformed fetus
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a malformed or crushed fetus requires the majority to emerge to be considered born. Rabbi Elazar argues that even if the head emerges with the body, it does not exempt; Rabbi Yochanan holds that the head exempts only when it emerges alone, but if the head is with the body, the head exempts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the rule that a malformed or crushed fetus requires the majority to emerge to be considered born.
Rabbi Elazar argues that even if the head emerges with the malformed body, it does not exempt the fetus from needing the majority to emerge.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that the head exempts only when it emerges alone; if the head is with the body, the head exempts the fetus from needing the majority.

items.text: Attributing the dispute to Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Attributing the dispute to Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan hinges on Shmuel's statement that the head does not exempt in the case of fetuses. One opinion holds that Shmuel's rule applies only to a complete fetus, while the other extends it to a malformed one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan hinges on Shmuel's ruling that the head does not exempt in the case of fetuses.
The Gemara resolves that both agree on a complete fetus, but dispute a malformed one: one opinion holds Shmuel's rule applies only to a complete fetus, the other extends it to a malformed one.

items.text: Alternative version: Both reject Shmuel
items.text_en: Alternative version: Both reject Shmuel
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation states that both Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan reject Shmuel's ruling, and they agree that a properly formed fetus's head exempts; the dispute is only about a malformed fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the dispute, stating that the Mishnah's case of a malformed fetus implies that a properly formed fetus's head exempts from the laws of childbirth impurity.
The alternative version concludes that both Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan reject Shmuel's ruling that the head does not exempt in the case of miscarriages.

items.text: Independent tradition: Head as majority of limbs
items.text_en: Independent tradition: Head as majority of limbs
items.desc_en: Some teach this discussion independently: Rabbi Elazar says the head is not like a majority of limbs, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is, and they dispute based on Shmuel's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces an independent tradition of the dispute.
Rabbi Elazar states that the head is not like a majority of limbs.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the head is like a majority of limbs.
The gemara explains that they dispute based on Shmuel's ruling about the head not exempting in miscarriages.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a malformed or crushed fetus requires the majority to emerge, implying that a properly formed fetus's head exempts. This challenges Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that the head exempts even when with the body. Rabbi Yochanan reinterprets the Mishnah to refer to a malformed or complete but crushed fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing the Mishnah that a malformed or crushed fetus requires the majority to emerge, implying that a properly formed fetus's head exempts, which contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's position.
Rabbi Yochanan reinterprets the Mishnah to refer to a malformed or complete but crushed fetus, so that the head does not exempt even when the body is intact.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah uses the word 'אוֹ' (or), which distinguishes between a malformed and a crushed fetus, not treating them as the same category.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah means: a malformed or complete fetus, and both are crushed, so the majority is required.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid's explanations of the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid's explanations of the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yosei: the first Tanna requires the majority for a malformed fetus, but the head exempts a properly formed one; Rabbi Yosei requires the majority of a properly formed fetus. Rav Zevid objects and clarifies that Rabbi Yosei requires the majority of the head for viability.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yosei regarding the ruling for a malformed fetus.
Rav Pappa explains that the first Tanna requires the majority for a malformed fetus, but the head exempts a properly formed one, while Rabbi Yosei requires the majority of a properly formed fetus.
Rav Zevid objects that Rav Pappa's explanation implies that for a malformed fetus the majority does not exempt, contradicting the principle that the majority is like the whole.
Rav Zevid clarifies that Rabbi Yosei requires the majority of the head for viability, resolving the objection.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Zevid's interpretation
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Zevid's interpretation
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that a properly formed fetus's head exempts, and Rabbi Yosei requires the majority of the head for viability. The baraita further defines 'majority of the head' according to Rabbi Yosei, Abba Chanan, and others.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Zevid's interpretation: for a properly formed fetus the head exempts, and Rabbi Yosei requires the fetus to emerge in its proper form for viability.
The gemara asks what constitutes 'proper form for viability' and answers: when the majority of the head has emerged.
The gemara asks what constitutes the majority of the head, and Rabbi Yosei answers: when his temples emerge.

sub.text: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua defines the majority of the head as when his forehead emerges.
Some say (יש אומרים) that the majority of the head is when the 'horns of his head' (the fontanelles) become visible.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on a woman who miscarries an unknown substance
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on a woman who miscarries an unknown substance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman who miscarries an unknown substance observes the stringencies of both male and female, and if unsure if it was a fetus, also observes niddah. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that if she crossed a river and miscarried, she brings a sacrifice, following the majority of women who give birth to viable offspring. The Gemara challenges this from the Mishnah and from a case of an animal, resolving that the Mishnah deals with a woman not known to be pregnant, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's case is when she was known to be pregnant.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman who miscarries an unknown substance observes the stringencies of both male and female, and if unsure if it was a fetus, also observes niddah.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a woman who crossed a river and miscarried brings a sacrifice, following the majority of women who give birth to viable offspring.
The Gemara challenges from the Mishnah: why must she observe niddah if we follow the majority?
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with a woman not known to be pregnant, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's case is when she was known to be pregnant.
A baraita is cited: an animal that went out full and came back empty has a firstborn of uncertain status.
The Gemara objects: why is it uncertain? Follow the majority of animals that give birth to viable offspring.
Ravina answers: the majority is undermined because this animal did not discharge turbid liquids beforehand.

The Gemara objects: if all birthing animals discharge turbid liquids, then this animal's lack of discharge would prove it gave birth to a non-viable offspring, making the subsequent offspring a definite firstborn; rather, say that most birthing animals discharge, and since this one did not, the majority is undermined.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's objection
items.desc_en: When Ravin came, he reported that Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina raised an objection from a baraita, but he did not know what the objection was.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina raised an objection from a baraita, but Ravin does not know what the objection is, and the Gemara asks what it is.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of a woman who left full and returned empty, bringing three clean weeks and ten alternating weeks. Beit Shammai requires 95 immersions, Beit Hillel 35, and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says one immersion at the end suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who left full and returned empty, bringing three clean weeks and ten alternating weeks of impurity and purity.
Beit Shammai rules that she serves for 35 days and immerses 95 times.
Beit Hillel rules that she immerses only 35 times.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda rules that a single immersion at the end suffices.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Why not serve in the fourth week?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Why not serve in the fourth week?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the woman does not serve in the fourth week, given that the blood is pure. It suggests that this implies we do not follow the majority, but then rejects that reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the woman does not serve in the fourth week, since the blood she sees then is pure.
The Gemara objects that this implies we do not follow the majority (רוב).

items.text: Alternative explanation: Distant birth
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Distant birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: perhaps her birth was distant, so the fourth week is still impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the meaning of the earlier statement 'I do not know what the refutation is' could be, given the difficulty with the fourth week.
The Gemara answers that perhaps her birth was distant, so the fourth week is still within the impure period.

items.text: Further challenge: Fifth week and daily uncertainty
items.text_en: Further challenge: Fifth week and daily uncertainty
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges why she does not serve in the fifth week, which is pure, and then analyzes the fourth week's daily uncertainty between end of birth and beginning of menstruation, requiring seven clean days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: the fifth week is entirely pure, so why does the Mishnah not permit her to serve (engage in marital relations) during that week?

The Gemara explains: regarding the fourth week, each day we are uncertain whether it is the end of the birth period or the beginning of menstruation, and the twenty-eighth day itself might be the start of menstruation, requiring seven clean days.
The Gemara objects: but on the twenty-first day (the first day of the fourth week) she should be permitted to serve, since it is not yet subject to the uncertainty of the twenty-eighth day.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon's concern
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon's concern
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who forbids such practice lest she come to doubt. She may serve at night if she saw blood in the evening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who forbids such practice lest she come to doubt, and notes that she may serve at night if she saw blood in the evening.

items.text: Explanation of the 95 immersions
items.text_en: Explanation of the 95 immersions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Beit Shammai's calculation: immersions at night for weeks one and two (possible male or female birth), and during the day for weeks two and three (possible zabah). The night immersions in week three follow Beit Shammai's own view that a long day requires immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins explaining Beit Shammai's 95 immersions: in week one, immersions are at night, because the woman might be a יולדת זכר (one who gave birth to a male).
In week two, immersions are at night (possible female birth) and during the day (possible male birth with זיבה (zavah status)).
In week three, immersions are during the day, because the woman might be a יולדת נקבה בזוב (one who gave birth to a female with zavah status).
The night immersions in week three follow Beit Shammai's own view that a long day (טבולת יום ארוך) requires immersion.

items.text: Resolving the missing day in Beit Shammai's count
items.text_en: Resolving the missing day in Beit Shammai's count
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that after subtracting the third week's immersions, 94 days remain, but Beit Shammai's count requires 95. Rav Yirmiyah of Difti explains that if the woman came before us at twilight, we give her an extra immersion.

items.text: Beit Hillel's missing 35 days
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's missing 35 days
items.desc_en: For Beit Hillel, who say a long day's immersion is not required, the Gemara asks what the 35 days are for. It answers that 28 are as we said, and the fifth week we immerse every night because it might be the end of her menstrual period.

items.text: Why ten weeks?
items.text_en: Why ten weeks?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why ten weeks are needed when eight and a half would suffice. It answers that since the Tanna taught half a week, he continues, and since he taught 'week of impurity', he also taught 'week of purity'.

items.text: Excluding the immersion of a זבה
items.text_en: Excluding the immersion of a זבה
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the immersion of a זבה (zavah). It answers that only immersions before intercourse are counted, not after. For Beit Shammai, who count after intercourse, the Gemara objects that they should also count the זבה's immersion, but the reply is that we are dealing with childbirth, not זיבה. The Gemara then asks about a woman giving birth in a state of זיבה, and answers that such a case is counted, but pure זיבה is not.

items.text: The first week's immersion and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: The first week's immersion and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the first week she comes to us, we immerse her during the day, lest her counting days be completed each day. This follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires counting in our presence. The Gemara then asks why not immerse her at the end of the first week, and answers that we are not dealing with one day a week. It then asks why not immerse her on the first day she comes, lest she be a שומרת יום כנגד יום, and answers that we are dealing with a גדולה זבה, not a קטנה.

items.text: Three conclusions from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Three conclusions from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives three conclusions: that it follows Rabbi Akiva requiring counting in our presence; that it follows Rabbi Shimon who says the Sages forbade doing so lest she come to doubt; and that immersion at its proper time is a mitzvah, unlike Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda who says the last immersion suffices.

items.text: Mishnah: Miscarriage on day 40 or 41
items.text_en: Mishnah: Miscarriage on day 40 or 41
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who miscarries on day 40 need not worry about a child; on day 41 she sits for a male, female, and menstruation. Rabbi Yishmael says day 41 is for a male and menstruation, day 81 for male, female, and menstruation, because a male is formed in 41 days and a female in 81. The Sages say both are formed in 41 days.

items.text: Gemara: Why mention male?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why mention male?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a male is mentioned, since the laws of impurity and purity for a female are already stated. The question is cut off at the end of the segment.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that discusses the case of a woman who sees blood on day 34 and again on day 41, becoming confused until day 48, and similarly for a female.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's statement and the Sages' objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's statement and the Sages' objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael says that day 41 for a male and day 81 for a female are treated as both the end of impurity for the previous birth and the beginning of impurity for the next. The Sages object that one cannot derive laws of creation from laws of impurity.

items.text: Cleopatra's maidservants as a proof
items.text_en: Cleopatra's maidservants as a proof
items.desc_en: The Sages bring a story about Cleopatra's maidservants who were examined and found to have both male and female fetuses at 41 days. Rabbi Yishmael dismisses this as a proof from fools.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's Torah proof and the Sages' counter
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's Torah proof and the Sages' counter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael brings a Torah proof from the verse 'teiled' (she gives birth) indicating an additional birth for a female. The Sages explain the maidservants' case as due to a drug, but Rabbi Yishmael counters that some bodies do not accept the drug.

items.text: Another story and the Sages' response
items.text_en: Another story and the Sages' response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael brings another story about Cleopatra's maidservants found with male at 41 and female at 81 days. The Sages say no proof from fools, as the female may have been conceived later. Rabbi Yishmael suggests a guard was appointed, but the Sages counter that there is no guardian for forbidden relations.

items.text: Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the dispute by stating that the signs of male and female are identical at 41 days, so the maidservants' case is inconclusive.

items.text: The Sages' ruling and its necessity
items.text_en: The Sages' ruling and its necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Sages' opinion is identical to the Tanna Kamma, and explains that the repetition is to teach that despite Rabbi Yishmael's scriptural support, the halakha follows the majority.

items.text: Aggadic description of the fetus
items.text_en: Aggadic description of the fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai describes the fetus in the womb like a folded notebook, with a light, learning Torah, and being sworn before birth. The section concludes with a parable from the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's beginning
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's beginning
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement by Rabbi Elazar, which is cut off.

items.text: The fetus likened to a floating nut
items.text_en: The fetus likened to a floating nut
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to explain the term 'gozi' (my cutting off) as an oath, and Rabbi Elazar compares the fetus in the womb to a nut floating in a bowl of water, which sinks when pressed.

items.text: The three trimesters of pregnancy and the verse for hidden formation
items.text_en: The three trimesters of pregnancy and the verse for hidden formation
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that the fetus dwells in different parts of the womb during the three trimesters, and at birth it turns and emerges, causing labor pains. Rabbi Elazar cites a verse indicating that the fetus is 'embroidered' in the lower parts of the earth.

items.text: Why labor pains are greater for a female
items.text_en: Why labor pains are greater for a female
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a female fetus emerges face-down (like the manner of intercourse), while a male emerges face-up, causing greater pain for the female.

items.text: The effect of intercourse during pregnancy
items.text_en: The effect of intercourse during pregnancy
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that intercourse in the first three months is harmful to both mother and fetus, in the middle months it is harmful to the mother but good for the fetus, and in the last months it is good for both. A baraita warns that intercourse on the ninetieth day is like shedding blood, but Abaye says one may continue, trusting that God protects the simple.

items.text: The three partners in a human being
items.text_en: The three partners in a human being
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that there are three partners in the creation of a person: the father contributes the white substance (bones, sinews, nails, etc.), the mother contributes the red substance (skin, flesh, hair, etc.), and God gives spirit, soul, facial features, and other faculties. At death, God takes His portion and leaves the parents' portions, as Rabbi Pappa notes in a folk saying.

items.text: Wonders of fetal development: God's ways vs. human ways
items.text_en: Wonders of fetal development: God's ways vs. human ways
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili expound on verses showing God's wonders in fetal development: unlike a human who puts a vessel with its opening upward, God places the fetus in an open womb with its opening downward; unlike a human whose heavy objects sink, the fetus rises as it grows; unlike seeds that each grow in its own kind, all fetuses become one species; and unlike a dyer whose dyes all become one color, each fetus develops its distinct features.

items.text: The parable of the two merchants and the hidden miracle
items.text_en: The parable of the two merchants and the hidden miracle
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef interprets a verse about God's anger turning to comfort, using a parable of two merchants: one is pricked by a thorn and curses, but later learns his friend's ship sank and thanks God. Rabbi Elazar adds that even the beneficiary of a miracle does not recognize it.

items.text: The selection of the pure drop and the counting of Israel's issues
items.text_en: The selection of the pure drop and the counting of Israel's issues
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina bar Pappa teaches that a person is formed only from the purest part of the drop, like winnowing. Rabbi Avahu connects this to David's praise. He further expounds that God counts the 'quarters' (menstrual cycles) of Israel to know when the drop for a righteous person will come, and Balaam's eye was blinded for peering into this. Rabbi Yochanan adds that God assisted in the conception of Issachar.

items.text: Who determines the sex of the child: woman or man?
items.text_en: Who determines the sex of the child: woman or man?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak quoting Rabbi Ami states that if the woman emits seed first, she bears a male; if the man emits first, she bears a female. The Sages initially said this without proof, until Rabbi Tzadok explained from the verse about Leah's children that males are attributed to females and females to males. The Gemara begins to discuss another verse about multiplying children.

items.text: Teaching on delaying intercourse to produce male children
items.text_en: Teaching on delaying intercourse to produce male children
items.desc_en: Rav Katina and Rava discuss the practice of delaying ejaculation to ensure male offspring, citing a verse that credits such men as if they multiplied descendants.

items.text: Dispute on timing of conception
items.text_en: Dispute on timing of conception
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Ami says a woman conceives only close to her menstrual period, while Rabbi Yochanan says close to her immersion. The Gemara explains the derivation of the word 'chet' as purification.

items.text: Teachings on male and female birth
items.text_en: Teachings on male and female birth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Ami teaches that when a male is born, peace comes to the world, and he brings his sustenance with him. A female comes with nothing and must beg for support.

items.text: Reasons for post-childbirth offerings and periods
items.text_en: Reasons for post-childbirth offerings and periods
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that a woman brings a sacrifice because she swears in pain not to cohabit again. Rav Yosef objects that she is willful and needs a sin-offering. The Gemara explains the different periods for male and female births and the timing of circumcision.

items.text: Reason for niddah period
items.text_en: Reason for niddah period
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir explains that the Torah mandated a seven-day niddah period because a husband becomes accustomed to his wife and disgusted; the separation makes her beloved again.

items.text: Questions on gender differences
items.text_en: Questions on gender differences
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai's students ask why men pursue women, why men face downward and women upward, why men are appeased easily, and why women's voices are pleasant. Each answer is based on the source of creation.

items.text: Mishnah on Samaritan women
items.text_en: Mishnah on Samaritan women
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that Samaritan girls are considered niddot from birth, and Samaritans transmit impurity through lower and upper bedding because they engage in intercourse with niddot. They are not liable for entering the Temple or burning terumah due to uncertainty.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's ruling: if they see blood, even Jewish women are impure; if not, even Samaritans are pure. Rava bar Rav Acha bar Rav Huna citing Rav Sheshet explains the case is about uncertainty, and the tanna is concerned for a minority.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's ruling on minors
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's ruling on minors
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the mishnah's author as Rabbi Meir, who holds that a minor boy and girl cannot perform chalitzah or yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the mishnah's author as Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita that a minor boy and girl do not perform חליצה (chalitzah) or יבום (yibbum).

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Sages agree with Rabbi Meir that chalitzah is invalid for minors, but question why yibbum is also prohibited. Rabbi Meir answers due to the risk of the minor being a saris or aylonit, while the Sages counter that one follows the majority, and most minors are not infertile.

sub.desc_en: The Sages agree with Rabbi Meir that chalitzah is invalid for minors, but ask why yibbum is also prohibited.
Rabbi Meir answers that a minor male might be a saris (infertile) and a minor female might be an aylonit (infertile), so yibbum could lead to unintentional incest.
The Sages object that one should follow the majority (רוב), and most minors are not infertile, so the concern is unfounded.

items.text: Gemara's question and support from cases of immersion
items.text_en: Gemara's question and support from cases of immersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir considers only a common minority, but here the minority is common, as illustrated by cases where a girl was immersed before her mother due to concern for early niddah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir's concern for a common minority extends to an uncommon minority, challenging the application of his principle here.

The Gemara counters that this minority is indeed common, citing a baraita with stories from Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi, and Rav Yosef where a girl was immersed before her mother due to concern for early niddah.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Yosef's case and the law of anointing
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Yosef's case and the law of anointing
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi's cases were due to terumah of the Land of Israel, but Rav Yosef's case in Babylonia is needed for the law of anointing with terumah oil, which is equated to drinking via a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Yosef's case was needed, since Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi's cases were due to terumah of the Land of Israel, but in Babylonia terumah is only forbidden for eating, not touching.

Mar Zutra answers that Rav Yosef's case was needed for the law of anointing with terumah oil, which is equated to drinking via the verse 'ולא יחללו את קדשי בני ישראל' (they shall not profane the holy things of the children of Israel).
The Gemara objects that drinking is already included in eating, so the verse must be to include anointing as equivalent to drinking.
The Gemara offers an alternative proof from the verse 'ותבא כמים בקרבו וכשמן בעצמותיו' (it comes like water into his innards and like oil into his bones), equating anointing with drinking.

items.text: Distinction between Babylonian and Palestinian practice
items.text_en: Distinction between Babylonian and Palestinian practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the same concern does not apply to us (Babylonians), and answers that since we expound the extra 'ishah' verses and separate girls when they see blood, the Sages did not decree immersion; but they did not expound and do not separate, so a decree was made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the same concern about immersion before the mother does not apply to us (Babylonians).

The Gemara answers that since we (Babylonians) expound the extra 'אישה' verses and separate girls when they see blood, the Sages did not decree immersion; but they (Palestinians) did not expound and do not separate, so a decree was made.

items.text: The age of niddah: halakha vs. scriptural support
items.text_en: The age of niddah: halakha vs. scriptural support
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the derivation of a one-day-old girl being a niddah from the extra 'ishah' verse, and a three-year-old for intercourse, leading to a contradiction. Rava resolves that both are halakha, and the verses are mere support, but the Gemara questions which is halakha and which is scriptural.

items.text: Deriving that 'Ish' excludes a man from red discharge
items.text_en: Deriving that 'Ish' excludes a man from red discharge
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the extra 've-ishah' teaches that a ten-day-old girl is eligible for zavah. This is needed because zavah is less stringent than niddah. Two verses are used to exclude a man from the red discharge of niddah and from semen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the extra 'איש' (man) in the verse excludes a man from the red discharge of niddah.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives a ten-day-old girl's eligibility for zavah from 'וְאִשָּׁה' (and a woman), and questions why this derivation is needed—could it not be learned from the laws of niddah?
The Gemara explains that the derivation is necessary because zavah is less stringent than niddah—a zavah only needs to wait one day, so one might think she is not included without the explicit verse.

The Gemara objects that the verse could have been written only for zavah, and the exclusion of a man from red discharge would still be learned; the Gemara concedes and reinterprets the extra verse as excluding a man from red discharge.
The Gemara resolves that two exclusions are needed: one to exclude a man from semen (שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע) and one to exclude him from blood (דָּם).

items.text: Debate on whether a one-day-old male can be a zav
items.text_en: Debate on whether a one-day-old male can be a zav
items.desc_en: Tanna teaches that 'ish ish' includes a one-day-old infant for zavah impurity, according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yishmael argues it is unnecessary because 'la-zachar' includes any male, and 'ish ish' is merely the Torah speaking in human language.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited regarding males: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'אִישׁ אִישׁ' (each man) that a one-day-old male is impure with zavah, while Rabbi Yishmael argues that 'לַזָּכָר' (to the male) already includes all males, and 'אִישׁ אִישׁ' is merely the Torah speaking in human language.

The Gemara notes that the baraita implies the verse includes a one-day-old, but a contradiction arises from another baraita that limits zavah to a nine-year-old male, deriving a nine-year-old from 'וְאִישׁ' (and a man).
Rava explains that both are halachot (הלכות) supported by verses, but the Gemara questions which is the halacha and which is the verse, noting that a verse is written generally.
The Gemara resolves that the nine-year-old is the halacha (הלכה) and the one-day-old is derived from the verse, and the verse is needed to exclude a woman from white discharge (לובן).

items.text: Resolving a contradiction between one-day-old and nine-year-old
items.text_en: Resolving a contradiction between one-day-old and nine-year-old
items.desc_en: A baraita states 'ish' only includes a nine-year-old, not a one-day-old. Rava explains that one-day-old is halakha, and nine-year-old is from a verse. The verse that seems to include the one-day-old actually excludes a woman from white discharge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the baraita (seg 5-6) teaches that the verse includes a one-day-old, but another baraita (seg 7) teaches that 'איש' only includes a nine-year-old, not a one-day-old.

Rava explains that both laws are halakhot (הלכות) that the Sages merely attached to verses; the Gemara then questions which is the halakha and which is the verse, rejecting the possibility that the one-day-old is the halakha because the verse for the nine-year-old is written in general terms.

The Gemara resolves: the nine-year-old is the halakha (הלכה), and the one-day-old is derived from the verse; the verse that seems to include the one-day-old actually serves to exclude a woman from white discharge (לובן).

items.text: Why both males and females are written for zav
items.text_en: Why both males and females are written for zav
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes both 'zachar' and 'nekevah' for zavah impurity. It answers: they are needed because males are strict regarding sightings like days, but females are strict regarding ones (accidental impurity), so each context requires its own verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah needs to write both the laws for males and females regarding zavah, and answers that each is necessary: males are impure through multiple sightings like days, while females are impure through אונס (accidental emission), so neither can be derived from the other.

The Gemara answers that both verses are necessary: males are strict regarding sightings (ראיות) like days, but females are strict regarding accidental impurity (אונס), so each context requires its own verse.

items.text: explaining 'mishkav tachton ka-elyon' for Kutim
items.text_en: explaining 'mishkav tachton ka-elyon' for Kutim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says Kutim make the lower bedding impure like the upper. The Gemara clarifies: it does not mean every mattress under the zav is impure (obvious), but rather the lower bedding of one who has intercourse with a niddah is like the upper of a zav — only impure for food and drink. The source for the upper of a zav is 'everyone who touches all that is under him'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that Cuthim (Samaritans) render the lower bedding like the upper bedding, and explains that this means the lower bedding of a niddah's partner is like the upper bedding of a zav, which only imparts impurity to food and drink, and derives this from the verse 'תַּחְתָּיו' (under him).
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means the lower bedding of one who has intercourse with a niddah is like the upper of a zav, only impure for food and drink.
The Gemara asks for the source that the upper of a zav only impurifies food and drink, citing the verse 'everyone who touches all that is under him'.

items.text: Derivation of the zav's upper bedding impurity
items.text_en: Derivation of the zav's upper bedding impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'and whoever touches anything that was under him' refers to the upper bedding of a zav, and 'the one who carries' refers to the carried object. The verse teaches that this impurity is light, affecting only food and drink.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks that the phrase 'under him' cannot refer to the zav's lower bedding, since that is already derived from the verse 'and whoever touches his bed', and explains that it refers to the upper bedding of the zav.

The Gemara explains that 'the one who carries' refers to the carried object, and the verse detaches it from severe impurity and brings it to light impurity, teaching that it only imparts impurity to food and drink.

items.text: Objection: Could it include people and garments?
items.text_en: Objection: Could it include people and garments?
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: perhaps the light impurity still includes people and garments, but not causing garment impurity. The Gemara answers that 'yitma' implies only a light impurity.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: perhaps the light impurity still includes people and garments, but not causing garment impurity.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'יִטְמָא' (it shall be impure), which implies only a light impurity, excluding people and garments.

items.text: Derivation of the ba'al niddah's lower bedding impurity
items.text_en: Derivation of the ba'al niddah's lower bedding impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the impurity of the lower bedding of a ba'al niddah from the verse 'and her niddah be upon him'. It limits the impurity to food and drink, excluding the ability to make a משכב ומושב that contaminates people and garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the impurity of the lower bedding of a ba'al niddah?
A baraita is cited: the verse 'ותהי נדתה עליו' teaches that the ba'al niddah is impure for seven days, but not that he rises to her level of impurity.
The Gemara explains: the verse 'ותהי נדתה עליו' teaches that just as the niddah contaminates people and earthenware vessels, so too the ba'al niddah contaminates them.
The Gemara objects: perhaps just as the niddah makes a משכב ומושב (bed and seat) that contaminates people and garments, so too the ba'al niddah should make such a משכב ומושב.
The Gemara resolves: the verse 'וכל המשכב אשר ישכב עליו יטמא' teaches that the ba'al niddah's lower bedding is limited to contaminating only food and drink, not people or garments.

items.text: Rav Achai's objection and Rav Asi's answer
items.text_en: Rav Achai's objection and Rav Asi's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Achai objects that the light impurity might still include people and garments. Rav Asi answers that 'yitma' implies only a light impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achai objects that the light impurity might still include people and garments, not just food and drink.
Rav Asi answers that the word 'יִטְמָא' (it shall be impure) implies only a light impurity, excluding people and garments.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate the application of כלל ופרט
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate the application of כלל ופרט
items.desc_en: An attempt to apply a כלל ופרט derivation is rejected by Abaye because the verses are separated. Rava argues that 'וכל' is a ריבוי, allowing the derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes applying a כלל ופרט (general followed by specific) derivation to limit the bo'el niddah's impurity to only a משכב ומושב (bed and seat).

Abaye objects that the verse 'יִטְמָא שִׁבְעַת יָמִים' (he shall be impure for seven days) interrupts the context, making this a כלל ופרט המרוחקין (separated general and specific), which cannot be used for derivation.
Rava counters that the derivation is still valid because the word 'וכל' (and every) is a ריבוי (amplification), not a פרט (specification), so the rule of כלל ופרט does not apply.

items.text: Rabbi Yaakov's objection and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov's objection and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov objects that just as a niddah's touch and bedding are equal in severity, so too a ba'al niddah's touch and bedding should be equal in leniency. Rava answers that 'עליו' implies a burden, limiting the impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov objects that just as a niddah's touch and bedding are equal in severity, so too a ba'al niddah's touch and bedding should be equal in leniency.
Rava answers that the word 'עליו' (upon him) implies a burden, limiting the impurity to a specific leniency.

items.text: Discussion of the Mishnah's ruling on ba'alei niddot and zavot
items.text_en: Discussion of the Mishnah's ruling on ba'alei niddot and zavot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah refers to married women. It then discusses the counting of clean days for a zava, with Rabbi Meir's statement, Rami bar Chama's objection, and Rava's resolution involving a case close to sunset.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'because they are ba'alei niddot' (those who engage in intercourse with menstruants), asking whether all of them are indeed ba'alei niddot.
Rabbi Yitzchak Magdela'ah answers that the Mishnah refers specifically to married women (נשואות), not all women.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir states that if women sit for every type of blood, it is a great enactment for them.
Rabbi Meir clarifies that the enactment applies only when they see red blood and complete it with green blood.
Rabbi Meir offers an alternative explanation: the day she stops bleeding counts toward the seven clean days.
Rami bar Chama objects: why should she count that day, since we hold that a partial day is considered like a full day (מקצת היום ככולו)?
Rava responds: if so, how could seminal emission (שכבת זרע) interrupt the counting of clean days for a zava, given the principle of a partial day being like a full day?
The Gemara resolves: if she saw blood in the middle of the day, indeed it would not interrupt; here we are dealing with a case where she saw close to sunset.
The Gemara digresses to question the scriptural basis for this distinction, concluding that the verse itself is forced to accommodate this interpretation.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about a פולטת שכבת זרע
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about a פולטת שכבת זרע
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a woman who emits semen after relations interrupts her זיבה count. The daf ends with this question.

items.text: Gemara's resolution on whether a zav's touch interrupts his counting
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution on whether a zav's touch interrupts his counting
items.desc_en: Rava initially challenges the assumption that a zav's touch would interrupt his counting, but the Gemara resolves that only tum'at zivah interrupts, not mere touch. The argument uses a parallel from the zav himself to establish the principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether a zav's mere touch (without emitting zivah) interrupts his counting.
Rava objects that even if touch interrupts, it cannot interrupt seven days, as the zav's own rule limits interruption to one day like his wife.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְאַחַר תִּטְהָר' (and after she becomes pure) teaches that no tum'ah (ritual impurity) interrupts between the seven clean days.
Rava objects that the same verse would apply to the zav himself, yet he does interrupt his counting.
The Gemara resolves that only טומאת זיבה (zivah impurity) interrupts the counting, not mere touch, and applies the same principle to the zav's wife.

items.text: Rav Pappa's encounter and the baraita on doubtful tum'ah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's encounter and the baraita on doubtful tum'ah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa visits a place and meets a scholar named Rav Shmuel. He challenges him with a contradiction between a Mishnah that says we do not burn terumah for doubtful tum'ah and a baraita that lists six cases where we do. Rav Shmuel initially answers with a case of a Kutite haver, but Rav Pappa objects. Rav Shimi bar Ashi then offers a resolution involving a Kutite who immersed and stepped on a haver's garments, creating a double doubt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa arrives at a place called Tuvakh and is told by an old woman that a scholar named Rav Shmuel is there, and she blesses him to be like Rav Shmuel.

Rav Pappa infers that Rav Shmuel is God-fearing, goes to him, and raises a contradiction between the Mishnah that says we do not burn תרומה (priestly portion) for doubtful טומאה (ritual impurity) and a baraita that lists six cases where we do.
Rav Pappa cites the baraita that lists six doubtful cases for which we burn תרומה (priestly portion), including the case of garments of an עַם הָאָרֶץ (an ignoramus).
Rav Shmuel (through Rav Pappa's blessing) answers that the baraita deals with a כותי חבר (a Kutite who is a haver, i.e., scrupulous in purity laws).
Rav Pappa objects: do you consider a כותי חבר (a Kutite haver) to be a בועל נדה (one who has intercourse with a menstruant)?

Rav Pappa leaves Rav Shmuel and goes to Rav Shimi bar Ashi, who suggests resolving the contradiction with a case of a Kutite who immersed and stepped on a haver's garments, which then touched תרומה (priestly portion).

Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains that the Kutite's immersion removes the טומאת עם הארץ (impurity of an ignoramus), and the doubt about being a בועל נדה (one who has intercourse with a menstruant) is a double doubt.

Rav Shimi bar Ashi elaborates that even if the Kutite had intercourse recently, there is a doubt whether he completed the emission of semen, creating a ספק ספיקא (double doubt), and we do not burn תרומה (priestly portion) for a double doubt.

The Gemara objects: why not consider the impurity of the garments of an עַם הָאָרֶץ (ignoramus), since the garments of an ignoramus are a מדרס (treading impurity) for פרושים (those scrupulous in purity)?
Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that the case involves a naked Kutite, so there is no issue of garment impurity.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the status of Sadducee women
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the status of Sadducee women
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Sadducee women who follow their fathers' ways are like Kutite women, but if they follow Israel's ways they are like Israelite women. Rabbi Yosei says they are always like Israelite women until they explicitly follow their fathers' ways. The Gemara debates the default status (setama) and concludes from Rabbi Yosei's statement that the first Tanna holds the default is like Kutite women.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: Sadducee women who follow their fathers' ways are like Kutite women; if they follow Israel's ways they are like Israelite women; Rabbi Yosei says they are always like Israelite women until they explicitly follow their fathers' ways.

The Gemara raises a dilemma: what is the default status of a Sadducee woman when her custom is unknown? It attempts to infer from the Mishnah but finds contradictory implications from the first and last clauses, concluding that no inference can be drawn from this Mishnah.

The Gemara resolves the dilemma by citing Rabbi Yosei's statement, from which it infers that the first Tanna holds the default status is like Kutite women, and concludes that this is the correct understanding.

items.text: Story of a Sadducee and the halakhic discussion about his spittle
items.text_en: Story of a Sadducee and the halakhic discussion about his spittle
items.desc_en: A story is told about a Sadducee whose spittle fell on a High Priest's garments, causing the priest to turn pale and rush to his wife. The Gemara questions why the spittle is not considered a source of tum'ah from an am ha'aretz. Abaye answers it was a Sadducee haver, but Rava objects that a Sadducee haver would be a bo'el niddah. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts an incident where a Sadducee's spittle fell on the High Priest's garments, causing the priest to turn pale and rush to the Sadducee's wife.
The wife reassures the High Priest that even Sadducee women fear the perushim and show their blood to the Sages, so the garments are pure.
Rabbi Yosei testifies that all Sadducee women in his neighborhood show blood to the Sages except one who died as a punishment.
The Gemara asks why the High Priest did not consider the spittle impure due to the Sadducee being an am ha'aretz.
Abaye answers that the case involved a Sadducee haver who is meticulous about purity.
Rava objects that a Sadducee haver would still be a bo'el niddah, so the spittle should be impure.
Rava begins to offer an alternative explanation, but the text cuts off, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Background: Am ha'aretz impurity during the pilgrimage
items.text_en: Background: Am ha'aretz impurity during the pilgrimage
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that during the pilgrimage, the Sages treated the impurity of an am ha'aretz as pure, based on the verse that makes all Israelites 'companions'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that during the pilgrimage, the Sages treated the impurity of an am ha'aretz as pure, based on the verse that makes all Israelites 'companions'.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: a gentile woman's blood and a metzora's pure blood (Beit Shammai deem pure, Beit Hillel compare to her saliva and urine); a woman who gave birth and hasn't immersed (Beit Shammai compare to saliva/urine, Beit Hillel deem impure wet or dry); and agreement that a woman with a zavah discharge is impure wet or dry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the first case: Beit Shammai deem a gentile woman's blood and a metzora's pure blood pure, while Beit Hillel compare them to her saliva and urine.
The Mishnah presents the second case: a woman who gave birth and hasn't immersed — Beit Shammai compare her blood to saliva and urine, while Beit Hillel deem it impure wet or dry.
The Mishnah concludes with the agreed case: both schools agree that a woman with a zavah discharge is impure wet or dry.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why don't Beit Shammai apply the decree of gentile zavim?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why don't Beit Shammai apply the decree of gentile zavim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Do Beit Shammai not accept the rabbinic decree that gentiles are considered zavim in all respects, based on the verse 'Speak to the children of Israel'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai reject the principle that gentiles do not contract זוב (gonorrhea-like discharge) impurity by Torah law, but the Sages decreed they are like זבים (gonorrhea-like discharge sufferers) for all purposes.

items.text: Beit Shammai's answer: Distinction based on a distinguishing mark (היכר)
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's answer: Distinction based on a distinguishing mark (היכר)
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai respond that the decree about gentile zavim was stated regarding males, not females. For a gentile woman, they cannot make her blood impure like Torah law (wet and dry) because that would equate it to Torah impurity, nor can they make it impure only wet (like a zav) because that would create a split within Torah law. They instead make a distinguishing mark (היכר) by treating her blood as pure, so that her saliva and urine (which are rabbinic) are recognized as such. The Gemara explains that saliva and urine are common, so the Sages decreed on them, but blood is uncommon, so they did not decree.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai answer that the decree about gentile zavim was stated regarding males, not females, and explain the dilemma: treating a gentile woman's blood as impure both wet and dry would equate it to Torah law, while treating it as impure only wet would create a split within Torah law.

The Gemara objects that if a distinguishing mark (היכר) is made with her blood, then her saliva and urine should also be treated as pure, and Beit Shammai responds that the mark makes it known that saliva and urine are rabbinic.

The Gemara asks why not make the mark on saliva and urine instead and treat blood as impure, and answers that saliva and urine are common so the Sages decreed on them, but blood is uncommon so they did not decree.

items.text: Rava's ruling: Zov of a gentile woman is impure, her semen is pure
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: Zov of a gentile woman is impure, her semen is pure
items.desc_en: Rava states that a gentile woman's zov (discharge) is impure even for Beit Shammai, because a distinguishing mark can be made with her semen (which is pure). Her semen is pure even for Beit Hillel, because the Sages made a distinguishing mark so as not to burn terumah and sacrifices on its account. The Gemara explains that zov is not dependent on an action, so the Sages decreed on it; semen is dependent on an action, so they did not decree.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a gentile woman's zov (discharge) is impure even for Beit Shammai, and her semen is pure even for Beit Hillel.
The Gemara explains that zov is impure because a distinguishing mark can be made with her semen (which is pure).
The Gemara explains that semen is pure because the Sages made a distinguishing mark so as not to burn תרומה (priestly portion) and sacrifices on its account.
The Gemara objects: why not make a distinguishing mark with zov and declare semen impure instead?
The Gemara resolves: zov is not dependent on an action, so the Sages decreed on it; semen is dependent on an action, so they did not decree.

items.text: Supporting evidence: A gentile woman who emits semen from an Israelite
items.text_en: Supporting evidence: A gentile woman who emits semen from an Israelite
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: A gentile woman who emits semen from an Israelite is impure; a Jewish woman who emits semen from a gentile is pure. The Gemara initially suggests this means completely pure, but concludes it means pure from Torah law but impure rabbinically. The text continues with a statement that an Israelite's semen is impure everywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a gentile woman who emits semen from an Israelite being impure and a Jewish woman who emits semen from a gentile being pure, and initially suggests that 'pure' means completely pure, but concludes it means pure from Torah law but impure rabbinically.
The Gemara cites a concluding statement that an Israelite's semen is impure everywhere, reinforcing the distinction between Israelite and gentile semen.

items.text: Impurity of semen in a gentile woman and purity of gentile's semen
items.text_en: Impurity of semen in a gentile woman and purity of gentile's semen
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a gentile's semen is pure everywhere, even in a Jewish woman's body, except for its urine. The Gemara questions whether this purity is only biblical but rabbinically impure, and concludes that it is pure even rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a gentile's semen is pure everywhere, even in a Jewish woman's body, except for its urine.
The Gemara questions whether the purity is only biblical but rabbinically impure.
The Gemara objects that if urine were biblically impure, it would be impure, but it is not, so the purity must be absolute.
The Gemara concludes that the purity is even rabbinically, as proven by the urine exception.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about semen in a gentile woman after three days
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about semen in a gentile woman after three days
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether a Jew's semen in a gentile woman's body is impure after three days, considering whether the body decomposes differently for Jews and gentiles. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Mar states that a Jew's semen is impure everywhere, even in a gentile woman's body.
Rav Pappa asks about the status of a Jew's semen inside a gentile woman's body.
The Gemara clarifies that Rav Pappa's question applies only after three days, not within three days.
Rav Pappa poses a dilemma: whether a Jew's semen decomposes due to mitzvot, while a gentile's does not, or whether gentiles' eating of vermin causes decomposition, leaving the question unresolved.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Beit Hillel's reasoning for pure blood of a leprous woman
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's reasoning for pure blood of a leprous woman
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the verse 'to the male' and 'to the female' includes a leprous male and female for their sources, meaning the pure blood of a leprous woman is impure. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to her blood, not other sources.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of Beit Hillel regarding the pure blood of a leprous woman.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the verse 'to the male' and 'to the female' includes a leprous male and female for their sources, implying the pure blood of a leprous woman is impure.
The Gemara asks what 'her sources' refers to, and suggests it cannot be other sources since that would be derived from the male.
The Gemara resolves that 'her sources' refers to her blood, to render impure her pure blood.

items.text: Beit Shammai's objection and Beit Hillel's response
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's objection and Beit Hillel's response
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai argues that a female leper cannot be derived from a male leper due to differences in obligations. Beit Hillel responds that if the Torah wrote only 'female', we would derive the male a fortiori, so the verse 'to the male' is used to include the female's blood.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai objects that a female leper cannot be derived from a male leper because the male has obligations (uncovering the head and tearing garments, and prohibition of marital relations) that the female lacks.

Beit Hillel responds that if the Torah had written only 'female', we would derive the male a fortiori, so the verse 'to the male' is used to include the female's blood of purity (דַּם טׇהֳרָה) for impurity.

items.text: Beit Shammai's alternative objection and Beit Hillel's counter
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's alternative objection and Beit Hillel's counter
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai argues that a male leper cannot be derived from a female because a female zavah is impure even by accident, unlike a male zav. Beit Hillel responds that they are discussing a leper, not a zav, and Beit Shammai counters that they compare any impurity.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai objects that the male cannot be derived from the female because the female is impure even from an unavoidable emission.
Beit Hillel objects that Beit Shammai is mixing the laws of a leper with those of a zav.
Beit Shammai responds that they are objecting based on any impurity.

items.text: Alternative explanation: 'to the male' includes any male
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: 'to the male' includes any male
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is given: Beit Shammai interprets 'to the male' to include any male, big or small, while Beit Hillel derives this from 'this is the law of the zav'.

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation: Beit Shammai interprets 'לַזָּכָר' to include any male, whether adult or minor.
Beit Hillel derives the inclusion of minors from the verse 'זֹּאת תּוֹרַת הַזָּב'.

items.text: Rav Yosef's question about a minor zav's first sighting
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's question about a minor zav's first sighting
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a minor zav's first sighting imparts impurity by touch, based on the verse linking zav to semen. Rava resolves it by citing 'this is the law of the zav' to include both adult and minor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a minor zav's first sighting imparts impurity by touch, given the verse linking zav to semen, and whether the minor's lack of seminal impurity exempts the first sighting or if the possibility of a second sighting joining to make him a zav renders it impure.

Rava resolves the question by citing the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַזָּב' (this is the law of the zav), which includes both adult and minor, teaching that just as an adult's first sighting imparts impurity, so too does a minor's first sighting.

items.text: Rav Yosef's question about a leper's first sighting by carrying
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's question about a leper's first sighting by carrying
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a leper's first sighting imparts impurity by carrying, questioning if the discharge is considered a spring. Rava cites a verse to suggest it is impure, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether the first emission of a leper imparts impurity through carrying.
Rav Yosef presents a dilemma: whether the place of discharge is considered a spring and imparts impurity, or not.
Rava begins to resolve by citing the verse 'זוֹבוֹ טָמֵא הוּא' and questioning whether it applies to a simple zav.

items.text: Initial inference about zav and metzora
items.text_en: Initial inference about zav and metzora
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that a metzora's first emission is not a full spring (ma'ayan) like a zav's, since the Torah needed a special verse to include the second emission. This implies that the place of emission (mekom zivah) is not considered a spring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that a metzora's first emission is not a full spring (ma'ayan) like a zav's, since the Torah needed a special verse to include the second emission, implying that the place of emission (mekom zivah) is not considered a spring.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's objection from the scapegoat
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's objection from the scapegoat
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta challenges Rava: perhaps the verse refers to a regular zav (not a metzora), and the scapegoat proves that causing impurity to others does not imply impurity for oneself.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta challenges Rava's proof: perhaps the verse refers to a regular zav (not a metzora), and the scapegoat shows that causing impurity to others does not imply impurity for oneself.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: the verse includes metzora
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: the verse includes metzora
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the verse 'Zot Torat HaZav' includes both large and small zav, and the extra word 'lazachar' is used to include a metzora for his springs, comparing him to a full zav who imparts impurity through carrying (masa).

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the difficulty by citing the verse 'זאת תורת הזב' (this is the law of the zav) which includes both large and small zav, and the extra word 'לזכר' (for the male) includes a metzora for his springs, and 'לנקבה' (for the female) includes a metzora'at for her springs.

Abaye argues that the Torah compares a metzora to a full zav (זב גמור), so just as a full zav imparts impurity through carrying (משא), so too the first sighting of a metzora imparts impurity through carrying.

items.text: Rav Huna: first emission of zav imparts impurity through ones
items.text_en: Rav Huna: first emission of zav imparts impurity through ones
items.desc_en: Rav Huna teaches that a zav's first emission imparts impurity even when caused by ones (accident), based on a comparison to seminal emission.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna teaches that a zav's first emission imparts impurity even when caused by ones (accident), based on a comparison to seminal emission.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from a baraita about examining the zav
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from a baraita about examining the zav
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: for the first emission, we examine the zav; is this for impurity? The Gemara initially suggests it is for impurity, but then deflects: the first is for impurity, the second for the offering, as per the verse 'mibesaro' excluding ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about examining the zav after the first emission and asks whether this examination is for impurity.
The Gemara deflects: the first examination is for the offering, not for impurity.
The Gemara brings another baraita about examining the zav on the second emission and argues that since the second is for impurity, the first must also be for impurity.
The Gemara resolves: the first examination is for the offering and the second for impurity, as per the verse 'mibesaro' excluding ones.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and the dispute over 'etim'
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and the dispute over 'etim'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says they examine even on the third day because of the offering, implying the first Tanna says it is because of impurity. The Gemara rejects this: all agree it is for the offering, and they dispute whether to expound the word 'et' (including the third day) or not.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: zav is lenient and stringent compared to ba'al keri
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: zav is lenient and stringent compared to ba'al keri
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that the zav was included in the category of ba'al keri but was singled out to be lenient (not impure through ones) and stringent (other stringencies).

items.text: Clarifying the leniency and stringency of the second sighting of a zav
items.text_en: Clarifying the leniency and stringency of the second sighting of a zav
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a zav's second sighting makes him a source of midras impurity. It initially assumes this refers to the first sighting, but then corrects that Rabbi Yitzchak explains the second sighting comes to both be lenient (not impure due to ones) and stringent (makes midras).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a zav's second sighting makes him a source of midras impurity.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yitzchak's statement refers to the first or second sighting, initially assuming the first sighting, which would imply a leniency.
The Gemara objects that the first sighting cannot impose midras impurity, so the statement must refer to the second sighting.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the second sighting comes to both be lenient (not impure due to ones) and stringent (makes midras).

items.text: Rav Huna's description of the physical differences between zov and semen
items.text_en: Rav Huna's description of the physical differences between zov and semen
items.desc_en: Rav Huna describes zov as resembling barley water, coming from dead flesh, and being thin like the white of a spoiled egg, while semen comes from living flesh and is thick like the white of a fresh egg.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna describes the physical differences between זוב (zov) and שכבת זרע (semen): זוב resembles barley water, comes from dead flesh, and is thin like the white of a spoiled egg, while semen comes from living flesh and is thick like the white of a fresh egg.

items.text: Debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on a yoledet who saw blood without immersing
items.text_en: Debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on a yoledet who saw blood without immersing
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel argues that a yoledet who has not immersed and sees blood is impure, similar to a niddah. Beit Shammai counters that a yoledet who immersed is pure, unlike a niddah. Beit Hillel responds with the case of a yoledet b'zov, where immersion after counting pure days purifies, but without immersion she remains impure. Beit Shammai dismisses this as not a valid proof.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: the blood of a yoledet who has not immersed is debated by Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
Beit Hillel asks Beit Shammai: do you not agree that a niddah who has not immersed and sees blood is impure?
Beit Shammai counters: you cannot compare, because a niddah is impure even after immersion, but a yoledet who immersed and sees blood is pure.
Beit Hillel objects: the case of a yoledet b'zov proves the point — after counting pure days, immersion purifies, but without immersion she remains impure.
Beit Shammai dismisses the objection, saying the same law applies and that is the answer.

items.text: Reconciling the dispute with the Mishnah's statement of agreement
items.text_en: Reconciling the dispute with the Mishnah's statement of agreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel actually disagree, given the Mishnah says they agree that a yoledet b'zov is impure wet and dry. It resolves that the dispute is when she counted pure days, while the agreement is when she did not count. A baraisa confirms that when she counted but did not immerse, each follows its own view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel actually disagree, given the Mishnah states they agree that a yoledet b'zov (woman who gave birth in a state of זוב) is impure wet and dry.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the dispute applies when she counted her pure days, while the agreement applies when she did not count.
A baraisa confirms that when a yoledet b'zov counted but did not immerse and then saw blood, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel each follow their own view.

items.text: Rav and Levi debate whether the yoledet has one or two ma'ayanot
items.text_en: Rav and Levi debate whether the yoledet has one or two ma'ayanot
items.desc_en: Rav holds there is one ma'ayan that becomes impure or pure by Torah decree. Levi holds there are two ma'ayanot, one pure and one impure, that alternate. The practical difference is in cases of continuous flow from within seven days to after seven, etc., where Rav's view leads to leniency at the start and stringency at the end, and Levi's view the opposite.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the yoledet has one ma'ayan (source of blood) which the Torah alternately renders impure and pure.
Levi counters that there are two ma'ayanot (sources), one pure and one impure, which alternate opening and closing.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rav's and Levi's views, listing cases of continuous flow from within the seven or fourteen days to after their completion.
The Gemara explains that according to Rav, the beginning of the flow is lenient (the blood is pure) and the end is stringent (the blood is impure).
The Gemara explains that according to Levi, the beginning is stringent and the end is lenient, opposite to Rav.

items.text: Challenging Levi from the Mishnah about a yoledet who did not immerse
items.text_en: Challenging Levi from the Mishnah about a yoledet who did not immerse
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Levi from the Mishnah where Beit Hillel says the blood of a yoledet who did not immerse is impure wet and dry. If there are two ma'ayanot, why is it impure? Levi answers that the case is one of continuous flow, and Beit Shammai themselves hold there is one ma'ayan. The difference between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel according to Rav is whether impurity depends on days alone or days and immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Beit Hillel rules that the blood of a yoledet who did not immerse is impure wet and dry, challenging Levi's position.
The Gemara assumes the yoledet stopped bleeding, and questions why according to Levi (who holds two ma'ayanot) the blood would be impure wet and dry.
Levi answers that the case involves a continuous flow (שופעת), and Beit Shammai themselves hold there is one ma'ayan.
The Gemara asks: according to Levi, the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is clear, but according to Rav, what is the difference between them?
The Gemara answers that the difference between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel according to Rav is whether impurity depends on days alone or days and immersion.

items.text: Further challenge from the agreement on yoledet b'zov
items.text_en: Further challenge from the agreement on yoledet b'zov
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Levi again from the Mishnah where all agree a yoledet b'zov is impure wet and dry. Levi again says it is a case of continuous flow. The Gemara asks why this teaching is necessary, and Levi explains it is needed for Beit Shammai, who hold one ma'ayan and that impurity depends on days, but for a yoledet b'zov who needs counting, they agree she is impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a challenge to Levi's position by citing the Mishnah where all agree that a woman who gives birth in a state of זוב (abnormal discharge) is impure whether wet or dry.
The Gemara initially assumes that the woman stopped counting her clean days, and questions how this fits with Rav's view of a single source (מעין אחד) versus Levi's view of two sources (שני מעיינות).
The Gemara notes that for Rav it is fine, but for Levi it is difficult, so Levi explains that here too it is a case of continuous flow (שופעת).

The Gemara asks why the teaching is necessary if it is continuous flow, and Levi explains it was needed for Beit Shammai, who hold one source and that impurity depends on days, but for a יולדת בזוב (woman giving birth with abnormal discharge) who needs counting, they agree she is impure.

items.text: Deriving the need for seven clean days for a yoledet b'zov
items.text_en: Deriving the need for seven clean days for a yoledet b'zov
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a derivation from the verse 'd'votah titma' to include the yoledet b'zov requiring seven clean days. It notes that according to Rav, who holds one ma'ayan, this is necessary, implying Levi's view may differ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous discussion by adducing a baraita that derives from the verse 'דְּוֹתָהּ תִּטְמָא' (her impurity) that a yoledet b'zov (one who gave birth in a zav-like state) must count seven clean days.
The baraita lists three inclusions from 'דְּוֹתָהּ תִּטְמָא': one for her husband, one for nights, and one for the yoledet b'zov requiring seven clean days.
The Gemara notes the baraita fits Rav's view that there is a single ma'ayan (source), making the seven clean days necessary; the derivation for Levi is cut off at the end of the section.

items.text: First objection to Levi from the requirement of seven clean days
items.text_en: First objection to Levi from the requirement of seven clean days
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to Levi who says there are two sources, why does a woman need seven clean days? A minimal cessation should suffice. The Gemara answers: she needs to cease for a minimal amount so that it counts toward her seven clean days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Levi: if there are two sources, why require seven clean days? A minimal cessation should suffice.
The Gemara answers: she needs to cease for a minimal amount so that it counts toward her seven clean days.

items.text: Second objection to Levi from the baraita of three seasons
items.text_en: Second objection to Levi from the baraita of three seasons
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a woman who needs three seasons of cessation. For Rav, who holds one source, three seasons are needed. For Levi, a minimal cessation should suffice. The Gemara answers: she needs to cease for a minimal amount so that it counts toward three seasons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a woman whose days of pregnancy and nursing combine to count toward three seasons of cessation.
