The Gemara objects: for Rav, who holds one source, three seasons are needed; for Levi, who holds two sources, a minimal cessation should suffice.
The Gemara answers: she needs to cease for a minimal amount so that it counts toward three seasons.

items.text: Objection to Rav from the law of blood after the pure blood
items.text_en: Objection to Rav from the law of blood after the pure blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to Levi, a woman who sees blood after the pure blood is only impure for that moment, consistent with two sources. But according to Rav, why is she not impure retroactively for a full day? The Gemara answers: because there is no time interval, and the Sages did not decree retroactive impurity from examination to examination when there is no full day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita: according to Levi, a woman who sees blood after the pure blood is only impure for that moment, but according to Rav, why is she not impure retroactively for a full day?
The Gemara answers: because there is no time interval (a full day) to trigger retroactive impurity.
The Gemara objects further: even without a full day, why not decree retroactive impurity from examination to examination?
The Gemara resolves: since there is no full day interval, the Sages did not decree retroactive impurity from examination to examination in this case.

items.text: Objection to Levi from the case of a woman in זוב who counted but did not immerse
items.text_en: Objection to Levi from the case of a woman in זוב who counted but did not immerse
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to Rav, a woman in זוב who saw after counting but before immersion is impure for wet and dry, consistent with one source. But according to Levi, why is she impure for dry? Levi answers: he follows the Tanna who says they agree. Alternatively, the case is of a woman giving birth to a female in זוב, where the first week stopped and the second did not, and days without seeing count toward her זוב count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita about a woman in זוב who counted clean days but did not immerse and then saw blood: according to Rav it is consistent, but according to Levi, why does she transmit impurity both wet and dry?
Levi answers that he follows the Tanna who holds that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree in this case.
The Gemara objects to the alternative explanation that the woman was a שופעת (continuous flow), because the baraita explicitly says she counted clean days.
The Gemara resolves: the case involves a woman who gave birth to a female while in זוב, where the first week stopped and the second did not, and days without seeing count toward her זוב count.

items.text: Final ruling: halakha follows Rav
items.text_en: Final ruling: halakha follows Rav
items.desc_en: Ravina reports that Mar Zutra taught that the halakha follows both Rav and Levi stringently. Rav Ashi and Marimar rule that the halakha follows Rav both leniently and stringently, and the Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rav in all cases.

sub.desc_en: Ravina reports to Rav Ashi that Mar Zutra taught that the halakha follows both Rav and Levi stringently.
Rav Ashi and Marimar rule that the halakha follows Rav both leniently and stringently, and the Gemara concludes accordingly.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The status of a woman in hard labor
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The status of a woman in hard labor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says a woman who experiences three days of pain within the eleven days of zivah, then has a respite of a full day, and gives birth, is a yoledet b'zov. Rabbi Yehoshua defines the respite as a night and a day like Shabbat. The Mishnah then discusses the duration of קישוי: Rabbi Meir says up to forty or fifty days, Rabbi Yehuda says her month, and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say no more than two weeks.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman in hard labor and presents Rabbi Eliezer's position: if she experienced three days of pain within the eleven days of zivah, then had a respite of a full day, and gave birth, she is a yoledet b'zov.
Rabbi Yehoshua defines the required respite as a night and a day like Shabbat, specifying that the respite is from pain, not from blood.

sub.text: Mishnah's dispute on duration of קישוי
sub.text_en: Mishnah's dispute on duration of קישוי
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records the dispute on the maximum duration of קישוי (labor pain): Rabbi Meir says up to forty or fifty days, Rabbi Yehuda says her month, and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say no more than two weeks.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Does every woman in hard labor become a niddah? Rav says she is a niddah for the day, Shmuel says we are concerned she might have a discharge, and Rabbi Yitzchak says she is nothing. The Gemara objects with the Mishnah's statement. Rava resolves: In days of niddah she is a niddah, in days of zivah she is pure, and a baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's blanket statement that a woman in hard labor is a niddah, asking whether every woman in hard labor is indeed a niddah.
Rav answers that a woman in hard labor is a niddah only for the day of the pain.
Shmuel answers that we are concerned she might have a discharge, so she is treated as a niddah.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that a woman in hard labor is nothing (not a niddah at all).
The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah which explicitly states that a woman in hard labor is a niddah.
Rava resolves the contradiction: in days of niddah she is a niddah, but in days of zivah she is pure.

items.text: Details of the baraita and Chananya's opinion
items.text_en: Details of the baraita and Chananya's opinion
items.desc_en: The baraita details cases: if pain precedes a respite before birth, she is a yoledet b'zov; if respite precedes pain, she is not. The rule: קושי סמוך ללידה is not yoledet b'zov, שופי סמוך ללידה is. Chananya ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua adds: if her pain began on the third day, even if the entire day is respite, she is not yoledet b'zov.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with examples: if pain precedes a respite before birth, she is a יולדת בזוב (one who gives birth as a זבה).

The baraita continues with opposite cases: if respite precedes pain, she is not a יולדת בזוב, and states the principle: קושי סמוך ללידה (pain adjacent to birth) exempts, שופי סמוך ללידה (respite adjacent to birth) renders her a יולדת בזוב.
חנניה בן אחי רבי יהושע (Chananya ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua) adds: if her pain began on the third day, even if the entire day is respite, she is not a יולדת בזוב.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the baraita's rule
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the baraita's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'כללו של דבר' comes to include, and answers: it includes Chananya's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'כללו של דבר' (the principle of the matter) in the baraita comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it comes to include the ruling of חנניא (Chananya), son of Rabbi Yehoshua's brother.

items.text: Scriptural derivation for blood from the fetus
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation for blood from the fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'דמה' that blood comes from herself, not from the fetus. It considers the alternative of אונס (accident) and rejects it, concluding that birth is a greater אונס. A counter-argument is raised and dismissed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that blood comes from the woman herself, not from the fetus.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'דָּמָהּ' (her blood) that blood comes from herself, not from the fetus.

The Gemara raises an alternative: perhaps the exclusion is for אונס (accident), not for the fetus, and then resolves that the verse 'וְאִשָּׁה כִּי יָזוּב' already includes accident, so 'דָּמָהּ' must exclude the fetus.
The Gemara justifies the distinction: the fetus is purified after birth, whereas accident has no subsequent purification.
A counter-argument is raised: accident should be purified, as accident in a male זב is pure, but the Gemara notes that no accident is found in a woman.
The Gemara concludes with an alternative: birth itself is the greatest accident, so the fetus is excluded and accident is included.

items.text: Derivation for zivah and the source for קושי in zivah days
items.text_en: Derivation for zivah and the source for קושי in zivah days
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the same logic to the word 'זבה' and then seeks the source that קושי in zivah days is pure. Resh Lakish suggests the word 'תשב' implies another sitting like this, but is rejected. Avuh d'Shmuel derives from 'וטמאה שבועים כנדתה' that zivah blood is pure, and this refers to קושי in zivah days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the logic of 'דמה' applies to zivah, then for niddah as well the word 'זבה' should exclude blood due to childbirth.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'זבה' excludes only blood due to childbirth, not due to coercion, because coercion is already included in the general phrase 'כי תהיה זבה'.
Resh Lakish derives from the word 'תשב' (she shall sit) that there is another 'sitting' like the days of purity, namely קושי (labor pains) during the eleven days of zivah, which is pure.
The Gemara objects that the verse could equally refer to קושי during the days of niddah, not specifically zivah.

Avuh d'Shmuel resolves the issue by citing the verse 'וטמאה שבועים כנדתה' (she shall be impure two weeks as in her niddah), implying that her zivah blood is pure, and this refers to קושי during the eleven days of zivah.

items.text: Clarification of the verses
items.text_en: Clarification of the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without the word 'דמה', one might have thought that 'כנדתה ולא כזיבתה' applies even to שופי, so the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Now that the verse 'וטמאה שבועים כנדתה' (and she shall be impure two weeks as in her menstruation) is written, why is the term 'דמה' (her blood) needed?

The Gemara answers: Without 'דמה', one might have thought 'כנדתה ולא כזיבתה' (as in her menstruation and not as in her ziva) applies even to שופי (resting from labor), so the verse teaches us otherwise.

items.text: Story of Sheila bar Avina and Rav Asi's enforcement
items.text_en: Story of Sheila bar Avina and Rav Asi's enforcement
items.desc_en: Sheila bar Avina ruled like Rav. On his deathbed, Rav told Rav Asi to 'צנעיה' (restrain him), but Rav Asi misunderstood as 'גדייה' (excommunicate him). After Rav's death, Rav Asi learned Rav had retracted, but Sheila did not comply, leading to a confrontation where they boasted of their lineage. Rav Asi fell ill and died from alternating hot and cold treatments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Sheila bar Avina ruled like Rav, and on his deathbed Rav told Rav Asi to 'צנעיה' (restrain him), but Rav Asi misunderstood as 'גדייה' (excommunicate him).
After Rav's death, Rav Asi asked Sheila bar Avina if he knew that Rav had retracted, and when Sheila doubted it, Rav Asi excommunicated him.
Sheila bar Avina boasted of his lineage as unbreakable iron, and Rav Asi countered with his own lineage as brass that breaks iron.
Rav Asi fell ill and died from alternating hot and cold treatments.

items.text: Opening story about Sheila's death and the rabbis' lottery
items.text_en: Opening story about Sheila's death and the rabbis' lottery
items.desc_en: A story is told about Sheila who, suspecting he would be asked a difficult question by Rav, asked his wife to prepare provisions. He died, and the rabbis saw a myrtle branch flying from one bed to another, indicating they had conducted a lottery (פייסא) for his position.

sub.desc_en: The story recounts that Sheila, suspecting Rav would question him, asked his wife for provisions, then died; the rabbis saw a myrtle branch flying between beds, indicating they conducted a lottery (פייסא) for his position.

items.text: Rava's question: Does קושי interrupt זיבה?
items.text_en: Rava's question: Does קושי interrupt זיבה?
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a קושי (difficult labor) interrupts the counting of זיבה days. The question is whether it is considered a דבר המטמא (something that imparts impurity) like the days of niddah, which interrupts, or a דבר הגורם (something that causes impurity) which does not interrupt.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a קושי (difficult labor) interrupts the counting of זיבה days, considering whether it is a דבר המטמא (something that imparts impurity) like niddah days, which interrupts, or a דבר הגורם (something that causes impurity) which does not interrupt.

items.text: Abaye's proof from אונס and Rava's counter with Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from אונס and Rava's counter with Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that an אונס (accidental emission) in זיבה proves that even a non-causative event interrupts. Rava counters that אונס is itself causative, citing a mishnah that a third sighting requires examination. For Rabbi Eliezer, who requires examination even for the third, it is non-causative and does not interrupt.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that an אונס (accidental emission) in זיבה proves that even a non-causative event interrupts the counting.
Rava counters that אונס is itself causative, citing a mishnah that a third sighting requires examination.
Rava concludes that for Rabbi Eliezer, who requires examination even for the third sighting, the emission is non-causative and does not interrupt.

items.text: Attempted proof from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on the fourth sighting
items.text_en: Attempted proof from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on the fourth sighting
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from Rabbi Eliezer's statement that the fourth sighting does not require examination, suggesting it is for interruption (סתירה). It is rejected: it is for impurity by carrying (משא). Another attempt: it is for the sacrifice (קרבן), not interruption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from Rabbi Eliezer's statement that the fourth sighting does not require examination, suggesting it is for interruption (סתירה).
The Gemara rejects the proof: the examination is to determine impurity by carrying (משא), not for interruption.
The Gemara brings another baraita to prove that Rabbi Eliezer's examination is for interruption.
The Gemara rejects again: the examination is for the sacrifice (קרבן), not for interruption.
The Gemara concludes that for Rabbi Eliezer, a non-causative substance negates the count, and asks what the halakha is for the Rabbis.

items.text: Proof from the baraita of Avuh deRabbi Avin
items.text_en: Proof from the baraita of Avuh deRabbi Avin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis hold. A baraita states: 'What does his זוב cause? Seven days, therefore it interrupts seven; what does his קרי cause? One day, therefore it interrupts one.' This proves that only a causative thing (גורם) interrupts, not a non-causative one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve the dilemma by citing a baraita from the father of רבי אבין (Rabbi Avin), which states that what a זוב (ziva) causes—seven days of impurity—therefore it negates seven clean days, while a קרי (seminal emission) causes only one day of impurity, so it negates only one day.

The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if it merely meant that זוב (ziva) imparts impurity for seven days, it should have said 'just as his זוב is impure for seven days'; rather, it teaches that a causative substance (גורם) negates the count, while a non-causative one does not, and concludes that this is the proof.

items.text: Abaye's conclusion: קושי does not interrupt in זיבה
items.text_en: Abaye's conclusion: קושי does not interrupt in זיבה
items.desc_en: Abaye states the accepted ruling: קושי does not interrupt in זיבה. If you find a tanna who says it does, that is Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states the accepted ruling that קושי (difficult birth) does not interrupt the counting of זיבה (gonorrhea-like discharge), and any tanna who says it does is following Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.

items.text: Debate on whether לידה interrupts or counts in זיבה
items.text_en: Debate on whether לידה interrupts or counts in זיבה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Marinus says that לידה does not interrupt in זיבה. The question is whether it counts (עולה) toward the seven clean days. Abaye says it neither interrupts nor counts; Rava says it does not interrupt but does count. Rava brings proofs from verses, and Abaye offers alternative interpretations.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Marinus states that לידה (childbirth) does not interrupt (סותרת) the counting of clean days in the context of זיבה (a zavah's discharge).
The Gemara raises an inquiry: does לידה count (עולה) toward the seven clean days of זיבה, even though it does not interrupt?
Abaye rules that לידה neither interrupts nor counts toward the seven clean days.
Rava rules that לידה does not interrupt but does count toward the seven clean days.
Rava cites a baraita from the verse 'וְאַחַר תִּטְהָר' (and after she becomes pure) to argue that no impurity should interrupt the clean days, supporting that לידה counts.
Rava argues: if לידה counts, then no impurity interrupts; but if it does not count, then the birth itself creates an interruption, contradicting the verse.
Abaye counters that the verse only means that טומאת זיבה (impurity of זיבה) should not interrupt, not that לידה itself cannot interrupt.
Rava cites another baraita: the verse 'מִזּוֹבָהּ' (from her discharge) excludes impurity from a נגע (skin lesion) and from לידה, implying that לידה is not excluded from counting.
Abaye rejects the baraita's second clause, saying one should only teach 'מִזּוֹבָהּ' excludes a נגע, not לידה.

Rava objects: if the baraita only excludes a נגע, that rule is already derived from the verse 'וְכִי יִטְהַר הַזָּב מִזּוֹבוֹ' (when the zav is cleansed from his discharge), so the baraita must also exclude לידה.
The Gemara resolves that Abaye distinguishes between a זב (male zav) and a זבה (female zavah), and both derivations are necessary.

items.text: Need for both זב and זבה verses
items.text_en: Need for both זב and זבה verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah needed to write the law of זב and זבה separately: each has a unique leniency that might lead one to exempt the other, so both are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a potential redundancy: since a זב (male with discharge) does not transmit impurity through אונס (unintentional emission), one might think a זבה (female with discharge) who does transmit through אונס should be exempt, so both verses are needed.
The Gemara concludes that both verses are indeed necessary because each has a unique leniency that could lead to exemption of the other.

items.text: Abaye's derivation from "דותה תטמא"
items.text_en: Abaye's derivation from "דותה תטמא"
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a beraita that expounds the verse "דותה תטמא" to include the woman's husband, the nights, and a woman who gives birth in a state of זוב, requiring seven clean days. The Gemara clarifies that the clean days are from blood, not from childbirth.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces his derivation from the verse "דותה תטמא" to include the woman's husband.
The baraita continues to expound the verse to include the nights and a woman who gives birth in a state of זוב (a discharge), requiring seven clean days.
The Gemara asks whether the clean days are from childbirth (i.e., free of childbirth impurity) or from blood.
The Gemara answers that the clean days are from blood, not from childbirth.

items.text: Abaye's second derivation and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Abaye's second derivation and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Abaye cites another beraita comparing the days of childbirth to the days of menstruation, concluding that days unfit for זוב do not count toward the seven clean days. Rava objects that this is the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that a woman in such days even סותרת (invalidates previous clean days).

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a beraita comparing the days of childbirth to the days of menstruation, concluding that days unfit for זוב do not count toward the seven clean days.
Rava objects that this beraita reflects only Rabbi Eliezer's view, who holds that such days even סותרת (invalidate previous clean days).

items.text: Debate on deriving possible from impossible
items.text_en: Debate on deriving possible from impossible
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can derive a case that is possible from one that is impossible. Rav Ahadbui bar Ami and Rav Sheishet offer different resolutions: one attributes the view to Rabbi Eliezer who allows such derivation, while the other says the verse itself makes the comparison unavoidable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can derive a case that is possible (possible) from one that is impossible (impossible).
Rav Ahadbui bar Ami resolves that the view is Rabbi Eliezer's, who holds that one can derive possible from impossible.
Rav Sheishet resolves that the verse itself makes the comparison unavoidable, regardless of the general principle.
An alternative version attributes to Rav Ahadbui bar Ami citing Rav Sheishet that the view is Rabbi Eliezer's, while Rav Pappa says the verse itself makes the comparison unavoidable.

items.text: Dispute on a woman who rested from both pain and blood
items.text_en: Dispute on a woman who rested from both pain and blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a woman who experienced pain for three days. An inquiry arises: if she rested from both pain and blood, what is her status? Rav Chisda rules she is טמאה, while Rabbi Chanina rules she is טהורה, each offering a parable about a king and his troops.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, introducing the case of a woman who experienced pain for three days.
The Gemara raises an inquiry: if the woman rested from both pain and blood, what is her status?
Rav Chisda rules that she is טמאה (ritually impure).
Rabbi Chanina rules that she is טהורה (ritually pure).
Rabbi Chanina offers a parable: a king who goes out with his troops — it is known that they are the king's troops, implying that cessation of pain and blood together indicates purity.
Rav Chisda counters: all the more so the king needs more troops, implying that cessation of both indicates impurity.

items.text: Refutation of Rav Chisda from Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Chisda from Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehoshua says a woman who rests from pain but not from blood is pure, implying that if she rests from both she is pure, refuting Rav Chisda. Rav Chisda defends himself by distinguishing between resting from both and resting only from pain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehoshua says a woman who rests from pain but not from blood is pure, implying that if she rests from both she is pure, which refutes Rav Chisda.

Rav Chisda defends himself by distinguishing between resting from both pain and blood (which is certainly impure) and resting only from pain (where one might think the pain has not fully ceased), and the Mishnah teaches that even in the latter case she is pure.

items.text: Refutation of Rabbi Chanina from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Refutation of Rabbi Chanina from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a Mishnah about a woman who experienced pain for three days and then rested for a full day. It suggests that the Mishnah implies she rested from both pain and blood, refuting Rabbi Chanina. Rabbi Chanina explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where the pain began on the third day, and she rested only from pain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a woman who experienced pain for three days within the eleven-day זוב (zavah) period, rested for a full day, and then gave birth — she is classified as a יולדת בזוב (a woman who gives birth while in a state of זוב).
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's formulation: if it describes three days of pain followed by a full day of rest, why mention three days? Two days of pain and one of rest would suffice.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: it means she rested from both pain and blood, and this refutes Rabbi Chanina's position that such a woman is pure.

Rabbi Chanina rejects the refutation, explaining that the Mishnah refers to a case where the pain began on the third day and she rested only from pain, not from blood, thereby excluding his own view that such a woman is pure.

items.text: Duration of labor pain and dispute on days counted
items.text_en: Duration of labor pain and dispute on days counted
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about the duration of labor pain, resolving that it refers to a weak woman versus a healthy one. Rabbi Levi and Rav dispute which days the fetus purifies: only days fit for זבה or also days fit for counting a זבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about the duration of labor pain, asking how forty days can be less than fifty.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a weak woman (חולה) and a healthy one (בריאה).
Rabbi Levi states that the fetus purifies only during days fit for a זבה (zavah).
Rav argues that the fetus purifies even during days fit for counting a זבה (zavah).
Rav Adda bar Ahavah introduces a discussion about Rav's reasoning, but the move is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening statement: Even days suitable for counting zivah
items.text_en: Opening statement: Even days suitable for counting zivah
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that even days that are suitable for counting the zivah period (i.e., days when a woman could potentially be a zivah) are included in the ruling that the fetus purifies the woman from zivah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that even days suitable for counting the zivah period are included in the ruling that the fetus purifies the woman from zivah.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Levi regarding which days the fetus purifies
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Levi regarding which days the fetus purifies
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about Rabbi Meir's opinion on the duration of labor (40-50 days). It questions how this fits with the views of Rav and Levi. Rav holds that the fetus purifies even days suitable for a minor zivah, while Levi holds it only purifies days suitable for a major zivah. The Gemara explains their scriptural derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah that records Rabbi Meir's opinion that the duration of labor pain is forty to fifty days.
The Gemara questions how the mishnah fits with the views of Rav and Levi: it is understandable for Rav (per Rav Adda bar Ahava), but difficult for Levi.
Levi responds that the mishnah does not state she is pure in all those days; rather, days of menstruation render her a menstruant, and only days of זיבה (zivah) are pure.
An alternative version states that Rabbi Levi explicitly rules that the fetus purifies only days suitable for a major זבה (zavah), deriving this from the verse 'יָמִים רַבִּים' (many days).
Abba Shaul reports in Rav's name that the fetus purifies even days suitable for a minor זבה (zavah), deriving this from the words 'יְמֵי' and 'כׇל יְמֵי' written in the verse.

items.text: Challenge to both Rav and Levi from the mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to both Rav and Levi from the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges both Rav and Levi from the mishnah that states Rabbi Meir says a woman can be in labor for 40-50 days. The mishnah does not say she is pure throughout; rather, if she labors during her niddah days she is a niddah, and during zivah days she is pure. This contradicts the earlier statement that the fetus purifies all days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita says Rabbi Meir allows up to forty-five days, which is difficult for both Rav and Levi — but the baraita does not say 'pure in all of them'; it distinguishes between niddah and zivah days.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's baraita on 150 days of labor and the sages' objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's baraita on 150 days of labor and the sages' objection
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir says a woman can be in labor for 150 days without zivah occurring. He explains the calculation: 2 days before her period, 7 niddah, 2 after niddah, 50 purified by the fetus, 80 for a female, 7 niddah, and 2 after niddah. The sages object that this would allow labor all her days without zivah. Rabbi Meir responds that there is no labor for miscarriages.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir states that a woman can be in labor for 150 days without zivah occurring, and he explains the calculation of the days.
The sages object that according to Rabbi Meir's calculation, a woman could be in labor all her days without zivah occurring.
Rabbi Meir responds that the sages' concern about miscarriages is unfounded, because there is no labor (קושי) for miscarriages.

items.text: Baraita on 100 days without zivah and its lesson
items.text_en: Baraita on 100 days without zivah and its lesson
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that a woman can see blood for 100 days without zivah occurring, with a similar calculation. The Gemara explains that this teaches that it is possible for the opening of the womb (פתיחת הקבר) to occur without blood, contradicting one who says it is impossible.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a woman can see blood for 100 days without zivah occurring, detailing the calculation of days.
The Gemara explains that this baraita teaches that it is possible for the opening of the womb (פתיחת הקבר) to occur without blood, contradicting one who says it is impossible.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion in the name of Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion in the name of Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon that a woman's labor period is sufficient for her month (i.e., she is not a zivah during labor). The Gemara explains how this can be lenient or stringent: if she labors 2 days at the end of the eighth month and 1 at the beginning of the ninth, she gives birth with zivah; but if she labors 1 day at the end of the eighth and 2 at the beginning of the ninth, she does not give birth with zivah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon that a woman's labor period is sufficient for her month, and this can be lenient or stringent.
The baraita explains the lenient case: if she labors two days at the end of the eighth month and one at the beginning of the ninth, she gives birth with זוב (zivah status).
The baraita explains the stringent case: if she labors one day at the end of the eighth month and two at the beginning of the ninth, she does not give birth with זוב (zivah status).

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's inference and Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's inference and Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava infers from Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the appearance of the fetus (שיפורא) causes the labor, not the days. The Gemara questions this based on Shmuel's statement that a woman only gives birth after 271-273 days. The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement follows the practice of the early pious ones, who only had relations on Wednesday nights to avoid birth on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava infers from Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the appearance of the fetus (שיפורא) causes the labor, not the days.
The Gemara objects by citing Shmuel's statement that a woman only gives birth after 271-273 days, implying the days matter.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement follows the practice of the early pious ones, who only had relations on Wednesday nights to avoid birth on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's question on the duration of קשי
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the duration of קשי
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a woman in hard labor is not considered to have violated Shabbat until the fourth day, and clarifies that the Mishnah means from the fourth day onward.

items.text: Mar Zutra's explanation of the pious ones' practice and the duration of pregnancy
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's explanation of the pious ones' practice and the duration of pregnancy
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra explains that the early pious ones refrained from relations from the fourth day because the gematria of 'הריון' is 271, corresponding to the maximum pregnancy days. He further states that even for those who hold that a nine-month pregnancy cannot be shortened, a seven-month pregnancy can be shortened, as derived from Hannah's pregnancy.

items.text: Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon's opinion and Shmuel's explanation of the Rabbis' view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon's opinion and Shmuel's explanation of the Rabbis' view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon state that קשי does not last more than two weeks. Shmuel explains the Rabbis' reasoning from the verse 'וטמאה שבועים כנדתה', implying that the days of זיבה are pure, and asks how many weeks are meant.

items.text: The Baraisa on the maximum days of קשי and the Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: The Baraisa on the maximum days of קשי and the Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The Baraisa teaches that a woman can be in hard labor for 25 days without becoming a זבה, detailing the breakdown of days. The Gemara questions the wording 'without a child' and, through Rav Sheshet and Rava, clarifies that the statement refers to a place where there is a child, but for a miscarriage, three days suffice.

items.text: Mishnah: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding blood during the eighty days
items.text_en: Mishnah: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding blood during the eighty days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman in hard labor during the eighty days after a female birth sees pure blood until the child is born, but Rabbi Eliezer declares it impure. The Sages argue that if the leniency applies to blood during easy labor, it should apply to hard labor as well. Rabbi Eliezer responds that the leniency only exempts from זיבה, not from נדה.

items.text: Gemara: The Baraisa version of the dispute and additional arguments
items.text_en: Gemara: The Baraisa version of the dispute and additional arguments
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraisa that parallels the Mishnah. The Sages present two additional kal vachomer arguments: one comparing קשי after birth to שופי after birth, and another comparing קשי during the eighty days to שופי during the eighty days. Rabbi Eliezer consistently responds that the leniency only removes זיבה, not נדה.

items.text: Rava's support for Rabbi Eliezer and the Gemara's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's support for Rabbi Eliezer and the Gemara's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the Sages' own principle that blood comes from herself and not from the child supports Rabbi Eliezer, as the verse 'וטהרה ממקור דמיה' implies blood from herself. The Gemara questions whether this applies only to days of נדה, but concludes that the word 'תשב' teaches a single sitting for all days.

items.text: Mishnah: The eleven days of presumed purity
items.text_en: Mishnah: The eleven days of presumed purity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all eleven days (between periods of נדה) are presumed to be pure, introducing the next topic.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman sat without examining, or was negligent, raped, or willful without examining, she is pure. If her vest period arrived and she did not examine, she is impure. Rabbi Meir adds that if she was in hiding and her vest arrived without examination, she is pure because fear suppresses blood. The Mishnah then rules that during the days of the zav, zavah, and the one observing a day for a day, they are presumed impure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who sat without examining, was negligent, raped, or willful without examining — she is pure.
The Mishnah states that if her vest period arrived and she did not examine, she is impure.
Rabbi Meir adds that if she was in hiding and her vest period arrived without examination, she is pure because fear suppresses blood.
The Mishnah concludes that during the days of the zav, zavah, and the one observing a day for a day, they are presumed impure.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Rav Yehuda's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Rav Yehuda's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what halakha is the opening clause taught? Rav Yehuda answers: To say that a woman in her zivah period does not need to examine herself. The Gemara objects: From the fact that the seifa teaches 'she sat and did not examine', it implies that ab initio she does need examination! The Gemara resolves: The seifa refers to the days of niddah, and the Mishnah is saying: All eleven days are presumed pure and do not require examination, but during her niddah days she does require examination.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what halakha is the opening clause of the Mishnah taught?
Rav Yehuda answers: To say that a woman in her zivah period does not need to examine herself.
The Gemara objects: From the seifa which teaches 'she sat and did not examine', it implies that לכתחילה (ab initio) she does require examination!

The Gemara resolves: The seifa refers to the days of niddah, and the Mishnah is saying: All eleven days are presumed pure and do not require examination, but during her niddah days she does require examination; the seifa's ruling of 'she sat and did not examine — pure' applies to the niddah days.

items.text: Rav Chisda's alternative explanation and objection
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's alternative explanation and objection
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says the opening clause is only necessary for Rabbi Meir, who holds that a woman without a fixed vest is forbidden to have relations. The Gemara objects: If so, why did Rabbi Meir say 'he must divorce her and never take her back'? Because she might become lax during niddah days.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the Mishnah's ruling is only necessary for Rabbi Meir, who holds that a woman without a fixed vest (וסת) is forbidden to have relations during her niddah days, but during her zivah days she is presumed pure.

The Gemara objects: If Rav Chisda's explanation is correct, why did Rabbi Meir rule that he must divorce her and never take her back? The answer is that she might become lax (קלקול) during her niddah days.

items.text: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah as dealing with a woman with a vest
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah as dealing with a woman with a vest
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the seifa deals with a woman who has a vest, implying the entire Mishnah is about such a woman. It then reinterprets the Mishnah as missing a clause: All eleven days are presumed pure and permitted to her husband, but during niddah she is forbidden. In what case? For a woman without a vest; but one with a vest is permitted but requires examination. The Gemara then resolves the apparent contradiction between the reisha and seifa by stating the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, who distinguishes between hiding and not hiding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the seifa (later clause) of the Mishnah mentions a woman whose time of her vest (fixed cycle) arrived and she did not examine, implying the entire discussion is about a woman who has a vest.

The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah as missing a clause: all eleven days are presumed pure and permitted to her husband, but during niddah she is forbidden; this applies to a woman without a vest, but one with a vest is permitted yet requires examination.

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the reisha and seifa by stating the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, who distinguishes between hiding (which causes fear that clears blood) and not hiding.

items.text: Rava's interpretation and refutation
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation and refutation
items.desc_en: Rava says the opening clause teaches that a woman in her zivah period does not render impure retroactively (me'et le'et). The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states a niddah, zavah, etc., all render impure retroactively. This is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's ruling teaches that a woman in her zivah period does not render impure retroactively (מעת לעת).
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists a niddah, zavah, etc., all of which render impure retroactively, concluding that this is a refutation of Rava.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Chiya's interpretation and support from a story
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya's interpretation and support from a story
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya says in the name of Shmuel: The opening clause teaches that a woman does not establish a fixed vest during her zivah days. Rav Yosef says he had not heard this teaching. Abaye then recounts that Rav Yosef himself taught a related ruling: If a woman was accustomed to seeing on day 15 and changed to day 20, both are forbidden; and Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that this applies only when day 15 is from her immersion (i.e., day 22 from her sight), which falls in niddah, but day 15 from her sight falls in zivah and does not establish a vest.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya reports in Shmuel's name that the Mishnah's opening clause teaches that a woman does not establish a fixed vest (וסת) during her zivah days.
Rav Yosef states that he had not heard this teaching before.
Abaye reminds Rav Yosef that he himself taught a ruling: if a woman changed her pattern from day 15 to day 20, both days are forbidden for marital relations.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, as reported by Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, as reported by Abaye
sub.desc_en: Abaye further recalls that Rav Yehuda said in Shmuel's name that the ruling applies only when day 15 is counted from her immersion (falling in niddah), but day 15 from her sight (falling in zivah) does not establish a vest.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about concern for a possible vest
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about concern for a possible vest
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asked Rav Yehuda of Diskarta: Even if a vest is not established during zivah, should we at least be concerned about it? Rav Yehuda was silent. Rav Pappa then attempts to resolve the question himself, citing the case of a woman accustomed to seeing on day 15 who changed to day 20, where both are forbidden, implying concern.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rav Yehuda of Diskarta: Even if a vest is not established during zivah, should we at least be concerned about it?
Rav Yehuda of Diskarta remains silent and does not answer Rav Pappa.
Rav Pappa attempts to resolve the question himself by citing the case of a woman who changed from day 15 to day 20, where both are forbidden, implying concern.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel's ruling on counting days
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel's ruling on counting days
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states that the dispute about a woman who saw blood on day 15 after her immersion (day 22 from her sighting) and then changed to day 27 applies only when the second sighting occurs on day 27, because when she returns to day 22, she falls within the days of zivah, and the Mishnah rules both are forbidden, indicating we are concerned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states that the dispute about a woman who saw blood on day 15 after her immersion (day 22 from her sighting) and then changed to day 27 applies only when the second sighting occurs on day 27, because when she returns to day 22, she falls within the days of zivah, and the Mishnah rules both are forbidden, indicating we are concerned.

items.text: Rav Pappa's interpretation of the counting
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's interpretation of the counting
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the 22 days are counted from day 22, while niddah and its opening are counted from day 27.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that the 22 days are counted from day 22, while niddah and its opening are counted from day 27.

items.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's challenge and proof
items.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's challenge and proof
items.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua challenges Rav Pappa, suggesting that the 22 days might also be counted from day 27, placing her within the days of niddah. He brings a proof from a hen that lays and skips days, showing that when she resumes, she follows the pattern of the most recent interval.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua challenges Rav Pappa, suggesting that the 22 days might also be counted from day 27, placing her within the days of niddah.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's proof from a hen
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's proof from a hen
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brings a proof from a hen that lays and skips days, showing that when she resumes, she follows the pattern of the most recent interval.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks about Resh Lakish's statement that a woman can establish a fixed cycle within the days of zivah but not within niddah, while Rabbi Yochanan says she can establish a cycle within niddah. He presents a case of sightings on Rosh Chodesh and the 5th, and now she saw on the 5th but not on Rosh Chodesh, implying counting from Rosh Chodesh.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks about the practical case illustrating the dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding whether a woman can establish a fixed cycle (וסת) within the days of niddah.
Rav Pappa proposes a case: a woman saw on Rosh Chodesh and the 5th repeatedly, and now saw on the 5th but not on Rosh Chodesh, implying counting from Rosh Chodesh.
Rav Pappa infers that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a woman can establish a cycle within niddah implies counting from Rosh Chodesh, contradicting the earlier assumption.

Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that Rabbi Yochanan's case is different: a woman saw on Rosh Chodesh, Rosh Chodesh, the 25th, and Rosh Chodesh, where the extra days are attributed to additional blood.
The gemara notes that when Ravin and other seafarers came, they reported the tradition in accordance with Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's interpretation.

items.text: Rav Huna's clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Rav Huna's clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: Rav Huna responds that Rabbi Yochanan's case is different: when she saw on Rosh Chodesh, Rosh Chodesh, and the 25th, and then Rosh Chodesh, we say it is due to an excess of blood, not a fixed cycle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna corrects Rav Pappa's understanding: Rabbi Yochanan's case is when she saw on Rosh Chodesh, Rosh Chodesh, and the 25th, and then Rosh Chodesh, where we attribute the extra sighting to an excess of blood, not a fixed cycle.

items.text: Conclusion: Support for Rav Huna's view
items.text_en: Conclusion: Support for Rav Huna's view
items.desc_en: When Ravin and all who descend to the sea arrived, they reported the ruling in accordance with Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes that when Ravin and all who descend to the sea arrived, they reported the ruling in accordance with Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a child born by caesarean section does not require the mother to observe days of impurity or purity, nor does it obligate a sacrifice. Rabbi Shimon disagrees, considering it like a normally born child. It then discusses that women become impure from internal blood, but a zav or ba'al keri only when their impurity exits externally, and a person eating terumah who feels arousal must hold his membrum and swallow the terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a child born by caesarean section (יוצא דופן) does not require the mother to observe days of impurity or purity, nor a sacrifice, while Rabbi Shimon considers it like a normally born child.
The Mishnah states that women become impure from internal blood, but a zav or ba'al keri only when their impurity exits externally.

The Mishnah rules that a person eating תרומה (priestly portion) who feels arousal must hold his membrum and swallow the terumah, and that such emissions impart impurity in any amount, even as small as a mustard seed or less.

items.text: Gemara's first question and scriptural derivation for the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and scriptural derivation for the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish asks the reason of the Rabbis, deriving from the verse 'When a woman conceives and gives birth to a male' that birth must be through the place of conception. Rabbi Shimon interprets the same verse to include a caesarean birth. The Rabbis use the word 'teled' to include a tumtum and androgynos.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish asks what is the reason of the Rabbis who exempt a caesarean birth from the laws of impurity.
The Gemara derives from the verse 'אִשָּׁה כִּי תַזְרִיעַ וְיָלְדָה זָכָר' that birth must be through the place of conception, excluding a caesarean section.
The Gemara objects: how does Rabbi Shimon interpret the same verse? He learns that even a birth resembling conception renders the mother impure.

sub.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Shimon's reason
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Shimon's reason
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Shimon's own reason for including a caesarean birth.
Resh Lakish answers that Rabbi Shimon derives from the word 'תֵּלֵד' to include a caesarean birth.

sub.text: Gemara's answer for the Rabbis' use of 'teled'
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for the Rabbis' use of 'teled'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis use the word 'תֵּלֵד' to include a טומטום (tumtum) and אנדרוגינוס (androgynos), countering a possible exclusion from the terms 'זָכָר' and 'נְקֵבָה'.

items.text: Bar Leviai's teaching and the Rabbis' response
items.text_en: Bar Leviai's teaching and the Rabbis' response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives from Bar Leviai's teaching that 'leven' and 'levat' include any son or daughter. The Rabbis use these words to obligate a sacrifice for each son and each daughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon derives the inclusion of a יוצא דופן (caesarean-section birth) from Bar Leviai's teaching that 'לבן' and 'לבת' include any son or daughter, regardless of birth mode.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis use the words 'לבן' and 'לבת' to obligate a separate sacrifice for each son and each daughter, not to include a יוצא דופן.

items.text: Tanna's teaching before Rav Sheishet and the Rabbis' additional derivation
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching before Rav Sheishet and the Rabbis' additional derivation
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Sheishet that the verse 'Zot torat hayoledet' teaches that a woman can bring one sacrifice for multiple births, but not for a birth and a zivah together, nor for births before and after the completion of days. The Rabbis need 'leven o levat' despite 'zot' to exclude a case of twins from one pregnancy.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Sheishet that the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיּוֹלֶדֶת' teaches that a woman can bring one sacrifice for multiple births.
The Tanna asks whether a woman could bring one sacrifice for both a birth and a zivah (abnormal discharge), or for two separate sins (eating blood and eating forbidden fat).
The Tanna asks whether a woman could bring one sacrifice for births before and after the completion of days, and answers that 'זֹאת' excludes this.
The Rabbis explain that despite 'זֹאת', the words 'לְבֵן אוֹ לְבַת' are needed to exclude a case of twins from one pregnancy, where one might think a single sacrifice suffices.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and the debate on the source for consecration
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and the debate on the source for consecration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Shimon concedes that a caesarean birth is not consecrated for sacrifices, deriving from a gezerah shavah of 'leidah' from a firstborn. The Gemara debates whether to learn from a firstborn or from a human, concluding that the firstborn is more similar because it involves the mother and is subject to piggul, notar, and tamei.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Shimon concedes a caesarean birth is not consecrated for sacrifices, deriving this via a גזירה שווה of 'לידה' from firstborn, just as a firstborn requires 'פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם'.
The Gemara objects: why not learn the גזירה שוה from a human birth, where a caesarean birth is considered a valid birth?
The Gemara suggests: it is more logical to learn from firstborn because both involve the mother (אמו).
A counter-argument is raised: learning from a human is more logical because a human birth is פָּשׁוּט (ordinary and straightforward) compared to an animal.
The Gemara proposes a new reason: firstborn is more similar because consecrated animals are subject to piggul, notar, and tamei, which apply to sacrifices but not to humans.
A counter-argument lists human advantages (simple, male, holy, a gift); but the Gemara concludes the firstborn has more similarities (הנך נפישן), settling the debate.

items.text: Supporting baraita from Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives three exclusions from the verse 'Zot torat ha'olah hi ha'olah', supporting Rabbi Yochanan's position.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives three exclusions from the verse 'זאת תורת העולה היא העולה' (This is the law of the burnt offering, it is the burnt offering), supporting Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: disqualifications that do not cause descent
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: disqualifications that do not cause descent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where an olah that was slaughtered at night, whose blood was spilled, or whose blood left the courtyard, if it ascended the altar, it does not descend.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists disqualifications (slaughtered at night, blood spilled, blood taken outside the courtyard) for which an olah that ascended the altar does not descend.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's expansion and scriptural derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's expansion and scriptural derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon expands the list to include many other disqualifications, such as the leftover (notar), the impure (tamei), and those slaughtered outside their proper time or place, and derives from the verse "This is the Torah of the olah" that all offerings that ascend do not descend.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon opens by stating that from the Torah he only has a valid olah (עולה) offering, and then lists many disqualifications that he seeks to include.
Rabbi Shimon continues listing additional disqualifications and asks: from where (מניין) are these included?
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הָעוֹלָה' (This is the Torah of the olah), deriving that one Torah law applies to all that ascend, so if they ascended they do not descend.

items.text: Exclusion of severe disqualifications and the hermeneutical question
items.text_en: Exclusion of severe disqualifications and the hermeneutical question
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether one might include disqualifications like a rove'a (animal that copulated with a human) or a terefah, and excludes them via the word "zot" (this). It then asks: what distinguishes the included from the excluded?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility of including severely disqualified animals (e.g., rove'a, terefah) under the rule that if they ascend the altar they do not descend.
The Gemara answers that the word 'זֹאת' (this) excludes these severe disqualifications from the rule.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes the included disqualifications from the excluded ones, seeking a hermeneutical principle.

items.text: Opening statement: The principle of inclusion and exclusion
items.text_en: Opening statement: The principle of inclusion and exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a general principle: after the Torah included and excluded certain cases, one can say that those whose disqualification was in the sanctuary are included, while those whose disqualification was not in the sanctuary are excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a general principle: after the Torah included and excluded certain cases, one can say that those whose disqualification was in the sanctuary are included, while those whose disqualification was not in the sanctuary are excluded.

items.text: Question and initial answer about יוצא דופן
items.text_en: Question and initial answer about יוצא דופן
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's exclusion of יוצא דופן refers to sacrificial animals or firstborn animals. Rav Huna bar Rav Natan suggests it refers to a firstborn, but the Gemara objects that a firstborn is derived from the verse 'פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם'. The Gemara then considers it refers to sacrificial animals, but objects that it is derived from the word 'אִמּוֹ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's exclusion of יוצא דופן (a birth through the side) refers to sacrificial animals (קדשים) or firstborn animals (בכור).

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan answers that the exclusion refers to a firstborn animal (בכור).
The Gemara objects that a firstborn is already derived from the verse 'פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם' (opener of the womb), so no separate exclusion is needed.
The Gemara alternatively suggests that the exclusion refers to sacrificial animals (קדשים), but then objects that this too is derived from the word 'אִמּוֹ' (its mother).

items.text: Resolution: Two verses needed for sacrificial and non-sacrificial animals
items.text_en: Resolution: Two verses needed for sacrificial and non-sacrificial animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if it refers to sacrificial animals, two verses are necessary: one for a non-sacred animal that gave birth through the wall and was then consecrated, and one for a sacred animal that gave birth through the wall, since the offspring of sacred animals are sanctified at their formation. But if it refers to a firstborn, one verse suffices, so the first interpretation is correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if the verse refers to sacrificial animals, two verses are necessary: one for a non-sacred animal that gave birth through the wall and was then consecrated, and one for a sacred animal that gave birth through the wall, since the offspring of sacred animals are sanctified at their formation.
The Gemara concludes that if the verse referred to a firstborn, one verse would suffice, so the first interpretation (sacrificial animals) is correct.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah's list and final conclusion
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah's list and final conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara finds support from the Mishnah's list of disqualified animals (רובע, נרבע, etc.), which are derived from other verses, showing that two verses are needed for both non-sacred and sacred animals. Thus, the Mishnah's exclusion of יוצא דופן refers to sacrificial animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that its position is supported by the Mishnah's list of disqualified animals (רובע, נרבע, מוקצה, נעבד, and כלאים).
The Gemara objects that these disqualifications are already derived from other verses (e.g., 'מן הבהמה' for רובע and נרבע, 'מן הבקר' for נעבד, 'מן הצאן' for מוקצה and נוגח).
The Gemara further objects that the disqualification of כלאים (kil'ayim) is derived from the verse 'שור או כשב או עז', and that of נדמה (a doubtful species) from the same verse.
The Gemara resolves that two verses are needed: one for non-sacred animals and one for sacred animals, and similarly here two verses are required for יוצא דופן.

items.text: Baraita: Woman in labor and יוצא דופן
items.text_en: Baraita: Woman in labor and יוצא דופן
items.desc_en: A Baraita discusses a woman who suffers labor pains for three days and then gives birth through a Caesarean section: the Sages consider her a יולדת בזוב, while Rabbi Shimon disagrees. The Gemara explains the dispute in the first clause, and Ravina clarifies the second clause about the blood being impure, where they argue about a case where the fetus emerged through the wall.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites a dispute: a woman in labor for three days who delivers via Caesarean section is considered a יולדת בזוב (a woman who gives birth in a state of זוב) according to the Sages, while Rabbi Shimon disagrees; additionally, the blood emerging from the womb is impure, but Rabbi Shimon declares it pure.
The Gemara asks: the first clause is understandable given each side's known positions, but on what basis do they dispute in the second clause?
Ravina explains that the dispute in the second clause concerns a case where the fetus emerged through the wall (דופן) of the womb, not through the birth canal.

items.text: Summary of the previous dispute
items.text_en: Summary of the previous dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis each follow their own reasoning regarding whether blood from the womb causes impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara summarizes that Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis each follow their own reasoning regarding whether blood from the womb causes impurity.

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to the previous explanation, arguing that the case is about a fetus emerging through the side, and the dispute is about whether the source in its place is impure or pure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to the previous explanation, arguing that the case is about the head (the fetus's head) and that the word 'משם' (from there) implies the place of the fetus.

Rav Yosef resolves the objection by explaining that the case involves a fetus emerging through the side (דופן), and the dispute between the Sages is about whether the source in its place (מקור מקומו) is impure or pure.

items.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan argue about whether one who deems the blood impure also deems the woman impure; Rabbi Yochanan holds that even the one who deems the blood impure deems the woman pure, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that one who deems the blood impure also deems the woman impure, and one who deems the blood pure also deems the woman pure.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that even the one who deems the blood impure deems the woman pure.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan supports his position with a verse taught by Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, showing that a woman is not impure until her discharge exits through her genitals.

items.text: Impurity of a detached source and sweat
items.text_en: Impurity of a detached source and sweat
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia rules that a detached source renders the woman impure, but only with evening impurity. Rabbi Yochanan adds that if the source emits two drops like pearls, she is impure with evening impurity, but not with seven-day impurity.

sub.text: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that a detached source (מקור) renders the woman impure, citing a verse.
The Gemara asks whether this impurity is seven-day impurity or evening impurity, and rejects seven-day impurity because the Torah said blood, not a piece.
The Gemara resolves that it is only evening impurity (טומאת ערב).
Rabbi Yochanan adds that a source that sweats two drops like pearls renders the woman impure, but only with evening impurity.
The Gemara specifies that only two drops cause impurity, but one drop is presumed to come from elsewhere.

items.text: Definition of the external chamber
items.text_en: Definition of the external chamber
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the definition of the external chamber (בית החיצון) where all women become impure. Reish Lakish defines it as where a young girl can see, Rabbi Yochanan defines it as up to the labia, and a baraita defines it as the place of treading, explained by Rav Yehuda as where the husband treads.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all women become impure through the external chamber (בית החיצון).
The Gemara asks for the definition of the external chamber.
Reish Lakish defines the external chamber as the area visible when a young girl sits.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that Reish Lakish's definition would make the area exposed like a creeping creature, which is not the case.
Rabbi Yochanan defines the external chamber as up to the labia (בין השיניים).
The Gemara asks whether the labia (בין השיניים) itself is considered inside or outside the external chamber.
A baraita taught by Rabbi Zakkai resolves that the labia itself is considered inside the external chamber.
A baraita defines the external chamber as the place of treading (מקום דישה).
The Gemara asks what 'place of treading' means.
Rav Yehuda explains that the place of treading is where the husband treads during intercourse.

items.text: Impurity of a woman who emits semen
items.text_en: Impurity of a woman who emits semen
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that a woman who emits semen becomes impure, but Rabbi Shimon argues she is like her husband, only impure when the impurity exits. The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between one who serves and one who emits, and explains that the case involves one who immersed for her service.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'בבשרה' that a woman's impurity applies both internally and externally, and extends this to a זבה (zavah) and a פולטת שכבת זרע (woman who emits semen).
Rabbi Shimon argues that a woman who emits semen is like her husband: she only becomes impure when the impurity exits to the outside.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon himself says that impurity of a hidden place (בית הסתרים) does not normally impart impurity, but the Torah decreed it for semen, contradicting his position here.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a woman who actively serves (משמשת) and one who passively emits (פולטת).
The Gemara questions how a פולטת (emitter) can be exempt, since she must have served; the answer is that she immersed for her service (טבלה לשמושה), so the emission is after immersion.

items.text: Rava's statement and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's statement and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether serving with evening impurity suffices, citing Rava that a woman who serves is forbidden to eat terumah for three days. The Gemara resolves that the case is where she was immersed in her bed, implying that Rava's case is when she walks to immerse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether serving with evening impurity (טומאת ערב) suffices, citing Rava's statement that a woman who serves is forbidden to eat terumah for three days because she will inevitably emit seed.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where she was immersed in her bed, implying that Rava's case is when she walks to immerse, lest she emit seed while walking.

items.text: Rava's resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction in Rava's earlier statement by distinguishing between a woman who turns over (mit'hapekhet) and one who does not. The Torah's leniency applies only when she does not turn over, but if she turns over within three days, she is prohibited from eating terumah because she will inevitably discharge semen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's position: if the concern is that some semen remained, the Mishnah should have said 'we are concerned lest some remained' rather than 'we are concerned.'

Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a woman who turns over (מתהפכת) and one who does not: the Torah's leniency applies only when she does not turn over, but if she turns over within three days she is prohibited from eating תרומה (priestly portion) because she will inevitably discharge semen.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's question to Abaye: ro'ah or nogá'at?
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's question to Abaye: ro'ah or nogá'at?
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna asks Abaye whether a woman who discharges semen is considered a 'ro'ah' (one who sees a discharge) or a 'nogá'at' (one who merely touches it). The practical difference involves whether she requires a full day of counting (soter), whether she transmits impurity in any amount, and whether she transmits impurity inside as outside. The Gemara explores the possibilities based on whether the Mishnah is known, and focuses on Rabbi Shimon's opinion.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna asks Abaye whether a woman who discharges semen is classified as a 'ro'ah' (one who sees a discharge) or a 'nogá'at' (one who merely touches it).

The Gemara explains that the practical difference between the two classifications involves whether she requires a full day of counting (soter), whether she transmits impurity in any amount, and whether she transmits impurity inside as outside.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the question's background
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the question's background
sub.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes that if Rav Shmuel bar Bisna knew the Mishnah, then according to the Rabbanan she is a 'ro'ah', and according to Rabbi Shimon she is a 'nogá'at'.
The Gemara suggests that if he did not know the Mishnah, it is reasonable that she is a 'nogá'at'.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution of the question's scope
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the question's scope
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that he knew the Mishnah, and his question was only according to Rabbi Shimon's opinion.
The Gemara clarifies that the question about transmitting impurity inside as outside was not asked; the question was only about soter and transmitting impurity in any amount.

sub.text: Gemara's formulation of the unresolved question
sub.text_en: Gemara's formulation of the unresolved question
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the unresolved question: does Rabbi Shimon's principle that she is like her husband apply only to impurity inside as outside, but for soter and transmitting impurity in any amount she is a 'ro'ah', or is there no difference?

items.text: Alternative version and resolution: ro'ah is the ruling
items.text_en: Alternative version and resolution: ro'ah is the ruling
items.desc_en: An alternative version suggests that Rav Shmuel bar Bisna had not heard the Mishnah, and his question was based on a comparison to the stringency of ba'alei kerayin at Sinai. Abaye initially rules that she is a ro'ah, and Rava and Rav Yosef concur. However, Abaye later retracts, explaining that Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies only to impurity inside as outside, but for soter and impurity in any amount, she is a ro'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna had not heard the Mishnah, and his dilemma was based on the stringency of בעלי קריין (men with seminal emissions) at Sinai, suggesting she might be a רואה (one who experiences an emission).
The Gemara raises the counter-possibility: perhaps we cannot derive halakhot from Sinai, as it was a novelty, since זבים (zavin) and מצורעים (lepers) are more stringent yet were not excluded.
Abaye rules that she is a רואה (one who experiences an emission); Rava and Rav Yosef concur, but Rav Shmuel bar Bisna complains they all repeat the same answer.

Abaye retracts his earlier answer, explaining that Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies only to impurity inside as outside, but for סותר (negating the count) and טומאה בכל שהוא (impurity in any amount), she is a רואה (one who experiences an emission).

items.text: Baraita on zavot and yoledet, and the case of a yoledet who descends to immerse
items.text_en: Baraita on zavot and yoledet, and the case of a yoledet who descends to immerse
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a niddah, zavah, shomeret yom keneged yom, and yoledet all transmit impurity inside as outside. The Gemara questions why yoledet is listed separately, and resolves that it refers to a case where she descended to immerse from impurity to purity. Rabbi Zeira cites Rav's ruling that if blood is dislodged during the descent she is impure, but during the ascent she is pure. Rabbi Yirmeya questions this, and Rabbi Zeira directs him to Rabbi Avin, who compares it to the impurity of a kosher bird's carcass in the throat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a נידה (menstruating woman), זבה (zavah), שומרת יום כנגד יום (one who observes a clean day), and יולדת (woman after childbirth) all transmit טומאה (impurity) inside as outside.

The Gemara questions why יולדת (woman after childbirth) is listed separately, since if the blood is from her menstrual days she is a נידה (menstruating woman), and if from her זיבה (ziva) days she is a זבה (zavah).
The Gemara answers that the case is necessary when the יולדת (woman after childbirth) descended to immerse from impurity to purity.
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) cites רב (Rav) that a יולדת (woman after childbirth) who descended to immerse and blood was dislodged during the descent is impure, but during the ascent she is pure.
רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeya) objects to רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) that the blood is a טומאה בלועה (encapsulated impurity) and should not impart impurity.
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) directs רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeya) to ask רבי אבין (Rabbi Avin), who nodded in agreement when the explanation was given.
רבי אבין (Rabbi Avin) explains that the Sages treated this blood like the carcass of a kosher bird that imparts impurity to garments in the throat, and the Gemara questions the comparison.

items.text: Clarifying the case of a woman who immersed while a fetus was inside
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of a woman who immersed while a fetus was inside
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the immersion is effective for the fetus that later emerges, given that it was inside. It explains that the immersion also benefits the blood inside, so it also benefits the fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the immersion is effective for the fetus, given that when it emerges it should be impure.
The Gemara answers that the immersion benefits the blood inside, so it also benefits the fetus, and the baraita teaches this.

items.text: Distinction between days of Niddah and Zivah for a woman giving birth
items.text_en: Distinction between days of Niddah and Zivah for a woman giving birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a woman who gives birth is classified as a Niddah if it occurs during her Niddah days, and as a Zavah if during her Zivah days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the previous discussion and states the rule: a woman giving birth is classified as a Niddah if during her Niddah days, and as a Zavah if during her Zivah days.

items.text: Case of a dry birth and the concern of the fetus's head emerging
items.text_en: Case of a dry birth and the concern of the fetus's head emerging
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a dry birth where no blood is emitted, and explains that the concern is when the fetus's head emerges outside the vestibule, citing Rav Oshaya's decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah is dealing with, and answers that it is a dry birth, questioning how it can be that a dry birth has impurity inside like outside.
The Gemara explains that the case is where the fetus's head emerged outside the vestibule, citing Rav Oshaya's decree about such a situation.
The Gemara cites Rav Oshaya's decree that there is a concern the fetus might extend its head outside the vestibule, which creates impurity.

items.text: Story of Rava and the man who heard a fetus cry
items.text_en: Story of Rava and the man who heard a fetus cry
items.desc_en: A man asked Rava if he could walk on Shabbat to attend to a fetus that cried before Shabbat but was not born until Shabbat. Rava initially permitted it, but later realized the man knew the law and inquired further, concluding that the fetus had emerged its head outside the vestibule, making circumcision not override Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story about a man who came before Rava and asked whether he may walk on Shabbat to attend to a fetus that cried; Rava initially permitted it.
After the man left, Rava questioned why the man would ask if he already knew the law, and pursued him to clarify the exact circumstances.
The man explained that he heard a fetus cry on Shabbat eve but it was not born until Shabbat.
Rava concluded that the fetus had already emerged its head outside the vestibule, making the circumcision a מילה שלא בזמנה (non-timely circumcision) which does not override Shabbat.

items.text: First inquiry: Is a woman's inner space 'absorbed' or 'hidden'?
items.text_en: First inquiry: Is a woman's inner space 'absorbed' or 'hidden'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a woman's inner space is considered 'absorbed' (בָּלוּעַ) or 'hidden' (בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים). The practical difference is if a friend inserts an olive-sized piece of carrion there: if absorbed, it does not transmit impurity; if hidden, it transmits impurity through carrying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a woman's inner space is considered 'absorbed' (בָּלוּעַ) or 'hidden' (בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים), with the practical difference being whether an olive-sized piece of carrion inserted there transmits impurity through carrying.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate the status of a woman's inner space
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate the status of a woman's inner space
items.desc_en: Abaye says it is 'absorbed', Rava says it is 'hidden'. Rava cites a baraita about impurity of hidden places. Abaye adds that even if it were hidden, it does not transmit impurity due to a Scriptural decree.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava state their positions: Abaye says the woman's inner space is considered 'absorbed' (בָּלוּעַ), while Rava says it is 'hidden' (בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים).
