Rava cites a baraita to support his view, stating that the impurity in a woman's inner space is considered 'hidden' (בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים).
The baraita explains that impurity in a hidden place does not normally transmit impurity, but here it is a Scriptural decree.
Abaye responds with two reasons: first, the impurity is 'absorbed' (בְּלוּעָה), and second, even if it were 'hidden' (בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים), it does not transmit impurity due to a Scriptural decree.

items.text: Second inquiry: Is the place of a pure bird's carcass 'absorbed' or 'hidden'?
items.text_en: Second inquiry: Is the place of a pure bird's carcass 'absorbed' or 'hidden'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the same question regarding the mouth: if a friend inserts an olive-sized piece of carrion into his mouth, the same distinction applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: is the place of a pure bird's carcass in the mouth considered 'absorbed' or 'hidden'?
The Gemara explains the practical difference: if a friend inserts an olive-sized piece of carrion into his mouth, the status determines whether it imparts impurity by carrying.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate the status of a pure bird's carcass in the mouth
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate the status of a pure bird's carcass in the mouth
items.desc_en: Abaye says it is 'absorbed', Rava says it is 'hidden'. Abaye cites a baraita that a carcass of a kosher bird does not transmit impurity in the mouth, and a kal vachomer from a pure bird's carcass is rejected by the verse 'בָּהּ'. The verse 'וְהָאוֹכֵל' teaches that the measure for touching and carrying is an olive's bulk.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava state their positions on the status of a pure bird's carcass in the mouth: Abaye says it is 'absorbed' (בָּלוּעַ), Rava says it is 'hidden' (בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים).
Abaye cites a baraita that a carcass of a kosher bird does not transmit impurity in the mouth, based on the verse 'נְבֵלָה וּטְרֵפָה לֹא יֹאכַל לְטׇמְאָה בָהּ'.

The gemara raises a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a pure bird's carcass, which has no impurity outside, has impurity inside, then a kosher bird's carcass, which has impurity outside, should certainly have impurity inside.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'בָּהּ' (in it), which limits the impurity to the specific carcass mentioned, not to another.
The gemara explains that the verse 'וְהָאוֹכֵל' teaches that the measure for touching and carrying is an olive's bulk (כְּזַיִת), just as for eating.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a creeping creature or carcass in one's fist
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a creeping creature or carcass in one's fist
items.desc_en: Rava rules: if a creeping creature is in one's fist, it is pure (since it is a hidden place for touch); if a carcass is in one's fist, it is impure (since it transmits impurity through carrying). If one inserts a creeping creature in his fist into the airspace of an oven, it is impure, and the Gemara explains that this is not obvious because one might think the Torah said 'its interior' only for a specific case.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules: a creeping creature in one's fist is pure (since it is a hidden place for touch), but a carcass in one's fist is impure (since it transmits impurity through carrying).

The Gemara explains: a creeping creature only impurifies through direct contact, and a hidden place is not subject to contact impurity; a carcass, however, impurifies through carrying even in a hidden place.

sub.text: Rava's additional ruling and Gemara's resolution
sub.text_en: Rava's additional ruling and Gemara's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rava adds: if one inserts a creeping creature in his fist into the airspace of an oven, it is impure; the Gemara notes this is obvious, but explains that one might have thought the Torah only said 'its interior' for a specific case, so the ruling is necessary.

items.text: Reish Lakish on the law of היסט for a zav
items.text_en: Reish Lakish on the law of היסט for a zav
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish teaches that if a zav carries a tube in his armpit and moves a pure person with it, the pure person remains pure; but if a pure person carries a tube in his armpit and moves a zav with it, the pure person becomes impure. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for this distinction, deriving that the zav's היסט is unique in that it imparts impurity only when done directly by his body.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states the law: a tube in a zav's armpit moving a pure person does not transmit impurity, but a tube in a pure person's armpit moving a zav does transmit impurity.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of this distinction.

The Gemara explains that the verse 'וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִגַּע בּוֹ הַזָּב' teaches that a zav's היסט (movement) is unique in imparting impurity only when done directly by his body (מאברוי), not through an intermediate object.

items.text: Mishnah: Zav and ba'al keri do not impart impurity unless emission is from the body
items.text_en: Mishnah: Zav and ba'al keri do not impart impurity unless emission is from the body
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a zav and a ba'al keri do not impart impurity unless the emission comes from their body, as derived from verses: for a zav, 'from his flesh', and for a ba'al keri, 'from him'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a zav and a ba'al keri do not impart impurity unless the emission comes from their body, citing the verses 'from his flesh' for a zav and 'from him' for a ba'al keri.

items.text: Gemara's question on holding the penis while urinating
items.text_en: Gemara's question on holding the penis while urinating
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance for a ba'al keri to hold his penis while urinating, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer forbids holding the penis while urinating. Abaye and Rava resolve the contradiction: Abaye says it refers to a thick cloth, Rava says even a thin cloth is permitted because once the urine is expelled, it is no longer an issue. The Gemara supports Rava's view with a metaphor about the eye.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance for a ba'al keri to hold his penis while urinating, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer forbids it as if bringing a flood.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by saying the Mishnah refers to holding through a thick cloth.
Rava argues that even a thin cloth is permitted because once the urine is expelled, it is no longer an issue, and he is not concerned about adding more urine.
A baraita is cited with a metaphor: holding the penis while urinating is like putting a finger in the eye, which causes repeated tearing.
The Gemara explains that Rava dismisses the metaphor because repeated warming of the urine at that moment is uncommon.

items.text: Shmuel's first statement: seminal emission requires full-body sensation
items.text_en: Shmuel's first statement: seminal emission requires full-body sensation
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that any seminal emission that does not involve the entire body's sensation does not impart impurity, based on the term 'שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע' implying it must be capable of causing pregnancy. The Gemara raises an objection from a case of nocturnal emission where the body is found warm, and Rav Huna resolves it by saying it refers to one who had intercourse in a dream, which necessarily involves sensation.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that any seminal emission that does not involve the entire body's sensation does not impart impurity, based on the term 'שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע' implying it must be capable of causing pregnancy.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: one who had nocturnal emission and found his body warm is impure, implying sensation is not required.
Rav Huna resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers to one who had intercourse in a dream, which necessarily involves sensation.

items.text: Shmuel's second statement: emission must shoot like an arrow
items.text_en: Shmuel's second statement: emission must shoot like an arrow
items.desc_en: An alternative version of Shmuel's statement says that seminal emission must shoot like an arrow to impart impurity. The Gemara notes the practical difference between the two versions: a case where the emission is dislodged with sensation but exits without sensation.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version of Shmuel's statement says that seminal emission must shoot like an arrow to impart impurity.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two versions of Shmuel's statement.
The Gemara answers that the difference is a case where the emission is dislodged with sensation but exits without sensation.

items.text: Rava's dilemma: emission dislodged with sensation but exits without
items.text_en: Rava's dilemma: emission dislodged with sensation but exits without
items.desc_en: Rava raises a dilemma: if the emission is dislodged with sensation but exits without sensation, what is the law? The Gemara attempts to resolve it from a case of a ba'al keri who immersed and later urinated, becoming impure, but distinguishes because most of the emission exits with sensation.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a dilemma: if the emission is dislodged with sensation (הרגשה) but exits without sensation, what is the law?
The Gemara attempts to resolve the dilemma from the case of a ba'al keri who immersed and later urinated, becoming impure, but distinguishes because most of the emission exits with sensation.

items.text: Alternative version: emission that does not shoot like an arrow still imparts impurity
items.text_en: Alternative version: emission that does not shoot like an arrow still imparts impurity
items.desc_en: Another version states that Shmuel said: any seminal emission that does not shoot like an arrow does not cause pregnancy, but it still imparts impurity, as derived from the verse 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִהְיֶה טָהוֹר מִקְּרֵה'—even any קרי.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Shmuel said: any seminal emission that does not shoot like an arrow does not cause pregnancy, but it still imparts impurity, as derived from the verse 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִהְיֶה טָהוֹר מִקְּרֵה'—even any קרי.

items.text: Rava's three dilemmas: gentile who had a thought, zavah who had urine dislodged, and gentile zavah
items.text_en: Rava's three dilemmas: gentile who had a thought, zavah who had urine dislodged, and gentile zavah
items.desc_en: Rava raises three dilemmas: (1) A gentile who had a thought (of impurity) and then immersed—what is the law? (2) A zavah whose urine was dislodged and then immersed—what is the law? (3) A gentile zavah whose urine was dislodged—what is the law? Each is left unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a dilemma: a gentile who had a seminal thought (הרהר) and then descended and immersed for conversion — what is the law regarding his impurity?

The Gemara analyzes the dilemma: if we follow the moment of uprooting (עקירה), that might apply only for stringency, but here it would be a leniency; or perhaps there is no difference. The dilemma is left unresolved (תיקו).
Rava raises a second dilemma: a זבה (zavah) whose urine was dislodged (נעקרו) and then she descended and immersed — what is the law?

The Gemara analyzes: if we follow the moment of uprooting, perhaps that applies only to semen which cannot be held back, but urine can be held; or perhaps there is no difference. The dilemma is left unresolved (תיקו).
Rava raises a third dilemma: a gentile זבה (zavah) whose urine was dislodged — what is the law? (The text is cut off, but the dilemma is introduced.)

items.text: Teiku on a gentile woman zavah who immersed
items.text_en: Teiku on a gentile woman zavah who immersed
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a gentile woman who was a zavah and immersed while holding the semen inside her. It considers whether the semen is considered as if it exited after immersion, depending on whether we follow the principle of 'after the removal' or not, and whether the distinction between a Jewish woman (whose tum'ah is de'oraita) and a gentile woman (whose tum'ah is derabbanan) matters. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses an unresolved question (תיקו) about whether a gentile woman who was a zavah and immersed while still retaining semen inside her transmits impurity afterward, given the possible distinction between her rabbinic-level impurity and a Jewish woman's biblical-level impurity, and whether the principle of 'after the removal' (בתר עקירה) applies.

items.text: Shiur for zav and derivation from verses
items.text_en: Shiur for zav and derivation from verses
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that a zav requires a minimum shiur of the size of a seal of an amah, based on the verse 'or his flesh be sealed from his flow'. The Mishnah, however, says they are metamei in any amount. The Gemara explains that Shmuel follows Rabbi Natan, who says this in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, but the Sages disagree. The Gemara then analyzes the scriptural derivations for the shiur, the distinction between wet and dry, and the counting of three sightings for a korban and two for tum'ah, citing Rabbi Simai.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a זב (zav) imparts impurity in any amount, but Shmuel says he requires a minimum the size of a seal of the amah, citing the verse 'אוֹ הֶחְתִּים בְּשָׂרוֹ מִזּוֹבוֹ' (or his flesh be sealed from his issue).
The Gemara objects: But we learned in the Mishnah that they impart impurity in any amount! It answers that Shmuel follows Rabbi Natan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, but the Sages did not agree.
The Gemara asks: What is the reason of Rabbi Yishmael? It answers: Because the verse says 'אוֹ הֶחְתִּים בְּשָׂרוֹ מִזּוֹבוֹ' (or his flesh be sealed from his issue).
The Gemara asks: And what do the Sages derive from that verse? They need it to teach that a moist discharge imparts impurity, but a dry one does not.
The Gemara asks: And Rabbi Yishmael? He derives that halakha from the word 'רָר' (run) in the verse.

The Gemara asks: And what do the Sages derive from 'רָר'? They use it for counting: 'זוֹבוֹ' (his issue) is one, 'רָר בְּשָׂרוֹ' (his flesh run) is two, 'אֶת זוֹבוֹ' (his issue) is three, teaching that a זב (zav) with three sightings is liable to bring a קרבן (offering).

The Gemara explains that the verse 'אוֹ הֶחְתִּים בְּשָׂרוֹ מִזּוֹבוֹ טָמֵא' teaches that a partial issue is impure, indicating that a זב (zav) with two sightings imparts impurity to משכב ומושב (bed and seat). It then asks: And Rabbi Yishmael, from where does he derive the counting? He derives it from Rabbi Simai.
A ברייתא (baraita) cites Rabbi Simai: The verse counted two and called him 'טמא' (impure), and three and called him 'טמא' — two for impurity, three for the offering.

items.text: Alternative derivation for zav's shiur
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for zav's shiur
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the opinion that derives both the shiur and the counting from the verse 'zot tihyeh tum'ato bezovo'. It then explains what is done with the verse 'ish ish ki yihyeh zav mibesaro' (to require that the flow comes from his flesh) and the phrase 'zovo tamei' (to teach that the flow itself is tamei).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to the one who derives both the shiur and the counting from the verse 'זֹאת תִּהְיֶה טוּמְאָתוֹ בְּזוֹבוֹ' (This shall be his impurity in his issue), what does he do with the verse 'אִישׁ אִישׁ כִּי יִהְיֶה זָב מִבְּשָׂרוֹ' (When any man has an emission out of his flesh)?
The Gemara answers: He requires that verse to teach that the discharge must emerge from his flesh.
The Gemara asks: Why do I need the phrase 'זוֹבוֹ טָמֵא' (his issue is impure)?
The Gemara answers: It teaches that the issue itself is impure.

items.text: Shiur for shikvat zera: ro'eh vs. noge'a
items.text_en: Shiur for shikvat zera: ro'eh vs. noge'a
items.desc_en: Rav Chanilai in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon states that shikvat zera is metamei the ro'eh in any amount, but the noge'a requires a ke'adasah. The Gemara challenges this from the Mishnah which says 'metam'in bechol shehen', and initially assumes it refers to the noge'a, but concludes it refers to the ro'eh. A brayta comparing shikvat zera and sheretz is brought, and the Gemara attempts to prove that the shiur for noge'a is ke'adasah, but Rav Adda bar Ahavah deflects by saying the brayta compares the 'name' (type) of tum'ah, not the shiur. The Gemara then questions whether sheretz itself is not metamei in any amount, citing the Mishnah about limbs and ke'adasah, and answers that a limb is different because it is considered as a full ke'adasah. Finally, the Gemara explains the difference in tum'ah between shikvat zera and sheretz: one is between small and large, not between Jew and gentile.

sub.text: Rav Chanilai in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rav Chanilai in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanilai states in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon that shikvat zera (seminal emission) is metamei (imparts impurity) to the ro'eh (one who sees it) in any amount, but to the noge'a (one who touches it) requires a ke'adasah (lentil-sized amount).
The Gemara challenges: we learned in the Mishnah that they (zav, zava, niddah, and yoledet) are metamei in any amount — does this not refer to the noge'a (one who touches)?
The Gemara answers: no, the Mishnah refers to the ro'eh (one who sees the emission), not the noge'a.
The Gemara brings a baraita that compares shikvat zera and sheretz (carcass of a creeping animal), stating that shikvat zera is metamei in any amount, unlike sheretz.
The Gemara asks: does this baraita not refer to the noge'a (one who touches)?
The Gemara answers: no, it refers to the ro'eh (one who sees).
The Gemara objects: but the baraita compares shikvat zera to sheretz, and sheretz is metamei through contact (נגיעה), so the comparison implies shikvat zera is also metamei through contact.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah deflects: the baraita compares the 'name' (type) of tum'ah (impurity), not the shiur (measurement).
The Gemara questions: does sheretz not impart impurity in any amount? But we learned in a Mishnah that limbs have no fixed measure, and less than a ke'adasah of sheretz is listed.
The Gemara answers: a limb is different because it is considered as a full ke'adasah (lentil-sized amount) in its entirety, as if it were missing a bit, would it still be metamei?
The Gemara asks: what is the difference in tum'ah (impurity) between shikvat zera and sheretz? If it is between a Jew and a gentile, there is also a difference between a sea mouse and a land mouse.
The Gemara resolves: the difference is between a small amount and a large amount (i.e., the shiur for tum'ah varies by size).

items.text: Derivation for noge'a in shikvat zera and the tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Derivation for noge'a in shikvat zera and the tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the source for including the noge'a in shikvat zera is the verse 'o ish', and that the tannaim disagree: some say 'dun minah u-minah' (derive from sheretz both the mode of tum'ah and the shiur), while others say 'dun minah v'okei b'atreh' (derive the mode but keep the shiur as is). Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan challenges Rav Pappa, suggesting that the 'o ish' might come from the verse about shikvat zera itself, and that all agree on 'dun minah u-minah'. The Gemara concludes that the tannaim are divided, some supporting Rav Pappa and some supporting Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens by stating that the source for including the one who touches (נוגע) shikvat zera is the verse 'אוֹ אִישׁ', and that the tannaim dispute the implications.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the tannaitic dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the tannaitic dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the tannaim are divided: some say 'דון מינה ומינה' (derive from sheretz both the mode of tum'ah and the shiur), while others say 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה' (derive the mode but keep the shiur as is).

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration of the first position
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration of the first position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates that according to the view 'דון מינה ומינה', just as sheretz conveys tum'ah through contact (נגיעה) and requires a shiur of a lentil (כעדשה), so too shikvat zera requires a lentil's worth for the one who touches.

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration of the second position
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration of the second position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates that according to the view 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה', the mode of tum'ah (contact) is derived from sheretz, but the shiur remains as per shikvat zera itself — any amount (במשהו) for both the one who sees and the one who touches.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan challenges Rav Pappa, suggesting that the 'אוֹ אִישׁ' might come from the verse about shikvat zera itself (ויקרא טו:לב), and that all tannaim agree on 'דון מינה ומינה'.
The Gemara concludes that the tannaim are divided, some supporting Rav Pappa and some supporting Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan.

items.text: Mishnah: Status of a one-day-old infant
items.text_en: Mishnah: Status of a one-day-old infant
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a one-day-old female is metamei as a niddah, and a ten-day-old female is metamei as a zavah. A one-day-old male is metamei as a zav, metamei with negaim, metamei with tum'at met, is eligible for yibbum, exempts from yibbum, enables eating terumah, and disqualifies from terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing laws of a one-day-old female infant who can become a niddah, a ten-day-old female who can become a zavah, and a one-day-old male infant who can become a zav, have negaim, and various other halachic capacities.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a one-day-old infant inherits and bequeaths, and if killed the killer is liable, and he is considered a full groom for his father, mother, and all relatives.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a one-day-old infant inherits and bequeaths, and if killed the killer is liable, and he is considered a full groom for his father, mother, and all relatives.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the laws of a one-day-old infant from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the laws of a one-day-old infant from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for each law listed in the Mishnah: a one-day-old female is a niddah, a ten-day-old female is a zavah, a one-day-old male is a zav, he is impure with negaim and corpse impurity, he obligates yibbum, exempts from yibbum, permits eating terumah, and disqualifies from terumah. The Gemara explains why both verses for disqualification are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the Mishnah's law that a one-day-old female is a niddah, and cites a baraita deriving it from the extra 'וְאִשָּׁה' in the verse.
The Gemara asks the source for a ten-day-old female being a zavah, and cites a baraita deriving it from the same extra 'וְאִשָּׁה'.
The Gemara asks the source for a one-day-old male being a zav, and cites Rabbi Yehuda's derivation from the double 'אִישׁ אִישׁ'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka objects that the derivation is unnecessary, as the verse 'וְהַזָּב אֶת זוֹבוֹ לַזָּכָר וְלַנְּקֵבָה' already includes any male or female regardless of age, and the double 'אִישׁ אִישׁ' is merely the Torah speaking in human language.
The Gemara cites the verse 'אָדָם כִּי יִהְיֶה בְעוֹר בְּשָׂרוֹ' to derive that a one-day-old male is impure with negaim, as 'אָדָם' includes any person.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וְעַל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת אֲשֶׁר הָיוּ שָׁם' to derive that a one-day-old male is impure with corpse impurity, as 'נֶפֶשׁ' includes any soul.
The Gemara cites the verse 'כִּי יֵשְׁבוּ אַחִים יַחְדָּו' to derive that a one-day-old male obligates yibbum, as 'אַחִים' includes brothers who had any existence together in the world.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וּבֵן אֵין לוֹ' to derive that a one-day-old male exempts from yibbum, as the deceased has a son.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וִילִיד בֵּיתוֹ הֵם יֹאכְלוּ בְלַחְמוֹ' and reads it as 'יַאֲכִילוּ' to derive that a one-day-old male permits eating terumah.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וְזֶרַע אֵין לָהּ' to derive that a one-day-old male disqualifies from terumah, as the woman has seed.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'seed' (a born child) — even a fetus should disqualify, and answers that the verse 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' excludes a pregnant woman.

The Gemara explains that both verses are needed: 'וְזֶרַע אֵין לָהּ' alone might imply that only a born child disqualifies because it changes the woman's body from one entity to two, but a fetus that remains one entity might not disqualify, so the Torah wrote 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' to include the fetus.

The Gemara explains that conversely, 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' alone might imply that only a fetus disqualifies because it fills the body, but a born child that leaves the body empty might not disqualify, so both verses are necessary.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's case: a kohen with two wives
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's case: a kohen with two wives
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a one-day-old infant rather than a fetus. Rav Sheishet answers that the Mishnah deals with a kohen who has two wives, one divorced and one not, and has a one-day-old son from the divorced wife who disqualifies the father's slaves from terumah, excluding the opinion of Rabbi Yosei who says a fetus also disqualifies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a one-day-old infant rather than a fetus, which should also disqualify.
Rav Sheishet answers that the Mishnah deals with a kohen who has two wives, one divorced and one not, and has a one-day-old son from the divorced wife.
Rav Sheishet explains that the one-day-old son disqualifies the father's slaves from eating תרומה (priestly portion), excluding the opinion of Rabbi Yosei who says a fetus also disqualifies.

items.text: Explaining 'inherits and bequeaths'
items.text_en: Explaining 'inherits and bequeaths'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a one-day-old can both inherit and bequeath. Rav Sheishet explains: he inherits from his mother's property to bequeath to his paternal brothers. Only a one-day-old, not a fetus, because the fetus might die first and a son does not inherit his mother while still in the womb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a one-day-old can both inherit and bequeath, noting that if he inherits from his father and bequeaths to his paternal brothers, the brothers could simply inherit directly from the father.

Rav Sheishet explains that the one-day-old inherits from his mother's property to bequeath to his paternal brothers, and this applies only to a one-day-old, not a fetus, because the fetus might die first and a son does not inherit his mother while still in the womb.

items.text: Clarification of the stillborn's movement
items.text_en: Clarification of the stillborn's movement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that a stillborn does not move, citing an incident where a stillborn moved three times. Mar bar Rav Ashi explains that such movement is like the twitching of a lizard's tail, not a sign of life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that a stillborn does not move, citing an incident where a stillborn moved three times.
Mar bar Rav Ashi explains that such movement is like the twitching of a lizard's tail, not a sign of life.

items.text: Two versions of Mar bar Rav Yosef's ruling on a posthumous son
items.text_en: Two versions of Mar bar Rav Yosef's ruling on a posthumous son
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef cites Rava: a son born after the father's death does not reduce the firstborn's share, requiring the verse 'and they bore to him'. In Pumbedita, they taught that such a firstborn does not take a double portion, requiring 'he shall acknowledge'. The halakha follows all these statements.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef cites Rava that a son born after the father's death does not reduce the firstborn's share, requiring the verse 'וְיָלְדוּ לוֹ' (and they bore to him).

sub.text: Pumbedita version of Mar bar Rav Yosef's teaching
sub.text_en: Pumbedita version of Mar bar Rav Yosef's teaching
sub.desc_en: In Pumbedita they taught that a firstborn born after the father's death does not take a double portion, requiring the verse 'יַכִּיר' (he shall acknowledge), which is absent.
The halakha follows all these statements of Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava.

items.text: Liability for killing a stillborn and its status for mourning
items.text_en: Liability for killing a stillborn and its status for mourning
items.desc_en: One who kills a stillborn is liable, as the verse 'any soul' includes all. The stillborn is considered a full groom for his parents and relatives regarding mourning. This follows the view that if it is known the months were completed, it is a viable birth, unlike Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who considers a child that did not survive 30 days a doubtful case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one who kills a stillborn is liable, citing the verse 'any soul' to include all cases.
The Gemara asks for what halachic purpose the stillborn is considered a full groom for his parents and relatives, and Rav Pappa answers: regarding mourning.

The Gemara clarifies that this ruling follows the view that if it is known the months were completed, it is a viable birth, unlike Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who considers a child that did not survive 30 days a doubtful case.

items.text: Mishnah: The three-year-old girl's legal capacities
items.text_en: Mishnah: The three-year-old girl's legal capacities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a girl of three years and one day can be betrothed through intercourse; if a yavam has intercourse with her, he acquires her; she incurs the death penalty for adultery; she renders her husband impure through niddah; if married to a priest she eats terumah; intercourse with a disqualifier disqualifies her from the priesthood; and intercourse with a relative incurs the death penalty while she is exempt. Below that age, it is like putting a finger in the eye.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a girl of three years and one day can be betrothed through intercourse, acquired by a yavam, liable for adultery, renders her husband impure through niddah, eats terumah if married to a priest, is disqualified from the priesthood by a disqualifier, and incurs the death penalty for intercourse with relatives while she is exempt.
The Mishnah concludes that below this age, intercourse is like putting a finger in the eye, causing pain without lasting effect.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages on the exact age
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages on the exact age
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Meir says a three-year-old girl can be betrothed, while the Sages say three years and one day. The difference is either the eve of Rosh Hashanah (Rabbi Yannai's academy) or that 30 days in a year count as a year (Rabbi Yochanan). An objection is raised from another baraita where Rabbi Meir includes even a two-year-old and one day, but the Sages still say three years and one day.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the dispute: Rabbi Meir says a three-year-old girl is betrothed through intercourse, the Sages say three years and one day.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions.
The academy of Rabbi Yannai answers: the difference is the eve of Rosh Hashanah (the last day of the third year).
Rabbi Yochanan offers a different answer: the difference is whether thirty days in a year are considered a year.
The Gemara raises an objection from another baraita where Rabbi Meir includes even a two-year-old and one day, but the Sages still say three years and one day.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan's view aligns with a Tanna who considers one day in a year as a year, but Rabbi Yannai's view is difficult because it contradicts that principle.

items.text: The inquiry about the nature of virginity
items.text_en: The inquiry about the nature of virginity
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: do the signs of virginity come and go, or do they only heal after three years? The practical difference is illustrated with a case of intercourse within three years and after three years.

items.text: Rav Chiyya's objection
items.text_en: Rav Chiyya's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Ika challenges the assumption that a wound within three years does not heal immediately, suggesting it might heal right away, which would undermine the previous case.

items.text: Alternative practical difference
items.text_en: Alternative practical difference
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a different case: if blood is found both within three years and after three years, the question is whether it is blood of virginity or menstrual blood.

items.text: Rav Chisda's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda argues that the Mishnah's phrase 'like putting a finger in the eye' implies that virginity comes and goes, just as an eye waters repeatedly.

items.text: Story of Yostani before Rabbi
items.text_en: Story of Yostani before Rabbi
items.desc_en: A story is told of Yostani, daughter of Asverus ben Antoninus, who came before Rabbi and asked about the age for marriage and pregnancy, expressing regret for lost years.

items.text: Discussion on pregnancy of minors
items.text_en: Discussion on pregnancy of minors
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a girl under three can become pregnant, citing a baraita about three women who use a contraceptive, and discusses the age of a minor, with differing opinions from Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

items.text: Story of a woman before Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Story of a woman before Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A woman who was violated before age three asks Rabbi Akiva about her eligibility for the priesthood. He initially rules her fit, but after her parable, he rules her unfit, and explains to the students that the halacha is from Sinai.

items.text: Mishnah: The nine-year-old boy
items.text_en: Mishnah: The nine-year-old boy
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a nine-year-old boy who has relations with his yevamah acquires her, but cannot divorce until he matures, and discusses other halachic consequences.

items.text: Gemara: The need for a get and chalitzah
items.text_en: Gemara: The need for a get and chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says he cannot give a get until he matures, and explains that his intercourse is like a ma'amar of an adult, requiring both a get and chalitzah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Ages for Vows and Dedications
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Ages for Vows and Dedications
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a girl of eleven years and one day has her vows examined, while at twelve years and one day they are binding; similarly for a boy at twelve and thirteen years. Before these ages, even if they claim knowledge, their vows are void; after, even if they claim ignorance, their vows are valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the ages for examining and binding vows for girls and boys, and the rule that before these ages vows are void and after they are valid.

items.text: Gemara's Questions on the Mishnah's Redundancies
items.text_en: Gemara's Questions on the Mishnah's Redundancies
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah includes both the age for examination and the age for binding vows, and why it mentions the period of examination. It explains that without these, one might think examination is perpetual or limited to thirty days. It also justifies the inclusion of the clause about before and after the time, to prevent reliance on the children's own statements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state both that a girl's vows are examined at eleven and that they are binding at twelve, since the latter follows from the former.
The Gemara answers that without the second clause, one might think examination continues forever even after adulthood; the Mishnah teaches that at twelve vows are binding without examination.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah also needs to state that one examines throughout the twelfth year, given that it already said vows are binding at twelve.
The Gemara answers that without this clause, one might think examination is limited to thirty days; the Mishnah teaches that examination continues throughout the entire twelfth year.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to mention examination at eleven years old, since the two clauses about twelve years already cover the law.
The Gemara answers that without this clause, one might think a sharp girl should be examined at eleven; the Mishnah teaches that examination only begins at twelve regardless of intelligence.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state the rules for before and after the time, since they can be inferred from the earlier clauses.

The Gemara answers that without these clauses, one might rely on the children's own statements about their knowledge; the Mishnah teaches that before the time their vows are never valid and after the time always valid regardless of their claims.

items.text: Dispute Between Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on Gender Differences
items.text_en: Dispute Between Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on Gender Differences
items.desc_en: A Tosefta records that Rabbi says the rules for a girl apply to a boy and vice versa, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reverses them. Rav Chisda explains Rabbi's reasoning from the verse 'And the Lord built the rib' indicating women have extra understanding. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning is given by Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak: because a boy is frequently at his teacher's house, cunning enters him first.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta records the dispute: Rabbi holds that the rules for a girl apply to a boy and vice versa, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reverses them.
Rav Chisda explains Rabbi's reasoning: the verse 'וַיִּבֶן ה׳ אֶת הַצֵּלָע' (And the Lord built the rib) teaches that women were given extra understanding (בינה יתירה) compared to men.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar uses the same verse for a different teaching: that God braided Eve's hair, as in coastal cities they call braiding 'building' (בנייתא).
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak explains Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning: because a boy frequents his teacher's house, cunning (ערמומית) enters him first, so boys develop understanding earlier.

items.text: The Question of 'Within the Time' – Before or After?
items.text_en: The Question of 'Within the Time' – Before or After?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the period 'within the time' (the year of examination) is treated as before or after the age of majority for purposes of liability. It clarifies that this question is not about vows but about punishments. Rav and Rabbi Chanina say it is like before, while Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say it is like after. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: is the period 'within the time' (the year of examination) treated like before the time or after the time?
The Gemara clarifies that the question is not about vows (where the rule is clear) but about punishments.
Rav and Rabbi Chanina both say that 'within the time' is like before the time.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi both say that 'within the time' is like after the time.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic: 'וזאת לפנים בישראל' (and this was before in Israel) to remember that Rav and Rabbi Chanina's view (within time = before) is the earlier one.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's Challenge and Rava's Response
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's Challenge and Rava's Response
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna attempts to prove from the Mishnah's wording that 'within the time' is like before, but Rava counters that the same reasoning could prove it is like after. The Gemara concludes that Rav Hamnuna's proof is from the Mishnah itself: after the time, if the child has not brought two pubic hairs, he is still a minor, implying that the case of 'within the time' involves those who have brought hairs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges by citing the Mishnah's ruling about 'after the time' to infer that 'within the time' is like 'before the time'.
Rava counters that from the Mishnah's first clause one could equally infer that 'within the time' is like 'after the time'.
The Gemara rejects Rava's objection, explaining that Rava misunderstood Rav Hamnuna's reasoning as deriving from an extra Mishnah clause.

The Gemara resolves that Rav Hamnuna's proof is from the Mishnah itself: 'after the time' must refer to a child who has brought two pubic hairs, implying that 'within the time' is like 'before the time'.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to the earlier assumption
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to the earlier assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling that a girl who brings two hairs within the time is considered as after the time, citing a baraita about a boy of thirteen who vows. Rabbi Zeira's objection shows that within the time is like before the time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier assumption that a girl who brings two hairs within the time is considered as after the time, arguing that within the time should be like before the time.
Rabbi Zeira cites a baraita about a boy of thirteen who vows, showing that within the time is like before the time.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita proves that within the time is like before the time, presenting a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of the earlier position.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution as a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution as a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman suggests that the issue is a dispute between Tannaim: whether hair growth before the proper age is a mere 'shuma' (growth) or a 'siman' (sign of maturity).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the objection by presenting the issue as a Tannaitic dispute: hair growth before the proper age is either mere 'שומא' (a growth) or a 'סימן' (a sign of maturity), with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holding it is a sign.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Tannaitic baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Tannaitic baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: it first says hair from nine to twelve is 'shuma', implying thirteen is 'siman', but then says thirteen is 'siman', implying the earlier statement was about 'shuma'. It asks if this reflects a dispute about whether within the time is like after or before the time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the first clause implies that thirteen is a siman, but the second clause states thirteen is a siman, implying the first clause was about shuma; it then asks whether this reflects a dispute about whether תּוֹךְ זְמַן (within the time) is like after the time or before the time.

items.text: Alternative resolutions of the contradiction
items.text_en: Alternative resolutions of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers several alternative explanations: either the entire baraita is about a girl, with the first part by Rabbi and the second by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar; or both parts are about a boy, with reversed attributions; or both are by one authority but distinguish between a boy and a girl.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by asserting that all agree תוך זמן כלפני זמן (within the period is like before the period), and the baraita's first part is Rabbi's view about a girl, while the second part is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view about a girl.
The Gemara offers a second resolution: both parts are about a boy, with the first part by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the second by Rabbi.
The Gemara offers a third resolution: both parts are by Rabbi, but one refers to a boy and the other to a girl.
The Gemara offers a fourth resolution: both parts are by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, but one refers to a boy and the other to a girl.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and a supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and a supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says hair is a 'siman' only if it remains attached. A baraita supports this: hair from nine to twelve is 'shuma' if still attached, but Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda calls it a 'siman'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Kruspadai, son of Rabbi Shabbtai, adds that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's ruling that hair is a permanent sign applies only when the hairs are still attached to the body.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda states that hair is a 'siman' (sign of maturity).
Rabbi Kruspadai qualifies that the hair is a 'siman' only if it is still attached (עוֹדָן בּוֹ).

A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Kruspadai's condition, stating that from nine to twelve years old, if the hairs are still attached, they are considered a temporary growth, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says they are a permanent sign.
A baraita supports the distinction: hair from nine to twelve is 'shuma' (a mere mark) if still attached, but Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda calls it a 'siman'.

items.text: Rava's ruling on within the time and a contradiction
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on within the time and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rava rules that within the time is like before the time. He also says a girl of twelve can refuse (mi'un) but not perform chalitzah. The Gemara notes a contradiction: if she is an adult, she should perform chalitzah, and Rava himself said a girl who reached the age of majority is presumed to have signs.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that within the time is like before the time, and a girl of twelve can refuse (mi'un) but not perform chalitzah.
The Gemara objects: if she cannot refuse, she is an adult, so she should perform chalitzah.
The Gemara objects further: Rava himself said a girl who reached the age of majority is presumed to have signs, so there is no doubt.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction regarding chalitzah and mi'un
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction regarding chalitzah and mi'un
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rava's presumption applies only when not examined; here they examined and found no signs. But then she could refuse? Concern that the signs may have fallen off. The discussion distinguishes between the opinions of Rav Pappa and Rav Pappei regarding concern for fallen signs, and concludes that for chalitzah we are concerned, but for mi'un we rely on the presumption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rava's presumption applies only in an unspecified case (בסתמא), but here they examined and found no signs, so it does not apply.
The Gemara asks: if so, she should be able to perform מיאון (refusal), but the ruling says she cannot.
The Gemara answers that we are concerned (חוששין) that the signs may have fallen off, so she cannot perform מיאון.
The Gemara objects: this works for the one who says we are concerned, but for the one who says we are not concerned, what can be said?
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Pappei regarding concern for fallen signs.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute applies only regarding חליצה (levirate release), but for מיאון (refusal) everyone agrees we are concerned.
The Gemara objects: does it follow that the one who says 'we are concerned' means she performs חליצה? He only said 'we are concerned' in general.
The Gemara resolves: actually, they did not examine her, and for חליצה we are concerned, but Rava's presumption applies only for מיאון, while for חליצה she requires examination.

items.text: Rav Dimi's halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi from Nehardea rules that we are concerned the signs may have fallen off, but only if the betrothal was within the time and the intercourse after the time, creating a Torah-level doubt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi of Nehardea rules that we do worry about falling off, but only in a case where he betrothed her within the time and consummated after the time, creating a Torah-level doubt, but not from the outset.

items.text: Rav Huna's principle about vows and a supporting challenge
items.text_en: Rav Huna's principle about vows and a supporting challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if one consecrates and then eats, he is lashed, based on the verse 'Ish ki yaflei' linking the ability to vow with the prohibition 'lo yachel devaro'. Rav Huna bar Yehuda brings a challenge to support Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if a minor consecrated an animal and then ate it, he is lashed, based on the verse 'איש כי יפליא לנדר' and 'לא יחל דברו', linking the prohibition of violating one's word to the ability to make a vow.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda brings a supporting citation to aid Rav Huna's position.

items.text: Opening question: Is a minor liable for a sacrifice on his consecration?
items.text_en: Opening question: Is a minor liable for a sacrifice on his consecration?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inference from a verse equating minor and adult for certain prohibitions, asking whether one might think a minor is liable to bring a sacrifice for misusing his consecrated property. It concludes with a scriptural exclusion: 'zeh hadavar' (this is the matter) limits liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inference: since the verse equates a minor with an adult for intentional false oath, prohibition, and 'בל יחל' (do not profane), one might think a minor is liable to bring a sacrifice for misusing his consecrated property.
The Gemara resolves: the verse says 'זה הדבר' (this is the matter), limiting liability to this specific case and excluding a minor's consecration.

items.text: Clarifying the liability for issur and bal yachel
items.text_en: Clarifying the liability for issur and bal yachel
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the previous statement holds that one is liable for 'issur' and 'bal yachel'. It questions whether 'issur' refers to the prohibition of 'bal yachel' itself, and analyzes the status of a mufla samukh l'ish. It deduces that a minor eating neveilot leads to a court obligation to separate him, and explains the case as one where the minor consecrated and others ate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the mishna teaches liability for issur and bal yachel, and proposes that 'issur' refers specifically to the prohibition of 'bal yachel'.
The Gemara questions the status of a mufla samukh l'ish (a minor near majority): if his vows are biblical, he should be liable to lashes; if rabbinic, there is no issur for those warned about him.
The Gemara deduces that a minor eating neveilot requires the court to separate him, and explains the case as one where the minor consecrated and others ate.

items.text: Dispute liability for others eating the minor's consecration
items.text_en: Dispute liability for others eating the minor's consecration
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a disagreement: according to the one who says 'he consecrated and others ate — they are flogged', the answer works; but for the one who says they are not flogged, what can be said? It cites the dispute between Rav Kahana and Rabbi Yochanan/Reish Lakish, and offers the resolution that it is rabbinic with a scriptural support (asmachta).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the one who says 'he consecrated and others ate — they are flogged', the earlier resolution works; but for the one who says they are not flogged, what can be said?
The Gemara cites the dispute: Rav Kahana says they are not flogged, while Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both say they are flogged.
The Gemara resolves: the prohibition is rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן), and the verse is merely a scriptural support (אסמכתא).

items.text: Analysis of the dispute's basis
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute's basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara restates the dispute between Rav Kahana and Rabbi Yochanan/Reish Lakish regarding whether others are flogged for eating the minor's consecration, explaining that they disagree about whether a mufla samukh l'ish is considered a full biblical adult or only rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates the dispute between Rav Kahana and Rabbi Yochanan/Reish Lakish regarding whether others are flogged for eating the minor's consecration.
The Gemara asks what underlies their disagreement.
The Gemara explains that they disagree about whether a mufla samukh l'ish (a minor near majority) has biblical or only rabbinic status.

items.text: Challenge from the law of an orphan girl's vow
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of an orphan girl's vow
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya challenges: an orphan girl who vowed can have her husband annul it. If mufla samukh l'ish is rabbinic, then (rabbinic) marriage annuls a rabbinic vow; but if it is biblical, can rabbinic marriage annul a biblical vow? Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers: whichever view, the husband can annul because if it's biblical, the minor is like one eating neveilot and courts are not obligated to separate him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya challenges: if mufla samukh l'ish is biblical, how can rabbinic marriage annul a biblical vow, as seen in the case of an orphan girl whose husband annuls her vow?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers: whichever view, the husband can annul because if it's biblical, the minor is like one eating neveilot and courts are not obligated to separate him.

items.text: Objection and resolution with Rabba bar Leivai and Rav Pinchas
items.text_en: Objection and resolution with Rabba bar Leivai and Rav Pinchas
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: when she grows up, she (the orphan) relied on the initial annulment (so it must be effective). Rabba bar Leivai answers: the husband annuls every hour, provided he had relations (the annulment applies ongoing). Another objection notes that a husband cannot annul vows taken before marriage, resolved by Rav Pinchas citing Rava that a woman vows with her husband's consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: when she grows up, she eats based on the initial annulment, implying the annulment was effective, contradicting the idea that the husband's annulment is only rabbinic.
Rabba bar Leivai answers that the husband annuls every hour, provided he had relations, so the annulment applies continuously.
The Gemara objects that a husband cannot annul vows taken before marriage, contradicting the idea of ongoing annulment.
Rav Pinchas cites Rava that a woman vows with her husband's consent, so the vow is not truly prior and the husband can annul it.

items.text: Support from terumah of a minor
items.text_en: Support from terumah of a minor
items.desc_en: Abaye attempts to bring proof from a baraita: a minor who has not grown two pubic hairs — Rabbi Yehuda says his terumah is not terumah; Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: before the age of vows it is not terumah, after it is terumah. The Gemara initially assumes Rabbi Yosei holds terumah nowadays is biblical, but then corrects that Rabbi Yosei actually holds it is rabbinic, as supported by a tradition in Seder Olam (attributed to Rabbi Yosei) that the third conquest lacked the inheritance, so terumah is only rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: Abaye brings a baraita about a minor who has not grown two pubic hairs: Rabbi Yehuda says his terumah is not terumah; Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between before and after the age of vows.
The Gemara initially assumes Rabbi Yosei holds that terumah nowadays is biblical, and questions how a rabbinic-level minor could fix biblical-level tevel.
The Gemara corrects that Rabbi Yosei actually holds terumah nowadays is rabbinic, resolving the difficulty.
The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Yosei really hold that? A baraita in Seder Olam (attributed to Rabbi Yosei) states that the third conquest lacked inheritance, implying terumah is biblical.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yosei taught Seder Olam but does not hold its view; he personally holds terumah nowadays is rabbinic.
The Gemara adds supporting evidence from a baraita about dough that became mixed or leavened with terumah, implying the discussion continues.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi Yosei's view and continuing support
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi Yosei's view and continuing support
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan notes that Rabbi Yosei taught Seder Olam but did not necessarily hold its view. This is supported by a baraita about dough that became mixed with terumah or leavened with terumah leaven, implying Rabbi Yosei does treat terumah as a real issue. The text cuts off but continues into further discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan identifies Rabbi Yosei as the author of Seder Olam, which states that terumah is not biblical in the third era.
The gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei taught Seder Olam but did not personally hold its view that terumah is only rabbinic.
The gemara cites a baraita about dough mixed with terumah or leavened with terumah leaven, implying that Rabbi Yosei treats terumah as a real issue, supporting the resolution.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on challah for a doubtful mixture
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on challah for a doubtful mixture
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a mixture of terumah and chullin that is doubtful is liable for challah but not invalidated by a tevul yom, according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda; Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon exempt it from challah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a doubtful mixture of terumah and chullin is liable for challah but not invalidated by a tevul yom according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon exempt it from challah.

items.text: Gemara's initial explanation and question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial explanation and question
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether terumah and challah are d'oraita or d'rabbanan in the present era. It questions how Rabbi Yosei can exempt challah if he holds challah is d'oraita, since a rabbinic doubt would not override a biblical obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: one who holds תרומה (priestly portion) is דאורייתא (biblical) holds חלה (dough offering) is also biblical; one who holds תרומה is דרבנן (rabbinic) holds חלה is also rabbinic, and then a rabbinic doubt can override a rabbinic obligation.
The Gemara questions: if Rabbi Yosei holds חלה is biblical, how can a rabbinic doubt override a biblical obligation?
The Gemara answers: perhaps Rabbi Yosei holds that תרומה in the present era is biblical, but חלה is rabbinic.

items.text: Rav Huna's tradition and the debate on challah's status
items.text_en: Rav Huna's tradition and the debate on challah's status
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua reports that the Rabbis of Rav's academy held that even if terumah is rabbinic, challah is biblical, based on the seven years of conquest and seven of division. He counters that even if terumah is biblical, challah is rabbinic, citing a brayta that the verse 'when you come' refers to the entire nation's entry, not the partial return under Ezra.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua reports that the Rabbis of Rav's academy held that even if תרומה (priestly portion) is rabbinic, חלה (dough offering) is biblical.
They argue that during the seven years of conquest and seven of division, the Israelites became obligated in חלה but not in מעשר (tithe), showing חלה's biblical status.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua counters that even if תרומה is biblical, חלה is rabbinic, based on a different interpretation.
He cites a ברייתתא (baraita) that the verse 'בבאכם' (when you come) requires entry of the entire nation, not just a partial return under Ezra.
The gemara concludes that when Ezra brought the exiles up, not all of them ascended, so the obligation of חלה under Ezra was only rabbinic.

items.text: Mishnah: The three stages of a woman (Pagga, Bochal, Tzemel)
items.text_en: Mishnah: The three stages of a woman (Pagga, Bochal, Tzemel)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a parable of a woman's development: Pagga (childhood), Bochal (youth), and Tzemel (maturity). In the first two stages, the father retains rights to her findings, earnings, and annulment of vows; once she reaches Tzemel (bagrut), the father has no authority.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the parable of a woman's three stages: Pagga (childhood) and Bochal (youth).
The Mishnah rules that in the first two stages the father retains rights to her findings, earnings, and vow annulment, but once she reaches Tzemel (bagrut) he has no authority.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute on the physical signs of bagrut
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute on the physical signs of bagrut
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the simanim (signs) of bagrut: Rabbi Yosei HaGlili says when a crease forms under the breast; Rabbi Akiva says when the breasts droop; Ben Azzai says when the nipple darkens; Rabbi Yosei says when one places a hand on the nipple and it sinks and lingers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks what are the physical signs of bagrut (puberty), and Rabbi Yosei HaGlili answers: when a crease forms under the breast.
Rabbi Akiva gives his sign: when the breasts droop.
Ben Azzai gives his sign: when the nipple darkens.
Rabbi Yosei gives his sign: when one places a hand on the nipple and it sinks and lingers before returning.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for Pagga, Bochal, Tzemel
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for Pagga, Bochal, Tzemel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms: Pagga is from the verse 'the fig tree has formed its unripe figs'; Bochal is from the Mishnah about figs that ripen, and Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rav that it means when their heads whiten; alternatively, from the verse 'my soul loathed them'. Tzemel is explained as 'she has become full' (bagrut).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'Pagga' refers to a young girl, citing the verse about the fig tree forming its unripe figs, and 'Bochal' refers to the days of youth, citing the Mishnah about figs that ripen and Rabba bar bar Chana's statement in the name of Rav that this means when their heads whiten.
The Gemara offers an alternative scriptural source for 'Bochal' from the verse 'my soul loathed them', and explains 'Tzemel' as meaning 'she has become full' (bagrut).

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of simanim and Shmuel's actions
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of simanim and Shmuel's actions
items.desc_en: Shmuel clarifies that the 'crease' is not literal but when she puts her hands behind her back and it appears as a crease. He tested his maidservant and paid her four zuz for her embarrassment, consistent with his view that Canaanite slaves are for labor, not shame. The Gemara also notes Shmuel's, Rav Nachman's, and Rav Sheshet's practices with slaves. Rabbi Yosei's 'oketz' is explained as the nipple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that Rabbi Yosei HaGlili defines the sign of puberty as the appearance of a crease.
Shmuel clarifies that the crease is not literal but is seen when she puts her hands behind her back, creating the appearance of a crease under the breast.
The Gemara reports that Shmuel tested his maidservant for the sign and paid her four zuz for her embarrassment.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel's payment aligns with his view that Canaanite slaves are given for labor, not for shame.

sub.text: Gemara's note on practices of other rabbis
sub.text_en: Gemara's note on practices of other rabbis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel designated a specific slave for himself, Rav Nachman exchanged slaves, and Rav Sheshet entrusted slaves to Arabs, warning them to beware of Israelites.

sub.text: Shmuel's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's term
sub.text_en: Shmuel's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's term
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'עוקץ' (oketz) means in Rabbi Yosei's statement, and Shmuel answers that it refers to the nipple.

items.text: Brayta: Additional opinions on simanei bagrut
items.text_en: Brayta: Additional opinions on simanei bagrut
items.desc_en: A brayta lists further signs: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok says when the breasts shake; Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says when the tip of the nose darkens (emended by Rav Ashi to 'when the tip of the nose splits'); Rabbi Yosei says when the areola becomes hard; Rabbi Shimon says when it becomes soft.

sub.desc_en: The brayta opens by asking what are the signs of physical maturity (בגרות), and Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok gives his opinion: when the breasts shake.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says the sign is when the tip of the nose darkens, but the gemara objects that this would describe an old woman.
Rav Ashi emends the text to read 'when the tip of the nose splits' instead of darkens.
Rabbi Yosei says the sign is when the areola becomes hard.
Rabbi Shimon says the sign is when the areola becomes soft.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The Kaf and the Three Signs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The Kaf and the Three Signs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the 'kaf' (a fleshy protuberance) and lists three signs given by the Sages for a woman: paggah (unripe), bochal (ripe), and tzemel (wilted), corresponding to stages of pubic hair growth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the 'kaf' (fleshy protuberance) and lists three signs—paggah, bochal, and tzemel—corresponding to stages of pubic hair growth, as taught by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of the Kaf and Ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of the Kaf and Ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains the kaf as a swollen place above the genitals that flattens as the girl grows. The Sages asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whose opinion is the halacha, and he replied that the halacha follows all of them to be stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'kaf' (כַּף) in the Mishnah refers to.
Rav Huna explains that the 'kaf' is a swollen place above the genitals that flattens as the girl grows.
The Sages ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whose opinion among the Tannaim is the binding law (הלכה).
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that the halacha follows all opinions to be stringent (להחמיר).

items.text: Digression: The Tzurian Courtyard
items.text_en: Digression: The Tzurian Courtyard
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited about the 'Tzurian courtyard' which is liable for maaser. Various Tannaim define it differently: Rabbi Shimon says it is where vessels are guarded, Rabbi Akiva says if one opens and one locks it is exempt, Rabbi Nechemya says if one is not embarrassed to eat there it is liable, Rabbi Yose says if one can enter without being questioned it is exempt, and Rabbi Yehuda says the inner courtyard is liable and the outer exempt. The Gemara concludes that the halacha follows all of them to be stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Chinana bar Rav Ika, one of whom teaches the baraita about the Tzurian courtyard.
The baraita defines the Tzurian courtyard as one liable for מעשר (tithe), with Rabbi Shimon's position that it is where vessels are guarded.
The Gemara asks what 'Tzurian courtyard' means.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana explains in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that in Tyre they post a guard at the courtyard entrance, and then cites Rabbi Akiva's position that if one opens and another locks, it is exempt.
Rabbi Nechemya states that if one is not embarrassed to eat there, the courtyard is liable for מעשר (tithe).
Rabbi Yose states that if one can enter without being questioned, the courtyard is exempt from מעשר (tithe).
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between an inner courtyard (liable) and an outer one (exempt).

sub.text: Sages' question and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling
sub.text_en: Sages' question and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Sages ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whose opinion is the הלכה (binding law), and he rules that the law follows all of them to be stringent.

items.text: Mishnah: Age of Majority for Ailonit and Saris
items.text_en: Mishnah: Age of Majority for Ailonit and Saris
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman of twenty who has not grown two pubic hairs must bring proof that she is twenty and is an ailonit, and she does not perform chalitzah or yibbum. Similarly, a man of twenty who has not grown two hairs must bring proof and is a saris. Beit Hillel says twenty, Beit Shammai says eighteen. Rabbi Eliezer says the male follows Beit Hillel and the female follows Beit Shammai because women mature earlier.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a twenty-year-old woman without two pubic hairs: she must bring proof of her age, is classified as an אַיְילוֹנִית (a woman incapable of puberty), and does not perform חליצה (levirate release) or ייבום (levirate marriage).
The Mishnah states the parallel rule for a twenty-year-old man without two hairs: he must bring proof, is classified as a סָרִיס (a eunuch), and does not perform חליצה or ייבום.
Beit Hillel sets the age at twenty, while Beit Shammai sets it at eighteen for both male and female.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that the male follows Beit Hillel (age twenty) and the female follows Beit Shammai (age eighteen), because women mature earlier than men.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction and Resolution Regarding Saris Signs
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction and Resolution Regarding Saris Signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a nine-year-old and a twenty-year-old without hair are both considered minors? Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says this applies only if signs of saris are present. Rava supports this from the Mishnah's wording. If no signs, until when? Rabbi Chiya says until the majority of his years. Rabbi Chiya would instruct to fatten or thin the person to see if signs appear due to thinness or fatness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah treats a nine-year-old and a twenty-year-old without hair as equivalent minors.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when signs of a saris (a eunuch) are present.
Rava supports this by noting that the Mishnah explicitly says 'and he is a saris,' confirming the inference.
The Gemara asks: if no signs of saris are present, until what age is the person considered a minor?
Rabbi Chiya teaches: until the majority of his years (i.e., half his expected lifespan plus one).
Rabbi Chiya would instruct to fatten a thin person or thin a fat person to determine if the signs were due to thinness or fatness.

items.text: Debate: Calculation of Years – From Day to Day or Calendar Year
items.text_en: Debate: Calculation of Years – From Day to Day or Calendar Year
items.desc_en: Rav rules that all years in this chapter are calculated from day to day (i.e., from the exact date of birth). Ulla says only what is explicitly taught is from day to day. The Gemara questions Rav from a baraita of Rabbi Yose ben Kippar and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that seem to use calendar years. It resolves that these are Tannaitic disputes. The Gemara then derives from verses that years for sacrifices, walled cities, and ancestral fields are from day to day.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that all years in this chapter are calculated from day to day (מֵעֵת לְעֵת).
Ulla says that only what is explicitly taught in the Mishnah is calculated from day to day; otherwise, it is not.
The Gemara questions Rav: if all years are from day to day, why does the Mishnah explicitly mention 'one day' only in some cases?
The Gemara objects with a baraita where Rabbi Yose ben Kippar and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi treat a year that has passed 30 days as a full calendar year, contradicting Rav's day-to-day calculation.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is between Tannaim, and cites a baraita that years for sacrifices, walled cities, ancestral fields, and the Hebrew slave are all calculated from day to day.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives from the verse 'כֶּבֶשׂ בֶּן שְׁנָתוֹ' that the year for sacrifices is the animal's own year, not a calendar year, and similarly derives for walled cities and ancestral fields.

items.text: Opening Mishnah (partial) on selling produce
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah (partial) on selling produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the sale of produce over two years, noting that sometimes three harvests are sold in two years.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may sell two harvests over two years, sometimes selling three harvests in two years.

items.text: Derivation of six years for a Hebrew slave
items.text_en: Derivation of six years for a Hebrew slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the six years of service for a Hebrew slave, citing the verse 'Six years he shall serve, and in the seventh' to include the seventh year as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the six years of service for a Hebrew slave, and answers by citing the verse 'Six years he shall serve, and in the seventh' to include the seventh year as well.

items.text: Dispute about the purpose of 'that which is in the son and daughter'
items.text_en: Dispute about the purpose of 'that which is in the son and daughter'
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel and Rav Yosef debate whether the phrase 'that which is in the son and daughter' refers to valuations or to the stages of a yotzei dofen. Abaye asks if they disagree, but they clarify they are not arguing, each stating a different application.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what halachic purpose is the phrase 'that which is in the son and daughter' written?
Rav Giddel in the name of Rav answers: It refers to the laws of valuations (ערכין).
Rav Yosef answers: It refers to the stages of a yotzei dofen (a child born by cesarean section).
Abaye asks: Do you two disagree with each other?
They reply: No, each of us stated a different application, and we do not dispute.

items.text: Proof that they do not disagree and explanation of their positions
items.text_en: Proof that they do not disagree and explanation of their positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a proof that Rav Giddel and Rav Yosef do not disagree, as Rav rules that the halacha for all stages of yotzei dofen is from birth. It then explains why each holds his view: one derives from the written verses, the other notes that the phrase should have been 'that which is in the male and female'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a proof that Rav Giddel and Rav Yosef do not disagree, because if they disagreed, the one who holds for ערכין (valuations) would not hold for יוצא דופן (a child delivered by caesarean section), yet Rav ruled that the halacha for all stages of יוצא דופן is from birth.

The Gemara explains why the one who holds for ערכין (valuations) does not also hold for יוצא דופן (caesarean section): he derives the rule from the written verses, requiring a parallel to the explicitly written cases.

The other authority (Rav Yosef) explains that the phrase 'שֶׁבַּבֵּן וְשֶׁבַּבַּת' (that which is in the son and daughter) should have been 'שֶׁבַּזָּכָר וְשֶׁבַּנְּקֵבָה' (that which is in the male and female), indicating a different derivation.

items.text: Halacha like Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar and Rabbi Zeira's inquiry
items.text_en: Halacha like Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar and Rabbi Zeira's inquiry
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Elazar rules the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar in the name of Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Zeira seeks to learn this from the master himself, and upon ascending, finds Rabbi Elazar who explains the reasoning: in all other chapters the Tanna teaches 'one day', but here he does not, implying the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar who spoke in the name of Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Zeira expresses his desire to ascend and learn this ruling directly from the master (Rabbi Elazar).

Upon ascending, Rabbi Zeira finds Rabbi Elazar, who explains that the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar because in all other chapters the Tanna teaches 'one day', but here he does not, implying the ruling is reasonable.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter on yotzei dofen
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter on yotzei dofen
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter on yotzei dofen with the phrase 'Hadran alach Yotzei Dofen'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter on yotzei dofen with the standard concluding formula.

items.text: Mishnah: Signs of puberty and yibbum
items.text_en: Mishnah: Signs of puberty and yibbum
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the halacha when the lower sign (pubic hair) appears before the upper sign (breasts): the woman may perform chalitzah or yibbum. If the upper sign appears before the lower, which is impossible, Rabbi Meir says she may not, while the Sages say she may, because the lower can precede the upper but not vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the halacha: when the lower sign (pubic hair) appears before the upper sign (breasts), the woman may perform חליצה (chalitzah) or יבום (yibbum).
Rabbi Meir rules that if the upper sign appears before the lower, which is impossible, the woman may neither perform חליצה (chalitzah) nor יבום (yibbum).
The Sages argue that she may perform חליצה (chalitzah) or יבום (yibbum), because the lower sign can precede the upper but the upper cannot precede the lower.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'even though it is impossible' since the case is that the upper sign came. It explains that 'came' is for Rabbi Meir, and 'even though impossible' is for the Rabbis. It then clarifies why the Mishnah includes this phrase: to teach that it is truly impossible, and the sign must have fallen off. It also notes that in a case where we checked and did not find the lower sign, the Rabbis would agree with Rabbi Meir that the upper sign came first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'even though it is impossible' since the case explicitly states that the upper sign came.
The Gemara explains that 'came' refers to Rabbi Meir's position, and 'even though impossible' refers to the Rabbis' position.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah could have simply stated the dispute without the phrase 'even though impossible', since the impossibility is obvious.
