The Gemara explains that without the phrase, one might think the dispute is about whether to worry about the minority of cases where the upper sign comes first, so the Mishnah teaches that it is truly impossible.

The Gemara concludes that in an unspecified case the dispute applies, but if we checked and did not find the lower sign, the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Meir that the upper sign came first and then fell off.

items.text: Biblical support for the order of signs
items.text_en: Biblical support for the order of signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses to support the order of signs. For Rabbi Meir, the verse 'Your breasts were formed and your hair grew' supports the lower sign preceding the upper. For the Rabbis, the verse is interpreted to mean that once breasts are formed, it is known that hair has grown. Another verse is similarly explained, with an alternative interpretation that 'shadei' refers to breasts, and God tells Israel that once breasts come, youth comes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Rabbis can explain the verse 'שָׁדַיִם נָכוֹנוּ וּשְׂעָרֵךְ צִמֵּחַ' (Your breasts were formed and your hair grew), which seems to support Rabbi Meir's order of lower sign before upper, while the Rabbis hold the opposite order.
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis interpret the verse to mean that once the breasts are formed, it is known that the hair has already grown, thus the upper sign (hair) precedes the lower (breasts).

The Gemara raises a second question: for Rabbi Meir, the verse 'בַּעְשׂוֹת מִמִּצְרַיִם דַּדַּיִךְ לְמַעַן שְׁדֵי נְעוּרָיִךְ' (when from Egypt your breasts were made for the sake of the breasts of your youth) supports his order, but for the Rabbis it should be reversed.
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis interpret this verse similarly: once the breasts come, it is known that youth (the upper sign) has already come.

An alternative answer is offered: the word 'שְׁדֵי' (breasts) is written entirely in the context of breasts, and God tells Israel that once breasts come, youth comes, implying the lower sign precedes the upper.

items.text: Opening poetic verse on breasts
items.text_en: Opening poetic verse on breasts
items.desc_en: A verse is cited describing the development of breasts as a sign of maturity, but the Gemara will clarify that the lower sign is the halakhic determinant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a poetic verse describing the development of breasts as a sign of maturity, but the context will clarify that the lower sign is the halakhic determinant.

items.text: Derivation that women are like men: one sign suffices
items.text_en: Derivation that women are like men: one sign suffices
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know to rely on the lower sign. Rav Yehudah citing Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael derive from a verse that a woman is equated to a man for all penalties: just as a man is judged by one sign (lower), so too a woman. The Gemara then refines this: like a man, the lower sign, not the upper.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that we rely on the lower sign (תחתון) for a woman's puberty?

sub.text: Rav Yehudah citing Rav and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael derive from the verse 'איש או אשה כי יעשו' that a woman is equated to a man for all penalties: just as a man is judged by one sign, so too a woman.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the one sign could be either the upper or the lower sign, not specifically the lower.
The Gemara resolves: just as a man's sign is the lower one (pubic hair) and not the upper (breasts), so too a woman's sign is the lower one.

items.text: Baraita: Once lower sign appears, ignore upper
items.text_en: Baraita: Once lower sign appears, ignore upper
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok that the sages in Yavneh ruled: once the lower sign comes, we no longer pay attention to the upper sign.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports this: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok said that in Yavneh they would explain that once the lower sign appears, we no longer pay attention to the upper sign.

items.text: Dispute about which sign comes first based on lifestyle
items.text_en: Dispute about which sign comes first based on lifestyle
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that city girls get the lower sign first due to bathing, while village girls get the upper sign first due to grinding. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that rich girls get the right side first due to lounging, while poor girls get the left side first due to carrying water or siblings.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that city girls get the lower sign first due to bathing, while village girls get the upper sign first due to grinding.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that rich girls get the right side first due to lounging, while poor girls get the left side first due to carrying water or siblings.

items.text: Dispute about left side preceding right
items.text_en: Dispute about left side preceding right
items.desc_en: The Sages state that the left side precedes the right. Rabbi Chanina ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua says that never did the left precede the right except in one case in his neighborhood, and it reverted.

sub.text: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Chanina ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Chanina ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: The Sages taught that the left side precedes the right side; Rabbi Chanina ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua says the left side never preceded the right except in one case in his neighborhood where it did and then returned to normal.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua disputes the generalization, asserting that the left side never preceded the right except in one case in his neighborhood, and even that case reverted.

items.text: Baraita: Women may examine girls; dispute about reliability
items.text_en: Baraita: Women may examine girls; dispute about reliability
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that all girls who need examination are examined by women, and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yishmael would delegate to their wives/mothers. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between before, during, and after the 'perek' (the year of puberty), limiting women's examinations. Rabbi Shimon allows women even during the perek, but only for stringency, not leniency. Examples are given for mi'un and chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general rule that all girls who need examination are examined by women, and cites the practice of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yishmael who delegated this to their wives or mothers.
Rabbi Yehuda limits women's examinations to before and after the perek (the year of puberty), but not during the perek, because one may not rely on women for doubtful matters.
Rabbi Shimon permits women to examine even during the perek, but only for stringency (החמיר) and not for leniency (הקל).
The baraita provides examples of the stringency/leniency distinction: a woman may say 'she is גדולה (an adult)' to prevent mi'un, or 'she is קטנה (a minor)' to prevent chalitzah, but not the reverse.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute about examination timing
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute about examination timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes Rabbi Yehuda's position: before the perek, examination is needed to rule out moles; after the perek, Rava's chazakah (presumption that signs have come) applies, but examination is still needed for chalitzah. During the perek, women do not examine because it is like after the perek but without Rava's chazakah. Rabbi Shimon holds that during the perek is like before the perek, requiring examination. The Gemara then clarifies that the statement about women being believed only for stringency is attributed to Rabbi Yehuda regarding the perek period.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda's statement that women examine girls before and after the perek.
The Gemara explains that before the perek, examination is needed to rule out moles.
The Gemara questions why examination is needed after the perek, given Rava's chazakah (presumption that signs have come).
The Gemara answers that Rava's chazakah applies only for mi'un (refusal), but for chalitzah (release from levirate marriage) examination is still needed.
The Gemara resolves that during the perek, women do not examine because it is like after the perek but without Rava's chazakah, so they cannot rely on women's examination.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that during the perek is like before the perek, requiring examination to rule out moles.
The Gemara asks who teaches the statement that a woman is believed only for stringency but not for leniency.
The Gemara answers that it is Rabbi Yehuda's position, applying specifically to the perek period.

items.text: Alternative explanations for the Mishnah's redundancy
items.text_en: Alternative explanations for the Mishnah's redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes two alternative reasons for the Mishnah's seemingly redundant clause: either it follows Rabbi Shimon's view after the chapter, rejecting Rava's presumption, or it intends to teach a 'similar case' (כיוצא בו). The first alternative is challenged and resolved by noting that the Mishnah wants to align with the majority opinion, and the second is preferred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's clause follows Rabbi Shimon's view after the chapter, rejecting Rava's presumption.
The Gemara objects that the clause is redundant, as the first part of the Mishnah already stated the same ruling.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah intends to align with the majority opinion, but this is obvious since the rule is that the law follows the majority.
The Gemara resolves that the clause is needed to teach a 'similar case' (כיוצא בו), countering a potential inference from Rabbi Meir's scriptural support.

items.text: Mishnah: Classifications of vessels and limbs
items.text_en: Mishnah: Classifications of vessels and limbs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three parallel classifications: vessels that absorb liquid also emit it, but some emit without absorbing; limbs with a nail have bone, but some have bone without a nail; items susceptible to midras impurity are also susceptible to corpse impurity, but some are susceptible to corpse impurity without being susceptible to midras.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a classification: every clay vessel that absorbs liquid also emits it, but some emit without absorbing.
The Mishnah presents a second classification: every limb that has a nail also has bone, but some have bone without a nail.

The Mishnah presents a third classification: everything susceptible to midras impurity is also susceptible to corpse impurity, but some are susceptible to corpse impurity without being susceptible to midras.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the vessel classification
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the vessel classification
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's vessel classification: a vessel that absorbs liquid is invalid for purification water and invalid due to a crack (גסטרא), while one that only emits is valid for purification water but still invalid due to a crack. Rav Asi teaches that the measure for clay vessels is by absorbing liquid, and the mention of emitting liquid is only for the matter of a crack, as Mar Zutra explains that one does not apply the principle of 'bring a crack to a crack'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's vessel classification: a vessel that absorbs liquid is invalid for purification water and invalid due to a crack (גסטרא), while one that only emits is valid for purification water but still invalid due to a crack.
Rav Asi teaches that the measure for clay vessels is by absorbing liquid, and the mention of emitting liquid is only for the matter of a crack (גסטרא).

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman's explanation
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman's explanation
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra explains the reason: one does not apply the principle of 'bring a crack to a crack' (הבא גסטרא לגסטרא) to disqualify a vessel that emits liquid.

items.text: Baraita: How to test a clay vessel
items.text_en: Baraita: How to test a clay vessel
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the practical test for determining if a clay vessel absorbs liquid: one brings a basin full of water and places the pot inside; if the pot absorbs water, it is known to absorb liquid, otherwise it only emits.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the practical test for a clay vessel: placing it in a basin of water to determine if it absorbs liquid (כונס משקה) or only emits (מוציא משקה).

items.text: Mishnah: Tests for a pot's absorption or emission
items.text_en: Mishnah: Tests for a pot's absorption or emission
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei describe methods to test whether a pot absorbs liquid (a defect) or emits it (sound). Rabbi Yehuda suggests placing the pot in hot water or fire; Rabbi Yosei forbids fire lest it over-seal the pot and only permits embers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda describes the first test: turning the pot upside down in water to see if water enters (indicating a hole that absorbs) or not (indicating a hole that only emits).
Rabbi Yehuda offers an alternative test: placing the pot on fire to see if the fire holds liquid back (emission hole) or not (absorption hole).
Rabbi Yosei objects to the fire test, arguing that fire can seal the pot, and instead recommends using hot ash; he also adds a drip test to identify an absorption hole.

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the difference between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the difference between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda?
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the difference between the first Tanna (Tanna Kamma) and Rabbi Yehuda is whether forced absorption counts as absorption (כינוס על ידי הדחק).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what difference exists between the first Tanna (Tanna Kamma) and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the testing method for earthenware vessels.
Ulla answers that the difference lies in whether forced absorption (כינוס על ידי הדחק) is considered absorption.

items.text: Impurity of a limb without a fingernail
items.text_en: Impurity of a limb without a fingernail
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any limb with a fingernail conveys impurity via touch, carrying, and tent. If it has bone but no fingernail, it only conveys impurity via touch and carrying. Rav Ḥisda, citing 'our great master' (Rav), rules that an extra finger with bone but no nail conveys impurity via touch and carrying, as per a ruling of Rabbi Yochanan when the finger is not counted on the hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a limb with a fingernail conveys impurity via touch, carrying, and tent; a limb with bone but no fingernail conveys impurity only via touch and carrying.
Rav Ḥisda, citing 'our great master' (Rav), applies the Mishnah's rule to an extra finger with bone but no nail, ruling it conveys impurity via touch and carrying but not tent.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Ḥana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Ḥana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Ḥana adds a qualification in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the extra finger conveys impurity only when it is not counted as part of the hand.

items.text: Vessels fit for sitting and impurity of midras
items.text_en: Vessels fit for sitting and impurity of midras
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that whatever is susceptible to midras impurity is also susceptible to corpse impurity. The Gemara asks what is excluded, and answers: a se'ah or tarkav measure that is not designated for sitting, as derived from a baraitha: 'which the zab sits upon' excludes vessels that are moved when needed for work.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that whatever is susceptible to midras impurity is also susceptible to corpse impurity, and there is something that is susceptible to corpse impurity but not to midras impurity.
The Gemara asks what is excluded by the Mishnah's formulation.
The Gemara answers that it comes to include a se'ah or tarkav measure that is not designated for sitting.
A baraita is cited that questions whether a se'ah or tarkav that is overturned and sat upon would be impure.
The baraita resolves that the verse 'which the zab sits upon' excludes vessels that are moved when needed for work, as they are not designated for sitting.

items.text: Eligibility to judge: monetary vs. capital cases
items.text_en: Eligibility to judge: monetary vs. capital cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one fit to judge capital cases is fit for monetary cases, but not vice versa. Rav Yehuda says this excludes a mamzer. The Gemara notes a parallel Mishnah that includes a ger, and explains that both are necessary: one might think a ger is fit because he can enter the congregation, but a mamzer cannot; conversely, one might think a mamzer is fit because he comes from a valid seed, unlike a ger.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anyone fit to judge capital cases is fit for monetary cases, but not vice versa.
Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah's exclusion of those fit only for monetary cases includes a mamzer (bastard).
The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah where Rav Yehuda similarly explains that the exclusion includes a mamzer, and notes that one Mishnah includes a ger (convert) and the other a mamzer.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: if only the ger were taught, one might think a mamzer is excluded because he cannot enter the congregation.
Conversely, if only the mamzer were taught, one might think a ger is excluded because he comes from a flawed seed; therefore both are needed.

items.text: Eligibility to judge vs. testify
items.text_en: Eligibility to judge vs. testify
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who is fit to judge is fit to testify, but not vice versa. Rabbi Yochanan says this excludes a blind person in one eye, and then asks who is the authority for this ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one who is fit to judge is fit to testify, but not vice versa.
The Gemara asks what new case the Mishnah's exclusion comes to include.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah excludes a blind person in one eye from judging but not from testifying.
The Gemara asks whose authority supports this ruling.

items.text: Derivation that judging requires sight and excludes relatives
items.text_en: Derivation that judging requires sight and excludes relatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's source as Rabbi Meir, who derives from a biblical analogy that court cases must be judged by day and cannot involve a blind judge, just as with negaim. It also derives that negaim cannot be judged by relatives, analogous to court cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's source as Rabbi Meir, who derives from a biblical analogy that court cases must be judged by day, just as with negaim.
Rabbi Meir further derives that court cases cannot involve a blind judge, just as with negaim, and that negaim cannot be judged by relatives, analogous to court cases.
The baraita raises an objection that if court cases require three judges, then negaim should also require three priests, but the verse teaches that even one priest may view negaim.

items.text: The blind judge in Rabbi Yochanan's neighborhood
items.text_en: The blind judge in Rabbi Yochanan's neighborhood
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a blind person could judge, given Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the law follows the anonymous Mishnah which disqualifies a blind person. It resolves that Rabbi Yochanan found another anonymous Mishnah allowing night sessions, and explains why that Mishnah is preferred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that a blind person in Rabbi Yochanan's neighborhood was judging cases, and Rabbi Yochanan said nothing to him.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan could allow this, given his own ruling that the halakha follows an anonymous mishnah.
The Gemara cites the mishnah that one blind in one eye is fit to testify but not to judge, and notes that Rabbi Yochanan himself explained this.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan found another anonymous mishnah that allows judging monetary cases at night, which contradicts the comparison to leprous marks.
The Gemara asks why the second anonymous mishnah is preferred over the first.
The first answer: an anonymous mishnah representing the view of many Sages is preferable.
The second answer: the mishnah in Sanhedrin is preferred because it teaches the halakha in the context of the laws of judges.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for tithes and impurity of foods
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for tithes and impurity of foods
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything liable for tithes is susceptible to food impurity, but not vice versa. The Gemara explains that the additional category includes meat, fish, and eggs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything liable for tithes is susceptible to food impurity, but there are items that are susceptible to food impurity yet not liable for tithes.
The Gemara asks what additional items are included in the category of foods susceptible to impurity but not liable for tithes.
The Gemara answers that the additional items are meat, fish, and eggs.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for pe'ah and tithes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for pe'ah and tithes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything liable for pe'ah is liable for tithes, but not vice versa. The Gemara explains that the additional category includes figs and vegetables, which are exempt from pe'ah due to the general rule of pe'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: anything liable for pe'ah is liable for tithes, but there are items liable for tithes that are not liable for pe'ah.
The Gemara asks what additional items are included in the category of things liable for tithes but not for pe'ah.
The Gemara answers that the additional items are figs and vegetables, which are exempt from pe'ah according to the general rule of pe'ah.
The Gemara cites a baraita that lists the five conditions for pe'ah liability: food, guarded, grown from the earth, harvested all at once, and stored for preservation.

The baraita explains each condition: 'food' excludes certain plants, 'guarded' excludes ownerless produce, 'grown from the earth' excludes mushrooms, 'harvested all at once' excludes figs, and 'stored for preservation' excludes vegetables.

The Gemara contrasts the tithe rule, which lacks the last two conditions (harvested all at once and stored for preservation), thereby explaining why figs and vegetables are liable for tithes but not for pe'ah.

items.text: Discussion of onions and mushrooms
items.text_en: Discussion of onions and mushrooms
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case of onions and vegetables, citing a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Sages about pe'ah. It then quotes Rabbi Yochanan regarding mushrooms initially grown for animal feed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if onions and garlic are among the vegetables, they are obligated in pe'ah.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei says pe'ah is taken from each bed of onions, while the Sages say one pe'ah suffices for all.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement via Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement via Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan: mushrooms initially planted for animal feed, but then reconsidered for human consumption, are exempt from ma'aser.

items.text: Opening statement: intention during attachment is not considered intention
items.text_en: Opening statement: intention during attachment is not considered intention
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that items require intention at the time of detachment, because intention during attachment is not considered valid intention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that items require intention at the time of detachment, because intention during attachment is not considered valid intention.

items.text: Rava's proof from the thirteen rules of a kosher bird carcass
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the thirteen rules of a kosher bird carcass
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita listing thirteen rules about a kosher bird carcass, one of which is that it requires intention but not preparation. He argues that this proves intention during life is not considered intention, and similarly intention during attachment is not considered.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita listing thirteen rules about a kosher bird carcass, one of which is that it requires intention but not preparation, and argues that this proves intention during life is not considered intention, and similarly intention during attachment is not considered.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's explanation and the hen of Yavneh
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's explanation and the hen of Yavneh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the case involves a fledgling that fell from a roof, where no one had intention for it. Abaye challenges him with the case of the hen of Yavneh, which was deemed impure without intention. Rabbi Zeira initially says it was a wild chicken, but Abaye rebukes those who laughed, explaining it was a domesticated hen that rebelled, and 'wild' means it became wild from its owner.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the case involves a fledgling that fell from a roof, where no one had intention for it.
Abaye challenges Rabbi Zeira with the case of the hen of Yavneh, which was deemed impure without intention.
Rabbi Zeira initially says it was a wild chicken.
The sages laugh and object that a wild chicken is a non-kosher bird and cannot become impure.
Abaye rebukes those who laughed, explaining it was a domesticated hen that rebelled, and 'wild' means it became wild from its owner.

items.text: Rav Papa's alternative explanation and the marsh hen
items.text_en: Rav Papa's alternative explanation and the marsh hen
items.desc_en: Rav Papa says it was a marsh hen, consistent with his view that a male marsh hen is forbidden but a female is permitted. Marimar taught that the female marsh hen is forbidden, but the rabbis saw it trample and eat, which is the reason for leniency.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that the case involved a marsh hen (תרנגולתא דאגמא), consistent with his view that a male marsh hen is forbidden but a female is permitted.
Marimar taught that the female marsh hen is forbidden, but the rabbis saw it trample and eat, which is the reason for leniency.

items.text: Baraita on a fledgling that fell into a vat and the dispute with Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Baraita on a fledgling that fell into a vat and the dispute with Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if a fledgling fell into a vat and one intended to give it to a Samaritan, it is impure; if to a dog, it is pure. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri argues it is impure even for a dog, using a kal vahomer: if it imparts severe impurity without intention, it should impart light impurity without intention. The Sages counter that severe impurity does not descend to that level, but light impurity does. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri cites the hen of Yavneh as a proof, but they respond that Samaritans were there and intended it for food.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: a fledgling that fell into a vat is impure if intended for a Samaritan, pure if for a dog; Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri argues it is impure even for a dog.

sub.text: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri's kal vahomer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri's kal vahomer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri argues by kal vahomer: if the fledgling imparts severe impurity without intention, it should impart light impurity without intention.
The Sages reject the kal vahomer: severe impurity does not descend to that level, but light impurity does.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri cites the hen of Yavneh as a proof that light impurity can be imparted without intention.
The Sages reject the proof: Samaritans were present at Yavneh and had intended the hen for food, so intention was present.

items.text: Clarifying the location: city or village?
items.text_en: Clarifying the location: city or village?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the case is in a city or village. In a city, no intention is needed; in a village, intention is required. Rabbi Zeira bar Hanina resolves that it is in a city, but the vat was covered, making it like a village.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the case is in a city (כרכים) or village (כפרים), citing a baraita that in cities no intention is needed.
The Gemara rejects the village option, citing a baraita that in villages intention is required.
Rabbi Zeira bar Hanina resolves that it is in a city, but the vat was covered, making it like a village where intention is required.

items.text: Repeated kal vahomer and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Repeated kal vahomer and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri repeats his kal vahomer, and the Sages respond. Rava explains that 'does not descend to that level' means that severe impurity does not apply to a dog, so the kal vahomer is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object again: No — if you said regarding severe impurity that it does not descend to that level, can you say regarding light impurity that it does descend?

items.text: Opening argument: kal vachomer from severe impurity to light impurity
items.text_en: Opening argument: kal vachomer from severe impurity to light impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer argument: if severe impurity (neveilat of a non-kosher animal), which is lighter because it does not produce something similar (i.e., does not become a source of impurity like itself), nevertheless conveys impurity without intent, then light impurity (neveilat of a kosher bird), which is more stringent because it does produce something similar (i.e., can become a source of impurity like itself), should certainly convey impurity without intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer argument: if severe impurity (neveilat of a non-kosher animal) conveys impurity without intent because it is lighter (does not produce something similar), then light impurity (neveilat of a kosher bird) should certainly convey impurity without intent because it is more stringent (does produce something similar).

items.text: Abaye's objection: the kal vachomer is flawed
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: the kal vachomer is flawed
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the kal vachomer is actually reversed: severe impurity is lighter (kila) because it does not produce something similar, yet it conveys impurity without intent; light impurity is more stringent (chamira) because it does produce something similar, so it should certainly convey impurity without intent. This is a valid kal vachomer, but the Gemara will reject it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the kal vachomer is actually reversed: severe impurity is lighter (קיל) because it does not produce something similar, yet it conveys impurity without intent; light impurity is more stringent (חמיר) because it does produce something similar, so it should certainly convey impurity without intent.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's reinterpretation: the argument is about hechsher
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's reinterpretation: the argument is about hechsher
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the original argument was not about intent but about hechsher (preparation by water): severe impurity does not require hechsher, so it conveys impurity without hechsher; light impurity requires hechsher, so it does not convey impurity without hechsher.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet reinterprets the original argument: the distinction is not about intent but about hechsher (preparation by water) — severe impurity does not require hechsher, while light impurity does.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: neveilat of a kosher bird does not require hechsher
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: neveilat of a kosher bird does not require hechsher
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Sheshet: a mishnah states that neveilat of a kosher bird requires intent but not hechsher. The Gemara then distinguishes between hechsher of a sheretz (which it does not need) and hechsher of water (which it might need). It cites the school of Rabbi Yishmael's derivation from the verse "al kol zera zerua" that only items that do not ultimately convey severe impurity require hechsher, but neveilat of a kosher bird ultimately conveys severe impurity (through the throat), so it does not require hechsher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Sheshet by citing a mishnah that explicitly states neveilat of a kosher bird does not require hechsher.
The Gemara distinguishes: the mishnah only exempts it from hechsher of a sheretz (שרץ), but it still requires hechsher of water.
The Gemara questions why hechsher of a sheretz is not needed, and suggests that the same reasoning should exempt it from hechsher of water as well.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'עַל כׇּל זֶרַע זֵרוּעַ' that only items which do not ultimately convey severe impurity require hechsher, excluding neveilat of a kosher bird which does convey severe impurity through the throat.

items.text: Rava's (or Rav Pappa's) conclusion: no severe or light impurity in the world
items.text_en: Rava's (or Rav Pappa's) conclusion: no severe or light impurity in the world
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Pappa) concludes that the original argument is not about comparing severe and light impurity, but rather about the general principle that no impurity (whether severe or light) requires intent to convey impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Pappa) concludes that the original argument is not about comparing severe and light impurity, but rather about the general principle that no impurity (whether severe or light) requires intent to convey impurity.

items.text: Rava's statement: Rabbi Yochanan agrees that intent for connection is valid for tithes
items.text_en: Rava's statement: Rabbi Yochanan agrees that intent for connection is valid for tithes
items.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Yochanan agrees that regarding tithes, intent to connect (machshevet chibbur) is considered valid intent. Rava proves this from a mishnah about se'ah, ezov, and kornit in a courtyard: if they were guarded, they are liable for tithes. The Gemara explains that this is a case where they were initially planted for animal consumption, but if the courtyard guards them (i.e., they are intended for human use), they become liable.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Yochanan agrees that regarding tithes, intent to connect (מחשבת חיבור) is considered valid intent.
Rava asks: From where do I derive this?
Rava cites a mishnah (Ma'asrot 3:9) about savory, hyssop, and thyme in a courtyard: if they were guarded, they are liable for tithes.
The Gemara asks: What are the circumstances?
The Gemara objects: If they were initially planted for human consumption, does it need to be stated that they are liable?
The Gemara answers: Rather, it is a case where they were initially planted for animal consumption, yet if guarded they are liable, showing that intent while attached is valid.

Rav Ashi rejects the proof: The mishnah deals with plants that grew spontaneously, which are assumed to be for human consumption, and the condition of guarding determines liability, not intent while attached.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and Rava's resolution: the principle is about species
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and Rava's resolution: the principle is about species
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: there is a mishnah that says everything liable for tithes is susceptible to food impurity, but if Rava's principle is correct, there are items (like those planted for animals but guarded) that are liable for tithes but not susceptible to food impurity. Rava resolves that the mishnah means every species that is liable for tithes is susceptible to food impurity, not every individual item.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects by citing a mishnah that states everything liable for tithes is susceptible to food impurity, and argues that if Rava's principle were correct, there would be items (like those planted for animals but guarded) that are liable for tithes but not susceptible to food impurity.
Rava resolves the objection by clarifying that the mishnah means every species that is liable for tithes is susceptible to food impurity, not every individual item.

items.text: Support for Rava's interpretation from a parallel mishnah and Rav Shimi bar Ashi's proof
items.text_en: Support for Rava's interpretation from a parallel mishnah and Rav Shimi bar Ashi's proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rava's interpretation from a parallel mishnah about first shearing and priestly gifts, where a treifah is liable for first shearing but not for gifts, which would contradict the mishnah's statement if taken literally. Ravina explains that the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who exempts a treifah from first shearing. Rav Shimi bar Ashi then brings a proof from a mishnah about one who declares his vineyard ownerless: it is liable for pe'ah but exempt from tithes, contradicting the mishnah that says everything liable for pe'ah is liable for tithes, proving that the mishnah refers to species.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that Rava's interpretation is supported by the parallel mishnah's continuation, which states that everything liable for first shearing is liable for priestly gifts, but there are items liable for gifts and not for first shearing; if the mishnah were taken literally, a treifah (טריפה) would be a counterexample, being liable for first shearing but exempt from gifts.
Ravina resolves the objection by identifying the mishnah as following Rabbi Shimon, who exempts a treifah (טריפה) from first shearing, thus removing the counterexample.

Rav Shimi bar Ashi brings a proof from a mishnah about one who declares his vineyard ownerless: it is liable for pe'ah (פאה) but exempt from tithes, which would contradict the mishnah that says everything liable for pe'ah is liable for tithes.
The Gemara concludes that the contradiction proves the mishnah refers to מין (species), not individual items, thus supporting Rava's interpretation.

items.text: Transition to a new mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's ruling on sowing diverse seeds
items.text_en: Transition to a new mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's ruling on sowing diverse seeds
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic from a mishnah: the Sages agree with Rabbi Akiva that one who sows fenugreek or mustard in two or three places gives pe'ah from each place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a mishnah stating that the Sages agree with Rabbi Akiva that one who sows fenugreek or mustard in two or three places gives pe'ah from each place.

items.text: The status of asafoetida (שֶׁבֶת) regarding tithes and impurity
items.text_en: The status of asafoetida (שֶׁבֶת) regarding tithes and impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that asafoetida, used for flavor, is subject to tithes and impurity. A contradiction is raised from a mishnah where Rabbi Akiva states that certain spices, including asafoetida, are bought with ma'aser money but do not contract food impurity. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects, and a ruling is established that they are neither bought with ma'aser money nor contract impurity. Rav Chisda and Rav Ashi resolve the contradiction by distinguishing between asafoetida used for seasoning (לְכָמָךְ) and for cooking (לִקְדֵרָה), concluding that the default use is for seasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that asafoetida (שֶׁבֶת) is subject to pe'ah and tithes, and therefore should contract food impurity, since it is used for flavor.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishnah where Rabbi Akiva lists spices, including asafoetida, that are bought with ma'aser money but do not contract food impurity.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects to Rabbi Akiva's position, arguing that if these items are bought with ma'aser money they should contract impurity, and if not, they should not be bought.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri reports that the sages voted and concluded that these items are neither bought with ma'aser money nor contract food impurity.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the mishnah's ruling applies specifically to asafoetida used for seasoning (לְכָמָךְ), not for cooking.

Rav Ashi refines the answer before Rav Kahana, arguing that the default use of asafoetida is for seasoning (לְכָמָךְ), citing a baraita about terumah and impurity to prove that only after it imparts flavor in a pot does it lose its food status.

items.text: Laws of first shearing, priestly gifts, and Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Laws of first shearing, priestly gifts, and Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything obligated in first shearing is obligated in priestly gifts, but not vice versa. Similarly, anything subject to biur (removal) is subject to Sabbatical year laws, but not vice versa. The Gemara provides examples: leaves of arum and ivy have Sabbatical year status but no biur, while their roots have both. The biblical source for biur is explained based on the availability of food for wild animals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: anything obligated in first shearing is obligated in priestly gifts, but not vice versa; anything subject to biur (removal) is subject to Sabbatical year laws, but not vice versa.
The Gemara provides examples: leaves of arum and ivy have Sabbatical year status but no biur, while their roots have both.

The Gemara cites the verse (Leviticus 25:7) to explain the biblical source for biur: as long as wild animals eat from the field, you may feed your domesticated animals in the house; when it is gone from the field, you must remove it from the house, and these leaves never fully disappear from the field.

items.text: Signs of kosher fish and animals
items.text_en: Signs of kosher fish and animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any fish with scales has fins, but some have fins without scales; any animal with horns has hooves, but some have hooves without horns. The Gemara explains that scales are the definitive sign of a kosher fish, and the Torah mentions fins to prevent misinterpretation. Rabbi Avahu and the school of Rabbi Yishmael explain that both signs are written to magnify the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any fish with scales has fins, and any animal with horns has hooves, but the converse is not always true.
The Gemara asks: since we rely on scales as the definitive sign of a kosher fish, why did the Torah also mention fins?
The Gemara explains: without fins, one might have misinterpreted 'scales' as meaning fins, so the Torah wrote both to prevent error.
The Gemara proves that 'קשקשת' (scale) means a covering, citing the verse about Goliath's armor of scales.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu and the school of Rabbi Yishmael explain that the Torah wrote both signs to magnify and glorify the Torah.

items.text: Blessings before and after food
items.text_en: Blessings before and after food
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything requiring a blessing after it requires a blessing before it, but not vice versa. The Gemara asks what is included: first, vegetables; according to Rabbi Yitzchak who blesses on vegetables, water; according to Rav Pappa who blesses on water, mitzvot; according to the Westerners who bless after removing tefillin, the blessing after mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: anything requiring a blessing after it requires a blessing before it, but not vice versa.
The Gemara asks what case is included by the Mishnah's 'yesh she'ta'un berakha lefanav ve'ein ta'un berakha le'acharav', and answers: vegetables.
The Gemara asks what case is included according to Rabbi Yitzchak, who already blesses on vegetables, and answers: water.
The Gemara asks what case is included according to Rav Pappa, who already blesses on water, and answers: mitzvot.
The Gemara asks what case is included according to the Westerners, who already bless after removing tefillin, and the answer is cut off (the text ends).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a girl who brings two pubic hairs is obligated in all mitzvot and may perform halitzah or yibbum; similarly, a boy becomes obligated and is eligible to be a rebellious son until his beard grows. Rabbi Yehudah requires the black hair to outnumber the white for the girl to be unable to refuse marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a girl who brings two pubic hairs is obligated in all mitzvot and may perform halitzah or yibbum, and a boy similarly becomes obligated and is eligible to be a rebellious son until his beard grows; Rabbi Yehudah requires the black hair to outnumber the white for the girl to be unable to refuse marriage.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why mention halitzah and yibbum?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why mention halitzah and yibbum?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that the girl may perform halitzah or yibbum, given that she is already obligated in all mitzvot. It answers that this excludes the opinion of Rabbi Yosei, who holds that only a man is subject to yibbum, but a woman, whether adult or minor, is not. The Mishnah teaches that only if she has two hairs is she considered like a man for yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to specify that the girl may perform halitzah or yibbum, given that it already stated she is obligated in all mitzvot.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's phrase excludes the opinion of Rabbi Yosei, who holds that only a man is subject to yibbum, and teaches that a girl with two hairs is considered like a man for this purpose.

items.text: Gemara's second question: Why repeat the obligation for the boy?
items.text_en: Gemara's second question: Why repeat the obligation for the boy?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah repeats that the boy is obligated in all mitzvot, since it already stated the same for the girl. It suggests that the repetition is to introduce the law of the rebellious son, but the Gemara concludes that the Mishnah simply elaborates on the boy's laws alongside the girl's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah repeats that the boy is obligated in all mitzvot, since it already stated the same for the girl.
The Gemara objects that if the repetition were only to introduce the law of the rebellious son, that law was already stated earlier in the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah simply elaborates on the boy's laws alongside the girl's, without introducing new content.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar rules like Rabbi Yehudah; story of Rabbi Yishmael's daughter
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar rules like Rabbi Yehudah; story of Rabbi Yishmael's daughter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Elazar that the halakhah follows Rabbi Yehudah. Rabbi Yehudah concedes that if the girl was intimate after bringing two hairs, she can no longer refuse marriage. Rav Kahana relates a story about Rabbi Yishmael's daughter who came to refuse marriage with her son on her shoulder, citing a teaching that a woman whose betrothal was a mistake may refuse even after intimacy. The Sages concluded that a daughter may refuse until she brings two hairs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yehudah's position regarding a girl's ability to refuse marriage (מיאון).
The gemara states that Rabbi Yehudah concedes that if a girl was intimate after bringing two pubic hairs, she can no longer refuse marriage (מיאון).
Rav Kahana's colleagues intended to rule in practice (עובדא) according to Rabbi Yehudah's lenient position, even if the girl had been intimate.

Rav Kahana objects by recounting a story about Rabbi Yishmael's daughter who came to the study hall to refuse marriage (למאן) with her son on her shoulder, and a great weeping erupted in the study hall.

sub.text: The Sages in the study hall
sub.text_en: The Sages in the study hall
sub.desc_en: The Sages exclaim in distress: 'Shall the offspring of that righteous man (Rabbi Yishmael) stumble over a matter that he himself taught?'

sub.text: Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel citing Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel citing Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah reports in the name of Shmuel citing Rabbi Yishmael that a woman whose betrothal was a mistake (קידושי טעות) may refuse marriage (ממאנת) even if she has a child on her shoulder.
The Sages concluded that a daughter may refuse marriage (ממאנת) only until she brings two pubic hairs; they explained the ruling but did not act upon it in practice.

items.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba reports a ruling to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba reports a ruling to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba reports to Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Chanina's students ruled like Rabbi Yehudah even after intimacy. Rabbi Yochanan then reports this to Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah, who sends a spy and expels them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba reports to Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Chanina's students ruled like Rabbi Yehudah even after intimacy.
Rabbi Yochanan reports the matter to Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah, who sends a spy and expels them.

items.text: Interpretations of 'the black outnumbers the white'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'the black outnumbers the white'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quotes Mar Ukva that 'the black outnumbers the white' does not mean literally, but that two hairs lie down and appear as if black outnumbers white. Rava says it means two hairs that encircle from lip to lip.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda quotes Mar Ukva explaining that 'the black outnumbers the white' does not mean literally, but that two hairs lie down and appear as if black outnumbers white.
Rava offers an alternative interpretation: 'the black outnumbers the white' means two hairs that encircle from lip to lip.

items.text: Discussion of follicles and the distinction between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya
items.text_en: Discussion of follicles and the distinction between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya
items.desc_en: Rav Helbo quotes Rav Huna that the two hairs require follicles at their roots. Rav Malkiyo quotes Rav Adda bar Ahavah that follicles are sufficient even without hairs. The Gemara then distinguishes between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya regarding their teachings, and Rav Ashi quotes Mar Zutra that Rabbi Chanina from Sura questions why the Tanna did not explicitly teach about follicles, concluding that even two hairs in one follicle suffice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Helbo quotes Rav Huna that the two hairs require follicles at their roots.

sub.text: Rav Malkiyo citing Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.text_en: Rav Malkiyo citing Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.desc_en: Rav Malkiyo quotes Rav Adda bar Ahavah that follicles suffice even without hairs.
Rav Chanina bar Rav Ika distinguishes between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya by listing which topics each taught.
Rav Pappa provides a mnemonic: Mishnah and baraita are attributed to Rav Malkiya, while Talmudic statements are attributed to Rav Malkiyo.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two identifications.
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in the topic of 'shifchot' (handmaidens).

sub.text: Rav Ashi quoting Mar Zutra citing Rabbi Chanina from Sura
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi quoting Mar Zutra citing Rabbi Chanina from Sura
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi quotes Mar Zutra that Rabbi Chanina from Sura questions why the Tanna did not explicitly teach about follicles.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna omitted explicit mention of follicles to teach that even two hairs in one follicle suffice.

items.text: Digression: Rava's interpretation of Job's complaint
items.text_en: Digression: Rava's interpretation of Job's complaint
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether two hairs in one follicle is possible, citing a verse from Job and Rava's explanation that Job blasphemed by suggesting a storm wind confused 'Job' with 'enemy', and God answered him with a storm.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether two hairs in one follicle is possible, citing a verse from Job.
Rava explains that Job blasphemed by suggesting a storm wind confused 'Job' with 'enemy', and God answered him with a storm.

items.text: Opening aggadic discussion about hairs
items.text_en: Opening aggadic discussion about hairs
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an aggadic statement from Iyov about the precision of God's creation of hairs and their follicles, and then resolves a contradiction regarding whether the same rule applies to the body and the head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an aggadic statement from Iyov about God's precise creation of hairs and their follicles, and questions whether the same precision applies to the body and the head.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the body and the head.

items.text: Location of the two hairs for puberty
items.text_en: Location of the two hairs for puberty
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the two hairs can be even one on the pubic area and one on the testicles. A baraita supports this with Rabbi Shimon's opinion allowing even one on the eyebrow and one on the belly, while Rav Chisda reports that the Rabbis require both hairs in one place.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the two hairs for puberty can be located even one on the pubic area and one on the testicles.
A baraita supports Shmuel's leniency, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon that the two hairs can be even one on the eyebrow and one on the belly.

sub.text: Rav Chisda reporting the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda reporting the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports that the Rabbis require both hairs to be in one place, rejecting the lenient positions.

items.text: Dispute on the age of mi'un for a minor girl
items.text_en: Dispute on the age of mi'un for a minor girl
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute about until when a minor girl can exercise mi'un: Rabbi Meir says until she brings two hairs, Rabbi Yehuda says until the black (pubic hair) predominates, Rabbi Yosei says until the crown (pubic area) is surrounded, and Ben Shlakok says until she can 'kalkel' (cover the area). Rabbi Shimon reports that when he asked Rabbi Akiva about this, Rabbi Akiva admitted he did not know the meaning of 'kalkel' and ruled like Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the question of until when a minor girl can perform refusal, and presents the first opinion of Rabbi Meir that it is until she grows two pubic hairs.
Rabbi Yehuda states that refusal is permitted until the black pubic hair predominates over the white skin.
Rabbi Yosei rules that refusal is allowed until the pubic area (the crown) is surrounded by hair.
Ben Shlakok says that refusal is permitted until the pubic area is filled with hair (kalkel).
Rabbi Shimon reports that חנינא בן חכינאי (Ḥanina ben Ḥakhinai) instructed him to challenge Rabbi Akiva with the testimony of Ben Shlakok in Yavne, which was not refuted.
Rabbi Akiva responds that he does not know the meaning of 'kalkel' and does not recognize Ben Shlakok, and rules that refusal is until she brings two pubic hairs, like Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Measurement of two hairs for the red heifer and negaim
items.text_en: Measurement of two hairs for the red heifer and negaim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the required length of two hairs for the red heifer and negaim: Rabbi Yishmael says enough to bend their roots to their tips, Rabbi Eliezer says enough to pinch with a fingernail, and Rabbi Akiva says enough to be taken with tweezers. The Gemara rules that the halakha follows all opinions to be stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule for two hairs in the red heifer and negaim, and cites Rabbi Yishmael's opinion that they must be long enough to bend their tips to their roots.
Rabbi Eliezer states his opinion that the hairs must be long enough to pinch with a fingernail.
Rabbi Akiva states his opinion that the hairs must be long enough to be taken with tweezers.
Rav Chisda reports in the name of Mar Ukva that the halakha follows all opinions to be stringent.

items.text: Mishnah: A woman who sees a ketem and zavah concerns
items.text_en: Mishnah: A woman who sees a ketem and zavah concerns
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who sees a ketem (stain) is considered 'mekulkelet' (impaired) and must be concerned for zavah impurity according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say there is no concern for zavah from stains. The Gemara identifies the Sages as Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, who says stains do not cause zavah but sometimes lead to it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens: A woman who sees a stain (כֶּתֶם) is impaired (מְקוּלְקֶלֶת) and must suspect זוב (zavah impurity) — Rabbi Meir's opinion.
The Sages disagree: stains carry no concern of זוב (zavah) impurity.
The Gemara identifies the anonymous 'Sages' as Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, who taught that stains themselves do not cause זוב (zavah) but sometimes lead to it.

items.text: When stains lead to zavah: three garments or two days
items.text_en: When stains lead to zavah: three garments or two days
items.desc_en: The baraita explains that stains lead to zavah when a woman wears three checked garments and finds a stain on each, or if she sees a discharge for two days and finds a stain on one garment. The Gemara questions why the case of two days and one garment is needed, and answers that it teaches that even in such a case she brings a sacrifice and it is eaten.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes two scenarios where stains lead to zavah: a woman wears three checked garments and finds a stain on each, or she sees a discharge for two days and finds a stain on one garment.

The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to mention the case of two days and one garment, since the case of three garments (where the stain is not from her body) already establishes concern, and the two-day case (where the stain could be from her body) should be even more obvious.
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that even in the two-day case, she brings a sacrifice and it is eaten, countering a possible assumption that such a sacrifice would not be eaten.

items.text: Rava's analysis: comparing stains to gris measurements
items.text_en: Rava's analysis: comparing stains to gris measurements
items.desc_en: Rava notes that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus convinced the Rabbis: just as a stain smaller than three gris in one place is not concerning because we attribute it to two days' discharge, so too three gris in one place should be attributed to two and a half from the body and half from food. The Rabbis reject this because there is a distinction of a gris and more per day. The Gemara then questions Rabbi Chanina's consistency regarding three places versus three garments.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus convinced the Rabbis: just as a stain smaller than three gris in one place is not concerning because we attribute it to two days, so too three gris in one place should be attributed to two and a half from the body and half from food blood.
The Rabbis reject Rava's claim, arguing that since it is possible to divide the stain into at least one gris and more per day, we do not attribute it to food blood.

The Gemara questions Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus's consistency: he is not concerned for three gris in one place, but is concerned for three places, yet earlier he said he is concerned for three robes but not three places on one robe.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus was speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning: for himself, three robes yes and three places no, but he asks them to concede that three gris in one place should be attributed to two and a half from the body and half from food blood.
The Rabbis again reject the claim, maintaining that since it is possible to divide the stain into at least one gris and more per day, they do not attribute it to food blood.

items.text: Baraita: threshold for concern with a stain
items.text_en: Baraita: threshold for concern with a stain
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that a woman who sees a stain must be concerned if it is large enough to be divided into three gris (a gris and more), but if not, she is not concerned. Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra quotes Rabbi Yosei that in either case she is concerned.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a woman who sees a stain must be concerned if it is large enough to be divided into three גריסין (split beans), which is a גריס ועוד (a split bean and more), but if not, she is not concerned.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra quoting Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra quoting Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: רבי יהודה בן אגרא (Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra) says in the name of רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) that in both cases — whether the stain is large enough or not — she must be concerned.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra and the Sages concerns a woman who examined herself during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but not during Rabbi Yosei's twilight. The Sages consider Rabbi Yosei's twilight as night, so the examination during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight suffices, while Rabbi Yosei himself considers twilight as uncertain. Rava adds that if her hands were in her eyes throughout twilight, the Sages' position is correct, but if she removed them, she might have seen blood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi states that Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's words apply when she did not examine, and the Sages' words apply when she examined.
The Gemara asks what exactly 'examined' and 'did not examine' mean in this context.
Rava explains that the case involves a woman who examined her body during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but did not examine her garment, and did not examine during Rabbi Yosei's twilight.
The Gemara explains that the Sages consider Rabbi Yosei's twilight as night, so the examination during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight suffices, while Rabbi Yosei himself considers twilight uncertain.
Rava objects that if her hands were in her eyes throughout twilight, the Sages' position is correct, but if she removed them, she might have seen blood.
The Sages respond that they only speak when she kept her hands in her eyes throughout twilight.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi's statement and resolution of contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi's statement and resolution of contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes Rabbi's statement, initially assuming that 'lo badkah' means she did not examine during Rabbi Yosei's twilight, leading to a contradiction about the status of bein hashemashot. It resolves that Rabbi meant: Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's words apply when she did not examine at all, and the Sages only disagree when she examined during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but not Rabbi Yosei's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates Rabbi's statement and asks what 'lo badkah' (did not examine) means.

The Gemara proposes that 'lo badkah' means she examined during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but not Rabbi Yosei's, and objects that this would imply Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra is concerned even when she examined during both twilights, which is absurd since she did examine.
The Gemara concludes that 'lo badkah' must mean she did not examine during either twilight, implying that if she examined during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but not Rabbi Yosei's, she is not concerned.
The Gemara infers that for Rabbi, Rabbi Yosei's twilight is night, and then asks what 'badkah' (examined) means in the second clause of Rabbi's statement.

The Gemara proposes that 'badkah' means she examined during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but not Rabbi Yosei's, and objects that this would imply the Sages are not concerned even when she examined during neither twilight, which is absurd since she did not examine.
The Gemara concludes that 'badkah' must mean she examined during both twilights, implying that if she examined only during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight, the Sages are concerned.
The Gemara infers that for Rabbi, Rabbi Yosei's twilight is a doubt (ספק), creating a contradiction within Rabbi's own statements.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting Rabbi's statement: Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's words apply when she did not examine at all, and the Sages only disagree when she examined during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but not Rabbi Yosei's.

items.text: Second baraita and contradiction within Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra
items.text_en: Second baraita and contradiction within Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra
items.desc_en: A second baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra rules that a woman who sees a stain is concerned only for a heavy flow, but Rabbi says he heard from him that she is concerned in both cases. The Gemara analyzes the meaning of 'badkah' in this context, leading to a contradiction within Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's own views about bein hashemashot. It resolves that there are two tannaitic traditions regarding Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's opinion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra rules in the name of Rabbi Yosei that a woman who sees a stain is concerned only for a heavy flow, not a light one.
Rabbi reports that he heard from Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra that she is concerned in both cases, and his words appear correct when she examined herself.

The Gemara asks what 'badkah' means here, and rejects the possibility that it means she examined during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight but not Rabbi Yosei's, because that would imply Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra holds she is not concerned even without any examination.
The Gemara concludes that 'badkah' means she examined during both twilights, implying that Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra holds she is not concerned if she examined only during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight.
The Gemara notes that this implies Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra considers Rabbi Yosei's twilight as night, contradicting his earlier position that it is a doubt.
The Gemara resolves that the contradiction in the version without Rabbi is not difficult, but the version with Rabbi remains problematic.
The Gemara concludes that there are two tannaitic traditions regarding Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's opinion about the status of bein hashemashot.

items.text: Clarification of twilight according to Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Clarification of twilight according to Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the twilight period according to Rabbi Yosei extends into Rabbi Yehuda's twilight, and this tanna holds that view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei's twilight period extends into Rabbi Yehuda's twilight, and this tanna holds that view.

items.text: Dispute about retroactive impurity of a stain
items.text_en: Dispute about retroactive impurity of a stain
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi holds that a woman who sees a stain imparts retroactive impurity to herself and to sacred items. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues that she does not impart impurity to herself, only to sacred items, lest her stain be more stringent than her actual sighting. The Gemara questions this, and then emends the baraita to say that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds she does not impart impurity even to sacred items.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi's position: a woman who sees a stain (כתם) imparts retroactive impurity to herself and to sacred items.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues that she imparts impurity to sacred items but not to herself, lest her stain be more stringent than her actual sighting.
The Gemara objects: we find that her stain is indeed more stringent than her sighting regarding sacred items, undermining Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning.
The Gemara emends the baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar actually holds that she does not impart impurity even to sacred items, so that her stain is not more stringent than her sighting in any respect.

items.text: Dispute about attributing a stain to a subsequent sighting
items.text_en: Dispute about attributing a stain to a subsequent sighting
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a woman who sees a stain and later sees actual blood. Rabbi says she may attribute the stain to the sighting for a full 24-hour period. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar limits this to the same day. Rabbi comments that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view corrects her status, while his own distorts it. The Gemara questions this, and Ravina suggests reversing the attribution. Rav Nachman rejects the reversal, explaining that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view corrects her halachic status regarding zivah, while Rabbi's distorts it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi's ruling: a woman who sees a stain and later sees blood may attribute the stain to the sighting within a 24-hour period.
רבי שמעון בן אלעזר (Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar) limits attribution to the same day only, and רבי (Rabbi) comments that his own view distorts her status while Rabbi Shimon's corrects it.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's view actually distorts her status, and רבינא (Ravina) proposes reversing the attribution.
רב נחמן (Rav Nachman) rejects the reversal, explaining that Rabbi Shimon's view corrects her halachic status regarding זיבה (zivah), while Rabbi's distorts it.

items.text: Inquiry about stains requiring an interruption of purity
items.text_en: Inquiry about stains requiring an interruption of purity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi whether stains require an interruption of purity (הפסק טהרה). Rabbi Asi is silent. Later, Rabbi Zeira finds Rabbi Asi teaching that a stain is attributed to a sighting for 24 hours, and infers that stains do require an interruption. Rabbi Asi confirms this, explaining that his earlier silence was due to being preoccupied.

sub.desc_en: רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) asks רבי אסי (Rabbi Asi) whether stains require an הפסק טהרה (interruption of purity) or not; Rabbi Asi is silent.
Later, Rabbi Zeira finds Rabbi Asi sitting and teaching that a stain is attributed to a sighting within 24 hours, according to רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi).

sub.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) says the attribution applies only if she examined herself; רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) says it applies even without examination.
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) infers from Rabbi Asi's teaching that stains require an הפסק טהרה (interruption of purity); Rabbi Asi confirms.
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) asks why Rabbi Asi was silent earlier, suggesting it was due to being preoccupied.
רבי אסי (Rabbi Asi) confirms that the halakha came back to him in the course of his studies.

items.text: Mishnah: Sighting on the eleventh day at twilight
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sighting on the eleventh day at twilight
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who sees blood on the eleventh day at twilight is in a state of uncertainty regarding the beginning and end of niddah and zivah. Similarly, days 40 for a male and 80 for a female at twilight are subject to error. Rabbi Yehoshua comments that if you are fixing the fools, come and fix the wise.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the case of a woman who sees blood on the eleventh day at twilight, creating uncertainty about niddah and zivah boundaries.
The Mishnah adds that similar uncertainty applies to days 40 for a male child and 80 for a female child at twilight.
Rabbi Yehoshua comments that if you are fixing the fools, come and fix the wise.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah and Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah and Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing, noting that the eleventh day is the end of zivah, not niddah. Rav Chisda explains that the Mishnah means: seeing on the eleventh day at twilight is the beginning of niddah and end of zivah; on the seventh day of her niddah, it is the end of niddah and beginning of zivah. The Gemara then begins to discuss Rabbi Yehoshua's statement about fixing fools and the wise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing, noting that seeing on the eleventh day should be the beginning of niddah and end of zivah, not end of niddah.

Rav Chisda explains that the Mishnah means: seeing on the eleventh day at twilight is the beginning of niddah and end of zivah; on the seventh day of her niddah, it is the end of niddah and beginning of zivah.

sub.text: Gemara's transition to Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's transition to Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss Rabbi Yehoshua's statement about fixing fools and the wise, quoting the Mishnah's continuation.

items.text: Correction of the Mishnah's terminology
items.text_en: Correction of the Mishnah's terminology
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah should read 'טוֹעוֹת' (mistaken women) rather than 'שׁוֹטוֹת' (foolish women), as the women are mistaken about their cycles, not foolish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara corrects the Mishnah's terminology from 'שׁוֹטוֹת' (foolish women) to 'טוֹעוֹת' (mistaken women), asserting that the women are mistaken about their cycles, not foolish.

items.text: Baraita: one day impure, one day pure
items.text_en: Baraita: one day impure, one day pure
items.desc_en: The baraita states that if a woman has a pattern of one impure day followed by one pure day, she may engage in intercourse on the eighth day and its preceding night, and four nights out of eighteen days. If she saw the flow in the evening, she may only engage on the eighth day itself.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the case of a woman who has a pattern of one impure day and one pure day, stating that she may engage in intercourse on the eighth day and its accompanying night.
The baraita adds that she may engage in intercourse four nights out of eighteen days, but if she saw the flow in the evening, she may only engage on the eighth day alone.
The baraita continues with the case of two impure days and two pure days, stating that she may engage in intercourse on the eighth, twelfth, sixteenth, and twentieth days.

items.text: Question on the second case and answers
items.text_en: Question on the second case and answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita does not allow intercourse on the fourteenth day in the case of two impure and two pure days. Rav Sheshet answers that this proves the 'gargeran' (a type of fig) taught in the Mishnah is forbidden. Rav Ashi answers that while the eleventh day does not require guarding, the tenth day does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita should also permit intercourse on the fourteenth day.
Rav Sheshet answers that this proves the 'גרגרן' (glutton) taught in the Mishnah is forbidden.
Rav Ashi answers that although the eleventh day does not require guarding, the tenth day does require guarding.

items.text: Further cases in the baraita
items.text_en: Further cases in the baraita
items.desc_en: The baraita continues with patterns of three, four, five, six, seven, and eight impure and pure days, specifying how many days the woman may engage in intercourse. For example, with three and three, she may engage for two days and then never again; with seven and seven, she may engage for a quarter of her days, i.e., seven out of twenty-eight.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that with a pattern of three impure and three pure days, the woman may engage in intercourse for only two days and then never again.
The baraita states that with a pattern of four impure and four pure days, she may engage for only one day and then never again.
The baraita states that with five and five, she may engage for three days; with six and six, she may engage for five days, and then never again.
The baraita states that with seven impure and seven pure days, she may engage for a quarter of her days, i.e., seven out of twenty-eight.
The baraita states that with eight impure and eight pure days, she may engage for fifteen days out of forty-eight.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the last case
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the last case
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the calculation for eight impure and eight pure days yields fourteen days of intercourse, not fifteen. Rav Adda bar Yitzchak answers that this proves that days of her menstrual period during which she does not see blood count toward the counting of her זיבה, which was a matter of dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the calculation for eight impure and eight pure days yields only fourteen days of permitted intercourse, not the stated fifteen.

Rav Adda bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by stating that this proves that days of her menstrual period during which she does not see blood count toward the counting of her זיבה (abnormal discharge), which was a matter of dispute.

items.text: Days of childbirth counting toward zavah count
items.text_en: Days of childbirth counting toward zavah count
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana brings a baraita about a woman who saw two days of bleeding and miscarried on the third, uncertain if it was a zavah or a birth. The baraita states that her days of childbirth without bleeding count toward her zavah count. Rav Pappa distinguishes this case because she might be a mother of a male, and the extra seven days count. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua challenges this, arguing that the same uncertainty applies to a mother of a female, and concludes that the days indeed count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether days of childbirth during which a woman does not see bleeding count toward her zavah (זבה) counting.

Rav Kahana brings a baraita about a woman who saw two days of bleeding and miscarried on the third, uncertain whether it was a zavah or a birth, and the baraita rules that her days of childbirth without bleeding count toward her zavah count.
Rav Pappa distinguishes the baraita's case because the woman might be a mother of a male, and the extra seven days of purity count toward her zavah count.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua challenges Rav Pappa, arguing that the same uncertainty applies to a mother of a female, and concludes that the days indeed count.

items.text: Calculation of days for a fixed pattern
items.text_en: Calculation of days for a fixed pattern
items.desc_en: A brief halakhic statement: if a woman has nine days of impurity and nine days of purity, she may engage in intercourse for eight days out of eighteen. For ten days of impurity and ten of purity, her days of intercourse equal her days of impurity, and similarly for any larger numbers.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states the halakhic calculation: for nine days of impurity and nine of purity, she may engage in intercourse eight days out of eighteen; for ten and ten, her days of intercourse equal her days of impurity, and similarly for any larger numbers.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
