Rava objects that Rabbi Meir's view is actually lenient, not stringent, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits attributing a stain to a gentile woman.
Rava reconciles the baraitot: the first baraita means she actually sees, while Rabbi Meir says even if she is only fit to see.

items.text: Baraita on attributing to a shomeret yom and a soferet shiv'a
items.text_en: Baraita on attributing to a shomeret yom and a soferet shiv'a
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches: a woman can attribute a stain to a shomeret yom keneged yom on her second day, and to a soferet shiv'a who has not immersed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: therefore, she (the shomeret) is fit and her friend is unfit; Rabbi says: she cannot attribute, therefore both are unfit. They agree she can attribute to a shomeret yom on her first day, to a yoshevet al dam tohar, and to a betulah whose blood is pure. The Gemara explains the need for the word 'therefore' in each opinion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a woman can attribute a stain to a shomeret yom keneged yom on her second day.

sub.text: Baraita continuation — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that she can also attribute to a soferet shiv'a who has not immersed, therefore the shomeret is fit and her friend is unfit.
Rabbi disagrees, ruling that she cannot attribute to a soferet shiv'a, therefore both women are unfit.
Both agree she can attribute to a shomeret yom on her first day, to a yoshevet al dam tohar, and to a betulah whose blood is pure.
The Gemara asks why Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement includes the word 'therefore' (לפיכך).
The Gemara answers that it is needed to counter Rabbi's position.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi's statement includes the word 'therefore' (לפיכך).
The Gemara answers that without 'therefore' one might think only the woman with the stain is unfit, but the other remains fit; the word teaches that both are unfit.

items.text: Rav Chisda's analogy and Rav Adda's objection
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's analogy and Rav Adda's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: a case of a tamei and a tahor who walked on two paths, one tahor and one tamei, is analogous to the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rav Adda objects: there, Rabbi's reasoning is that both are equally suspect; here, what difference does it make? Rav Chisda responds: ultimately, she requires immersion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asserts that the case of a tamei and a tahor walking on two paths, one tahor and one tamei, falls into the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rav Adda objects: there, Rabbi's reasoning is that both women are equally suspect; here, what practical difference does it make?
Rav Chisda responds: ultimately, she requires immersion anyway, so the dispute is relevant.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states: in a case of a tamei and a tahor, or even a tahor and a talui, who walked on two paths, one tamei and one tahor, everyone agrees that the tamei attributes to the talui and the tahor to the tahor.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that even in a case of a טמא (impure) and תלוי (doubtfully impure) person walking on two paths, one may attribute the impure to the doubtful and the pure to the pure, according to all opinions.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry about attributing a stain to another stain
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry about attributing a stain to another stain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi: may one attribute a stain to another stain? He clarifies that according to Rabbi, it is certainly not permitted; the question is according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi answers: yes, one may attribute, because there is no reason not to. The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to contradict this, and resolves it by attributing the two parts to different opinions or different days. Rav Ashi offers an alternative resolution.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi whether one may attribute a stain to another stain, clarifying that the question is only according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, not Rabbi.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi answers that one may attribute, giving the reason 'because there is no reason not to attribute'.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says one may not attribute a stain to another stain, yet allows attribution to a non-Jew or a woman sitting on a stain.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first clause to Rabbi and the second to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
An alternative explanation holds that both clauses follow Rabbi, distinguishing between the first and second day of the woman's counting.
Rav Ashi resolves that both clauses follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and there is no contradiction.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about lending a garment to a gentile
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about lending a garment to a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction between two statements about a woman who lends her garment to a gentile woman. Ravina explains that the first statement refers to the past (למפרע) and the second to the future (להבא), and clarifies that the borrower is a woman sitting on pure blood (יושבת על דם טוהר), not a woman with a stain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between past (למפרע) and future (להבא) contexts.
The Gemara objects that the contradiction still stands.
Ravina explains that the first statement refers to a woman who lent her garment to a gentile woman, and a בעלת כתם (woman with a stain) may attribute the stain to her.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'or to a woman sitting on the stain', not a gentile.
Ravina clarifies that the borrower is a woman sitting on pure blood (יושבת על דם טוהר), not a woman with a stain.

items.text: Rabbi Nehemya's reasoning and its extension
items.text_en: Rabbi Nehemya's reasoning and its extension
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Nehemya's reasoning for his lenient ruling, based on the verse "ונקתה לארץ תשב" — once she sits on the ground, she is clean. Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Nehemya would even purify a stain found on the outside of an earthenware vessel, and the Gemara clarifies that this is not obvious, as one might have thought we should decree against the outside due to the inside.

sub.desc_en: Rav Matna asks for Rabbi Nehemya's reasoning, and the Gemara explains it from the verse 'ונקתה לארץ תשב' — once she sits on the ground, she is clean.
Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Nehemya would even purify a stain found on the outside of an earthenware vessel.
The Gemara objects that this ruling is obvious, since the outside of a vessel is not a place of impurity.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling is not obvious, as one might have thought we should decree against the outside due to the inside, so the teaching informs us that no such decree applies.

items.text: Abaye's additional leniency for rags
items.text_en: Abaye's additional leniency for rags
items.desc_en: Abaye adds that Rabbi Nehemya would also purify stains found on rags (מטלניות) that are less than three by three handbreadths, as they are not fit for either the poor or the rich.

sub.desc_en: Abaye adds that Rabbi Nehemya would also purify stains on rags (מטלניות) smaller than three by three handbreadths, as they are unfit for both poor and rich.

items.text: Dispute over the halakha like Rabbi Nehemya
items.text_en: Dispute over the halakha like Rabbi Nehemya
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana taught that the halakha follows Rabbi Nehemya, but Rav Nachman objects, citing a case that came before the Sages where they declared the women impure. The Gemara then brings the baraita describing that case: two women grinding with a hand-mill, and a case of blood found on the rim of a bathtub or on an olive leaf, where the Sages ruled them impure.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana teaches in the name of Rav that the halakha (binding law) follows Rabbi Nehemya's lenient position.
Rav Nachman objects to Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana's ruling, noting that a case brought before the Sages led them to declare the women impure, contradicting the halakha like Rabbi Nehemya.

The Gemara explains the case: two women grinding with a hand-mill, with blood found in various positions relative to them, and a case of blood on a bathtub rim or olive leaf, brought before the Sages who ruled the women impure — supporting Rav Nachman's objection.

items.text: Resolving the dispute: Tannaitic disagreement
items.text_en: Resolving the dispute: Tannaitic disagreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that there is a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yaakov declares impure, Rabbi Nehemya declares pure, and the Sages ruled like Rabbi Nehemya. Thus, the earlier case that Rav Nachman cited must follow Rabbi Yaakov's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by declaring it a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yaakov declares impure, Rabbi Nehemya declares pure, and the Sages ruled like Rabbi Nehemya.

items.text: Mishnah: Three women sleeping in one bed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three women sleeping in one bed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of three women sleeping in one bed who find blood under one of them: all are impure. If one checked and was found impure, she alone is impure. They may attribute the stain to each other, and if none are fit to see blood, we consider them as if they were fit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of three women sleeping in one bed who find blood under one of them: all are impure, but if one checked and was found impure, she alone is impure; they may attribute the stain to each other, and if none are fit to see blood, we consider them as if they were fit.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about the status of her pure items
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about the status of her pure items
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says the Mishnah's case is when she checked herself at the time of her fixed period (שיעור וסת). He holds like Bar Pada, who distinguishes based on whether her husband brings a sin-offering, a suspensive guilt-offering, or is exempt. Rabbi Oshaya disagrees, saying even if her husband brings a sin-offering, her pure items are in suspense. The Gemara questions Rabbi Oshaya's logic and provides parables from Rabbi Yirmeya and Abaye to explain why blood might be delayed.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav limits the Mishnah's leniency to a case where the woman checked herself at the time of her fixed period (שיעור וסת).

The Gemara explains that Rav holds like Bar Pada, who distinguishes three levels: if her husband brings a sin-offering (חטאת) her pure items are definitely impure; if a suspensive guilt-offering (אשם תלוי) they are in suspense; if he is exempt, they are pure.
Rabbi Oshaya objects, ruling that even if her husband brings a sin-offering, her pure items are only in suspense, not definitely impure.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Oshaya's logic: in the case of a woman who checked at her fixed period, if blood actually existed, what could have delayed it from appearing?

Rabbi Yirmeya and Abaye provide parables — a child walking with an elder and a finger in the eye — to explain that blood can be delayed by internal factors, supporting Rabbi Oshaya's position that even when a sin-offering is brought, the pure items remain in suspense.

items.text: Baraitha: How women attribute stains to each other
items.text_en: Baraitha: How women attribute stains to each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraitha explaining how women attribute stains to each other: a pregnant woman attributes to a non-pregnant one, a nursing woman to a non-nursing one, an old woman to a young one, and a virgin to a non-virgin. If both are in the same category, this is the case where we consider them as if they were fit to see blood.

sub.desc_en: The baraitha opens by explaining how women attribute stains to each other, beginning with the case of a pregnant woman attributing to a non-pregnant one.
The baraitha lists additional cases: a nursing woman attributes to a non-nursing one, an old woman to a young one, and a virgin to a non-virgin.
The baraitha concludes that when both women are in the same category (e.g., both pregnant), we consider them as if they were fit to see blood, meaning they cannot attribute to each other.

items.text: Opening phrase linking to previous daf
items.text_en: Opening phrase linking to previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues from the previous daf, stating that the blood found is considered as if it were fit to cause impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the blood found is considered as if it were fit to cause impurity, linking to the previous daf.

items.text: Mishnah: Three women in one bed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three women in one bed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of three women sleeping in one bed, with blood found under one of them. It details the impurity rulings based on where the blood is found and whether they passed through the foot of the bed or over it. It also discusses cases where some or all of them checked and found themselves pure, and concludes with a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about the status of items with presumed impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of three women sleeping in one bed, detailing impurity rulings based on where blood is found relative to the wall.
The Mishnah clarifies that the previous distinctions apply only when the women entered via the foot of the bed; if they passed over the bed, all are impure.
The Mishnah presents the rules when one, two, or all three women examine themselves and are found pure.
The Mishnah compares the case of the women to a ritually impure pile of stones mixed with two pure piles, with analogous examination rules.
Rabbi Meir states that if all three piles are examined and found pure, they remain impure due to the presumption of impurity.
The Sages argue that one continues searching until reaching bedrock or virgin soil, implying the impurity may have been removed by an animal.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not differentiate in the first case (blood under the middle woman) but does differentiate in the latter cases (blood under the inner or outer woman). Rabbi Ami answers that the women are arranged in a line (interlocked).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first clause of the Mishnah does not differentiate based on location while the latter clause does.
Rabbi Ami answers that the first case refers to women lying intertwined, making location-based distinction impossible.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about the analogy
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about the analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah includes the analogy of the pure and impure piles. Rabbi Meir challenges the Sages why they disagree in the case of the piles but not in the case of blood. The Sages respond that in the pile case, a raven might have taken the impurity, but in the blood case, the source of the blood is unknown.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah includes the analogy 'to what is this similar?'.

sub.text: Rabbi Meir's challenge to the Sages
sub.text_en: Rabbi Meir's challenge to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir challenges the Sages: why do you disagree in the pile case but not in the blood case?
The Sages respond: in the pile case, a raven might have taken the impurity, but in the blood case, the source of the blood is unknown.

items.text: Three stories about checking for impurity
items.text_en: Three stories about checking for impurity
items.desc_en: Three baraitot are brought: Rabbi Meir tells a story about a sycamore tree in Kfar Saba where a skull was found after the wind uprooted it; Rabbi Yose tells a story about a cave where bones were found after workers dug; Abba Shaul tells a story about a rock in Beit Horon where a pit of bones was found using sheets. In each case, the Sages respond that the initial check was insufficient.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir tells a story about a sycamore tree in Kfar Saba that was presumed impure, was checked and found clean, but later a skull was found embedded in its roots after the wind uprooted it.
The Sages object that the story is no proof, because the initial check may not have been thorough enough.
Rabbi Yose tells a story about a cave in Shichin that was presumed impure, checked down to smooth bedrock and found clean, but later workers digging with axes found a mortar full of bones.
The Sages again object that the story is no proof, because the initial check may not have been thorough enough.

Abba Shaul tells a story about a rock in Beit Horon that was presumed impure but too large to check; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya devised a method using wet sheets to detect the impurity, and they found a large pit full of bones.

items.text: Identification of the pit and Rava's principle
items.text_en: Identification of the pit and Rava's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the pit as the one filled by Yishmael ben Netanya with corpses, and explains that Gedaliah is considered responsible because he did not heed advice. Rava states that a bad rumor, even if not to be accepted, must be heeded.

sub.desc_en: A baraita identifies the pit as the one filled by Yishmael ben Netanya with corpses, citing the verse that attributes the killing to Gedaliah.
The Gemara questions how the verse attributes the killing to Gedaliah when Yishmael actually killed them.
The Gemara explains that because Gedaliah should have heeded the advice of Yochanan ben Kareach but did not, Scripture considers him as if he killed them.
Rava states that a bad rumor (לישנא בישא), even though one need not accept it, one must be concerned about it.

items.text: Story of the Galileans and Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Story of the Galileans and Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: A story is told of Galileans who were rumored to have killed someone and came to Rabbi Tarfon for advice on hiding. He applied Rava's principle, telling them to hide themselves.

sub.text: Story of Galileans and Rabbi Tarfon
sub.text_en: Story of Galileans and Rabbi Tarfon
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates Rava's principle: Galileans suspected of murder ask Rabbi Tarfon to hide them, and he applies the rule that a bad rumor must be taken seriously, advising them to hide themselves.
The Galileans ask Rabbi Tarfon whether they should hide themselves.
Rabbi Tarfon reasons that since the rumor is a bad report (לישנא בישא) that must be heeded, he advises them to hide themselves.

items.text: Discussion about Moses' fear of Og
items.text_en: Discussion about Moses' fear of Og
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Moses feared Og but not Sihon, since they were brothers. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that Moses feared Og's merit from Abraham, as Og had informed Abraham about Lot's capture.

sub.desc_en: Gemara asks: 'And the Lord said to Moses: Do not fear' — since Sihon and Og were brothers, as Master said: Sihon and Og were sons of Achiyah bar Shamchazai; why did Moses fear Og but not Sihon?

items.text: Beginning of a baraita about a garment with a stain
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita about a garment with a stain
items.desc_en: A baraita begins discussing a garment that has a lost stain, stating that one passes seven detergents over it to nullify it. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar offers a different opinion, but the text cuts off.

sub.text: Baraita of the garment with a stain
sub.text_en: Baraita of the garment with a stain
sub.desc_en: A baraita states that a garment with a lost stain is treated with seven chemicals to remove it.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar begins his statement, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Checking for lost kilayim
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Checking for lost kilayim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a garment has lost a kilayim thread, one checks it by examining neighboring threads. If semen is lost, a new garment is checked with a needle, a worn one with sunlight. A baraita adds that a 'neighbor' is at least three fingerbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for checking a garment that lost a kilayim thread or semen stain.
A baraita defines the minimum size of a 'neighbor' thread as three fingerbreadths.

items.text: Garment with lost kilayim: selling to a gentile and burial shrouds
items.text_en: Garment with lost kilayim: selling to a gentile and burial shrouds
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a garment with lost kilayim cannot be sold to a gentile or used as a donkey saddle, but can be made into a burial shroud for a corpse. Rav Yosef deduces that this implies mitzvot will be nullified in the future. Abaye objects citing Rabbi Mani's statement that this leniency applies only for eulogizing, not for burial, but Rabbi Yochanan permits even for burial, consistent with his view that the dead are free from mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a garment with lost kilayim cannot be sold to a gentile or used as a donkey saddle, but may be made into a burial shroud for a corpse.
Rav Yosef deduces from the baraita that mitzvot will be nullified in the future (since the dead are exempt).
Abaye objects, citing Rabbi Mani quoting Rabbi Yannai that the leniency applies only for eulogizing, not for burial.
Abaye (or the gemara) rejects the objection, noting that Rabbi Yochanan permits even for burial.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan follows his own view, interpreting the verse 'among the dead I am free' to mean that once a person dies, he becomes free from mitzvot.

items.text: Dyeing a garment with lost kilayim to permit it
items.text_en: Dyeing a garment with lost kilayim to permit it
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that a garment with lost kilayim can be dyed and becomes permitted. Rava questions the source of this ruling. Rafram bar Papa answers that it is derived from a Mishnah about checking until one reaches a rock, assuming a crow took it; similarly, wool and linen do not take the same dye, so if the kilayim is not discernible, it is considered removed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a garment with lost kilayim (shatnez) can be dyed and becomes permitted.
Rava asks Rafram bar Papa: from where does the elder (Rav Chisda) derive this ruling?

Rafram bar Papa answers that it is derived from a Mishnah: just as one checks until reaching a rock and assumes a crow took the lost item, so too wool and linen do not take the same dye, so if the kilayim is not discernible, it is considered removed.

items.text: Uncertainty about pulling out a linen thread from a wool garment
items.text_en: Uncertainty about pulling out a linen thread from a wool garment
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that if one pulled a linen thread from a wool garment and is unsure if it was completely removed, the garment is permitted. The reason is that the Torah requires the mixture to be 'shu'a, tavui, ve'nuz' (combed, spun, and woven), and the rabbinic decree only applies when the mixture is certain. Rav Ashi objects that perhaps any one of these conditions suffices, but the halakha follows Mar Zutra because the Torah mentions them in one phrase.

sub.text: Mar Zutra's ruling (via Rav Acha bar Rav Yeiva)
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling (via Rav Acha bar Rav Yeiva)
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that if one pulled a linen thread from a wool garment and is unsure if it was completely removed, the garment is permitted.

The gemara explains that the Torah requires the mixture to be שׁוּעַ טָוּי וְנוּז (combed, spun, and woven), and the rabbinic decree only applies when the mixture is certain, so uncertainty permits the garment.
Rav Ashi objects that perhaps any one of these conditions (combed, spun, or woven) suffices to create the biblical prohibition.
The gemara rules that the halakha follows Mar Zutra because the Torah mentions all three conditions in one phrase, indicating they are all required together.

items.text: Colored garments and bloodstains
items.text_en: Colored garments and bloodstains
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a dyed garment is susceptible to impurity from a bloodstain, but Rabbi Natan bar Yosef says it is not, because colored garments were permitted to women only to be lenient regarding their stains. The Gemara questions the term 'permitted', implying they were initially forbidden, and explains that during the war of Aspasyanus, decrees were made against crowns and irus, and they sought to forbid colored garments but allowed them for leniency regarding stains.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a dyed garment is susceptible to impurity from a bloodstain, but Rabbi Natan bar Yosef argues it is not, because colored garments were permitted to women only to be lenient regarding their stains.
The Gemara questions the term 'תִּקְּנוּ' (they instituted), suggesting it implies a prior prohibition, and asks how colored garments could have been forbidden.
The Gemara explains that during the war of Aspasyanus, decrees were made against crowns and irus, and they sought to forbid colored garments but allowed them for leniency regarding stains.

items.text: Mishnah: Seven substances for removing a bloodstain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Seven substances for removing a bloodstain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists seven substances used to remove a bloodstain: tasteless saliva, ground bean water, urine, natron, and borit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing seven substances used to remove a bloodstain from a garment.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The seven cleansing agents and their application
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The seven cleansing agents and their application
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the seven agents (קִמוֹנְיָא, אַשְׁלָג, etc.) and states that if after applying them the stain does not disappear, it is a dye and purities are pure; if it disappears or fades, it is a ketem and purities are impure. It also defines 'tasteless saliva' and notes that the agents must be applied in order, each rubbed three times.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the seven cleansing agents and states that if after applying them the stain does not disappear, it is a dye and purities are pure.
The Mishnah states that if the stain disappears or fades, it is a ketem and purities are impure and require immersion.
The Mishnah defines tasteless saliva and the preparation of מי גריסין and מי רגלים.
The Mishnah rules that each agent must be rubbed three times in order; if done out of order or all at once, it is ineffective.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the identity of the agents
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the identity of the agents
items.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that 'neter' is Alexandrian neter, not Antipatrian. Rav Yehuda identifies 'borit' as ahlah, but a baraisa lists both borit and ahlah separately, leading to a resolution that borit is kabrita (a type of alkali). A contradiction arises regarding shevi'it laws, resolved by identifying borit as ahlah, with two varieties. Kimonya is identified as 'shlof dotz', and ashleg is identified by Shmuel as a substance found between pearls, extracted with an iron needle.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna specifies that the 'neter' used is Alexandrian neter, not Antipatrian neter.
Rav Yehuda identifies 'borit' as ahlah (a type of alkali).
The Gemara objects that a baraisa lists both 'borit' and 'ahlah' separately, implying they are distinct.
The Gemara resolves that 'borit' here refers to kabrita (a different type of alkali), not ahlah.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraisa listing both 'borit' and 'ahlah' in the context of shevi'it (sabbatical year) laws.
The Gemara objects that if 'borit' is kabrita (a mineral), it should not be subject to shevi'it laws, yet the baraisa includes it.
The Gemara resolves that 'borit' in the shevi'it context is actually ahlah.
The Gemara objects again that the baraisa lists both 'borit' and 'ahlah' separately.
The Gemara resolves that there are two varieties of ahlah, one called 'borit' and one called 'ahlah'.
Rav Yehuda identifies 'kimonya' as 'shlof dotz' (a type of plant or mineral).
Shmuel identifies 'ashleg' by consulting sailors, who say it is a substance found between pearls and extracted with an iron needle.

items.text: Baraisa: The case of tzapon and the order of agents
items.text_en: Baraisa: The case of tzapon and the order of agents
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that if the seven agents did not remove the stain but tzapon (soap) did, the purities are impure. The Gemara objects that tzapon also removes dye, so it clarifies: if six agents failed and then tzapon removed it, purities are impure, because if tzapon had been applied first it might have removed the stain, indicating it was a ketem.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that if the seven agents did not remove the stain but tzapon (soap) did, the purities are impure.
The Gemara objects that tzapon also removes dye, so the baraisa's ruling cannot distinguish stain from dye.

The Gemara resolves that the baraisa means if six agents failed and then tzapon removed it, the purities are impure, because if tzapon had been applied first it might have removed the stain, indicating it was a ketem.

items.text: Another baraisa and Rabbi Zeira's distinction
items.text_en: Another baraisa and Rabbi Zeira's distinction
items.desc_en: Another baraisa states that if the seven agents did not remove the stain but repeating them did, the purities are pure. Rabbi Zeira limits this: only purities prepared between the first and second washings are pure, but those after the second washing are impure, because the person was particular about the stain and it eventually came off.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if the seven agents did not remove the stain but repeating them did, the purities are pure.

Rabbi Zeira limits the baraita: only purities prepared between the first and second washings are pure, but those after the second washing are impure, because the person was particular about the stain and it eventually came off.

items.text: Question about intent and proof from Rabbi Chiya
items.text_en: Question about intent and proof from Rabbi Chiya
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Ashi whether the removal of a blood stain depends on intent (קפידא). Rav Ashi answers yes, citing a baraita where Rabbi Chiya says that definite menstrual blood can be removed with seven markers, implying intent matters.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Ashi whether the removal of a blood stain depends on intent (קפידא).
Rav Ashi answers yes, citing a baraita where Rabbi Chiya says that definite menstrual blood can be removed with seven markers, implying intent matters.
The gemara infers from the baraita that since the blood is definite menstrual blood yet can be removed, the matter depends on intent (קפידא).

items.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan about absorbed liquids
items.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan about absorbed liquids
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about earthenware vessels that absorbed liquids from a zav and were placed in an oven. Reish Lakish distinguishes between light and heavy liquids, while Rabbi Yochanan holds that only if the oven was heated does the liquid become significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about earthenware vessels that absorbed liquids from a zav and were placed in an oven; if the oven was heated, the oven becomes impure because the liquid will eventually emerge.
Reish Lakish distinguishes between light liquids, which require the oven to be heated, and heavy liquids, which render the oven impure even without heating.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that for both light and heavy liquids, the oven is impure only if it was heated, otherwise not.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and discussion about stains
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and discussion about stains
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish with a baraita about a garment that was immersed and treated with markers, yet the stain remained—it is considered dye and pure. Reish Lakish deflects, saying stains are rabbinic. The Gemara questions this with Rabbi Chiya's baraita, and Rav Ashi notes that Rabbi Chiya's ruling may not be authoritative.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish with a baraita about a garment that was immersed and treated with seven markers yet the stain remained, which is considered dye and the garment is pure.
Reish Lakish deflects by saying that stains are only rabbinic, not biblical, so the baraita does not apply to biblical blood.
The Gemara questions Reish Lakish by citing Rabbi Chiya's baraita that definite menstrual blood can be removed with seven markers, implying it is biblical.
Rav Ashi resolves that Rabbi Chiya's baraita is not authoritative because Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not teach it, so Rabbi Chiya's source is unknown.

items.text: Discussion about absorbed blood and Rav Kahana's distinction
items.text_en: Discussion about absorbed blood and Rav Kahana's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects again with a case of a quarter-log of blood absorbed in a house or garment. Rav Kahana explains that the leniency regarding a quarter-log is because the blood of a corpse (דם תבוסה) is rabbinic.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish by citing a baraita about a quarter-log of blood absorbed in a house or garment, where the ruling depends on whether the blood can be removed.
Rav Kahana answers that the leniency regarding a quarter-log of blood is because the blood of a corpse (דם תבוסה) is only rabbinic in nature.

items.text: Reish Lakish's objection and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan with a principle: any absorbed substance that cannot come out is pure, but if it can come out it is impure even if it hasn't come out. Rav Pappa resolves the dispute by distinguishing cases based on whether the substance can come out and whether the owner cares about it.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan with a principle: any absorbed substance that cannot come out is pure, but if it can come out it is impure even if it hasn't come out.

Rav Pappa resolves the dispute by distinguishing cases based on whether the substance can come out and whether the owner cares about it, explaining the disagreement is specifically about a case where it can come out but the owner does not care.

items.text: Opening statement on the condition of the husband's insistence
items.text_en: Opening statement on the condition of the husband's insistence
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a general principle: if the husband was particular about the saliva, it is considered significant; otherwise, it is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general principle: if the husband was particular about the saliva, it is considered significant; otherwise, it is not.

items.text: Definition of tasteless saliva and Rav Pappa's error
items.text_en: Definition of tasteless saliva and Rav Pappa's error
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines tasteless saliva as that of one who has not tasted anything since the previous evening. Rav Pappa thought it meant from the night before, but Rava corrects him: it means from the previous day, excluding one who ate earlier.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes 'tasteless saliva' and cites a baraita defining it as saliva from one who has not tasted anything since the previous evening.
Rav Pappa thought to rule before Rava that the baraita means one who ate nothing at night.
Rava rejects Rav Pappa's interpretation, noting the baraita says 'from the evening' (מבערב), not 'in the evening', to exclude one who ate earlier.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's definition and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's definition and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines tasteless saliva as that which has passed midnight and is accompanied by sleep. The Gemara challenges this, citing a baraita that one who slept all day does not have tasteless saliva, while one who was awake all night does. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a drowsy state.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan defining tasteless saliva as that which has passed midnight and is accompanied by sleep.
The Gemara objects that sleep cannot be the sole criterion, citing a baraita: one who slept all day does not have tasteless saliva, while one awake all night does.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a dozing state (מתנמנם), not full sleep.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a drowsy state (מתנמנם), not full sleep or full wakefulness.

items.text: Definition of a drowsy state
items.text_en: Definition of a drowsy state
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi defines a drowsy state as one who is neither fully asleep nor fully awake: if called, he responds but cannot recall a complex argument, yet if reminded, he remembers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a precise definition of the dozing state (מתנמנם).
Rav Ashi defines dozing as a state where one is neither fully asleep nor fully awake: responds when called but cannot reason, and remembers when reminded.

items.text: The effect of early morning study on saliva
items.text_en: The effect of early morning study on saliva
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who arose early and reviewed his lesson does not have tasteless saliva. Rav Yehuda bar Sheila in the name of Rav Ashi in the name of Rabbi Elazar defines the limit as when most of the speech of three hours has emerged.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who arose early and reviewed his lesson does not have tasteless saliva.
The Gemara asks for the time limit within which this applies.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Sheila quoting Rav Ashi quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Sheila quoting Rav Ashi quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Sheila quotes Rav Ashi quoting Rabbi Elazar that the limit is within the first three hours of the day, when most of one's speech has emerged.

items.text: Discussion on bean gruel water and Reish Lakish's view
items.text_en: Discussion on bean gruel water and Reish Lakish's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the mishnah's ruling on bean gruel water supports Reish Lakish, who said that tasteless saliva must be present with each and every one. It deflects, suggesting that the mouth's vapor is beneficial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the Mishnah's rule about 'grinding water' (מי גריסין) being the chewed pulp of beans, and asks whether this supports Resh Lakish's position.
The Gemara considers whether this supports Resh Lakish, who said that tasteless saliva must be present with each and every one of the three immersions.
The Gemara rejects the support, suggesting that perhaps the mouth's vapor (הבלא דפומא) is beneficial and suffices.

items.text: The mishnah is not like Rabbi Yehuda, and the meaning of 'over'
items.text_en: The mishnah is not like Rabbi Yehuda, and the meaning of 'over'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, who requires boiling bean gruel water and adding salt. It then asks how we know that 'over' means to precede, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse, while Abaye offers alternative proofs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, who requires boiling bean gruel water and adding salt.
The Gemara asks how we know that the word 'עוֹבֵר' (over) means to precede.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse (II Samuel 18:23) where 'וַיַּעֲבוֹר' means to pass ahead, proving the meaning.
Abaye offers alternative proofs from verses (Genesis 33:3 and Micah 2:13) where 'עָבַר' and 'וַיַּעֲבוֹר' indicate going before.

items.text: Definition of fermented urine
items.text_en: Definition of fermented urine
items.desc_en: A baraita defines the fermentation of urine as three days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about 'urine that has soured' (מי רגלים שהחמיצו) and cites a baraita defining its souring period.
A baraita answers that its souring period is three days.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on measurements for stains and the need to sift
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on measurements for stains and the need to sift
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all measurements of the Sages regarding stains require consideration of the person's age, gender, clothing, and season. Additionally, one must sift three times. Rabbi Yirmeya questions whether bringing and taking back counts as one or two siftings, and the matter is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all measurements of the Sages regarding stains require consideration of the person's age, gender, clothing, and season.
Rabbi Yirmeya questions whether bringing and taking back the garment counts as one sifting or two.
The question is left unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute about the order of sifting and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Dispute about the order of sifting and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Two baraitot conflict: one says the second sifting counts but not the first, the other says the first counts but not the second. Abaye resolves that both agree the second sifting counts, and the dispute is about terminology: 'first' refers to the first in order, and 'second' refers to the second in the act of passing.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita rules that if one passed the second sifting before the first, only the second counts, not the first.
The second baraita contradicts the first, ruling that the first sifting counts but not the second.

Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that both baraitot agree the second sifting counts, but they differ in terminology: 'first' refers to the first in order of sifting, and 'second' refers to the second in the act of passing.

items.text: Mishnah: A woman with a fixed cycle is sufficient with her time
items.text_en: Mishnah: A woman with a fixed cycle is sufficient with her time
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists the signs of a fixed menstrual cycle (וסת): yawning, sneezing, pain in the stomach or lower abdomen, discharge, and chills. If these occur three times, it establishes a cycle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any woman with a fixed period (וסת) is only required to observe her time, listing the signs of a period: yawning, sneezing, abdominal pain, discharge, chills, and similar symptoms; three occurrences establish a fixed period.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between time-based and body-based cycles
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between time-based and body-based cycles
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah is necessary, as it was already taught elsewhere. It answers that the earlier mishnah dealt with time-based cycles, while this one deals with body-based cycles. It then questions the term 'flowing' (שופעת), and Ulla bar Rav Illai begins to address it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah is necessary, as it was already taught elsewhere.
The Gemara answers that the earlier mishnah dealt with time-based cycles (וסתות דיומי), while this one deals with body-based cycles (וסתות דגופא).
The Gemara questions the term 'שופעת' (flowing), noting that it implies a continuous flow, which seems redundant.
Ulla bar Rav Illai begins to address the question, but the text cuts off at the end of the section.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question on additional signs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question on additional signs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists signs of impurity, including a flow of impure blood amidst pure blood and a sensation like shivering. The Gemara asks what the phrase 'and similarly, those like them' comes to include. Rabba bar Ulla answers: a woman whose head and limbs feel heavy, who trembles and is nauseous.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists signs of impurity: a flow of impure blood amidst pure blood and a sensation like shivering.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'and similarly, those like them' comes to include.
Rabba bar Ulla answers that the phrase includes a woman whose head and limbs feel heavy, who trembles and is nauseous.

items.text: Shmuel's statement and Abaye's alternative inclusion
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement and Abaye's alternative inclusion
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that for days, two occurrences establish a pattern; for vestot (fixed intervals), one; for what the Sages did not enumerate, three. The Gemara asks what the latter includes. Rav Yosef says it includes the same signs as before. Abaye objects that this is already taught, and instead suggests it includes cases where she ate garlic, onions, or pepper and saw blood.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chiyya citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Shmuel states the rule: for days, two occurrences establish a pattern; for vestot (fixed intervals), one; for what the Sages did not enumerate, three.
The Gemara asks what the third category ('what the Sages did not enumerate') includes.
Rav Yosef answers that it includes the same signs already listed in the Mishnah: headache, heavy limbs, shivering, and nausea.
Abaye objects that Rav Yosef's answer adds nothing new, since Rabbah bar Ulla already explained the Mishnah's phrase 'and similar to them' to include these very signs.
Abaye instead suggests that the category includes cases where she ate garlic, onions, or pepper and then saw blood.

items.text: Rav Yosef's recollection and the dispute on establishing a veset
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's recollection and the dispute on establishing a veset
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says he did not hear this tradition. Abaye reminds him that he taught them a baraita about a woman who changed her pattern from day 15 to day 20, and the ruling that both days are forbidden until three occurrences establish the new pattern. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that this is the view of Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, but the Sages say she need not repeat or triple. Abaye clarifies that 'repeat' refers to vestot and 'triple' to days. The Gemara notes that Shmuel teaches that Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi holds like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that he has not heard this tradition (the teaching about establishing a veset).

Abaye reminds Rav Yosef that he himself taught them a baraita about a woman who changed her pattern from day 15 to day 20, ruling that both days are forbidden until three occurrences establish the new pattern.
Abaye further reminds Rav Yosef that he taught them Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel that this baraita follows Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, but the Sages say she need not repeat or triple.
Abaye clarifies that 'repeat' refers to vestot (patterns) and 'triple' refers to days, resolving the apparent redundancy in the Sages' statement.
The Gemara notes that Shmuel's teaching implies that Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi holds like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, explaining why the attribution was necessary.

items.text: Mishnah: Vestot and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vestot and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman was accustomed to seeing at the beginning of her vestot, all purifications she performed during the vestot are impure; if at the end, they are pure. Rabbi Yosei adds days, hours, and vestot. If she was accustomed to seeing at sunrise, she is only forbidden at sunrise; Rabbi Yehuda says the entire day is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a woman accustomed to seeing at the beginning of her vestot: all purifications during the vestot are impure; if at the end, they are pure.
Rabbi Yosei adds that days, hours, and vestot are also considered.
If she was accustomed to seeing at sunrise, she is only forbidden at sunrise; Rabbi Yehuda says the entire day is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying Rabbi Yosei's position and resolving contradictions in Rabbi Yehuda's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying Rabbi Yosei's position and resolving contradictions in Rabbi Yehuda's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei's view with an example: a woman who sees every 20 days at 6 hours. If she misses, Rabbi Yehuda forbids the first 6 hours, while Rabbi Yosei permits until 6 hours and then is concerned. If she misses the 6 hours, Rabbi Yehuda forbids the entire day, Rabbi Yosei permits from mincha onward. A contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements is resolved: one baraita refers to one accustomed to seeing at the beginning of the day, the other at the end of the night.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Rabbi Yosei's concept of 'days, hours, and fixed patterns' with an example of a woman who sees every 20 days at 6 hours, and contrasts Rabbi Yehuda's stringency with Rabbi Yosei's leniency for the first 6 hours.
The baraita continues: if the 6 hours pass without seeing, Rabbi Yehuda forbids the entire day, while Rabbi Yosei permits from mincha onward.
The Gemara objects: but a baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda says the entire night is forbidden, contradicting the previous baraita's ruling about the day.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one baraita refers to a woman accustomed to seeing at the beginning of the day, the other to one accustomed to seeing at the end of the night.
A baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda forbids before her fixed time and permits after it.
Another baraita states the opposite: Rabbi Yehuda forbids after her fixed time and permits before it.
The Gemara resolves this contradiction similarly: one baraita refers to one accustomed to seeing at the end of the night, the other to one accustomed to seeing at the beginning of the day.

items.text: Rava's ruling and the derivation of separation near the veset
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and the derivation of separation near the veset
items.desc_en: Rava rules like Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara questions this, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yirmeya derives from a verse that one must separate from one's wife near her veset. Rava says the separation is for one onah. The Gemara clarifies that this means the same onah, not the next one. The two sources are necessary: one for purity, one for marital relations; and to teach that 'near her veset' means the same onah, not the next.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding the prohibition of marital relations near the veset.
The Gemara objects: Did Rava actually say this? It cites a baraita that seems to contradict his ruling.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yirmeya derives from the verse 'וְהִזַּרְתֶּם אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִטּוּמְאָתָם' that Israelite men must separate from their wives near the veset.
The Gemara asks: How long is the separation period?
Rava answers: The separation is for one עונה (a period of 12 or 24 hours, depending on context).
The Gemara asks: Does this mean the next עונה (after the veset), not the same one?
The Gemara resolves: No, it means the same עונה (the one in which the veset occurs).
The Gemara asks: Why do we need both sources (the baraita and Rava's ruling)?
The Gemara explains: The baraita alone might have been understood as applying only to טהרות (pure foods), not to marital relations; Rava's ruling teaches that it applies to marital relations as well.
The Gemara adds: And from Rava's ruling alone, one might have thought 'near her veset' means the next עונה; the baraita teaches that it means the same עונה.

items.text: Mishnah: Establishing and uprooting a veset
items.text_en: Mishnah: Establishing and uprooting a veset
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a woman changed her pattern from day 15 to day 20, both days are forbidden. After two occurrences, both are still forbidden. After three occurrences, day 15 is permitted and day 20 is established, because a woman does not establish a veset until three times, and does not become free from a veset until it is uprooted three times.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the initial case: a woman accustomed to seeing on day 15 changes to day 20; both days are forbidden.
The Mishnah completes the rule: after three occurrences on day 20, day 15 is permitted and day 20 is established, because a veset requires three times to be fixed and three times to be uprooted.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on establishing a veset through skipping
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on establishing a veset through skipping
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a woman saw bleeding on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of consecutive months. Rav holds she establishes a veset through skipping (dilug), while Shmuel requires three occurrences of the skip pattern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case of a woman who saw bleeding on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of consecutive months.
Rav rules that the woman establishes a veset (fixed menstrual pattern) through skipping (דילוג).
Shmuel requires three occurrences of the skip pattern to establish a veset through skipping.

items.text: Attempt to link to Tannaitic dispute and resolution
items.text_en: Attempt to link to Tannaitic dispute and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rav and Shmuel's dispute aligns with a Tannaic dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding a woman who married twice and each husband died. It then rejects this, explaining both agree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and their dispute is about whether the 15th counts in the skip pattern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel's dispute aligns with the Tannaic dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding a woman who married twice and each husband died.
The Gemara rejects the alignment, explaining that both agree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and their dispute is about whether the 15th day counts in the skip pattern.

items.text: Objection against Rav from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection against Rav from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought: a woman accustomed to seeing on the 15th who shifts to the 16th makes both days forbidden; shifting to the 17th permits the 16th but forbids the 15th and 17th. This seems to contradict Rav's view that three sightings establish a skip pattern. Rav answers that a 'mudah' (accustomed woman) is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Rav from a baraita: a woman accustomed to seeing on the 15th who shifts to the 16th makes both days forbidden, and shifting to the 17th permits the 16th but forbids the 15th and 17th, which seems to contradict Rav's view that three sightings establish a skip pattern.
Rav answers that a 'mudah' (accustomed woman) is different from the case of establishing a skip pattern, so the baraita does not contradict him.

items.text: Clarification of Rav's answer
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rav needed to state this: one might think that since she is accustomed and then uproots her pattern, two occurrences suffice to uproot; Rav teaches that even for a mudah, three are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav needed to state his ruling about a mudah (accustomed woman) at all.

The Gemara explains that Rav's statement was necessary to counter the possible assumption that a mudah (accustomed woman) who uproots her pattern could do so after only two occurrences; Rav teaches that even for her, three occurrences are required.

items.text: Objection against Shmuel and resolution
items.text_en: Objection against Shmuel and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought: a woman who sees on the 21st, 22nd, and 23rd establishes a veset; if she skips to the 24th, she does not. This contradicts Shmuel who requires three skips. Shmuel answers that the case is where she was accustomed to seeing on the 20th and shifted to the 21st, so the 21st is not a skip but a continuation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that a woman who sees on the 21st, 22nd, and 23rd establishes a veset, but if she skips to the 24th she does not, which contradicts Shmuel's requirement of three skips.

Shmuel resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita deals with a woman who was accustomed to seeing on the 20th and shifted to the 21st, so the 21st is not a skip but a continuation, and the Gemara confirms this from the baraita's language.

items.text: Rav Pappa: One occurrence creates concern but not establishment
items.text_en: Rav Pappa: One occurrence creates concern but not establishment
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that a woman does not establish a veset until three times, but she is concerned after one occurrence. He supports this from a mishnah and explains that without his statement, one might think concern only applies within her menstrual days; he teaches that even outside those days, she must be concerned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that a woman does not establish a fixed menstrual cycle until three times, but she must be concerned after one occurrence.
The Gemara asks what Rav Pappa is teaching us, citing the mishnah that already states that if a woman deviates from her accustomed day, both days are forbidden.
The Gemara explains that without Rav Pappa's statement, one might think concern applies only within her menstrual days; he teaches that even outside those days she must be concerned.

items.text: Rav Pappa: Three occurrences needed to uproot a veset
items.text_en: Rav Pappa: Three occurrences needed to uproot a veset
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that if a veset was established with three occurrences, three occurrences are needed to uproot it; but if established with two, one uproots it. He supports this from a mishnah and explains that without his statement, one might think each number corresponds; he teaches that three uproots three.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that a veset established with three occurrences requires three to uproot, but one established with two is uprooted by one.
The Gemara asks what Rav Pappa is teaching us, since the mishnah already states that a veset is established only after three times.

The Gemara answers that without Rav Pappa's statement, one might think that uprooting requires the same number of occurrences as the establishment; Rav Pappa teaches that three uproots three, but two is uprooted by one.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Pappa: a woman accustomed to seeing on the 20th who shifts to the 30th makes both days forbidden; if she misses the 20th and sees on the 30th, then misses the 30th and sees on the 20th, the 30th is permitted. This illustrates the principle of uprooting with one occurrence for a two-time pattern.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Pappa: a woman accustomed to seeing on the 20th who shifts to the 30th makes both days forbidden, and if she misses the 20th and sees on the 30th, she is permitted until the 30th but must be concerned for the 30th.
The baraita concludes that if she then misses the 30th and sees on the 20th, the 30th day becomes permitted, illustrating the principle of uprooting a two-time pattern with one occurrence.

items.text: Opening statement from previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening statement from previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The daf opens with a brief statement from the previous Mishnah, establishing that the twentieth day is forbidden because the menstrual cycle arrives on time.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the twentieth day is forbidden because the menstrual cycle arrives on time.

items.text: Mishnah: Women are like vines
items.text_en: Mishnah: Women are like vines
items.desc_en: The Mishnah compares women to vines, noting that some have red wine (blood), some black, some abundant, some scarce. Rabbi Yehuda adds that every vine has wine, and one without wine is like a 'dorkti' (a type of dried grape).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah compares women's virginity to vines, with Rabbi Yehuda adding that a vine without wine is like a 'dorketi' (a dry vine).
Rabbi Yehuda adds that every vine has wine, and one without wine is like a 'דורקתי' (a dried grape).

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of 'dorkti' and benefits of blood
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of 'dorkti' and benefits of blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'dorkti' as a cut-off vine. Rabbi Chiyya teaches that just as leaven is good for dough, so blood is good for a woman. Rabbi Meir adds that a woman with abundant blood has many children.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna explains that 'dorketi' means a cut-off generation (a vine that produces no wine).
Rabbi Chiyya teaches that just as leaven is good for dough, so blood is good for a woman.
A tradition in the name of Rabbi Meir states that any woman whose blood is abundant has many children.

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: This segment marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'Hadran alach ha'isha' (we return to you, the woman).

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the previous chapter with the formula 'we return to you, The Woman'.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a minor bride and a mature bride
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a minor bride and a mature bride
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: a minor who married before reaching puberty (Beit Shammai: 4 nights; Beit Hillel: until the wound heals), a girl who reached puberty and married (Beit Shammai: first night; Beit Hillel: until after Shabbat, 4 nights), and one who saw blood while still in her father's house (Beit Shammai: only the mitzvah intercourse; Beit Hillel: the entire night).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a minor bride who married before reaching puberty, presenting Beit Shammai's ruling of four nights and Beit Hillel's ruling of until the wound heals.
The Mishnah shifts to the case of a girl who reached puberty and married, with Beit Shammai giving the first night and Beit Hillel giving until after Shabbat (four nights).
The Mishnah shifts to the case of a girl who saw blood while still in her father's house, with Beit Shammai giving only the mitzvah intercourse and Beit Hillel giving the entire night.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's inference and a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's inference and a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak infers from the Mishnah's structure that even if the minor saw blood, Beit Hillel still gives her until the wound heals. A baraita supports this, stating Beit Hillel's ruling applies whether she saw blood or not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak infers from the Mishnah's structure that Beit Hillel's leniency applies even if the minor saw blood.
A baraita explicitly supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's inference, stating Beit Hillel's ruling applies whether she saw blood or not.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of 'until the wound heals'
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of 'until the wound heals'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav defines 'until the wound heals' as 'as long as it is bleeding' (nocheret). Shmuel questions this, defining it as 'as long as saliva is found in the mouth due to intercourse'. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak clarifies Rav's definition with practical examples of standing/sitting and different surfaces.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the practical definition of the Mishnah's phrase 'until the wound heals'.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav defines the period as 'as long as it is bleeding' (נוחרת).
Shmuel objects that the term 'נוחרת' (bleeding) is unclear and offers his own definition.
Shmuel defines the period as 'as long as saliva is found in the mouth due to intercourse'.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's clarification
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's clarification
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak clarifies Rav's definition with practical examples: standing vs. sitting, and different surfaces, to determine when the wound has healed.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Levi on 'she engaged in intercourse during the days'
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Levi on 'she engaged in intercourse during the days'
items.desc_en: A dispute arises: if a bride engaged in intercourse during the day (not at night), Rav says she does not lose the nights, while Levi says she does. The Gemara explains their reasoning based on the Mishnah's wording, and concludes with a support from Shmuel regarding entering a narrow breach on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: if a bride engaged in intercourse during the day, Rav says she does not lose the nights, while Levi says she does.
Rav explains his position: the Mishnah teaches 'until after Shabbat' (four nights), so daytime intercourse does not forfeit the nights.
Levi explains his position: the Mishnah's phrase 'four nights' actually means four עונות (day-night units), so daytime counts as one unit.
The Gemara asks Rav: if the Mishnah only means nights, why specify 'four nights' rather than just 'until after Shabbat'?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches proper conduct (אורח ארעא) — that intercourse is normally at night.
The Gemara asks Levi: if the Mishnah means four עונות, why does it also say 'until after Shabbat'?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that it is permitted לכתחילה (ideally) to engage in intercourse on Shabbat.
The Gemara supports Levi's position with Shmuel's ruling that one may enter a narrow breach on Shabbat even though it dislodges stones.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Assi on finding blood after a previous intercourse without blood
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Assi on finding blood after a previous intercourse without blood
items.desc_en: If a man engaged in intercourse and found no blood, then engaged again and found blood, Rabbi Chanina rules the woman is impure (since the blood should have come initially), while Rabbi Assi rules she is pure (perhaps the blood came later, as Shmuel claimed he could engage multiple times without blood). The Gemara notes that Shmuel's case is exceptional due to his size.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: if a man engaged in intercourse and found no blood, then engaged again and found blood, Rabbi Chanina rules the woman is impure (טמאה), while Rabbi Assi rules she is pure (טהורה).
Rabbi Chanina explains his ruling: if there were hymenal blood (דם בתולים), it should have come initially, so the later blood is menstrual and renders the woman impure.
Rabbi Assi explains his ruling: perhaps the blood came later, as Shmuel claimed he could engage in multiple acts of intercourse without blood, so the woman remains pure.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Assi's analogy
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Assi's analogy
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rabbi Assi's reliance on Shmuel's case, noting that Shmuel is exceptional due to his large size (רב גובריה), so his experience does not set a general precedent.

items.text: Gemara: Rav's ruling on a bogeret and an objection
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav's ruling on a bogeret and an objection
items.desc_en: Rav rules that a bogeret (mature maiden) is given only the first night, and only if she did not see blood; if she saw blood, she only has the mitzvah intercourse. An objection is raised from a story where Rabbi gave four nights out of twelve months, questioning whether this refers to a minor.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a bogeret (mature maiden) is given only the first night, and only if she did not see blood; if she saw blood, she only has the mitzvah intercourse and no more.
The Gemara raises an objection from a story where Rabbi gave four nights out of twelve months, questioning whether this refers to a minor, which would contradict Rav's ruling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a young bride is given four nights, starting from when the wound heals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a young bride is given four nights starting from when the wound heals.

items.text: First objection: allocating all four nights in adolescence
items.text_en: First objection: allocating all four nights in adolescence
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if all four nights are given during adolescence, that period is only six months long, not twelve, as per Shmuel's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if all four nights are allocated to adolescence, that period is only six months long, not twelve, as per Shmuel's statement, and the word 'בלבד' (only) excludes any longer period.

items.text: Second proposal: two in childhood and two in adolescence
items.text_en: Second proposal: two in childhood and two in adolescence
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests giving two nights in childhood and two in adolescence, but Rav Chinnana bar Shelemya's question about a bride who reaches the time to see blood under her husband is answered by Rav: all subsequent relations count as one, and the rest complete the four nights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes giving two nights in childhood and two in adolescence, then raises Rav Chinnana bar Shelemya's question: what is the law for a bride who reaches the time to see blood under her husband?
Rav answers that all subsequent relations count as one, and the rest complete the four nights.

items.text: Third proposal: one in childhood, two in adolescence, one in adulthood
items.text_en: Third proposal: one in childhood, two in adolescence, one in adulthood
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers giving one night in childhood, two in adolescence, and one in adulthood, arguing that if an adult woman gets extra nights, then adolescence reduces one from childhood and adulthood reduces one from adolescence; but if an adult woman gets no extra nights, she should only receive the mitzvah intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes giving one night in childhood, two in adolescence, and one in adulthood, arguing that if an adult woman gets extra nights, then adolescence reduces one from childhood and adulthood reduces one from adolescence.
The Gemara objects that if an adult woman receives no extra nights, she should only receive the mitzvah intercourse and nothing more.

items.text: Resolution: one in childhood and three in adolescence
items.text_en: Resolution: one in childhood and three in adolescence
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that one night is given in childhood and three in adolescence, explaining that each two-month period counts as one onah, not three months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that one night is given in childhood and three in adolescence, explaining that each two-month period counts as one onah, not three months.

items.text: Story of Minyamin Saksena'ah and Shmuel's reaction
items.text_en: Story of Minyamin Saksena'ah and Shmuel's reaction
items.desc_en: Minyamin Saksena'ah went to Shmuel's place intending to act like Rav even if the bride saw blood, but Shmuel said Rav did not distinguish between seeing and not seeing; Minyamin died on the way, and Shmuel applied the verse 'No harm befalls the righteous' to Rav.

sub.desc_en: Minyamin Saksena'ah traveled to Shmuel's place intending to act like Rav even if the bride saw blood.
Shmuel said that Rav did not distinguish between the bride seeing blood and not seeing blood.
Minyamin died on the way, and Shmuel applied the verse 'No harm befalls the righteous' to Rav.

items.text: Rav Chinnana's teaching on teeth and sustenance
items.text_en: Rav Chinnana's teaching on teeth and sustenance
items.desc_en: Rav Chinnana bar Shelemya said in Rav's name: once a person's teeth fall out, their sustenance diminishes, as per the verse about clean teeth and lack of bread.

sub.text: Rav Chinnana bar Shelemya in Rav's name
sub.text_en: Rav Chinnana bar Shelemya in Rav's name
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinnana bar Shelemya teaches in Rav's name that once a person's teeth fall out, their sustenance diminishes, citing the verse about clean teeth and lack of bread.

items.text: Baraita on a bride who sees blood while still in her father's house
items.text_en: Baraita on a bride who sees blood while still in her father's house
items.desc_en: The baraita states that if a bride sees blood while still in her father's house, Beit Hillel says she gets the entire night and a full onah, defined by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as a night and half a day. The Gemara questions whether so much time is needed and cites a contradiction regarding purifying vessels.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if a bride sees blood while still in her father's house, Beit Hillel says she gets the entire night and a full onah, defined by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as a night and half a day.
The Gemara questions whether so much time is needed and cites a contradiction regarding purifying vessels.
The Gemara introduces a baraita about purifying winepress and olive-press vessels, which sets up the contradiction.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Purification of baskets
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Purification of baskets
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between baskets made from different materials and specifies how they are purified: some are wiped, others are left to dry for twelve months. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that they are left from one pressing season to the next.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that baskets of certain materials are purified by wiping, while others require drying for twelve months, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel specifies the drying period as from one pressing season to the next.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: Difference between Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: Difference between Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma's, and explains the difference lies in the case of early and late ripening seasons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what difference exists between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since their positions seem identical.
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in the case of early (חָרְפֵי) and late (אַפְלֵי) ripening seasons.

items.text: Mishnah continued: Rabbi Yosei's alternative purification methods
items.text_en: Mishnah continued: Rabbi Yosei's alternative purification methods
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei offers immediate purification methods: scalding in hot water or steeping in olive water. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel cites Rabbi Yosei's opinion of placing them under a spout or in a spring. The Gemara corrects the Mishnah's comparison: the principle was stated regarding purities, not wine libations.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that one who wishes to purify baskets immediately may scald them in hot water or steep them in olive water.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel cites Rabbi Yosei's alternative method: placing the baskets under a spout with gushing water or in a flowing spring.
The Mishnah states that the required waiting period (עונה) for these methods is the same as that stated for wine libations (יין נסך) and for purities (טהרות).
The Gemara objects: 'To the contrary! We are dealing with purities (טהרות)!' — implying the Mishnah's comparison is backwards.
The Gemara corrects the Mishnah's wording: the principle was stated regarding purities (טהרות), and then applied to wine libations (יין נסך), not the reverse.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about the duration of an עונה
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about the duration of an עונה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that an עונה is either a full day or a full night. Rabbi Chana Sha'una quotes Rabbi Yochanan that it is half a day and half a night. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak resolves the dispute by attributing each to different seasons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How long is an עונה (a period)?

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that an עונה is either a full day or a full night.

sub.text: Rabbi Chana Sha'una citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chana Sha'una citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chana Sha'una (or some say Rabbi Chana bar Sha'una) reports in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan that an עונה is half a day and half a night.

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak resolves the dispute: the two statements are not contradictory — one refers to the season of Nisan and Tishrei (when day and night are equal), the other to the season of Tammuz and Tevet (when one is longer).

items.text: Gemara: Application to Niddah and alternative answer
items.text_en: Gemara: Application to Niddah and alternative answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to apply the half-day/half-night rule to Niddah but notes a textual discrepancy. It resolves by assigning different seasons. An alternative answer suggests that the leniency is due to the marriage contract (כתובה) which encourages the husband to finalize the marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to apply the half-day/half-night rule to Niddah, but notes a textual discrepancy in the Mishnah's phrasing.
The Gemara resolves the discrepancy by assigning different seasons: either a night of Nisan/Tishrei or a half-day/half-night of Tevet/Tammuz.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the leniency is due to the marriage contract (כתובה) which encourages the husband to finalize the marriage.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's ruling and challenge
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's ruling and challenge
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel rule that a bride who sees blood during relations performs the initial mitzvah intercourse and then separates. Rav Chisda challenges with a story where Rabbi gave four nights out of twelve months. Rava criticizes citing a story instead of a Mishnah. The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel acted in accordance with the later ruling of our Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both rule that the halakha is that the groom performs the initial mitzvah intercourse and then separates.
