Rav Chisda raises an objection from a story where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave a bride four nights within twelve months, contradicting Rav and Shmuel.
Rava criticizes Rav Chisda for citing a story rather than a mishna, explaining that Rav Chisda considers a practical incident a preferable source.

The Gemara notes that despite the criticism, the story still challenges Rav and Shmuel, and resolves that they acted in accordance with the later ruling of our Rabbis who voted that the groom performs the initial mitzvah intercourse and then separates.

items.text: Ulla's testimony and Rabbi Abba's question
items.text_en: Ulla's testimony and Rabbi Abba's question
items.desc_en: Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, when dealing with a minor bride, would extract the ruling with difficulty and conclude that he performs the mitzvah intercourse and separates. Rabbi Abba questions whether a scrupulous person should not complete intercourse, and Rav Ashi explains that if so, his heart would smite him and he would separate.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, when studying the case of a minor bride, extracted the halakha with great difficulty and concluded that the groom performs the mitzvah intercourse and then separates.
Rabbi Abba asks Rav Ashi: If so, should a scrupulous person not complete his intercourse?
Rav Ashi answers that if the Sages required him not to complete intercourse, his heart would smite him and he would separate entirely, so the ruling is not changed.

items.text: Baraita: Cases of continuous bleeding and dispute about blood appearances
items.text_en: Baraita: Cases of continuous bleeding and dispute about blood appearances
items.desc_en: A Baraita states that women who experience continuous bleeding from the four nights or from night to night must examine themselves. Rabbi Meir is stringent like Beit Shammai. For other sightings, one follows the appearance of the blood. Rabbi Meir distinguishes between menstrual and virginity blood, but Rabbi Yochanan reports that the Sages consider all blood appearances the same.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that all women who experience continuous bleeding from the four nights or from night to night must examine themselves.
The baraita reports that Rabbi Meir is stringent like Beit Shammai in all these cases.
The baraita rules that for other sightings between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, one follows the appearance of the blood.
Rabbi Meir distinguishes between menstrual blood and virginity blood by color, odor, and source.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rabbi Yosei citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rabbi Yosei citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that Rabbi Meir's view is individual, but the Sages consider all blood appearances the same.

items.text: Baraita: Woman who sees blood due to intercourse
items.text_en: Baraita: Woman who sees blood due to intercourse
items.desc_en: A Baraita rules that a woman who sees blood due to intercourse may engage in relations a first, second, and third time, but thereafter she may not until she divorces.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a woman who sees blood due to intercourse may engage in relations the first, second, and third times, but thereafter she may not until she divorces.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blood during relations
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blood during relations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a woman who sees blood due to intercourse. If she marries a second husband and sees blood, she may engage in relations three times; thereafter she must divorce and marry another. If she marries a third and sees blood, she may engage three times and then must examine herself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman who sees blood during relations with a second husband may engage three times, then must divorce and remarry; with a third husband, she must examine herself after three times.

items.text: Method of self-examination and leniencies
items.text_en: Method of self-examination and leniencies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how a woman examines herself using a tube with a wick to determine if blood comes from the source (uterus) or from the sides. If she has a wound or a fixed menstrual cycle, she may attribute the blood to those causes. Rabbi holds that a woman is believed to say she has a wound in the source.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks how a woman examines herself and describes the procedure with a tube and wick to determine if blood comes from the source or the sides.
The Mishnah states that if she has a wound or a fixed menstrual cycle, she may attribute the blood to those causes.
Rabbi adds that if the wound's blood differs from the menstrual blood, she cannot attribute it, but she is believed to say she has a wound in the source.

items.text: Dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that blood from a wound in the source is impure, while the Sages testified that such blood is pure. Ulla explains the difference between them: whether the place of the source is impure.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that blood from a wound in the source is impure, while the Sages testified that such blood is pure.
The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two positions.
Ulla explains that the dispute is about whether the place of the source itself is impure (מקור מקומו טמא).

items.text: Gemara's questions on the examination method
items.text_en: Gemara's questions on the examination method
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the practicality of the tube examination, and Shmuel explains it is a metal tube with its mouth attached inside. Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan why the woman cannot check with the third intercourse of the first husband or the first of the third; Rabbi Yochanan answers that not all fingers or powers are equal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the tube examination would tear the woman's flesh.
Shmuel explains that the tube is made of metal and its mouth is attached inside, so it does not tear.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks why the woman cannot check herself during the third intercourse with the first husband.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that not all fingers are equal, so the third intercourse may not replicate the earlier ones.
Reish Lakish asks why the woman cannot check herself during the first intercourse with the third husband.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that not all powers are equal, so the first intercourse with the third husband may not be comparable.

items.text: Stories of women who saw blood and their remedies
items.text_en: Stories of women who saw blood and their remedies
items.desc_en: Three stories: Rabbi tells Abdan to frighten a woman, causing a clot to fall, and declares her healed. Shmuel tells Rav Dimi to frighten another woman, but nothing falls, and Shmuel says she has no remedy. Rabbi Yochanan advises a woman who sees blood after immersion to go to the river and have relations there, or to reveal her condition to friends for prayers.

sub.desc_en: A woman came before Rabbi; he told Abdan to frighten her, a clot of blood fell, and Rabbi declared her healed.
A woman came before Shmuel; he told Rav Dimi to frighten her, but nothing fell, and Shmuel said she is a case of 'ממלאה ונופצת' (filling and overflowing) with no remedy.
A woman who saw blood after immersion came before Rabbi Yochanan; he suggested that perhaps the water of her city affected her, and advised her to go and have relations on the riverbank.

sub.text: Alternative versions of Rabbi Yochanan's advice
sub.text_en: Alternative versions of Rabbi Yochanan's advice
sub.desc_en: Two alternative versions: Rabbi Yochanan told her to reveal her condition to friends so they would wonder at her or pray for her, citing the principle that a טמא (impure person) must publicize their distress so many may seek mercy.

items.text: Rabbi's enactment and Rabbi Zeira's stringency
items.text_en: Rabbi's enactment and Rabbi Zeira's stringency
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rabbi enacted in the fields: if a woman sees blood one day, she sits six clean days plus that day; if two days, six plus two; if three, seven clean days. Rabbi Zeira states that Jewish women have adopted a stringency: even seeing a drop of blood like a mustard seed requires seven clean days.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports a precedent in Pumpedita where a woman was healed through a similar procedure.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef transmits a tradition that Rabbi enacted in the fields: a woman who sees blood for one day sits six clean days plus that day, for two days six plus two, for three days seven clean days.
Rabbi Zeira states that Jewish women have adopted a stringency: even seeing a drop of blood like a mustard seed requires seven clean days.

items.text: Rava's ruling on labor pains and Rav Pappa's challenge
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on labor pains and Rav Pappa's challenge
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a woman had labor pains for two days and miscarried on the third, she must sit seven clean days, because labor pains cannot occur without blood. Rav Pappa challenges that even minimal blood requires seven clean days per Rabbi Zeira's stringency. Rava distinguishes between a prohibition (issura) and a custom (minhaga).

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs Rav Shmuel to teach that a woman who had labor pains for two days and miscarried on the third must sit seven clean days, because labor pains cannot occur without blood.
Rav Pappa challenges Rava that even minimal blood requires seven clean days per Rabbi Zeira's stringency, so why specify two days of labor?
Rava distinguishes between a prohibition (איסורא) and a custom (מנהגא): the stringency applies only where women adopted it, not here.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a woman who agrees to marry and subsequent discussion
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a woman who agrees to marry and subsequent discussion
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a woman who was asked to marry and agreed must sit seven clean days. Ravina asks Rav Chanina about writing a ketubah for his son after four days, leading to a discussion about whether this applies to a minor who has not seen blood. Rava clarifies that the reason is due to desire, which applies to both adult and minor.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a woman who was asked to marry and agreed must sit seven clean days.
Ravina asks Rav Chanina about writing a ketubah for his son after four days, and Rav Chanina responds that he will wait an additional four days to complete seven clean days.
Ravina asks why the delay is needed, and Rav Chanina explains that Rava's ruling applies only to an adult who has seen blood, not to a minor who has not.
Rava clarifies that his ruling applies to both adult and minor, because the reason is due to desire (מחמדא), which applies to both.

items.text: Prohibition against using natron or sand for ḥafifah
items.text_en: Prohibition against using natron or sand for ḥafifah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a woman should not wash with natron (nether) because it abrades the skin, nor with sand because it causes clinging (and may create a ḥatzitzah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a woman should not perform ḥafifah (pre-immersion washing) with natron (נתר) because it abrades the skin, nor with sand (חול) because it causes clinging and may create a ḥatzitzah (interposition).

items.text: Amemar's ruling: only hot water for ḥafifah
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling: only hot water for ḥafifah
items.desc_en: Amemar in the name of Rava rules that a woman may only wash with hot water, not cold water, even if the cold water is heated by the sun. Cold water is prohibited because it stiffens the hair and causes it to loosen (making it prone to becoming a ḥatzitzah).

sub.text: Amemar in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Amemar in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Amemar rules in the name of Rava that a woman may only wash her hair with hot water, not cold water, because cold water stiffens the hair and causes it to loosen, making it prone to becoming a ḥatzitzah.

items.text: Rava's teaching on washing creases and the objection
items.text_en: Rava's teaching on washing creases and the objection
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that a woman should always be instructed to wash her creases (beit kameṭeha) with water. The Gemara objects from a baraita that states that hidden places (beit hakematim and beit hasetarim) do not require direct contact with water. The Gemara resolves that while they do not require actual water contact, they must be a place fit for water contact, as per Rabbi Zeira's principle: anything fit for blending (billah) does not require blending, but what is not fit for blending requires blending.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches that a woman should always be instructed to wash her creases (beit kameṭeha) with water.
The Gemara objects from a baraita that states that hidden places (beit hakematim and beit hasetarim) do not require direct contact with water.

The Gemara resolves that while hidden places do not require actual water contact, they must be a place fit for water contact, as per Rabbi Zeira's principle: anything fit for blending (billah) does not require blending, but what is not fit for blending requires blending.

items.text: Story of Rabbi's maidservant with a bone between her teeth
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi's maidservant with a bone between her teeth
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak relates an incident: the maidservant of Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) immersed, came up, and a bone was found stuck between her teeth. Rabbi required her to undergo another immersion, establishing that an interposing object invalidates the immersion.

sub.text: Ravin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak relates an incident where Rabbi's maidservant immersed and a bone was found between her teeth, and Rabbi required her to immerse again, establishing that a חוצץ (interposing object) invalidates immersion.

items.text: Rava's ruling on ḥatzitzah found after immersion and the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on ḥatzitzah found after immersion and the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava rules: if a woman immersed and found an interposing object on her, if she immersed close to her ḥafifah (i.e., on the same day), she does not need to repeat both ḥafifah and immersion; otherwise she must. An alternative version says: if she immersed on the same day as her ḥafifah, she does not need to repeat; otherwise she does. The Gemara explains the practical difference between these versions: whether one may do ḥafifah during the day and immerse at night (which is still considered close).

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a woman immersed and found an interposing object, if she immersed close to her ḥafifah (same day), she does not need to repeat both; otherwise she must.
An alternative version states that if she immersed on the same day as her ḥafifah, she does not need to repeat; otherwise she does.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two versions, and answers that it concerns whether one may do ḥafifah during the day and immerse at night (still considered close).

items.text: Prohibition against immersing on a clay vessel and the reason
items.text_en: Prohibition against immersing on a clay vessel and the reason
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a woman should not stand on a clay vessel and immerse. Rav Kahana thought the reason was a decree related to bathhouses (where one might come to use the vessel for other purposes), implying that standing on a stone (silta) would be fine. Rav Chanan from Nehardea corrected him: the actual reason is because it might tip over (due to fear), and a stone also might tip over.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a woman should not stand on a clay vessel and immerse.
Rav Kahana suggests the reason is a decree related to bathhouses, implying that standing on a stone (סִילְתָּא) would be fine.
Rav Chanan from Nehardea corrects him: the actual reason is because it might tip over (due to fear), and a stone also might tip over.

items.text: Beginning of Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's statement
items.text_en: Beginning of Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak begins a new ruling: a woman should not immerse... (the text cuts off at the end of the amud).

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak begins a ruling that a woman should not immerse, but the text cuts off at the end of the amud.

items.text: Opening statement about brine remnants
items.text_en: Opening statement about brine remnants
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that even if there is no visible interposition now, one must suspect that a brine remnant fell off during immersion, invalidating it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that even if there is no visible interposition now, one must suspect that a brine remnant (רִדְיוֹנֵי) fell off during immersion, invalidating it.

items.text: Shmuel's father's practice with daughters' mikvaot
items.text_en: Shmuel's father's practice with daughters' mikvaot
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Shmuel's father made mikvaot for his daughters in Nisan and spread them out in Tishrei, implying a concern for interpositions from seasonal changes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Shmuel's father made mikvaot for his daughters in Nisan and spread them out in Tishrei, demonstrating a concern for interpositions from seasonal changes.

items.text: Rav Giddel's ruling on cooked food interposition
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's ruling on cooked food interposition
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav that if a woman gave cooked food to her son and then immersed, her immersion is invalid even if no food is visible now, because it may have fallen off during immersion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav that a woman who gave cooked food to her son and then immersed has not fulfilled immersion, even if no food is visible now, because it may have fallen off during immersion.

items.text: Rami bar Abba on dried fish scales
items.text_en: Rami bar Abba on dried fish scales
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba rules that fish scales (ribdei dechusilta) are not interpositions within three days, but after three days they become interpositions.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba opens by stating that dried fish scales (רִבְדֵי דְּכוּסִילְתָּא) do not constitute a interposition (חציצה) within three days.
Rami bar Abba completes his ruling: after three days, the scales do become a interposition (חציצה).

items.text: Mar Ukva on pepper in the eye
items.text_en: Mar Ukva on pepper in the eye
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva rules that wet pepper in the eye is not an interposition, but dry pepper is; dry is defined as when it begins to fester.

sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva rules that wet pepper in the eye is not an interposition (חוֹצֵץ), but dry pepper is.
Mar Ukva defines dry pepper as from the time it begins to fester (לִירַק).

items.text: Shmuel on sand in the eye
items.text_en: Shmuel on sand in the eye
items.desc_en: Shmuel distinguishes between sand inside the eye (not an interposition) and sand on the eye (an interposition), unless the woman's eyes are discharging, in which case even on the eye is not an interposition.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that sand inside the eye (בתוך העין) is not an interposition (חוצץ) for immersion.
Shmuel adds that sand on top of the eye (על גבי העין) is an interposition.
Shmuel qualifies that if the woman's eyes are discharging (פורחות), even sand on top of the eye is not an interposition.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on opening or closing eyes excessively
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on opening or closing eyes excessively
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if a woman opens her eyes too much or closes them too much during immersion, her immersion is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if a woman opens or closes her eyes excessively during immersion, her immersion is invalid.

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbah bar Rav Huna on natural posture and tied hair
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbah bar Rav Huna on natural posture and tied hair
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that a woman must immerse in her natural posture, like a man appearing as a harvester or a woman as a weaver or nursing. Rabbah bar Rav Huna adds that a single tied hair is an interposition.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that a woman must immerse only in her natural posture, citing the Mishnah's examples of a man appearing as a harvester or olive-presser and a woman as a weaver or nursing her child.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna adds that even a single tied hair constitutes an interposition (חציצה) that invalidates the immersion.

items.text: Debate on ḥaṣiẓah: majority vs. minority, concern vs. non-concern
items.text_en: Debate on ḥaṣiẓah: majority vs. minority, concern vs. non-concern
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute about how many things interpose (ḥoẓeẓot). Rabbi Yoḥanan says only one. Rabbi Yitzḥak explains the Torah law: a majority that one is concerned about interposes, a majority not concerned about does not; the Sages decreed against a non-concerned majority because of a concerned majority, and against a concerned minority because of a concerned majority. The Gemara questions why they did not also decree against a non-concerned minority, and answers that this would be a decree upon a decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute about how many things interpose (חוצצות): an anonymous source says three do not interpose and two is uncertain, while Rabbi Yoḥanan says only one does not interpose.

Rabbi Yitzḥak explains the Torah law: a majority that one is concerned about interposes, a majority not concerned about does not; the Sages decreed against a non-concerned majority because of a concerned majority, and against a concerned minority because of a concerned majority.
The Gemara asks why the Sages did not also decree against a non-concerned minority because of a concerned minority.
The Gemara answers that the decree against a concerned minority is itself a decree, and one does not issue a decree upon a decree.

items.text: Dispute on when a niddah may immerse: Rav vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan
items.text_en: Dispute on when a niddah may immerse: Rav vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan
items.desc_en: Rav initially rules that a niddah who immerses at her proper time (on the seventh night) may only immerse at night, but one who immerses not at her proper time may immerse by day or night. Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that in either case she may only immerse at night, because of her daughter's habit (serakh bitah). The Gemara notes that Rav retracted and agreed with Rabbi Yoḥanan.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a niddah immersing at her proper time may only immerse at night, but one immersing not at her proper time may immerse by day or night.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that in either case she may only immerse at night, because of her daughter's habit.

sub.text: Gemara via Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Gemara via Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav retracted and agreed with Rabbi Yoḥanan, ruling that a niddah may only immerse at night in all cases.

items.text: Local enactments for daytime immersion due to danger
items.text_en: Local enactments for daytime immersion due to danger
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim instituted daytime immersion for niddot in their localities due to specific dangers: Rav Idi in Naresh because of lions, Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov in Papponia because of thieves, Rav Yehudah in Pumbedita because of cold, and Rava in Meḥoza because of river guards.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi instituted daytime immersion on the eighth day in Neresh due to lions.
Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov instituted daytime immersion in Pappunya due to thieves.
Rav Yehudah instituted daytime immersion in Pumbedita due to cold.
Rava instituted daytime immersion in Meḥoza due to gatekeepers.

items.text: Question about daytime immersion on the seventh day and the reason for prohibition
items.text_en: Question about daytime immersion on the seventh day and the reason for prohibition
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava and Abaye: since nowadays all women are considered uncertain zavot (safeik zavot), why not let them immerse on the seventh day during the day? The answer is because of Rabbi Shimon's interpretation of the verse "after she shall be clean" — that no impurity should interrupt between the seven days. The Sages said it is forbidden to do so, lest she come to doubt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava and Abaye: since all women are now considered uncertain zavot (ספק זבות), why not let them immerse on the seventh day during the day?

The Gemara answers that it is because of Rabbi Shimon's interpretation of the verse 'אחר תטהר' (after she shall be clean) — that no impurity should interrupt between the seven days, and immersion must be after the entire process.
The Sages ruled that it is forbidden to do so, lest she come to doubt (ספק) about her status.

items.text: Dispute on the interval between ḥafifah and tevilah: Rav Huna, Rav Ḥisda, Rav Yemar, and Marimar
items.text_en: Dispute on the interval between ḥafifah and tevilah: Rav Huna, Rav Ḥisda, Rav Yemar, and Marimar
items.desc_en: Rav Huna gives examples of permissible intervals between ḥafifah (preparation) and tevilah, using the analogy of Shabbat and festivals. Rav Ḥisda argues that we do not use the word "sheken" ("just as") to justify all cases; where possible it is possible, where not, not. Rav Yemar says we do use "sheken" except for the case of ḥafifah on Sunday and tevilah on Thursday, because that would correspond to a case that does not exist (since one can prepare on the night of the festival). Marimar rules that the halakhah follows Rav Ḥisda as reconciled by Rav Yemar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna lists three permissible intervals between ḥafifah (preparation) and tevilah (immersion), each justified by a parallel case of a woman who prepares on Shabbat eve and immerses after a festival.
Rav Ḥisda argues that we do not use the word 'שֶׁכֵּן' (just as) to justify all cases; where preparation is possible it is possible, where not, not.

Rav Yemar says we do use 'שֶׁכֵּן' except for the case of ḥafifah on Sunday and tevilah on Thursday, because that would correspond to a case that does not exist (since one can prepare on the night of the festival).
Marimar rules that the halakhah follows Rav Ḥisda as reconciled by Rav Yemar.

items.text: Inquiry about ḥafifah and tevilah both at night, and a related incident
items.text_en: Inquiry about ḥafifah and tevilah both at night, and a related incident
items.desc_en: A question is raised: may a woman perform ḥafifah at night and then immerse that same night? Mar Zutra forbids it, while Rav Ḥinnana from Sura permits it. Rav Adda relates to Rav Ḥinnana an incident involving the wife of Abba Mari the Exilarch, who was injured, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak went to appease her, and she asked what is now?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: may a woman perform ḥafifah (pre-immersion cleansing) at night and then immerse that same night?

sub.text: Mar Zutra and Rav Ḥinnana from Sura
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Ḥinnana from Sura
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra forbids the practice, while Rav Ḥinnana from Sura permits it.

sub.text: Rav Adda's challenge to Rav Ḥinnana
sub.text_en: Rav Adda's challenge to Rav Ḥinnana
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda challenges Rav Ḥinnana by citing an incident involving the wife of Abba Mari the Exilarch, who was injured, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak went to appease her, and she asked what is now the halachic situation.

items.text: Opening anecdote: Rava's initial ruling challenged
items.text_en: Opening anecdote: Rava's initial ruling challenged
items.desc_en: Rava initially taught that a woman may perform ḥafifah on Friday and immerse on Saturday night. Rav Pappa objects, citing Ravin's letter that forbids this, with the reason that ḥafifah and immersion must be immediate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a cryptic anecdote about a woman being asked if she lacks various items.
Rav Pappa objects to Rava's ruling that a woman may perform ḥafifah on Friday and immerse on Saturday night, citing Ravin's letter that forbids this.
Rav Pappa explains the objection: ḥafifah and immersion must be immediate (תֵּכֶף לַחֲפִיפָה טְבִילָה), and the gap violates this.
Rava retracts his earlier ruling and teaches in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a woman may not perform ḥafifah on Friday and immerse on Saturday night, citing the same requirement of immediacy.

sub.text: Gemara's question on the conflicting rulings
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the conflicting rulings
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes two conflicting rulings: one permits ḥafifah by day and immersion at night, the other requires ḥafifah only at night, and asks how both can be the binding law (הלכה).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one ruling applies when it is possible (to perform ḥafifah at night), the other when it is not possible.

items.text: Rava retracts and cites Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rava retracts and cites Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rava retracts his earlier statement, declaring it an error, and instead teaches in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a woman may not perform ḥafifah on Friday and immerse on Saturday night, because ḥafifah and immersion must be proximate.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches that a woman may perform ḥafifah (pre-immersion cleansing) on Friday and immerse on Saturday night.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's objection citing Ravin's letter
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection citing Ravin's letter
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Rava, citing Ravin's letter that a woman may not perform ḥafifah on Friday and immerse on Saturday night.
Ravin's letter rejects the practice, arguing that ḥafifah and immersion must be proximate (תיכף לחפיפה טבילה), and here they are not.

sub.text: Rava's retraction and citation of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rava's retraction and citation of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rava retracts his earlier statement, declaring it an error, and teaches in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a woman may not perform ḥafifah on Friday and immerse on Saturday night, because ḥafifah and immersion must be proximate.

items.text: Contradiction between two halakhot resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction between two halakhot resolved
items.desc_en: Two conflicting halakhot are stated: one permits ḥafifah by day and immersion at night, the other requires ḥafifah only at night. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where it is possible (to immerse at night) and where it is not possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two halakhic rulings: one permits ḥafifah by day and immersion at night, the other requires ḥafifah only at night.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where it is possible (to immerse at night) and where it is not possible.

items.text: Mishnah: Niddah's examination on day seven
items.text_en: Mishnah: Niddah's examination on day seven
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of a niddah who examined herself on the seventh morning and found herself pure or impure, and later found the opposite. It discusses the presumption of purity or impurity, and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding the time of separation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the first case: a niddah who examined herself on the seventh morning and found herself pure, did not separate at twilight, and later found herself impure — she remains in a presumption of purity.

The Mishnah presents the second case: she examined on the seventh morning and found herself impure, did not separate at twilight, and later found herself pure — she remains in a presumption of impurity.

The Mishnah adds the general rule: she imparts impurity retroactively for a full day or from the last examination, but if she has a fixed cycle (וסת), she only imparts impurity from the moment of discovery.
Rabbi Yehuda states: any woman who did not separate in purity from the time of the afternoon offering onward is in a presumption of impurity.
The Sages disagree: even if she examined on the second day of her niddah and found herself pure, did not separate at twilight, and later found herself impure — she remains in a presumption of purity.

items.text: Gemara: Rav and Levi debate definite vs. doubtful zavah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav and Levi debate definite vs. doubtful zavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rav and Levi applies to a case where she found herself impure both initially and later. Rav holds she is a definite zavah, Levi holds she is a doubtful zavah, as she may have stopped bleeding in between.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav says she is a definite zavah, Levi says she is a doubtful zavah.
The Gemara asks: To which case in the Mishnah does this dispute refer? It cannot be the first case, which rules she is presumed pure.
The Gemara objects: If it refers to the latter case, Levi's doubtful zavah is plausible, but Rav's definite zavah is problematic because she found herself pure initially.
The Gemara resolves: The dispute was stated independently, referring to a case where she found herself impure both initially and later.
The Gemara explains: Rav holds she is a definite zavah because she was impure at both checks; Levi holds she is a doubtful zavah because she may have stopped bleeding in between.

items.text: Levi's baraita and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Levi's baraita and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Levi teaches in a baraita that a woman who checks after the days (of zivah) and finds either pure or impure is considered a safek zavah and transmits impurity retroactively (me'et le'et). This challenges Rava's statement that a woman does not transmit impurity retroactively during her zivah days. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a case where she is still in her father's house (i.e., before marriage), and teaches that even though pure days intervene, she is not like the beginning of her niddah.

sub.desc_en: Levi teaches a baraita that a woman who checks after the days (of zivah) and finds either pure or impure is a safek zavah and transmits impurity retroactively (me'et le'et).
The Gemara raises a challenge to Rava's statement that a woman does not transmit impurity retroactively during her zivah days, citing Levi's baraita as a contradiction.
The Gemara notes that Rava has already been challenged once, and now they are adding this baraita as an additional challenge.

Rava answers that the baraita refers to a case where she is still in her father's house (before marriage), so the impurity retroactively applies only there, not during her zivah days in her husband's house.

The Gemara explains that one might have thought that since pure days intervene, she is like the beginning of her niddah and should not transmit impurity retroactively, so the baraita teaches that she does.

items.text: Establishing a fixed cycle during zivah days
items.text_en: Establishing a fixed cycle during zivah days
items.desc_en: The mishnah states 'if she has a fixed cycle' (veset). This challenges Rav Huna bar Chiyya quoting Shmuel, who said a woman does not establish a fixed cycle during her zivah days. The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement refers to uprooting a cycle, not establishing one, because during zivah her blood is withdrawn and she only needs to be concerned for the moment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna bar Chiyya quoting Shmuel, who said a woman does not establish a fixed cycle (וֶסֶת) during her zivah days, based on the mishnah's statement 'if she has a fixed cycle'.

Rav Huna bar Chiyya explains that Shmuel's statement refers to uprooting a cycle, not establishing one, because during zivah her blood is withdrawn (דָּמֶיהָ מְסוּלָּקִין) and she only needs to be concerned for the moment (דַּיָּהּ שְׁעָתָהּ).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and the debate about checking on the seventh day
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and the debate about checking on the seventh day
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says that if a woman checked on the seventh day and found pure, she is pure. The Sages object that since her hands are not constantly on her eyes (i.e., she might have seen during twilight), she could have become impure. The Gemara then recounts a story where Rabbi asked Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon about a niddah who checked on the seventh morning and found pure, but did not check at twilight, and later found impure. They ruled she is in a presumptive state of purity. The Gemara explores the logic behind this, concluding that once the chain of impurity is broken, it is broken.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states his opinion about a woman checking on the seventh day, and the Sages object that without constant monitoring she might have seen blood during twilight.
The Sages argue that since her hands were removed, she might have seen blood at twilight, comparing the seventh day to the first day of impurity.
The Gemara questions whether anyone actually holds that the first day is comparable to the seventh in this regard.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi asked Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon about a niddah who checked on the seventh morning and found pure but did not check at twilight, and later found impure.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's answer
sub.desc_en: They ruled that she is in a presumptive state of purity, and the same applies to checks on the sixth, fifth, fourth, third, and second days.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi did not ask about the first day, but concludes that once the chain of impurity is broken, it is broken even for the first day.
The Gemara reflects on what Rabbi originally thought, suggesting he was concerned about a presumptively open source of blood.

items.text: Mishnah: Zav and zavah who checked only on first and seventh days
items.text_en: Mishnah: Zav and zavah who checked only on first and seventh days
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a dispute: if a zav or zavah checked on day one and day seven and found pure, but did not check in between, Rabbi Eliezer says they are in a presumptive state of purity; Rabbi Yehoshua says only day one and day seven count; Rabbi Akiva says only day seven counts. The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer argues that counting with interruptions (serugin) violates the Torah's requirement of 'after, after' for all days. Rabbi Yehoshua counters with examples of a zav who had a seminal emission and a nazir who walked over graves, where counting with interruptions is valid. The Gemara distinguishes these cases. Finally, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon rule that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents the dispute: a zav and zavah who checked on day one and day seven and found pure, but did not check in between — Rabbi Eliezer says they are in a presumptive state of purity; Rabbi Yehoshua says only day one and day seven count; Rabbi Akiva says only day seven counts.

A baraita records Rabbi Eliezer's argument to Rabbi Yehoshua: counting with interruptions (סירוגין) violates the Torah's requirement of 'אחר תטהר' — 'after, after' for all days, without impurity intervening.

Rabbi Yehoshua counters: does Rabbi Eliezer not admit that a zav who had a seminal emission, and a nazir who walked over graves, count with interruptions (סירוגין), as the Torah says 'והימים הראשונים יפלו'?

The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's distinction: regarding the zav with a seminal emission, the Torah said 'לטמאה בה' — it only interrupts for that day, and there is no confusion between a zav and a בעל קרי (one with a seminal emission).

sub.text: Gemara's distinction for the nazir case
sub.text_en: Gemara's distinction for the nazir case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara further explains: regarding the nazir who walked over סככות ופרעות (shady trees and protruding graves), the Torah requires a genuine tent (אהל מעליא), and the rabbis only decreed impurity; thus rabbinic decrees are not confused with Torah law.

The Gemara concludes: but here (in the mishnah's case), if we are concerned that she might have seen blood, a ספק (doubt) would come to be confused with a וודאי (certainty), so Rabbi Eliezer's position stands.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's ruling
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's ruling
sub.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon rule: the words of Rabbi Eliezer are more convincing than Rabbi Yehoshua's, and Rabbi Akiva's more than all, but the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: New inquiry: checking on day one and day eight
items.text_en: New inquiry: checking on day one and day eight
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new question: what is the law if a zav or zavah checked on day one and day eight and found pure, but did not check on the intervening days? This is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved inquiry about a zav or zavah who checked on day one and day eight and found pure, but did not check on the intervening days.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Chanina regarding Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Chanina regarding Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer requires both the beginning and end of clean days (תחילתן וסופן) or only the beginning even without the end. Rav says only the beginning suffices, while Rabbi Chanina insists both are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer requires both the beginning and end of clean days (תחילתן וסופן) or only the beginning even without the end.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that only the eighth day counts, implying both beginning and end are needed. It deflects by identifying the disputants as Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva instead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that only the eighth day counts, implying both beginning and end are needed.
The Gemara deflects the objection by identifying the disputants in the baraita as Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva, not Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Rav's ruling on counting a clean day for a zavah
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on counting a clean day for a zavah
items.desc_en: Rav states that a niddah who separates in purity on her third day counts it toward her seven clean days. The Gemara corrects this to a zavah, as a niddah does not need counting.

sub.text: Rav's ruling via Rav Sheishet and Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav's ruling via Rav Sheishet and Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a niddah who separates in purity on her third day counts it toward her seven clean days.

items.text: Clarification of Rav's statement regarding Kutim
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav's statement regarding Kutim
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet questions whether Rav follows the Kutim who count the day of cessation. Rav's statement is clarified to exclude the third day, and applies when she did not check until the seventh day.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's question to Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's question to Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet asks whether Rav's ruling aligns with the Kutim, who count the day of cessation as part of the seven clean days.
The Gemara clarifies that Rav's statement excludes the third day, and applies specifically when she did not check until the seventh day.

items.text: Teaching both aspects: beginning without end and end without beginning
items.text_en: Teaching both aspects: beginning without end and end without beginning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav teaches both that beginning counts without end (from the earlier dispute) and that end counts without beginning (from this case), countering a potential assumption that only the former applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav teaches both that beginning counts without end (from the earlier dispute) and that end counts without beginning (from this case), countering a potential assumption that only the former applies.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yose's objection about a 'mistaken' woman
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yose's objection about a 'mistaken' woman
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina raises an objection from the case of a 'mistaken' woman (טועה). The Gemara infers from the practice of immersing her only at night that supervised counting (ספורים לפנינו) is required, otherwise she could immerse by day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Ravin's report that Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina raised a challenge from the case of a 'mistaken' woman (טועה).
The Gemara states it does not know the substance of the challenge, noting the established practice that in the first week she comes before us, we immerse her only at night, not by day.
The Gemara infers that if supervised counting (ספורים לפנינו) were not required, she could immerse by day, so the practice proves that supervised counting is indeed required.
The Gemara objects that the inference was already established as the view of Rabbi Akiva, who requires supervised counting.

items.text: Resolution: the objection follows Rabbi Akiva, not the Rabbis
items.text_en: Resolution: the objection follows Rabbi Akiva, not the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the requirement for supervised counting applies only according to Rabbi Akiva, not the Rabbis. It cites a mishnah about a 'mistaken' woman who immerses multiple times without supervised counting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the objection requiring supervised counting applies only according to Rabbi Akiva, who requires counting in our presence.
The Gemara cites a mishnah about a 'mistaken' woman who immerses multiple times without supervised counting, proving the Rabbis do not require counting in our presence.

items.text: Discussion of the 'mistaken' woman's immersions and a parable
items.text_en: Discussion of the 'mistaken' woman's immersions and a parable
items.desc_en: The Gemara details the number of immersions for various claims of the 'mistaken' woman, with Rava criticizing the ruling as illogical. A parable about orphans and oxen illustrates the principle that the end of a ruling should match its beginning. The Gemara concludes by clarifying the case of a woman who says she saw but doesn't know how many.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who says she saw one day of impurity immerses nine times: seven for niddah and two for zivah.
The Gemara asks what the eleven immersions are for a woman who saw during twilight, and Rav Yirmeya Midipti explains: eight for niddah and three for zivah.
The Mishnah states that a woman who says she never saw any impurity immerses fifteen times.
Rava criticizes the ruling as illogical, comparing it to a flawed judgment by barbers about oxen grazing.
A parable illustrates the principle that the end of a ruling should match its beginning, as an orphan boy points out the inconsistency in the barbers' judgment.
The Gemara applies the parable's principle: if a woman who says she saw gets nine or eleven immersions, why does one who says she never saw need fifteen?

The Gemara clarifies that the case of fifteen immersions applies to a woman who says she saw but doesn't know how many or whether during niddah or zivah days, and if she comes during the day we give her seven for niddah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a woman who appears at night
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a woman who appears at night
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between day and night appearances for a woman with a fixed period for zivah but not for niddah. It explains that for zivah, which has a fixed period, the time of day does not matter, while for niddah, which lacks a fixed period, appearing at night requires counting eight clean days, but appearing during the day does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah gives a woman who appears at night eight days for zivah and seven for niddah, since zivah itself requires eight clean days.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah actually gives seven for niddah and eight for zivah, and explains that for zivah, which has a fixed period, the time of day does not matter, while for niddah, which lacks a fixed period, appearing at night requires counting eight clean days, but appearing during the day does not.

items.text: Proof that counting before us is not required
items.text_en: Proof that counting before us is not required
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if counting before us were required, all these immersions would be unnecessary; she could just count seven and then immerse. This proves the Mishnah follows the Rabbis who say counting before us is not required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if counting before us were required, why would all these immersions be needed? She could just count seven and then immerse.
The Gemara concludes: this proves the Mishnah follows the Rabbis who say counting before us is not required.

items.text: Refinement of the Mishnah's case by Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Refinement of the Mishnah's case by Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef challenges Rav Ashi's explanation, suggesting the Mishnah's case is about a woman who counted but does not know how many days, or whether she counted at all. The Gemara adjusts the wording to 'I do not know if I counted or not' to avoid a missing immersion.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef challenges Rav Ashi's explanation, proposing that the Mishnah's case is about a woman who counted but does not know how many days, or whether she counted during days of menstruation or זיבה (abnormal bleeding), requiring fifteen immersions.
The Gemara objects that if she counted at least one day, she is missing one immersion from the required fifteen.
The Gemara resolves the objection by correcting the wording to 'I do not know if I counted or not,' eliminating the assumption that she definitely counted at least one day.

items.text: Mishnah: Impurity of certain corpses by carrying
items.text_en: Mishnah: Impurity of certain corpses by carrying
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a zav, zavah, niddah, yoledet, and metzora who died convey impurity by carrying until the flesh decays, but a dead gentile is pure from conveying impurity by carrying. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debate when a woman who died is considered a niddah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a zav, zavah, niddah, yoledet, and metzora who died convey impurity by carrying until the flesh decays, but a dead gentile is pure from conveying impurity by carrying.
Beit Shammai rules that all women who die are considered niddot (menstruants) for impurity purposes.
Beit Hillel rules that only a woman who died while actually menstruating is considered a niddah.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of 'by carrying' and the reason for the decree
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of 'by carrying' and the reason for the decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'by carrying' refers to carrying with a stone (as a weight), not direct carrying, as all corpses convey impurity by direct carrying. Rav explains the decree is due to fear of fainting, and a Tanna cites Rabbi Eliezer saying until the belly bursts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'by carrying' means, rejecting the possibility that it means direct carrying, since all corpses convey impurity by carrying.
The Gemara explains that 'by carrying' refers to carrying with a stone (as a weight), citing a verse about placing a stone over a pit.
Rav explains the reason for the decree: fear that one might faint (from the weight).
A Tanna cites Rabbi Eliezer's statement that the decree applies until the belly bursts.

items.text: Reason for the gentile's purity by carrying
items.text_en: Reason for the gentile's purity by carrying
items.desc_en: Rabbi explains that a dead gentile is pure from conveying impurity by carrying because his impurity during life is only rabbinic, not biblical.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi explains that a dead gentile is pure from conveying impurity by carrying because his impurity during life is only rabbinic, not biblical.

items.text: The Alexandrians' questions to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.text_en: The Alexandrians' questions to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the men of Alexandria asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya twelve questions: three of wisdom, three of aggadah, three of boorishness, and three of proper conduct. The first wisdom question repeats the Mishnah's ruling about impurity by carrying. The second asks about a daughter sent away (a divorcee's daughter) and whether she is permitted to a kohen, debating a kal vachomer from a widow to a kohen gadol.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna introduces that the men of Alexandria asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya twelve questions: three of wisdom, three of aggadah, three of boorishness, and three of proper conduct.
The men of Alexandria ask the first wisdom question: until when do the corpses of a zav, zava, niddah, yoledet, and metzora transmit impurity by carrying?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya answers: until the flesh decays.
The men of Alexandria ask the second wisdom question: what is the status of a daughter born from a forbidden remarriage (a divorcee who remarried her first husband) regarding marrying a kohen?

The Gemara presents a possible kal vachomer argument: if a widow to a kohen gadol, whose prohibition is not universal, produces a flawed son, then this daughter, whose prohibition is universal, should certainly produce a flawed son.
The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the kal vachomer is refuted because a widow to a kohen gadol is herself disqualified from terumah, unlike the daughter of a remarried divorcee.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya begins his response to the second question (the response is cut off in the source).

items.text: Opening statement: offspring of a forbidden union are not forbidden
items.text_en: Opening statement: offspring of a forbidden union are not forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that although the union itself is an abomination, the children born from it are not considered abominable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that although the union itself is an abomination (תועבה), the children born from it are not considered abominable.

items.text: Case of two lepers with mixed offerings
items.text_en: Case of two lepers with mixed offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where two lepers' offerings were mixed, one died, and the second's status is uncertain. Shmuel answers that the second should write his property to others, become poor, and bring a bird sin-offering for uncertainty, assuming his guilt-offering was already brought.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where two lepers' offerings were mixed, one died, and asks what the second should do.
Shmuel answers that the second leper should transfer his property to others, become poor, and bring a bird sin-offering for uncertainty.
The Gemara objects that the leper still has a guilt-offering obligation that cannot be fulfilled by a poor person's offering.
Shmuel resolves that the case assumes his guilt-offering was already brought before the mixing.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's challenge: which authority does Shmuel follow?
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's challenge: which authority does Shmuel follow?
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet questions Shmuel's ruling, noting that it depends on whether the guilt-offering or sin-offering determines the leper's status. He cites a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda (who follows the guilt-offering) and Rabbi Shimon (who follows the sin-offering), implying Shmuel's position is problematic.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Shmuel's ruling, arguing that if Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehuda (who holds that the guilt-offering (אשם) determines the leper's status), then once the guilt-offering established him as wealthy, he cannot bring a poor person's sin-offering.

The gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon holds that the sin-offering (חטאת) determines the leper's status, Rabbi Yehuda holds that the guilt-offering (אשם) determines it, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that the birds determine it.

Rav Sheshet further argues that if Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon (who holds that the sin-offering determines status), then even though the guilt-offering was not brought, the second leper could bring another guilt-offering with a condition, as Rabbi Shimon permits conditional offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's conditional offering method
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's conditional offering method
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Shimon, the leper could bring another guilt-offering conditionally, as taught in a baraita: he brings his guilt-offering and log of oil, stands at the Nicanor Gate, and stipulates that if he is a leper it is his offering, otherwise it is a peace-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the ruling follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the sin-offering (חטאת) determines the leper's status, then even if the guilt-offering (אשם) was not yet brought, the second leper could bring another guilt-offering conditionally, since Rabbi Shimon is known to allow conditional offerings.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Shimon taught that the leper brings his guilt-offering and log of oil the next day, stands at the Nicanor Gate, and stipulates that if he is a leper it is his offering, otherwise it is a peace-offering (שלמי נדבה).
The Gemara begins to note that that guilt-offering requires something, but the text cuts off at the end of the section.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Sages' objection
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Sages' objection
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the halakhot of a firstborn animal, and the Sages disagree with Rabbi Shimon because he brings sacrifices to the place of disqualification.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the halakhot of a firstborn animal: its slaughter is in the north, it requires application of blood on the thumb, laying of hands, libations, waving, and the breast and thigh, and it is eaten by male priests for one day and night.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Shimon because he brings sacrifices to the place of disqualification.

items.text: Shmuel's stance on Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Shmuel's stance on Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Shimon on one matter but disagrees on another.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Shimon on one matter but disagrees on another.

items.text: Three aggadic resolutions
items.text_en: Three aggadic resolutions
items.desc_en: Three apparent contradictions in verses are resolved: regarding God's desire for death, His acceptance of bribes, and His choice of Zion, each resolved by context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces three aggadic resolutions, beginning with the first: a contradiction between verses about God's desire for death is resolved by distinguishing between those who repent and those who do not.
The second resolution: a contradiction about God accepting bribes is resolved by distinguishing between before and after the decree.
The third resolution: a contradiction about God's choice of Zion is resolved by distinguishing between before and after Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter.

items.text: Three questions of burut (ignorance)
items.text_en: Three questions of burut (ignorance)
items.desc_en: Three foolish questions about impurity: Lot's wife, the Shunammite's son, and the resurrection of the dead, each answered by the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces three foolish questions (שְׁלֹשָׁה דִּבְרֵי בּוּרוּת) and presents the first: whether Lot's wife, who became a pillar of salt, can transmit ritual impurity (טומאה).
The Sages answer that a dead body transmits impurity, but a pillar of salt does not.
The second foolish question: whether the Shunammite's son, who was revived by Elisha, can transmit impurity.
The Sages answer that a dead body transmits impurity, but a living person does not.
The third foolish question: whether the dead who will be resurrected in the future require the purification ritual of the third and seventh days (הזאה שלישי ושביעי).
The Sages answer evasively: when they live, we will become wise regarding them.
An alternative version of the answer: when Moses our teacher comes with them (at the resurrection), we will know.

items.text: Three matters of derekh eretz: wisdom and wealth
items.text_en: Three matters of derekh eretz: wisdom and wealth
items.desc_en: Advice on becoming wise and wealthy: increase in study and reduce business, but ultimately prayer is needed; a parable of Rabbi Chiyya illustrates that both effort and divine gift are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The sages of Alexandria ask what a person should do to become wise.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers that one should increase time in study and reduce business.
The sages object that many have done this without success.
Rabbi Yehoshua resolves that one must pray for wisdom from God, citing Proverbs 2:6.
Rabbi Chiyya teaches a parable of a king who sends food from his own table to his beloved servants, illustrating that wisdom is a divine gift.
The Gemara asks what the parable teaches, and answers that both effort and prayer are necessary.
The sages of Alexandria ask what a person should do to become wealthy.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers that one should increase business and deal faithfully.
The sages object that many have done this without success.
Rabbi Yehoshua resolves that one must pray for wealth from God, citing Haggai 2:8.
The Gemara asks what this teaches, and answers that both honest business and prayer are necessary.

items.text: Third matter of derekh eretz: having male children
items.text_en: Third matter of derekh eretz: having male children
items.desc_en: Advice on having male children: marry a woman suitable for him.

sub.desc_en: The sages of Alexandria ask what a person should do to have male children.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers that one should marry a woman who is suitable for him.

items.text: The value of sanctifying oneself during intercourse and the reward for delaying
items.text_en: The value of sanctifying oneself during intercourse and the reward for delaying
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the practice of sanctifying oneself during intercourse to have worthy children. It notes that many did this without success, and advises prayer instead. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the reward for the fruit of the womb is given for those who delay themselves so that their wives conceive first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that one should sanctify himself at the time of intercourse.
The Sages of Alexandria object that many did this without success, and advise instead to pray to God for children, citing a verse.
The Gemara asks what the Sages' statement teaches us, and answers that prayer without proper conduct does not suffice.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the reward for the fruit of the womb is given to those who delay themselves so that their wives emit seed first.

items.text: Beit Shammai's reasoning that all men who die are zavim
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's reasoning that all men who die are zavim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explores the rationale of Beit Shammai, who hold that all men who die are zavim. It first considers a proof from the verse about Queen Esther, but rejects it because fear causes blood to congeal while terror loosens it. Instead, it cites a baraita about a decree to immerse vessels over all dead men to avoid shaming living zavim, which is the basis for Beit Shammai's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for the opinion of Beit Shammai.

The Gemara suggests that Beit Shammai's reason is from the verse about Queen Esther, where Rav taught that she began to menstruate due to fear, and similarly a dying woman sees blood due to fear of the Angel of Death.
The Gemara objects that a mishna teaches that trepidation eliminates the flow of menstrual blood, contradicting the idea that fear causes bleeding.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between anxiety (which contracts and stops blood) and sudden terror (which relaxes and causes blood to flow).

The Gemara objects that if the reason for Beit Shammai is fear, then they should also consider all men who die as zavim, but the verse 'from his flesh' excludes an issue due to circumstances beyond his control.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the real reason for Beit Shammai is a decree to immerse vessels over all dead men to avoid shaming living zavim, which is the basis for Beit Shammai's position.

items.text: Mishnah: A woman who dies and emits a quarter-log of blood
items.text_en: Mishnah: A woman who dies and emits a quarter-log of blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman dies and a quarter-log of blood emerges, it imparts impurity both as a bloodstain and in a tent. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees regarding bloodstain impurity because the blood was dislodged after death, but agrees in the case of a woman who died in childbirth. Rabbi Yosei adds that in that case it does not impart tent impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a woman who dies and emits a quarter-log of blood imparts impurity both as a bloodstain (כתם) and in a tent (אוהל).
Rabbi Yehuda disagrees regarding bloodstain impurity because the blood was dislodged after death, but concedes in the case of a woman who died in childbirth.
Rabbi Yosei adds that in the case of a woman who died in childbirth, the blood does not impart tent impurity.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Tanna Kamma holds that even though the blood was dislodged after death, it still imparts bloodstain impurity. Rabbi Ze'eri explains that the dispute is about whether the source (the uterus) is impure after death, which would affect the blood's status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that Tanna Kamma holds that blood dislodged after death still imparts bloodstain impurity, and questions this inference.
Rabbi Ze'eri explains that the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda is about whether the source (the uterus) is impure after death, which affects the blood's status.

items.text: The dispute about tent impurity and the concept of dam tevusah
items.text_en: The dispute about tent impurity and the concept of dam tevusah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda agrees in the case of a woman who died in childbirth, implying Tanna Kamma holds it imparts tent impurity as well. Rav Yehuda explains the dispute is about dam tevusah (blood of crushing). A baraita defines dam tevusah as blood from a slain person where it is uncertain whether it came from life or death, with a dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages. Rabbi Yehuda's opinion about a corpse whose blood drips into a pit is also cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that Rabbi Yehuda agrees in the case of a woman who died in childbirth.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehuda's concession that the Tanna Kamma must hold that the blood also imparts tent impurity.
Rav Yehuda explains that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda concerns the concept of דם תבוסה (blood of crushing).
A baraita is cited, defining דם תבוסה according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda as blood from a slain person where it is uncertain whether it came from life or death.
The Sages reject Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda's definition and instead rule that the impurity status depends on the location: in a private domain it is impure, in the public domain it is pure.
The Sages then provide their own definition of דם תבוסה: blood from a slain person where a quarter-log of blood emerged both during life and after death, with uncertainty about the majority.
Rabbi Yehuda states that a slain person from whom a quarter-log of blood drips into a pit is impure because the drop of death is mixed in, while the Sages declare it pure.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's consistency on blood nullification
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's consistency on blood nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the previous Mishnah is consistent with his principle that blood does not nullify blood. It then contrasts his view with Rabbi Shimon's regarding a crucified person, where Rabbi Yehuda is lenient due to a specific reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Rabbis' objection to Rabbi Yehuda is well-founded, and explains that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling follows his own principle that blood does not nullify blood.
A baraita contrasts Rabbi Shimon's ruling that a crucified person's dripping blood renders the ground beneath impure with Rabbi Yehuda's lenient ruling that the drop of death remains on the wood.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda should apply his own reasoning to the Mishnah's case, claiming that the drop of death remains on the bed.
The Gemara answers that a bed is different because it shakes, causing the blood to drip down.

items.text: Mishnah: Status of a woman after childbirth regarding purity
items.text_en: Mishnah: Status of a woman after childbirth regarding purity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the earlier and later rulings about a woman sitting on pure blood (after childbirth). Initially, she could pour water for the Paschal lamb; later, she is considered like one who touches a corpse for sacred matters, according to Beit Hillel, while Beit Shammai say she is like a corpse itself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the earlier ruling: a woman sitting on pure blood after childbirth could pour water for the Paschal lamb.
The Mishnah presents the later ruling of Beit Hillel: she is considered like one who touches a corpse for sacred matters.
Beit Shammai states a stricter position: she is like a corpse itself regarding ritual impurity.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction in the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction in the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the first clause implies that non-sacred items prepared with the purity of sacred items are like sacred, but the later clause implies they are not. It resolves by attributing the Mishnah to Abba Shaul, who holds that a טבול יום is only second-degree for sacred items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's first clause that the woman may pour water for the Pesach offering but not touch it, implying that non-sacred items prepared with the purity of sacred items (חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש) are treated like sacred items.

The Gemara objects by citing the later clause of the Mishnah, which states that she is only like a טמא מת for sacred items but not for non-sacred items, implying the opposite — that non-sacred items prepared with sacred purity are not like sacred items.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Abba Shaul, who holds that a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) is only a first-degree impurity for sacred items, so the first clause reflects his view that non-sacred items prepared with sacred purity are like sacred items.

items.text: Mishnah: Additional rulings on the woman after childbirth
items.text_en: Mishnah: Additional rulings on the woman after childbirth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the woman eats tithe, separates challah, and designates it. If her saliva or pure blood falls on terumah bread, it remains pure. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether she needs a final immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the woman after childbirth eats tithe, separates challah, designates it, and calls its name.
The Mishnah adds that if her saliva or pure blood falls on terumah bread, it remains pure.
Beit Shammai rules that she needs a final immersion.
Beit Hillel rules that she does not need a final immersion.

items.text: Gemara: Explanations of the Mishnah's details
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanations of the Mishnah's details
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each clause: eating tithe is based on the principle that one who immersed may eat tithe; separating challah shows that non-sacred items designated for challah are not like challah; the requirement to separate from adjacent produce; the concern about touching from outside is dismissed; and the ruling about saliva is based on the status of טבול יום's liquids.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement about eating tithe refers to the principle that one who immersed and ascended may eat tithe.
The Gemara explains that separating challah shows that non-sacred items designated for challah are not like challah itself.
The Gemara explains that the requirement to separate from adjacent produce is based on the principle of תרומה (priestly portion) from adjacent items.
The Gemara dismisses the concern that she might touch the challah from outside, teaching that no such decree is needed.

The Gemara cites a baraita that the liquids of a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) do not impart impurity, except for the liquids of a זב (gonorrheic) which are an אב הטומאה (primary source of impurity).

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the final immersion. Rav Katina answers: the case of a long טבול יום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the final immersion.
Rav Katina answers that the difference is the case of a long טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset).

items.text: Mishnah: Woman who sees blood on day eleven
items.text_en: Mishnah: Woman who sees blood on day eleven
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of a woman who sees blood on the eleventh day of the זבה period, immerses at evening, and then engages in relations. Beit Shammai rules that she renders the bed and seat impure and is liable for a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who sees blood on the eleventh day of the זבה period, immerses at evening, and then engages in relations.
Beit Shammai rules that the woman renders the bed and seat impure and is liable for a sacrifice.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute about immersion on the eleventh day
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute about immersion on the eleventh day
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the core dispute: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about a woman who immersed on the day after her period (the eleventh day of the zivah period), engaged in relations, and then saw blood. Beit Shammai holds she conveys tumah but is exempt from a korban; Beit Hillel calls this a 'gargeran' (a problematic case). They agree that if she saw within the eleven days, immersed at evening, and engaged in relations, she conveys tumah and is liable for a korban.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a woman who immersed on the eleventh day, engaged in relations, and then saw blood, with Beit Shammai holding she conveys טומאה (ritual impurity) but is exempt from a קרבן (offering), and Beit Hillel calling this a 'גרגרן' (problematic case), while they agree on the case of seeing within the eleven days and immersing at evening.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta that states Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on the law of a woman who immerses at night (invalid) and on a woman who sees within the eleven days. The only dispute is regarding the eleventh day itself: Beit Shammai holds she conveys tumah and is liable for a korban, while Beit Hillel exempts her from a korban.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta stating that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on two cases: a woman who immerses at night is invalid, and a woman who sees within the eleven days and immerses at evening and then has relations is liable for a korban.
The Gemara clarifies that the only dispute is regarding the eleventh day itself: Beit Shammai holds she conveys tum'ah and is liable for a korban, while Beit Hillel exempts her from a korban.

items.text: Debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai challenges Beit Hillel: why distinguish the eleventh day from within the eleven days? If it is similar for tumah, it should be similar for korban. Beit Hillel responds that within the eleven days, the following day joins for zivah, but the eleventh day does not. Beit Shammai then argues for consistency: either both tumah and korban apply, or neither. Beit Hillel counters that they apply tumah stringently but do not impose a korban leniently, and further points out an inconsistency in Beit Shammai's own position regarding the case of immersion on the day after.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai challenges Beit Hillel: why distinguish the eleventh day from within the eleven days? If it is similar for טומאה (ritual impurity), it should be similar for the קרבן (sacrifice).
Beit Hillel responds that within the eleven days, the following day joins for זיבה (zivah), but the eleventh day does not, so the cases are not analogous.
Beit Shammai argues for consistency: either both טומאה (impurity) and קרבן (sacrifice) apply, or neither.
Beit Hillel counters that they apply טומאה (impurity) stringently but do not impose a קרבן (sacrifice) leniently.
Beit Hillel points out an inconsistency in Beit Shammai's own position regarding the case of immersion on the day after, using their own logic against them.
Beit Hillel concludes that the consistent principle is to apply rules stringently (להחמיר) and not leniently (ולא להקל), resolving the debate.

items.text: Rav Huna's statement on Beit Shammai's position
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement on Beit Shammai's position
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that according to Beit Shammai, the woman's bedding on the second day (after immersion) conveys tumah even if she did not see blood, because if she had seen, it would convey tumah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that Beit Shammai declares her משכב ומושב (bed and seat) on the second day impure even though she immersed and did not see blood, because if she had seen, she would be impure, so now too she is impure.

items.text: Discussion between Rav Yosef, Rav Kahana, and Abaye
items.text_en: Discussion between Rav Yosef, Rav Kahana, and Abaye
